_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the hate brigaders trick you, if you are a fan of RTS games with an addictive and varied multiplayer experience then this game is for you. A lot of these negative reviews are being written by bitter company of heroes 2 fans, whom have no real argument. As to why these reviews claim company of heroes 3 is inferior to the second game, they employ talking points about the "bad for 2023 graphics" or the "poor quality audio" or whatever minor nitpick they deem is game ruining. As someone whose timeline with this franchise goes back to 2009 with the beta for Company of Heroes Online (which sadly shut down but also caused me to pick up the original CoH1+expansions), I remember falling in love with this franchise because of how exciting and novel gameplay features they debuted such as: squad system, retreating and victory point control elements amongst other features that are now considered staples of relic RTS games and other similar titles. But wait a second. What if I told you that most of these features were also in Dawn of War 1? And that a bunch of people back in the day said that CoH1 sucked because it was just a ww2 reskin of Dawn of War 1? This group of people i'm describing are not that different from the hate brigade we see today review bombing CoH3. In fact, the example i've laid out with the idea that CoH1=DoW1 but WW2 is just the beginning of this odd trend with RTS franchise fanboys that I can recognize. When Dawn of War 2 came out a lot of people hated on it as well because they claimed that it was just a watered down version of Dawn of War 1, or that it was (funnily enough) "just Company of Heroes but in Space". Now let's talk about company of heroes 2. Boy, what a disaster that game was on release. That game was almost widely considered to be hot garbage on release in comparison to a company of heroes 1 which had multiple expansion packs released by the 2013 release date of company of heroes 2. I could write an entirely separate essay about the issues CoH2 had during its early lifetime, but that would just detract from my current point here, so instead i'll just give a few short examples to illustrate how the issues with company of heroes 3 at release are quite minor compared to the ones with CoH2. CoH2 released with just two factions in comparison to the CoH1+xpacks four factions. Company of Heroes 2 also had many ridiculous balance issues and weird feature retcons at release, including no functional distance or accuracy system for units until months after release. CoH2 was also widely criticized at the time for including the in-game store and microtransactions, and many people considered the concept of commanders that you can purchase were "Pay-to-Win". Now thats just a few cherry picked examples from Company of Heroes 2, and well you probably didn't come here to read about why CoH2 sucked at release. You're here to read about whether Company of Heroes 3 sucks at release. Well Heres the TL;DR:    Company of Heroes 3 is a relatively safe and conservative sequel to a franchise that is considered uniquely great in the Real Time Strategy/Real Time Tactics genre. If you are new to the franchise, this title will be more friendly for you to learn than any previous one, as it contains many anti-frustration features and no-brainer additions that provide more opportunity for focusing on your tactics and strategy as opposed to mindless micromanagement compared to previous titles. If you are a returning fan of Company of Heroes then I would recommend you purchase this game if you enjoyed the Company of Heroes 1 style of gameplay over the Company of Heroes 2 style, as the US and Wehrmacht factions are more like their COH1 counterpart than the CoH2 versions. Also you get to do all the things you wish you could've done in previous titles, such as send your squads into battle ontop of tanks and hitch heavy weapon crews to trucks and other vehicles to haul them where they are needed. basically this game is 5/7 perfect score

_childDocuments_.review: One month after release many bugs, placeholder icons from CoH2, ugly or bad UI elements all remain issues. No new content has been added except an exploitative cash shop identical in form to what earned Warhammer 40,000: Darktide negative reviews.This game just came out, and in a poor state that many considered a rushed / early access release, yet the 1.1.0 update is mostly an embarrassing cash shop that isn't even enticing to the gullible.Credit to the developers who got many bugfixes into this patch, but I am changing my review to be negative, and it will likely stay that way for a long time.For multiplayer, this is a direct upgrade to Company of Heroes 2.I have hundreds of hours in COH2 (and likely thousands pre-steam in COH1), and have now had a day to queue multiplayer after finishing the DAK campaign and dipping my toes into the Italian 'Total War' campaign mode. While these campaigns are not on par with the excellence of the franchise's past, the DAK campaign was a lot of fun (except for the second mission, but finale was excellent!) and the Italian campaign mode is actually really cool—and I don't typically enjoy these campaign modes at all.The multiplayer is identical to the 'Tech Test' beta, if you played it. But that tech test, to me, was a pristine successor to the dated COH2 multiplayer. It does nothing to break the mold, but it is a breath of fresh air, new tech trees, new build orders, maps, meta, new balance issues to complain about... and if you loved COH1 or COH2 multiplayer, this is a great fit for you.Now, there are  issues that must be addressed...The menu and many UI elements appear like (or noticeably are) placeholders. You do not feel like this is a finished game when you launch and load the main menu. But you do when you are playing it. It's bizarre. Aesthetically its boring, and customisation features (face plates, player icons) are missing. There are no skins from achievements to equip, no way to view last match stats, no replays or observer mode. These are core features we should all expect to be in the game at launch. The 'Unique Colours' options, which helps identify players in 4v4 mode, has no colour theory behind it and causes unbelievable confusion and is mandatory to keep off until fixed, when this worked fine in COH2.These issues make this launch a disappointment. But yet, I love to play COH3, as I have loved to play COH since 2006.If you love Company of Heroes, and want to fight on the ladder or in skirmish, I promise you—get through the ugly unfinished menu and window dressing, and the best COH experience to date is there waiting for you as soon as you press play.It's hard to say if this is a recommendation or not. It's a bizarre type of unfinished release, where the gameplay is intact and solid. But its wonderfully fun, it's wonderfully COH, and therefore I give it my thumbs up.Pros:-Gameplay is a great refinement of the formula-Campaigns modes range from adequate to cool and unique-Variety of launch factions and new units to play with-Visuals are quite good (particularly destruction)-Voice lines are greatCons-Audio and SFX are subpar and sometimes bugged-Missing profile customisation features-Ugly placeholder Menu/UI elements-No unlocks or progression in game at launch-Price point is high for a video gameThanks for reading, see you on the battlefield!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not as unplayable as a lot of people make it seemed to be. Though I definitely expected more from a new entry to the COH series.As someone who mostly play AI matches. My biggest gripe has to be the minimal improvements to AI. In previous COH games, AI only keep up with the players through basically cheating. They know your fortifications, they read your build, they cheat resources and they have inhuman APM. As the case for COH3, it is exactly the same. AI refuses to put up an actual fight and will do anything to constantly harass  your points. It is so hard coded in AI even if you are surrounding their base with 5 Sherman they will send 3 squads of engineers to certain death just so they can send the 4th squad out to steal your points. So, If you feel like AI matches are kind of lackluster in COH 1 or 2 because you feel like the fight is just constantly patching up holes in your defense and no real showdown to lock in your attention. I'm sorry you won't get it here neither. AI is exactly the same, you will fend off harassment from AI and be forced to dance with them until you tech up and push them back once and for all with tanks.

_childDocuments_.review: Something about COH3 does not quite scratch the itch like COH2, and my two company bros agree. Despite all their trailers claiming maximum choice, there's actually less playstyles than coh2, less commanders/abilities, like 2 maps (5, feels like 2), and mostly crappier units. Also all the ones that are chopped up versions of bigger maps do not play as well. Sure graphics are great, sure breaching buildings is cool, sure the half-baked campaigns are there (just actually look at the first half of the afrikakorps maps before you fizzle out, like wow last minute decision). It's hard to put your finger on it. Maybe it is just balancing but it feels kinda like a gameplay choice, some units utterly suck while most of the elite infantry squads can dominate the map with 2 upgraded weapons for the price of 1 most of the time (double flames, double mgs, mostly for germans ofc). The anti-infantry AAs all kinda suck imo, except the OKW towable one. No more punishing noobs with your Crusader that deletes blobs with strafing fire ability, now it just goes boom.......................................... boom................................................ Unless you pay munitions, then its boom.........boom.........................boom............boom. It's not bad, but it's not as good. And that one is related to the early war period I believe, not balance. But many unit abilities feel that way - less tactical ability use and more just using the regular unit for combat. Nades are still good though and implemented well. And I guess the AA is good for planes considering they all die in 2-3 hits.The only thing that really stands out to me is the height advantage, that was a great addition imo. Also the rocket halftrack strike, graphically and damage, chefs kiss.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very much looking forward to the new twist on the CoH series. I bought the game in pre-sale, because it has thousands of hours in Coh2. I've played both the Alpha version and the Beta. But the final product is way off for me. The amount of buggies that the game contains is completely unbelievable. I played the African campaign first, which was really weak. I played it on the highest difficulty, and it was all about destroying what was on the map. It took time, but was it a challenge? It wasn't exactly fun either. Then I played the Italian campaign. I played 57 turns before the game always crashed at Piggatire Maggiore airport. If I try to conquer it. The game crashes. I try to work around it, but two turns later the game tells me that the Germans are moving their planes north and will use Piggatire Maggiore specifically, and the game crashes again. So far Relic hasn't fixed it, so I can't continue the campaign.What's really bad about CoH3 is the unit control. The units often don't execute the commands I give them at all. I sometimes have to press Retreat three times before a unit decides to retreat. Even the lag that is there is absolutely unbelievable. The enemy throws a grenade, I see it, and I click a little bit next to the unit to move. But nothing happens. It's only when the grenade explodes that the unit moves. And the tank and vehicle controls are probably even worse than the infantry. The system Relic has chosen is simply tragic. I'm very sorry I can't give a better rating. But this is really unplayable for the user.

_childDocuments_.review: Look how they massacred my boy. I cannot believe I am refunding a CoH game. UPDATE:  The first major content patch focused on releasing a PREMIUM MICROTRANSACTION STORE. Instead of fixing their broken game, they are too busy adding real-money cosmetics. In a $60 AAA title. ♥♥♥♥ these developers. UPDATE 2:After adding a microtransaction store in their first major update, they are now releasing a paid DLC instead of fixing the endless list of problems. Its hard to imagine what moron is in charge of this, but they destroyed one of the best RTS franchises ever. ORIGINAL REVIEW:CoH1 is one of my favorite games and the best RTS of all time. CoH3 is an unplayable buggy mess that looks, sounds, and runs like ♥♥♥♥.  Even if I look past all the other faults because of how much I love COH, I *literally* cannot play this game due to the zoom and stutter problems. My specs are comfortably above the "recommended". PROS:-Its supposed to be CoH-QoL improvements (e.g. auto-vault, auto-reinforce, etc.)NEUTRALS:-Campaign:  Although I've played hundreds of hours of COH, I've never played the campaign in any iteration of the game, so I have absolutely no opinion on that. I only play ranked multiplayer. -Mouse Pan Speed:  Default mouse pan speed is WAY too fast. Thankfully there is an option to reduce this (I recommend 50%).-Mod Support:  At first glance, this seems like it should belong in the "PROS" section, but given how poor the current audio/textures in the game are, it seems like the real reason they are supporting this out the gate is because they expect the community to fix their game. -Arcade style unit highlights: these didn't bother me, but they seem completely pointless (and I can understand why they bother other players). The player can only control the squad, not the individual units, so what point is there in highlighting the individual units and completely destroying the immersion?  CONS:-ZOOMED IN. You cannot see half the battle because the camera is SO CLOSE. Why am I playing the game with a microscope? Its not the like the textures are any good for me to look at. You cannot zoom out. (the previous games also had this issue to an extent)-Runs like ♥♥♥♥. I have an i7 9th gen with an RTX 2070.  3v3 is *literally* unplayable. 2v2 was a stuttering mess.  1v1 is "playable" but it is NOT smooth. (NOTE: I even reduced my gfx to 1920x1080 but it still stutters)-NO ONLINE RECONNECT (in 2023). If it crashes or you disconnect - too bad. -Hotkeys: QWERTY hotkeys.  NO LEGACY HOTKEYS. -Audio:  Why is everything so quiet? I've seen others mention that devs were going for "realism" instead of "Hollywood" -- I personally don't care about that. I need AUDIO CUES when playing a game. Can't hear anything unless you're zoomed in right on top of the action (this is also partly because if you aren't looking at something, it won't play the sounds, but the sounds it does play can barely be recognized....)-NO RANKED MODE:  Selecting multiplayer puts you directly into an unranked matchmaking lobby. -Default setting is borderless window withOUT mouse constraints. This setting is impossible to play. Laughable that it is the 'default' option. Bonus points: Mouse constraint setting does NOT save on quit. You have to do it each time you load the game. -HUD is unfinished and backwards in design.--Buildings DO NOT SHOW what unit they are building when you select them (its shown somewhere else on your hud). This is really important because it means you CANNOT CANCEL CONSTRUCTION via HOTKEY.  In order to cancel a unit that is being built, you have to click on the icon on the screen that shows you how far along the build progress is. This icon is always on your screen (to show you the build status) which means its possible to accidentally cancel a unit building due to misclick (selecting the building first is not necessary). This is a subtle but major flaw in the new HUD. --Text chat box is distorted. This is a really really amateur level mistake in a $60 game. --Tons of blank space, weird color choices, etc. This problem is magnified when you consider how immensely zoomed in the game already is. As others have said, it feels very much like a mobile UI.

_childDocuments_.review: How is there no ranked MP at launch? No level unlocks? No replays? No way to revisit post-game stats? No surrender? No changes since the betas aside from minor QOL fixes? Sure, I'm happy that building placement isn't broken anymore, but...? It's just so bland. 1v1, 2v2, 3v3, and 4v4 have ~2 maps each. The factions feel like reskins of each other. The armor selection is weak. Each faction only has 3 "special companies" which adds no flavor. You know EXACTLY what you're coming up against every match because each faction only has 1-2 viable "companies" and with them only 2-3 viable units. The camera is terrible. It's just way too zoomed in which makes it difficult to effectively control a large section of combat. The audio is lackluster and nothing has any real oomph to it - I'm using a 400w subwoofer with the bass cranked. For $90 CAD after taxes, this is an absolutely massive rip off in terms of content, polish, and everything else. There's absolutely nothing justifying the cost.However, if this were released in Early Access with a price to match - let's be honest, this is undeniably Early Access quality... All of the above gripes would be completely understandable (minus price of course). Right now, this is a $50 CAD game tops. Buying CoH3 right now is like paying someone to paint your entire house... But they only paint the trim and then bill you for the full job while saying, "we'll probably come back to add more paint later but for now we consider this job as completed".

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't good value, and I would not recommend buying this game. It shouldn't get more expensive, so I would suggest you save your money for now, and only buy once it is actually finished. If they've already got your money, they have no incentive to fix things.My issue are that:(1) key features that one would expect in a finished game are missing (eg, saving replays); (2) there appear to be significant balance or design issues beyond what one would expect at launch; (3) there are graphical issues (eg, guns floating in the air near soldiers instead of being held); (4) there are many bugs in game (for example, units getting stuck, including clipping through terrain and getting permanently stuck) and in menu (eg, post-game information closing randomly - possibly closing for everyone when the host closes it?);(5) there is evidence of cheapness/corner cutting - for example, recycling CoH2 icons. This isn't in itself a problem, but when combined with so many other issues, it feels like this was driven by cheapness rather than a deliberate choice;(6) In the first major update they brought in a store. Clearly the main issue is that there isn't extra monetisation for cosmetic items, and not that the game wasn't ready for release. (God forbid that they start introducing pay-to-win commanders so soon after launch, so far they haven't.)I technically got this game for free when I purchased a new computer (although that was part of the decision to buy), and would have even more upset had I paid.P.S. One of the best features about CoH in my view has been the music, but CoH3 music hasn't had the same impact for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This is exclusively a single player review and is comparative to other COH campaigns.COH3 has everything need to be great, the game mechanics, units, graphics etc. But in short there is a lack of unique scripted interesting missions, and the ones that do exist are too short with limited access to areas of the map, and are not tied well enough together with story or pacing. It's like getting all the perfect ingredients for a cake, and them just mixing them poorly.The first COH has 15 campaign missions. The first was a training mission, the next 3 were solid missions but very limited to ease you in to the game. The other 11 were all unique, interesting, relatively lengthy, quite open, often multistage missions. They were incredibly fun to play and to replay. The way the campaign was held together with some little intro and outro animations and a bit of in engine footage, was great. There was not outstanding dialogue or characters, but it was solid enough to give a filling of cohesion and progress to the whole thing. New units opened up as you went through the campaign so the pacing was good. Most of the missions allowed you to build a base and create the uniques you wanted to play with.Opposing fronts did the same, but with arguably even more mission variety, but split across 2 7/8 mission campaigns. But it was more of the good stuff.I replay the original and it's first expansion every few years. It's great fun.COH2 really dropped the ball on its campaign. Awful silly story, crappy looking CG cut scenes, poor pacing etc.Ardennes Assault was not bad. Some difficult solid unique scripted missions.So on to COH3. It has 2 campaigns. A standard 8 mission campaign in the desert which can be thought of as being kind of like half of opposing fronts, and a "full" Italian campaign which expands on the concept of Ardennes Assault.COH 3 African CampaignThe african campaign feels like it's almost there, but doesn't quite make it. Of the 8 missions most are very short. They jump a lot between missions where you have a fixed set of units and no base and missions where you can base build. I have nothing against a few missions where there is no base, COH1 did this for a few of its earlier missions. But in COH1 the missions got more complex with more options. It doesn't feel like the campaign here really opens up through most of it. When it finally starts to, its over. The pacing is odd as you will jump between being able to build and train large numbers of units one mission, to the next mission having a max of 6 units with no base. So this makes the pacing very odd. It's choppy. I would say there are about 3 full feeling missions where you get a good amount of freedom. The missions with set units would be better if they played out for the first part of the mission, then opened into full base building in the next phase of the same mission. To be fair the fixed unit missions are actually good, but fixed unit missions are not that much fun to play more than once as you can't really vary the approach.The story is fine and the way they approached it, having an axis campaign with the story told from a local who is fighting on the allied side, odd though it was, I think worked okay.So basically the issue is the missions are tOo small, to short, often with fixed units and as a result feel limited, with odd pacing. They have all the pieces for a great campaign, but then failed to make one by misunderstanding what actually makes the campaign missions fun and what gives the sense of progression through a campaign like COH1 and opposing fronts.The Italian Campaign.The main campaign has basically similar issues. At first it looks really exciting as there are a lot of missions, towns, harbours, airfields etc on the map, so it looks like it will be a really meaty long campaign with lots of missions, plus the added variety and complexity of being able to approach the missions with different companies, some in different orders, and with the complexities of doing so through a tactical map.However.... In actual fact most of the missions on the map are not unique story missions, they are skirmishes. They are just a random choice of run the enemy out of tickets, defend a couple of emplacements for a few minutes with fixed units, destroy the enemy base. They are fine as padding, which is what I assumed they would be, but they are not the padding, they are what you will spend most of the campaign doing. I would say for every 1 actual scripted story mission, you will play 3  standard types of skirmish missions.Put simply the campaign just doesn't have enough actual scripted full missions. It feels like just playing in skirmish mode, with the odd scripted mission chucked in.The skirmishes are also frustrating as they are very short. You can auto resolve already so if you choose to play the skirmish, why not at least let it be an intense push and pull battle. The placement defense missions only require you to defend for literally maybe 5 mins. The ticket base missions only have 250 tickets so the rounds are often over in under 10 mins.What this means is you spend most of the campaign jumping from one cookie cutter skirmish to the next, and then not being able to sink you teeth in to even that as by the time you get even a little way up the tech tree, by the time you have say your first heavy tank, the mission is over. The campaign is most like just playing a skirmish I COH1 but with the game forcing skirmish setting you don't want.To be fair, the scripted missions this campaign does have are actually reasonable. Most of them are quite good fun. They are still a little short, and the maps do this odd thing where most of the map is out of bounds the entire missions so you are only ever playing on say 50% of what's in the mini map, which to me looks like a way of the Devs just time saving and is really frustrating, but the missions are not bad by any stretch. But there are not enough of them, they are a little small, and the flow is broken by the 2 / 3 skirmishes that happen between. I hate looking at the campaign map at all the missions that could exist, but actually don't because they are just a generic skirmish.There are no real characters in the campaign to hold it all together. There are some different generals that give orders, but no characters that are kind of in the fight as it were.Here is what I wish they had done- Put some time into making more scripted missions. I would say at least double what exists.- Made the scripted missions longer and a bit more expansive with regard to the playable map area.- Tied it all together with a bit more of an intimate story with a bit more in the way of in engine cut scenes.- Made the skirmishes padding as opposed to the meat- Made the skirmishes longer with say higher ticket counts so you could sink your teeth in- Added some better thought out skirmsh mechanics and scenarios. For example they could have made it so the scripted campaign mission maps could later be counter attacked. This would have meant playing the skirmishs on unique maps. The attacks could be pretty strong and say wave based with some interesting variables relating to the overview map, company involved, at what point in the campaign it happened etc. This would have meant that although the same kind of counter attack would play out on different maps, it would be on interesting maps, tied better into the story, be quite long and intense.So the tldr. They created all the right stuff for a great COH single player campaign, but then made far to few unique scripted missions, made the missions they did create too short, forced them into map areas that are often too small, made too many of them without base building, for the most part didn't have much of a cohesive story to tie it together and give it weight and a feeling of progression, and make the way units become available make it feel like there is choppy progression.

Beside the lack of good lighting, textures, models and animations on ultra are fine. There should also be an option to change the voice lines of the units to native respective languages, e.g. Italians units speak Italian, German ones German and so on. All in all CoH3 is still a very good game, with really fun mechanics. I also quite enjoyed the campaigns, especially the Italian campaign. _childDocuments_.review: Short versionI've been a CoH enjoyer for many years unfortunately this latest instalment is missing the magic that made the previous titles great. I really wanted to leave a positive review of this game but ultimately the price point versus the delivered product does not equate. TL;DR - Spend your money on a more worthwhile title, return to this game when its on a deep sale.  Long versionThis instalment provides you with two main campaigns. The Africa Campaign is akin to classic CoH style and there are a plenty of enjoyable moments. I did find there to be some pacing issues and I never truly felt invested or as if the stakes were high. Ultimately it was an enjoyable campaign albeit a little cookie cutter.    The Italian Campaign is a nice innovative idea for the CoH series, and I enjoyed the idea of where that might lead. Hoping to utilise tactics on the game board to affect the enemy, cut off supplies, encircle and destroy etc. Unfortunately nothing you do seems to drastically affect the AI aside from "move here destroy army, move here take city" as such the momentum isn't maintained throughout the campaign and it becomes quite repetitive and basically just another skirmish mode. It also feels like a missed opportunity to not include cinematic's into the title as these could have very much enhanced the player experience. The Africa Campaign has a story board type intermission that I found to be lacklustre and rather boring, aside from this you only have the usual units running around the map aimlessly preamble prior to the start of missions.  Regarding sound, I had no issues I feel a lot of the sound is fine and implemented well although the explosions are lacking that impact or thud from previous titles. Dropping artillery or a bombing run on the map doesn't feel as impressive as it did.There are some new additions to the game such as tow-able weapon platforms, vehicle recovery, troops being carried in various way however I have not found these to be useful at any point. I feel more defensive structures such as being able to reinforce buildings or things that add to unit survive-ability would have been better game play additions.  The UI itself is not particularly intuitive and the game could use various quality of life improvements many of which players were hoping would be addressed in the coming patch (it was not). With regards to performance, the game performs decently with good load times however I have had some localised stuttering and lagging and about 3 crashes to date with some random frame drops. The game could still use some performance tweaks to bring it to standard.  With regards to replay-ability, the Africa Campaign provides none and the Italian Campaign provides very little if you want to avoid the grind, you might be able to differ your approach but ultimately everything is still the same. Leaving skirmishes and multiplayer as the sector of replay-ability.  With the latest patch entitled "Sapphire Jackal", Relic has shown they're indeed the true jackals with the release and implementation of their "store" feature being the focal point. Relic has shown they're more interested in micro transactions and cosmetics than they are the player base and I fear for the future of the title. Ultimately you will get some hours out of this game and definitely some enjoyable moments however the delivered product is not worth the price point and they should be held to a higher standard. This has been a lacklustre launch and instalment and it is for these reason that, at this time, I cannot recommend the game. Wait for a deep sale before purchasing, spend your money on a more worthwhile title.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE:It's encouraging to see the developers adding replay, progression, and graphics updates to the game, enhancing its 'finished' feel. It's great that both single-player and multiplayer enthusiasts are being catered to. However, upon seeing the expansion pack, it appears to be limited to battlegroup additions and premium skins. While I'm intrigued by the pricing, I believe a DLC, touted as an expansion, should offer more than just new battlegroups and skins. As someone who purchased the premium version, it's disappointing to realize that this pack is one of the promised DLCs from our version. While more gameplay is always enjoyable, the marketing and terminology used for this add-on (rather than an expansion) seem somewhat misleading. We'll have to wait and see.Older statement review:Take my review how you like, after playing the different tests and watching tons of gameplay and livestreams, while also playing a bit myself. Here is my review from someone who's put a ton of gameplay in CoH2 and 1.Campaigns:The total war-style turn-based campaign map mixed with real-time battles looks beautiful and is filled with lots of different systems. However, it becomes apparent that it's extremely linear in its execution. You have almost no effect or semblance of strategy on the world map; it's practically all window dressing to get to the really fun real-time battles. It's a shame and a wasted potential in terms of providing some form of "endless" replayability for solo players. Personally, I still find the Belgium theater campaign from CoH2 more impactful and hardcore than this. The second campaign is only 6 hours long and has lots of fun missions, but it also lacks the impact and historical essence of the original two campaigns. The cutscenes are all hand-drawn with no CGI, which is a step down in my opinion.Custom games:After you confusingly find the buttons to invite and kick players, you can treat yourself to the most basic custom game mode I've ever seen since Age of Empires 2 original. There are no progression tabs, no detailed scoreboards, and it's extremely buggy at times. That's it; there are no additional co-op missions like in CoH with those cool little visuals of historical battles on both the German and Soviet sides. There's nothing, just this super barebones custom game mode.Multiplayer:I'm happy to know that at least the NAT code and overall smoothness were present in multiplayer, and I didn't have much trouble starting a game. The only thing that stood out here was the utter lack of ranked matches, progression systems, or even emblem customization or clan systems. They released a game with tons of marketing focused on multiplayer and they took out the level system from CoH2. It wasn't much to begin with in previous games, but at least it was there, and you got some cool ribbons, challenges, and other little rewards from it.UI:The UI is generally good, but one complaint I have is that it takes up half of the screen. Additionally, the menus and visuals outside of gameplay still need some work. It may be a personal preference, but I do miss the interactive and visually appealing menus from the previous game.AI:Laughable is an understatement for the Medium difficulty; they do kind of give some challenges on Hard, but you can still totally crush any resistance with good flank tactics. They hardly reacted at launch, and after some patches, they do use cover better, but they still do super dumb things like driving through cities with tanks while being pummeled hard by anti-tank guns. Or not retreating at some points when they are clearly outgunned and under constant fire. The campaign AI does a better job, but they are mostly scripted to hold or attack points of interest, so they don't really work in dynamic ways to counter your offensive maneuvers.Graphics:Look, I'm not the kind of person who rants super hard if RTS games don't have the latest and best shadows or texture details. However, I do have a problem when a sequel to a 10-year-old game somehow looks worse than its predecessor. The ground, buildings, units, and animations all lack much-needed detail. It still looks like the alpha build they showed off a year ago.New additions:I really appreciate the addition of battlegroups to the game as it adds much-needed flavor and allows for different playstyles in multiplayer matches. It's evident that more will be added in the future because there's a large empty row underneath the existing three groups when opening the battlegroup customization. The introduction of unique systems for each faction is also a nice and welcome touch, even though some of them were a bit overpowered initially. It's clear that despite having the same factions as previous games, the developers did a good job of diversifying them in terms of playstyle, abilities, and weapons. The foundation is definitely there!Overall, I'm really disappointed in the state of CoH3, especially considering its very successful and content-rich predecessor. You would expect the game to meet the same standards or at least have the features present in previous titles. It's clear as day that this game was rushed, and the developers needed more time to polish and add necessary features. While the game is being marketed as a live service, and I don't mind that, especially if they are hinting at exploring other theaters with expansions and big updates, like most modern titles, this game just came out in early access with a 60 euros or more price tag. And i'm the idiot who bought the limited edition version...

_childDocuments_.review: Company of Heroes 3 is OK - just not as good as the original. The variation of units is decent if not exceptional (better than COH2 base game), the combat seems more visceral than COH2, but it feels like a lot of features are missing. The Italy campaign is a breath of fresh air (aside from a couple of crashing issues), but there is precious little late game content in a skirmish. AI is again acceptable but can be beaten by slow attrition. The graphics have not evolved sufficiently since COH2 (which was 10 years ago); when games like Plague Tale Requiem are challenging top end GPUs, this just isn't. That's not to say that there aren't framerate and optimisation issues (there are on a 4090). Overall there are the bones of a good game, but this feels like a Beta with later content to come as it is patched in (or as paid DLC). I don't feel this is worth the premium price. The whole game reeks of the studio being cheap & using an established name to draw you in to a substandard game. The first game was a true spaghetti carbonara, simple & easy but bravissimo. This ♥♥♥♥ put cream all over it & then added chicken & broccoli . . . & expects me to eat it because it shares the name of the first one. You cannot customise skins as easily as in the second game, heck it costs either real money or the in game currency to buy them. There were hardly any official maps & their idea of a good patch is to add in a handful every now & then. Did I mention that those maps they added already existed? Yeah, one of them was Semois from the first game. Cheap. There is no separate Italian faction . . . in a game set in the Italian theatre . . . mamma mia!!! Hey, you can buy a new battle group in the newest expansion (which isn't even worth an espresso but is over £10 at full price).One of the few things I enjoyed was the main campaign but if that was as enjoyable as it gets, there is a problem because even then it has major flaws. It shows you a map of Italy but also areas that are useless to take, nothing happens if you take Rome. The game ends abruptly after breaching the Winter Line, however quickly or slowly you decide to do it. So even single player is like munching on a soggy tiramisu, decent enough but underwhelming.This game, coupled with its horrific launch, is like someone offering to make you a pizza, & then you get a flatbread covered in ketchup. After ages complaining, they give you pineapple as a topping & mayonnaise on the side & expect you to be happy because they are making progress & adding to it. Anyone that says it is good is not right in the head. Sono tutti pazzi. It isn't worth the price even at 50% off. _childDocuments_.review: I've waited almost 2 months for a review on this game to address the initial problems and to wait for new content/fixes etc. to be added. Well seems like this is not the priority of Relic at this state. After the first "big" patch (1.1) 1-2 weeks ago we see minimal to no advancements in this regard, instead we are rewarded with an ingame shop in which you can buy with real money e.g. winter skins (very lol in the desert). There are major problems regarding not only the balance, but also the overall design of the factions, vehicle controlling (pathing), call-in units, abilities, broken stuff where you look, plenty of bugs as well as missing features from previous COH games. In addition, things like the main screen and tactical map are by far the worst in comparison to the other COH games. This combined with stuff I didn't mention yet leads to the point that you HAVE to play a certain way for each faction, if you don't do it it's already gg for you. Relic made the decision to add 4 playable factions for launch, which on paper is great, but lack of good game design and implementation leads to this crap we got now. In short, the game was launched half finished, and you will see this sooner or later. My advice, certainly don't buy at full price. Wait for sale or wait a year, maybe it's finished until then. Don't get me wrong, you can certainly enjoy this game for a while and you can have lots of fun with it, but eventually you'll notice the severe fundamental issues this game has and it will drain you a lot. For me this happend after 50-60 hours which is far below my expectations.The sad thing is, that I as a COH1 Fan really hoped to see this as a worthy sequel to this once great game, but it's just not. And based on the overall reviews, streams on twitch and current playerbase I'm certainly not alone.

_childDocuments_.review: This review was written after completing the Italy campaign and playing some multiplayer games.+ Amazing performance compared to COH2.+ Campaign map idea is great (execution could be better)+ Auto vaulting, towing, tank riding and auto reinforcing are useful QoL additions.+ Breaching and verticalty provide new fun tactical scenarios.+ Four factions at launch (COH2 only had two).+ The ability to play offline skirmishes against AI (instead of matchmaking).+ Far fewer bugsplats than COH2 at launch.+ Great and beautifully designed maps.+ Essence editor features are well expanded.+ Tactical break is nice to have (personally don't use it much).+ Destruction looks better (IMHO).+ Towing heavy weapons is really useful for the slightly faster matches.− The UI really needs some work.− The zoom level is ridiculous, it's 2023, come on Relic.− Currently no method to scale the HUD.− Currently no method to create custom user skins/camouflages (workshop).− Loudness of vehicle engines should be a bit louder.− The tactical map of the Italy campaign feels a bit clunky.− The AI on the Italy campaign map is really passive (no attempt to recapture).− Cannot continue playing after the end of a match.− No progression system with rewards for playing.□ Separate audio sliders for engines, explosions, music and general audio.□ Separate visual sliders for vibrance, sharpness and other basic visual settings.□ Multiple presets for color correction (War Thunder).□ More background sounds such as distant gunfire, birds, etc.□ More environmental elements such as day/night and weather effects.□ More customizability when setting up the campaign (like Civilization games).□ Option to (re)play the campaign with custom skins.□ An SAS battle group with vicker machine guns on jeeps.□ A roadmap with future additions / patches.COH3 could be a great game after some extensive polishing and tuning. Still, I can enjoy myself immensely with this game, and in the end, that is the goal.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a huge fan of the COH series since the first one came out in 2006, many hours in the previous two installments over the years. And I feel there is a lot to love about COH3 as well. But there are some caveats. I’ll start with the positives first.The SP experience is solid from my experience thus far, and I love the Total War style operation map and the detail that has gone into. It would be great to see some more expansion on it and look forward to see if the modding community can do anything with it.The tactical pause has been a huge benefit to me (I have a visual impairment). And thanks to this I can enjoy the game like I used to enjoy the previous titles when I could see much better.The game runs well and I have not had performance issues.And now for the issues…The multiplayer feels too fast for my taste, but it is still fun. I have not tried all the factions yet, but what is there seems a bit limited. This particularly true if you compare it to the variety of skills and abilities available in the campaign. I am sure this will be fleshed out more over time, but it does bare mention.There have been a few minor bugs and issues playing through the Italian theater campaign that has caused me to load saves here and there. Annoying, but not show stopping.I believe if you are a big fan of the series and not huge on multiplayer then I feel it is well worth the purchase price. If MP is solely your thing, I would wait for things to be fleshed out a bit more. Overall I feel it is a great game, but far from perfect at the moment. I look forward to seeing how it improves over time.

name: In Stars And Time
detailed_description: What would you do if you were forced to relive your failures over and over again? In Stars and Time tells the story of Siffrin and their adventurer friends—a found family bound together by fate in order to end the tyrannical reign of an evil king. But as victory is just within the party’s grasp, a tragedy occurs, the clock resets, and they have to do it all again . As Siffrin’s the only one who notices this loop, each new start wears away at his cheerful veneer, yet he keeps going in hopes he can end this temporal tragedy once and for all. In Stars and Time is a time-looping RPG adventure . With each loop, Siffrin gains a new perspective on the world around them, opening up new solutions to puzzles and allowing them to make better choices in conversation. Equip memories as armor, pray to the Change God to improve your team’s capabilities each loop, and challenge deadly foes to Rock, Paper, Scissors as Siffrin seeks the truth. ✦ Our Adventurers Siffrin (he/they): Stressed, depressed, and under duress. (Don’t worry about it. They’re doing fine.) The punmaster protagonist of our neverending tale. Mirabelle (she/her): A caring and nervous housemaiden mysteriously blessed by the god she so ardently follows. Isabeau (he/him): Defender with a heart of gold. Cares dearly for his people and his friends. Odile (she/her): The mature and nonsensical researcher studying…something. (No, she will not tell you what it is.) Bonnie (they/them): Wait a minute, who brought this kid along??? ✦ Features Save the world through the power of Rock, Paper, Scissors in strategic turn-based RPG combat encounters. Ignore the limits of time and space to fix your past mistakes by repeating the same two days over and over again. Equip the memories you have of your friends to make your party stronger in combat. Watch the fate of this world unfold as you escape the twists and turns of this endless(???) loop. Eat samossas with your friends! Get heckled by a cheeky ethereal being of infinite starlight . Pray to a god for good luck in your travels. You’re gonna need it. If any of this interests you, you might also want to play the game’s initial prototype, START AGAIN START AGAIN START AGAIN: A Prologue . While you don’t need to play it to understand In Stars and Time, it’s fun to see the game’s roots!

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, straight to the point. I wholeheartedly recommend this game, it's a fantastic experience through and through, and has given me a lot to mull over in my mind. This is with a caveat though, mainly that the first and second acts are really intent on setting things up, as it were, to the point of pretty much entirely railroading you aside from some simple side stuff. I have never really been a person to be bothered by extended set-ups in games, regardless of whether it makes things a slog, but (especially with reading some of the other reviews while stewing a bit on my thoughts) I do think it is pertinent to mention that. The game does open up MUCH more past act 2, so if you can get through that, you should be fine, unless the overall game-loop (yes, I hear your mental snickering) is not to your taste.Ok, basic "recommend or not?" stuff is over, I'm going to try and delve into my personal thoughts from here. This will be more than guaranteed to contain spoilers, so if you prefer to not be spoiled, don't read the rest.So, this game was really something, and being someone who has both played a LOT of games and loves to read stories, whether on the internet or with a physical book, my genuine thoughts as of writing this are that the game has really impressed me. I've been around the bend at this point in terms of interacting with media and video games, played stuff like Legend of the dragoon, and the original Artonelico, and I've read plenty of different genre's of fiction (stuff like Fablehaven, or the nausicaa manga), and watched plenty of shows. Now, I say this because of all the things I've read or watched or played over the years, In stars and time has actually managed to make me feel something no other game has, to my memory. It has actually managed to sicken me with pure, raw, dread. I mean like, actually made me feel ill when i was going through a certain part of the game. I've felt all sorts of things from interacting with stories, I've felt terror, I've teared up and on occasion cried when a story has actually touched me, I've even genuinely just simply felt satisfied with a story's conclusion very rarely. But never has a game actually made me tense up mentally from dread of what I know is going to happen so well that it's gotten such a visceral reaction out of me, and even sustained it, at that.For me personally, even if the only good part of the game was that section, I would still think VERY highly of the game and it's developer for managing to do that to me, as that is a fantastic experience and will probably be something I remember for a while. however, this was just a single section of the entire game, and this was just the most standout emotion and moment for me (I would ramble on about other particular parts for hours. Alas, word limit.)! To be honest, i'll have to wait a year or two to see if it really sticks, but for now, I would say that this is one of the best games I've ever played!P.S. insertdisc5, if your reading this, the king is my favorite character, it was a treat reading his entire speech at the Nostalgie achievement part, and even more of a treat when he completely turned around and called Siffrin out for having the audacity to try and "just talk things through" to a man who is literally freezing an entire country in time in order to fulfill his wish. The actual epitome of "YOU THOUGHT!". (his "death" was really beautiful too!)

_childDocuments_.review: In Stars and Time is a game that I think has made it's way into one of my top 10. It's not without it's flaws but I really feel like, specifically from a gameplay and story standpoint, this game really improves upon on the first game and makes it a much more enjoyable experience. I will say that I personally really enjoyed the game at first but found myself getting a little bored/frustrated during subsequent loops, it wasn't until I hit my 20th loop that I started having fun with the game again. I specifically liked how there was a lot of intrigue and expansion of the universe that I hadn't thought of but was well addressed. With that said, I am going to be going over some spoilers in the section below, so skip to the non blacked out part of this review if you haven't finished the game yet. While this game is kinda slow in places, I often felt that if I was messing up or missing something later in the game, that was on me. This game really knows how to communicate a lot and not waste your time if you don't let it. It's one of the rare pieces of timeloop media I felt a genuine interest and passion towards. It has something to say and says it well. All of the characters are great and the mechanics are really good. I would recommend getting this game first and then playing the prologue personally because that way the game will be more fun, but the first game did give me PTSD when it came to certain areas so there's that. Definitely a worthwhile game that has dreamy art, a cool story, a nice soundtrack, endearing characters, fun gameplay, and a lot of routes if you look for them. Don't skip this one, it's worth a playthrough!

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute gem of a game. It's one of those games that is an extremely slow burn initially and if you aren't invested in the story then it won't be for you. At first it was annoying for Siffrin to not be able to ask the questions I wanted to ask, or to look into what I wanted to look into until something clicked and I realised that Siffrin is a character with their own wants, needs and way of thinking. I wasn't supposed to be moulding Siffrin into some caricature of myself to puppeteer and make the decisions I would make like other RPGs, but rather I was meant to see through their perspective. Maybe it's a weird distinction to make and this only applies to me, but that initial frustration I felt came from this misunderstanding of what the game was presenting to me.I love the writing. A few things felt preachy here and there but when the sheer QUALITY of the story is this good then a few bumps are barely worth mentioning. Characters are lively and easily differentiated from one-another, the world itself feels so well-crafted as if there is more than the box we're put in. _childDocuments_.review: After playing this game for 45 hours (plus an additonal 35 on another platform), spanning two full playthroughs, and getting every single achievement (Getting all 43 in one run for that matter, since my second playthrough was from scratch on steam) I think I've spent more than enough time to leave a well informed review.Upon re-reading this I honestly can't say this is the most objective thing but uh.... well too late?Big rambling ahead. You have been warned.tldr: very good. good vibeo gaem. also contains The Horrors/Trauma. beware of the gut punches. Also may feel a bit slow at times.Let me preface this review with one more thing even if it isn't important: I have not played OMORI, or other RPGmaker games and the sort, so take this from the perspective of someone who is not familiarized with this type of game. This is effectively a whole new genre for me.This game KICKS ASS. It also will kick you in the stomach. Several times. Play the game. Do it. Don't spoil yourself, though, because that removes half the intrigue. The game's writing is REALLY good, and that's actually surprising to me. The characters themselves actually feel like they could be real people, at least in some way. Also, the OST is just a banger. There are a lot of really good tracks. Don't expect the gameplay and combat to blow you away, since it is still a turn-based RPG type game, but I found the way combat was designed and how a lot plays into each other to be pretty fun. For what it is, it's pretty solid but rarely difficult. Don't be surprised if gameplay feels a bit repetitive/frustrating later on; it's basically that way by design and is somehow used to the story's advantage. But, keep in mind there is actually a fair amount of QOL features to prevent the game from becoming entirely unfun and tedious.Just know that once you start, you'll probably get sucked into the loop yourself. It was surprisingly hard to put down for me. Now GO PLAY THE GAME. Or play the demo. Or read the rest and  play the game. Or don't at all! I don't really care.As I was saying, again this game is REALLY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. Like, it's an art piece in more than just the art/visuals. The game takes advantage of the fact that yes, this is in fact a video game, and lets you immerse yourself in the perspective of what I can best describe is the "literally me" protagonist who's got some Problems™, Siffrin, who got put in a time loop. I'll spare the details because I don't want to give spoilers, but you really get to experience firsthand what the time loop does to him over the course of the game. (Spoiler alert: Nothing Good)There's a lot of really good moments and plenty of The Horrors™ to go around as the game goes on. Also, the side content/quests are great and you shouldn't ignore them. This game practically begs you to go for that 100% completion (I rarely try to 100% my games. This was an exception).Once again, I also have to say. The OST is amazing. The story is something you don't want to be spoiled on. It's got some real gut punches sprinkled through, but also some really touching or funny moments to even things out. There's some real personality to the writing. The game somehow manages to make a child character not annoying and actually likeable, it's unbelievable I know. Oh, one last thing. The completely unapologetic integration of LGBTQ+ rep is unfathomably based, it's done very well and presented in a realistic and relatable way. Also yeah, there's the acknowledgement and inclusion of pronouns. Cry about it. ♥♥♥♥♥ and whine about it, even. It's a thing that exists, get over it. It's not the end of the world. It doesn't really matter anyways. I wanted to mention that part for the sole purpose of humoring myself knowing there's people that get butthurt at the mention of them.If I had to give it a number rating, this would be a 9/10 from me.I could definitely go on and on about this game if this wasn't a review, but that's what I'll leave it at. This is just my take. GO PLAY THE GAME AND SEE FOR YOURSELF!!! YOU (probably) WON'T REGRET IT! Form your own opinion about this!! Don't just take my word for it! On the fence? Again, there's a FREE DEMO sitting there, just waiting for you. What's the worst that could happen???

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game is a masterpiece. In my opinion, it is the best time loop game to date, and is on par with if not better than Omori and Undertale.REVIEWThis game felt very simple at first, and it was quite clear how time loops would play into the basic grand quest story we've come to love in RPGs. Until (hehe),  In case you didn't read that (good on you for staying spoiler free), I'm basically saying that there was a lot more depth to this than I had realised. There was so much lore, and I could really feel how this whole ordeal was affecting the character, and how that in turn impacted those around them. I was in awe.Here's a little blessing! You can skip through conversations you've already heard. And it doesn't feel like it was just added at the end to make everything faster, it feels so integrated and clear. You basically zone in and out of conversation!This game knows that playing through the same series of events over and over can get boring. It actually uses this to help you identify even more with our main character! Your feelings translate to the game, and the game as well as its characters actually seem to react to this feeling! Because of this, every single loop feels like its own new adventure.SUMMARYGraphics: 4/5 - I really like the art style! I think it really compliments the mood of the game, and I really appreciated how certain stylistic choices were actually addressed in the game's lore.Gameplay: 4/5 - Great gameplay overall! Interactions feel satisfying, and the simple yet engaging combat mechanics compliment the game's design. Soundtrack: 4/5 - Basic but nostalgic. It is used very well to make me feel anxious at times haha.Plot: 5/5 - I'm in love. I cried a lot, but that might just be who I am. It would appeal to those who liked titles such as Omori and Undertale, though it does feel quite different.Characters: 5/5 - I immediately connected with the little heroes of this game, and they all felt so unique and real. I adore how they interact with you as the game progresses.RECOMMENDATIONUm, hello? TRY THIS GAME???I'd recommend this game to you if you appreciate:- Undertale/Omori- Queer rep- Simple but meaningful world exploration with lots of backtracking- A deep or long story with lots of loreFINAL NOTEI'm editing this review months after I first played it and I just need to say that this replayability is incredible. I really adore this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Excels at gameplay/story integration and emotive writing, in a way that will probably turn a lot of people off.A great portion of ISAT isn't very fun. Although combat is novel, it gradually reveals itself to be fairly shallow as you use the same abilities over and over, getting lazier on strategy as it becomes no longer needed. It is fun to explore the detailed environments, but after a while they start feeling very samey and you're largely digging through things you've seen before. The character dialogue is excellent, but after you've read it a dozen times, you start wishing people weren't so long-winded. ISAT becomes a game you learn to speedrun with minor variations. Do all of this again but read this one book, pick up this one item, talk to this one person. You constantly are retreading your footsteps and teetering on the edge of a feeling of satisfaction which then gets pulled away from you as you realize you have to again backtrack to something you've seen before.All of this is by design. ISAT is very intent on putting you in Siffrin's shoes, and they are going through an experience that slowly wears its novelty and their mental state into dust. The game gets very dark and unpleasant, and even fellow schadenfreude enjoyers may find it begin to bum them out. You should probably consider doing what Siffrin can't, which is to take breaks to recover.Recommended, but specifically for the kind of person who enjoys wringing every last drop of enjoyment out of something and then reveling in the ashes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was incredibly charming! The story & the characters all felt so lovingly crafted, and the entire game was so charming from start to finish. I haven't gotten all the achievements yet, but I'm planning on going back and trying to get them, so maybe my (very small) grievances will be addressed there, but I do want to mention 2 things I felt were a bit lacking:- There's a moment at the climax of the story that I feel didn't give me enough catharsis; I felt there was a tonal transition missing between 2 very good moments, that would've made them both hit a lot harder. They're both back to back, and I found they were both really important an heartfelt moments, but I feel it would've went over better if there had been some sort of transition between the two.- There's a character that I wish I could've talked to at the end of the game. Maybe I missed something during my playthrough, so I may just have to keep playing, but with that said I do feel that there were certain small plot threads that I wish we could've known more about. Worldbuilding things that I thought would come back were left a bit in the air, but again maybe I just need to play more and/or we may get more stories related to them! Who knows!Even with those 2 small things though, I really do recommend this game. I very much enjoyed my time with it, I really care about the characters a lot, and I relate to Siffrin so much. If you're the type of person who goes back to their favorite stories because they miss the characters, I think this game will make you feel seen. The thematics around journeys (and their inevitable ends), wishes, promises, found family and love are all incredibly heartfelt, and feel very meta in that I, as the player, really felt seen in how stories matter to me.Another aspect I haven't touched upon is that this game is MUCH longer and has a lot more content than I was expecting. I love RPGMaker projects, and I never take how short a game is as a negative, but In Stars And Time kept surprising me with how it kept going, which I suppose is also very appropriate for the story and its thematics. I would say you are definitely getting a bang for your buck with this!Finally, my final argument: Isabeau is THE babygirl ever. I love him.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy games like Undertale, Detlarune, Oneshot, and other emotional character driven indie RPG games then this game is absolutely for you. The entire time I was playing this game I was making sure to search everywhere in the hopes of finding new dialogue options, new lore, and new character details. I didn't even find everything! I still have so so many questions about this games lore and I NEED it to become popular enough for people to make hour long videos that explain the games lore. Now in terms of game play I do think parts of the game are very tedious, which was probably by design. Going through the house over and over and over gets draining, but I feel like it helps put you in the mind space of Sif. Also after Sif gets past lvl 60ish all the sadnesses become more of minor annoyances. Combat was very.. basic rpg. When I first started playing I found the "rock paper scissors" mechanics a little... on the nose, but I didn't really care and by my 10th loop didn't even think about it. A part of me wished that fight mechanics could have been more than just "hit it with the craft its weak with until it dies" but the simple mechanics makes going through the same sadnesses over and over again more bearable. Last note: I like how the game displayed certain themes. Going through constant loops Sif was bound to have a mental break eventually. I felt uncomfortable and worried when it happened but in a good way. If someone is sensitive to certain topics and want to play the game I do recommend looking at the potential triggers so that you can makes the best decision for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I could kiss this game. I could marry this game. In Stars and Time is so heartwrenchingly good that I actually finished it two days after it came out last November, but I've been trying to figure out what I should even say in my review ever since. I love it! I think about it every single day! I have nothing but good things to say about this game, and I really want people to play it. This review does not technically contain spoilers, but I do talk a lot about the intro and the way the game handles its emotional highs, so if you want to go in completely blind, look away.The premise is so clever and so brilliantly executed. I love that it drops you into the very end of a fantasy RPG and encourages you to fill in the blanks. You are on a quest to save the country alongside the Chosen One. You are, essentially, the party’s rogue. You are not the main character. You are quiet and reserved, and you don’t join in on group hugs or talk about your feelings or your mysterious past, and all this is why you are simultaneously the best and worst possible candidate for a time loop. Siffrin was created in a lab to be bad at mindfulness. Siffrin absolutely refuses to let their party know that anything is wrong. You think to yourself, “Wow. It’s almost like this guy would actually rather die than ask for help.” AND THEN HE DOES! MULTIPLE TIMES!!! Oh, Siffrin. My dear friend Siffrin. You are like a little dog that I carry around in my purse. Very small. Very cute. Very good at going straight for the jugular. More than anything, I want to see you thrive. But the schadenfreude is truly exquisite. Anyway, you should buy this game if you want to watch a theatre kid descend into madness.A bit about the worldbuilding: The setting is fun and fresh and charming. Dormont has all the trappings of a cozy little starting (ending) village, and the game even riffs on things like the expectation that you’ll be allowed to waltz in and out of the villagers’ houses whenever you please. It starts off strong, and it only gets stronger as you go! And the magic system is rock paper scissors. This means that combat is super easy to get the hang of with minimal explanation. It also means that everyone gets to do cool poses when they kill a monster, which is awesome. Like, are you kidding me? Siffrin gets to wear a wizard hat AND do a peace sign? On a daily basis? I would be completely insufferable.Next, I have to mention the characters, because I adore them. ISAT’s character dynamics are so, so well-balanced. Their dialogue is so much fun no matter how many times you loop back, and their absolutely stellar chemistry makes every conversation a treat. The character writing is perhaps the biggest highlight of the game. It is genuinely phenomenal the whole way down, and it often hits much closer to home than you might expect from the silly writing style. No notes.ISAT also takes full advantage of its core concept, exploring the emotional repercussions of a time loop in a way that feels both fulfilling and deliciously evil. Remember what I said about the schadenfreude? Have you ever seen a character get thrown into a blender and left to puree so long that they start to completely lose their grip on reality? Would You Like To? If you enjoy time loops as a vehicle for tragedy, you will love ISAT. If you often find yourself wishing that other time loop stories would Go There, I can assure you that ISAT does. Things can be so much worse for Siffrin than you ever anticipated. You CAN and WILL make them worse. Life could be dream.Closing thoughts AKA unsolicited advice that you can skip over if you’d like:There are things in this game that are very easy to miss. If you’re big on lore (like me), I would recommend inspecting and experimenting as much as possible, and also keeping a few different save files for different points in the game. Ultimately, it is up to you whether or not you want to stop and smell the flowers, but you will always be rewarded for doing so. And finally–sometimes, yes, this game is tedious on purpose. This is not necessarily a bad thing. It has to be at least a little bit tedious, because it’s a story about being stuck in a time loop and reliving the same two days over and over again. You will have to backtrack, search an area, find nothing, loop back, realize Siffrin missed something, and go all the way back to search it again. For me, it wasn’t a problem, but for you, it might be. Personally, I barely noticed because I was so excited to see what happened next, but, y’know. Your mileage may vary. I’ve seen a lot of people complaining about this, so I felt like it was worth touching on. But I would also like to mention that you really can tell the developer paid a lot of attention to quality of life. ISAT isn’t really a roguelike, and you can skip around if you need to. It’s a very thoughtful game. It wants you to be frustrated sometimes, but its obstacles never feel spiteful. At the end of the day, it wants you to succeed. And I want it to succeed right back! I love it a lot. It was such a fun ride. If you’re even a little bit interested, you should definitely give it a try. I think you’ll be pleasantly surprised! I certainly was. If you made it this far, thanks for reading. Hope this was helpful, or at least entertaining. Have a good day.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of the nebulous "Indie RPG" subgenre, check it out!Comparisons to heavyweights like Omori and Undertale are inevitable, so i think it's more fruitful to talk about what's different from those.Siffrin, your main character, is experiencing a time loop that nobody else is aware of. It's like if you played Majora's Mask and Link had a party of friends with him. Those friends would be completely unaware. Wouldn't they find it... Kind of weird you know where all the keys are, all the boss weaknesses, and solve all the traps? Wouldn't he have some weight on his psyche from watching his friends die over and over and they don't even know? Would he find a way to communicate to them, or simply shoulder it all?If that kind of drama interests you, this game is great.-If you interacts with everything in an RPG to read the flavor text, this is for you.  One town and One dungeon never told me more about a game's world and setting so quickly.-Indie RPG's live and die on their music, and this doesn't slouch. Lots of small touches like music seamlessly changing from indoors to outdoors. Combat music is imposing and matches the suprising difficulty.-Cute characters with lots of energy and very animated poses. This is an already experienced RPG party that has reached their final dungeon, and you're simply joining in at the end, learning about their already established backstories.-Combat is on the face similar to OMORI, but is more difficult (Yes, actual difficulty! Death is a game mechanic!) and fast paced. There are ATB bars, cooldowns, necessary buffs, and swapping turns to open up minmaxing opportunities. Even the Jackpot, similar to Omori's "Release Energy", is more subdued and requires setup.-Never too difficult. you can always run to a savepoint to heal, or purposefully loop to grab extra healing items. You're never without options, and this is encouraged.If you're worried timelooping in an RPG would lead to repeating plot over and over and over, you can choose which savepoint you load from, and skipping dialog you've read before is an actual ability your character gains. It's explained awkwardly, but is a very funny way to solve it.tl;dr siffrin is cute

_childDocuments_.review: In Stars and Time was a game I had to obsessively finish - I could not, for the life of me, put it down. I was charmed by the initial demo, which spotlighted the game's combat system and charming art style. I wasn't even really intending to buy it at full price until I saw how fantastic and beautiful the fanart was, and I figured "There has to be something special about this game."And special it was.The experience of playing through this game has you mirroring a lot of the emotions held within it: the feelings of isolation, depression, and madness. Beyond that, using time loops as a mechanism to tell the story is ingenious, especially when you start to play more for efficiency than for experience. I chalk a lot of this up to the writer being incredibly experienced, but also due to the characters of ISAT being around for a long time. Their dialogue feels real, and I find myself feeling seen playing this game in a way that no one else has seen me. Not even my therapists, friends, or family understand me truly as well as I have felt this game has in multiple ways.This game is going to become a comforting new favorite of mine. I cannot begin to express the joy and relief I felt at reaching its ending. It felt almost like a personal journey just for me, like it reached out and touched me in just the right way. I can only hope other people who need this game find the same relief I did watching Siffrin and their friends. Please play it. Know that everything is going to be okay.

_childDocuments_.review: "In Stars and Time" is a very well written time loop story with turn based combat. The way the game uses the time loop mechanics to force the player to experience the same emotions the main character is experiencing is very clever. When the main character felt dread about repeating the same day over again, I felt dread, when the main character felt excited about a breakthrough, I felt excited as well. I will say though, the time loop nature of the story leads to some not fun parts, where you have to repeat roughly the same things over and over before the story really progresses (which I think is on purpose). This is slightly mitigated by how lovable and entertaining the characters and their interactions with each other are though, and it never truly felt like a chore to read the same scenes multiple times, especially when they often change based on what happens in the loop. But if you really want, there's a convenient skip button to fast forward through conversations you've already read. This is also one of the rare games that have made me cry real tears. Overall, I highly recommend to anyone who can be patient with the parts of the game that cause friction (like the battle system) and are prepared for an emotional narrative driven experience. (read the content warnings and take them seriously)

_childDocuments_.review: A time-loop story that begins at the end. Or so it seems. As Siffrin, you're tasked to enter the House of Change to defeat the King, in an apparently fairly standard JRPG affair, with quirky characters and a literal rock-paper-scissors based battle systems. Things go according to plan. Honed player reflexes kick in. And then, you die.From the top.The story is a thrilling mystery. It stars a small town, a decent size dungeon, and a fairly large cast of well defined characters. As you loop several times on your way to defeat the King, you uncover bits of intriguing backstory. The battle system gets more intricate as you meet stronger foes, learn their tells and your team gains more abilities. The character dialog is endearing, if a bit too energetic. You get into a confortable groove. And then, you die.From the top, again.The more you play, the more depth you uncover. The seemingly cheerful story lingers on the more psychologically scarring elements of the time prison. Siffrin progressively reveals hidden layers and trauma, as his frustration grows mirroring your own. The House holds few secrets now. Or does it? Check it again, from top to bottom, and back again. Every interaction could yield precious new information. Maybe you've seen this bit of dialog before. Maybe you haven't? Will you skip it, on the off chance it's changed? You both pay more attention and progressively lose focus. And so, you die.From the top, again.After enough loops, the systems grow frustrating. The looping structure is utterly merciless, forcing you to go over every excruciating moments you've already exhausted all possible outcomes of. New options become sparse. The battle system, too simplistic. Thankfully, Siffrin retains the experience they earn through each loop, making them progressively unstoppable. You can skip most of what you've been through before. Why bother to check every spot *again*? What interaction are you missing to progress this *specific* narrative thread? It's grating, infuriating. And then you uncover a critical piece of information, and everything becomes new again. Time to review all you've found so far. You know what you have to do.From the top, again.Ultimately, the game excels at its character interactions, with heartfelt and sincere moments of bonding. More than its psychological horror coating, more than its overarching lore puzzle, the game explores themes of found family, agency, consent and forgiveness, with moving (if a little didactic) ace/aro, trans, masc gay romance representation, and more. The pacing gets frantic, with back-loaded twists, culminating in emotional catharsis that may feel like it's going a bit everywhere at once - though still managing to land on its feet. After finishing the game, you're left with the sense you've experienced something precious, an individual voice echoing through the craft, a vision that shines through and overpowers the systemic warts, the questionable pacing, the dreary repetition. And once you must say goodbye to these people, you're left with a void to fill. Only one thing left to do.From the top, again!

territory, lets go over our main cast;The main character you play as is Siffrin "The Traveler" from a distant unknown land, he is the rouge of the group but they lead the way for the group due to an
