_childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge presents an intriguing setting where mythological and historical elements blend seamlessly, crafting a unique alternative history. The music adds to the allure, evoking a dark ambiance that feels fitting for the time period. Every Salutor's design is so well done and it was always exciting to see what kind of mythological beings are getting introduced here. (Krampus was my favorite but not maybe in combat) The combat system offers a unique twist on turn-based mechanics but some might mistake it for being card-based, in reality these "cards" are simply your skills, which you can customize by applying different effects suiting your playstyle. (DoT goated) I had some technical issues with wild crashing (particularly in combat) but just adjusting the graphics settings to be bit lower stabilized the game so a tip for those facing similar problems.Overall, The Thaumaturge was a pleasant surprise with its distinctive world and characters. However, it is Eurojank through and through, which could affect your enjoyment of it. Yet, if you approach it with expectation of Eurojank and want a fresh, unique RPG experience, I can recommend it to you. 8/10.With such a wealth of promising ideas, it would be a shame if The Thaumaturge didn't receive enough attention for a sequel.Heres a playlist of every video I made for different missable achievements of the game

_childDocuments_.review: another detective esc game with no fail state so its just clicking on the environment until quest moves along. _childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge is a game that I have disperate feelings about. The writing of this game is wonderful, drips with atmosphere and really engrosses you to Wiktor, the protagonist, and to the many other characters you meet throughout the journey. However, this writing is hampered by a few majors flaws that plague the game.the voice acting and graphics: This game sadly does not transcend its obviously lower than some budget. On top of this it does not try to stay within its bounds, the models and animations are, while designed well, rather unappealing to stare at for a long time. Most of the assets, especially the skin of characters, have a sort of glossy look to them. The voice acting is very mixed, with some performances like Wiktor, Rasputin, Ariel and Abaurcy standing out as good while some, mainly children and some minor characters feel like extras in a decent tv drama. The gameplay is good, feeling like disco elysium with the investigation and dialogue focus. While the combat is a bit lacking (I only had difficulty with a total of one fight) it is clear that that is not the focus of the game. The perception and conclusion loop, while it does get a bit tired seeing it as the only option 90% of the time, is a consistently fun way of interacting with the world and seeing Wiktor confront people with their secrets the first time he ever speaks with them is fun.The story flows well and the evolving mystery and twists kept me engrossed. the urban secrets are a fun way of using the games mechanics to create collectables. The side quests are fun and having more interaction with the side characters is a good thing. However there is a general lack of payoff for things the game tries to set up as important and some things which the game does not flag as things you should consider and despite the presence of two ending paths the linearity of the game does not inspire me to fully replay it immediatelyUltimately though the thaumaturge is a very enjoyable ~20 hour experience I would reccommend to anyone with a love of 'talking sims', invetigation, history or stories about magic.   - Good character writing- Good world building- Good premise- Fun, if acquired, gameplay loop- Interesting setting and world exploration- good variety of side quests  - Obvious lower budget through art and voice acting- Requires a particular taste in game to like- Deceptively linear at points- Most quests pan out the same or similar to each other

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game and thought it looked really interesting. After giving it an honest try I was very surprised at how it is. 8.5/10The game was good. Story is a little slow at the start and difficult to get a grasp of, but after hitting the 2nd act it really hooked me in. The combat is what let me stay until then.  While I'm not a huge fan of turn based fighting games but this one really hooked me. The salutors being part of the combat is a really fun way to give this game its own life and they've done it well.additional note, if you are a Polish speaker please use the Polish language for the audio, you can keep English subtitles but I think its quite a bit better in Polish than it is in English.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very interested in this game after playing the demo, but the full release fell very flat for me. _childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. Unique setting combined with the persona-like idea of fighting with peoples "flaws" in a turned based game is an intriguing idea.The execution, however, is bad. It’s a game in which we mostly talk, and while the writing is decent, the facial animations are beyond terrible, perhaps the worst I experienced in a few years.Another unique idea that falls flat on its tits is the turn-based combat system. You have no items to use, and (for the most part) no companions, leaving you with two choices per turn (you and your salutor’s). This system is basic but and boring when you fight against 1 or 2 people, but designers sometimes like to put Stanisław into a fight against 3 o 4 opponents, where the combat turns into a frustrating, half-baked mess of ill-conceived ideas (I was close to uninstalling the game with a few boss fights). And that’s even without mentioning the cognitive dissonance when one enemy shoots you with revolver for 6 dmg, while another hits you with fist for 14 dmg… wtf? It seems like the developer never could decide weather to leave all fight in the real of mind or physical. The end result is just weirdly unpleasant.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Its like a janky Persona 5, but instead of 2016 Tokyo it's 1905 Warsaw and instead of a harem of anime waifus you get Grigorij Jefimowicz Rasputin.tl;dr below:It's janky, a bit buggy, combat is pretty easy even on hard difficulty, progression system is 'existent' and investigations don't require much of thinking on player side.However, there is a certain charm to The Thamuaturge. Setting is fascinating - mostly historic, with a touch of fantasy. Graphic design is fantastic. Supernatural creatures look cool. Characters feel distinct. Environments feel very autenthic and have tons little, interesting details. If you look for historic photos of pre-WW1 Warsaw, ie. dworzec wiedeński, you'll see that much care was put into this aspect of the game. Music fits the setting and time period, same with stories presented in the context of the world. While I was not holding my breath when following the story beats, characters and events are interesting enough to not mindlessly blitz through quests.Combat and progression is pretty good "on paper", but those systems are not pushed to their limits. There are four "skills" to deveop that affect both combat and exploration/dialogues, but i never felt i needed to pick one. You get so much experience, that you can basically 'specialize' all of them, passing all skillchecks on clues for revealing information. In combat you have a set of 'human' active skills which you combine with passives giving various significant boons and each   Salutor has it's own active skills focused around some additional mechanics (ie. utilizing statuses). There are several 'winning strategies', but you can figure them out quickly and enemies don't do enough to stop you from executing them.If you play games to experience interesting worlds, alternative history or time periods not usually represented in media - The Thaumaturge is definitely worth checking out. Price is fair IMO. Otherwise, maybe wait for discount.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is surprisingly great though not without flaws ironically enough. When I first saw those games title screen I originally thought it was another World of Darkness title given how in the past few years we've been getting some decent World of Darkness games. _childDocuments_.review: It's 1905 and you're Wiktor Szulski, a prodigal son of Warsaw. Your father's untimely death has forced you to cease your wanderings about Europe and come home. You've been away for so long, you feel a little like a stranger to your own city. But first, you've got to clear your head and get out of the actual and proverbial woods. The only way to do that seems to be through this Rasputin (yes, that Rasputin), who helps you get back on your feet -- seemingly out of the goodness of his own heart.Just like dear old dad, you're a thaumaturge, a kind of wizard who can summon creatures bonded to you; one of them happens to be a childhood buddy of sorts. Another freaky thing thaumaturges can do is *sense* histories and feelings attached to objects by touch. This ability, as you can imagine, is extremely useful for nosing around in general and plays a pivotal role in your discovery of the whys and hows of your father's demise. Of course, there's lots more to discover as Warsaw is as rich as the Tsar himself when it comes to secrets. What are the forces allied with or against the Russian occupation and its associated ugliness like the secret police or Ohkrana? Why does this lonely painter dude exclusively paint fresh corpses that wash up on the banks of Powisle? What's the deal with your human childhood bestie, Abaurycy and how dare people call you a fancy boy when he exists? Will your sister prove to be a better candidate for taking over the family business, despite not being a magician? And just what does Rasputin believe in, anyway?At its best, The Thaumaturge is riveting and oddly soothing at the same time, kinda like a cosy murder mystery. The setting is beautiful and the atmosphere top notch. 11 Bit Studios manages to breathe life into 1905 Warsaw and imbue it with a level of detail where you almost feel like you're there. While Wiktor is no Miss Marple, the wonderful cast of characters (including the city!) that surrounds him is nothing short of magical. Watching him respond to people welcoming him back with a diverse range of reactions, nursing his pride by taking down people who have wronged him, agreeing to a haircut because some barber said he looks like a troglodyte... it's all great fun.I was really struggling in the beginning of the game, especially when I've just gotten to the city because I did not know that your Salutor tab spans more than one page. I was so frustrated that I had so many skill points but nowhere to put them. As it turns out, all I needed to do was scroll with my mouse wheel. While I found this mechanic a little on the unintuitive side, the game's internal wiki is otherwise actually pretty solid. I also ran into problems with video memory at times, which necessitated relaunching the game. This happened less after I turned my graphic settings down a notch. Other than that, the game ran mostly smoothly -- the janky moments where the graphics stutter tend to happen either during the loading screens or upon fast traveling to another district.Definitely give The Thaumaturge a shot. If you like losing yourself in RPGs with a good degree of mystery, richly established worlds and fascinating characters, this is your game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I like the game but there are two things I don't.:First off, I am not a fan of turn based combat. I played through the game on the hardest difficulty and found the combat boring and monotonous. Probably even worse on the easier difficulties. Not to mention, I got all the way to the end boss having one stat a point too low. This made the fight exponentially more difficult because I lacked the stat level to remove certain buffs. The game also reloaded right into the boss fight every time so I had to keep changing my attack loadout each and every time I died. All the previous autosaves before that were cutscenes leading up to the last boss so there was no way out of it. Quite annoying. Secondly, the dialogue can be annoying. There are times were you are often unable to complete a conversation and or progress in the story because you haven't wandered around the different areas of the map to find all the clues. Basically you will be stuck until you find everything they want you to find.Besides those things, the game has an interesting story and good graphics. There is a lot of decisions you can make that will have interesting impacts on the story. It also runs pretty well with the latest patch. The initial release had some issues when loading in areas during travel. The combat is probably the worst part of the game but there is a lot more to enjoy besides that. If you are into turn based combat then I would recommend this game at the full price. If you aren't really a fan of turned based combat, I would probably wait for a sale for $20. Also, the game does not have modern ideologies in it. It is true to the time period so it is nice and easy to get immersed in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could give this a good recommendation. I really want to. For the near 18 hours I played, I really enjoyed myself. The monster designs are fantastic, the story was compelling (though, yes, dialogue was a bit janky most of the time). A lot of people were talking about having issues running this, but I remarkably didn't run into a single crash for those near 18 hours. (I have this running off of a SSD if that makes any difference?). , nearing the end of hour 17, an error box popped up and the game crashed. Every time I attempted to re-open the game, the error box would pop up and the game would close itself before I even got to the main menu. The box in question? LowLevelFatalError[File:D:\TCWork\MainBuild\Engine\Source\Runtime\Core\Private\Serialization\Archive.cpp] [Line 751]BulkDatta compressed header read error. This package may be corrupt!I managed to find several guides (including one the devs had on their website) on how to fix the issue and have gone through each and every step, restarting my computer each time (as requested). Unfortunately, nothing has changed. I sent an email out to their tech support, detailing each and every thing I had done as well as supplying screenshots as proof (because I get it, IT - y'all can't trust most people to turn off and on their dang computers, let alone do all this convoluted file editing). They got back quickly - and copy pasted what was on their website for this error, as well as requesting screenshots I already sent.To say I'm frustrated would be an understatement.Considering this is an issue many people have come up against, I'm absolutely crushed that there is no real solution. I was so excited for this game and enjoyed my near 18 hours thoroughly, and am heart broken I can't see the rest of the story... And annoyed that the dev's tech support can't take the time to actually read the emails sent to them asking for help.Planning on returning this game if Steam allows it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is... it's pretty weird, let me sayIt's story and characters are positively amazing. Mesmerizing even. They are one of the better ones I have ever seen. Story is great and enriching, all kinds of historical tidbits entertaining. Little notes informing and really fun to read.And yet I can't recommend it.Because even with all of this amazing work put into story and characters, this game is boring. It just is. The whole gameplay loop is 80% running around clicking right mouse button, 10% repetitive combat to which no changes are made, first fight is almost exactly the same as end game fights. No gimmicks, no new stuff besides combo's and traits which change almost nothing. And last 10% is dialogue which is almost... curated. I don't know why, but I felt game pushing me towards this one certain response every time because it's response I "earned" by running around and clicking RMB.had this game been a light novel, I would push it into everyone's hands any chance I get. But in this format? Just no. It's too repetitve.and it's not like it couldn't be changed! Make You piece the clues Yourself instead of Victor doing it for You! Make You search for stuff instead of it being lightened up like christmas tree! Give us opportunity to carry sabre, hammer, rifle to change up our combat system! _childDocuments_.review: Traumaturge is heavily inspired by Witcher and Disco Elysium. In similar fashion to those games you have a Top down story based game with turns based combat and an open world you can investigate in early 19th century Poland with slavic mythological creatures. The story is pretty good and the narrative works with good pace. The game does an amazing job at showing off Poland as it was at that period, the combat is simple but you still have to plan your attacks. Everything about this game works well but scanning an entire city for notes so you can get some extra xp and finding clues by simply following a line sure does feel like a chore.

_childDocuments_.review: For a long time while I played to get my money's worth - I felt like the game wasn't worth recommending.And I still have my doubts;the tutorial area can complete a bit unexpectedly before you want it to;the combat is difficult to understand at first;the mid-game is a bit of a boring slog with a rather cumbersome time management system for the quests, most of which are only achievable in the afternoon - so you end up completing, waiting, completing, waiting, etc...;there is also a LOT of reading to do if you can be bothered (I tended to skip reading clues, and only reading conclusions).But decisions you make do have a visible effect on how the game unfolds.And it actually got really interesting in chapter 3 when you are quite close to the end of the game, and choosing how to conclude things.So, even though the game felt a little short, I think it might just be worth a recommendation if you get it on sale. (Maybe my play through would have been a lot longer if I read absolutely all the text it throws at you - and if that's your thing, then go for it.)

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot express enough how well this game is made. If you're a person who knows anything about Polish pre-independence  history (XIXth and early XXth century), you will be melting in absolute delight seeing just how much references to history did the makers of The Thaumaturge managed to pack into this game. Bonus points if you know a bit about Warsaw geography - you will enjoy the game even more! If you don't know Polish history, nor anything about Warsaw, I bet you will spend half of the time reading thorougly through every in-game note you find, looking in amazement at every in-game sketch there is (and probably spending your before-bedtime phone-scrolling time on sinking deeply into Wikipedia page with your eyes growing wider with wonder, seeing how many historical events, organizations and people are put into this game). Music - marvelous and climatic; visuals - fantastic; VFX - so enchanting! 10/10, especially if you're a history nerd.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has an interesting idea behind it. The idea of going around and catching monsters that inflate and feed off of people worst emotions and then using those same monsters to further your own goal is a lot of fun in my opinion. The gameplay is entertaining, the story is fun so far, and the characters are memorable for the most part.The game does have some issues from what ive experienced so far however. My main problem is with the dialogue. There have been times when ill be talking to an npc when they will say something that feels a little out of left field, or Wiktor will get asked a question and then no matter what option you pick he will just ignore whats asked of him. Its pretty easy to ignore for the most part and doesnt really ruin the experience at all, it just breaks the immersion a tiny bit. The combat system is simple and easy to grasp, and feels satisfying when you are able to plan and combo your and your Salutors moves together to wipe an enemy out. The fights for capturing your soon-to-be companions are also really cool and thematic, especially after the build up of having to figure out who they are attached to.All in all: Games fun, would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I have not loved a game this much since BG3 (and some of the play style reminds me a bit of BG3 - large maps, lots of quest options, lots of endings and variability, and turn-based strategic combat). This game feels so immersive in pre-WWI Poland. Every time I see something about the global political field mentioned, I stop to google it, and have been absolutely floored by how much of this game ties into authentic Polish history that I know woefully little about. Mixing wizards with alt-history stories based in real world events in a fun and educational setting? Count me IN. Also, although the accents for the voice actors are a bit funny in English and it doesn't take away much to listen in English other than being a bit humorous, try this game in Polish. It adds so much for me. All the VO actors are clearly Polish, they didn't change actors for English language (which is great), but consequently their English/American/time-period-specific accents vary widely from British to mock-1920s-American and aren't always super accurate. Absolutely no shade to the English VO work, it's well done and they clearly put a LOT of effort in, but I HIGHLY recommend playing this in the original Polish voiceover with English subtitles and text for full, beautiful, flawless immersion. It really adds another layer of depth in my experience. I'm absolutely in love with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game came out of nowhere and blew me away. My all-time favorite game is still The Witcher 3, in part because of the vibe it created through Slavic folklore and somber string music. While VERY different games, the vibe in The Thaumaturge took me back there. This game is entirely turn-based with a challenging combat system that took me some time to find my groove, which I appreciated. Choices influence the ending you get. The side quests were intriguing and rewarding. If you’re an English speaker, do yourself a favor and play in Polish with English subtitles. The English dub is… not great haha. All in all, highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge is a truly interesting combination of genres. Eastern Europe in general is a setting I'd like to see explored more often, particularly from the perspective of developers that have a personal history with the region.Overall, the best way I could describe the game is "Sherlock Holmes meets Persona". Essentially, the game is a relatively simple detective game that has you chasing down clues and learn about people in order to solve problems (or create them). After the prologue, it is surprisingly free-form, though does have one or two bottlenecks it needs you to clear before you can explore the rest of the map.When you're not exploring, you use salutors (demons, basically) that you've collected through various quests to combat a multitude of goons that woke up on the wrong side of bed that day. Health is split into actual life points and focus, think of posture bars from Sekiro, once their focus is down you can hit them with a finisher that will vary depending on your salutor. On top of that is a fairly thoughtless system of passive benefits that some enemies receive which are disabled by using salutors of a specific aspect, though a lot of the time simply dealing damage gets the job done.The few nitpicks I have with the game are too few to cast a blemish of the game. I thoroughly enjoyed my playtime and have earned a respect for the works of Fool's Theory, and am also excited to see how their work on The Witcher remake will turn out. I can heartily recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Lets be clear, this game is not an RPG. At least, not in the way most people probably thing of RPG games. It's also a game where the player never has a choice in anything you do.-There is no Gear-There are no stats (There kind of is, but not really)-Everything you do in the game is designed to hold you hand every step of the way. Go here and snap to look for stuff. Okay click all the stuff. Okay good job, your mission is done. Go over here and snap next. Repeat. You can't really fail.The setting is cool and the art direction is pretty good, but this is a visual novel sold as an RPG game. Combat clearly only exists for the sake of existing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art, a fascinating setting, and a compelling enough story. I finished it, and ultimately I don't regret it. But the exploration consists of following a red line, the investigation of reading flavour text until the game tells you the right answer, and the dialogue of choices that range from superficial to actively misleading. Add to that the extremely liberal use of a combat system so easy I played on the hardest difficulty and still never got the achievement for winning a fight on low health, and you have a game that fails in every aspect unique to the medium, while succeeding at things that can be delivered anywhere else.They should've written a book.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful. The setting is amazing. The creature design is just... TOP. The VA is absolutely amazing. And the story telling just... wow. The fighting system is very interesting, feels fresh but not foreign. New ideas but a familiar design. Same goes for the whole detective part of the game. The characters are so well written, everything pulls you in hard. There's a lot of text but it's soooo well written, too. The main character, Wiktor, sketches and you see so many scenes and things sketched by him and just... the RP, the dialogue options, the way you can shape him... the designs of the clothes, the street...and it's soooo calm and stressless while still being tense. Since fights are quasi-turned based, there's no stress or action (good for old people like me), you can take your time with everything, no dumb quick time events etc but it's far from boring.It draws you in. There is so much tension. ♥♥♥♥, I sweated on a part with Russian Roulette. Plus the decisions you have to make, there's so much depth and you might only realise that later when, in your dialogue options, something like [unavailable due to your previous decisions] shows up.there's one thing that amazes me about The Thamaturg. Every thing is enjoyable. Even damn collectables. Since they come as scenes - you don't collect "a thing", you collect a scene. You need to find it first (do bit of detective work) and once you found it, Wiktor will sketch it and you get the sketch of the scene as a collectable and it's just marvelous. You even get basically a quick animation with pencil sound of how the sketch comes to life.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Please for the love of God just add an option to skip combat/auto combat/ turn the combat animations even higher. It is utterly a dread to fight anything. All the animations are the same, the enemies are the same, it's literally a replay every damn turn.Actually a decent game if you didn't have to go through the slog of a combat. I will change my review if they add some mechanic around it.Later edit: probably one of the games I'm most torn up about lately. I think the story can be genuinely great, the visuals and the writing. It has some interesting elements and it's an interesting setting. However, I just find myself skipping through a lot of filler dialogue and trying to brute-force my way through combat to get it over with earlier. I think I'll just try to watch the endings on youtube.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing atmosphere so far in the game, very smartly written with an intriguing story and visually it looks great for an isometric game due to it’s strong art style. Combat system is quite simple so if you’re looking for a tactical challenge this won’t really scratch that itch, but it services the game well so far, fair warning I’m still quite early in the game so the battles might start becoming more complex but so far I one shotted all fights and flaws
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: I have made this game my home for 15 hours (and counting) here is my spoiler free review:-it is BEAUTIFUL! i have played on all graphics settings and despite some issues that i will bring up later in this review, this is Pre-WW1 eye candy.-as promised the story is gritty and involves topics that will shock the highest caliber pearl clutchers. (if you are sensitive to racial themes, abuse, and religions other than just Christianity please play with caution)-the Score in this game fits right in with the early 1900's theme that the game has, from the striking high chords of a violin, to the low tones of a cello, this score makes you nod off a tiny bit while wanting to use every sense to collect clues. (a hint for those in the know)The cons-THE STUTTER~~ Jesus mother Mary and god himself, i can not count on all ten fingers and all ten toes the ways i have tried to adjust the settings to stop the visual stuttering and pauses mainly in the bulk of the city, and in the middle of battles where it lies at its sludgy worst.-the Guidance system, there are a few flaws here but not so many that it is game breaking. Yes it is a thin red line that is hard to see at times but after clicking the button a few times i can usually find it, There are missions where this thing is utterly useless As the game is now, get it on sale and ignore the Deluxe edition if you aren't into extras unlike myself (got the deluxe content and drooled over the beautiful extras, thank you Devs and Artists). If you want the full experience even after reading the reviews, get it, play it, and try to see past all of the cons in this game, and see it for the masterpiece it could be.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge is an enjoyable adventure, with a compelling story, interesting combat and so-so investigation. There is *a lot* of reading. It does feel like your choices matter, but given how unclear the outcomes often are it does not always feel well handled. There are bugs, and for me one of them was a gamestopper, but the studio's tech support managed to resolve it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: After 30 hours, I finished the game with all side missions and collectables I could find on Story mode in my first playthrough.What are the postive things I can say about the game?- I like the round based battle system, I think the fights are very funny and amusing but also gets you into strategy thinking. A big plus point is that you can use all your Salutors in your battles, so there is no limit like in other games where you can equip only 3 out of 8.- The game has my humor and taste. Funny and great dialog options (I simply laughed a lot), great characters and an interesting story (It's something new), unexpecting and interesting events (also caused by the choices I made in the game) and so on. The Salutors are my favorites, I like these Horror Styles of them and finding them, was the best part of the game. I wanted to collect them all and I did collect them all (Even though it meant to play a bit evil muhahaha!)- To my surprise, I found out the game has 12 Endings. Which is good in my opinion. Means your choices are very important in many parts of the game to get a certain ending. And a reason to play more often and see the differences.- The game is very easy to play and wants you to enjoy it without doing big work.What negative can I say about the game?- Some or many little side missions are just walking missions without dialogs and scenes, they are just for gathering paintings and exp. Which was kinda boring, but I was glad that few had at least more interactions and one was even very important. Although I did wished for more for the rest ones. I guess it was a way to learn more about Poland (but I skipped the reading parts mostly so I can't say much ops)- The Battles can start to get a bit boring, because in the end every battle is the same without big changes. The Level system may grant you new moves but they are not that huge. But okay, I should not complain much about it since we are in the end just a normal person (with magician powers) and we fight against normal people and they can obviously don't do much than punching.If I would rate the game I would give it a 8 out of 10. I really enjoyed playing it in the end and I will definitely play it again.I will call this game also a little treasure in my gaming collection. Dziekuje!
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up on a whim and it was worth every penny.A wonderfully realised turn of the century Warsaw to explore and political and moral themes interwoven with a personal quest which is all excellently written and presented. The world is superbly realised and a joy to explore with multiple paths and endiings from your choices.Turn based combat based on swappable abilities isn't normally my thing but I enjoyed the tactical element of the combat and the variety of options available using different salutors and loadouts.It was the writing and presentation that kept me coming back though.It's a slow burner, stick a movie on the other screen and let the story unfold. Excellent game and I hope they make another.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: so far im loving the game i feel like your an investigator that has some cool abilites to get what you need done good or bad  keep in mind every decision you make has an effect,  alittle buggy unless its the graphic settings not sure but im loving the game so far i was so curious about this game before purchasimg it. just finished the game i love the story and how each answer you give changes outcomes 10 out of 10 story ending left me in complete shock.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game.  Great story.  Very interesting protagonist.  Excellent choices.The combat system is interesting.  Once you max out your trees, most fights are pretty easy, but then you get that one fight that kicks your butt & makes you reload.Also - shout out to frickin' Rasputin as a supporting character.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like this is a rough triple A game really. Is that anything? Spiders games feel the same too me. Like it is well loved by the devs, there is passion, creativity, and care for detail in the game design. Good vibes. I am really enjoying it. I love story rich games that allow for sporadic gaming when you feel like it, and I love games where you can get hooked on just looking at it and noticing small details, like a pretty teacup or good lighting in a room. I am not too far in yet, but so far am enjoying both the main and side quests. Even the silly little things like making visiting a place and getting a little sketch of it for some experience points. I did a very small early gameplay slice video, just showing very basic gameplay, graphics, menues etc. You can tell I guess in the video I am obsessed with zooming in places and just looking at things. Tables, lamps, dirt.. I'd buy it again already.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game, but it's not without its flaws.7/10A very interesting world and idea with salutors. I can imagine how cool an animated series or comicbook about this could be. Of the flaws, I will say that the game is too stretched out and the last fight with the boss is unbalanced. If the game was 15 hours shorter, it would only benefit it.If you don't want to lose your solutors in the last fight, then it's impossible to complete in the higher difficulty. Although these solutors are of no use later, there is not even a reward for saving them in battle.

_childDocuments_.review: caught my eye when I saw a trailer showing Wiktor's ability to read the emotions associated with the objects that he finds. Although in practice this detective work involved little more than running around slamming R2 on my controller, the concept was intriguing enough to warrant a purchase for me. I was also charmed by the graphical style of the game, the turn-of-the-century Polish setting, and the turn-based combat.When you hit R2 on your controller (if you're playing with a controller), you're not only shown a path to your selected objective (if applicable), but sparkly red specks may appear on your screen. If you move in the direction where the specks are most dense, they'll coalesce around objects that Wiktor can then investigate. One annoyance with this system for me was that certain objects are only visible when you are in the pertinent stage of a quest. Therefore, you can examine an entire room and find nothing, speak to a certain character to progress the quest, and then watch as the room becomes filled with objects to examine. The higher Wiktor's stats, the more objects overall that he is able to analyze and draw conclusions from. Some objects when found will display the message that Wiktor will need to raise one of his stats to effectively analyze it. The conclusions drawn can provide him with information needed to progress in a quest or the ability to manipulate a character in the game's world. Although the information that Wiktor gains is well-written, there are certainly a few times that the game begins to resemble more of a walking simulator, especially with respect to the many quests that are completed simply by interacting with a door and viewing a sketch.Wiktor upgrades his stats (as well as gaining attack cards and upgrade abilities) by leveling up. In a stroke of genius by developer Fool's Theory, every piece of intel that Wiktor finds (as well as any combat encounters he completes) gives him experience. Therefore, the game gives you a gameplay-centric reward for learning more about its world. You can become much more effective in combat simply by reading everything you can get your hands on. The strange thing about this system is that you can level up quite a few times just by wandering around, even if you aren't engaging in combat or with the game's main story. Although the writing was generally good, my favorite part of the game was easily the combat. Wiktor essentially begins with one "salutor," a ghostly creature that is drawn to a particular "flaw." As you progress through the game you can capture more - each is drawn to a particular flaw and has their own particular moveset in combat. Wiktor's first salutor looks sort of like a floating mummy with a cane. These salutors essentially function as combat partners for him, and you'll alternate between picking a combat action for Wiktor and picking one for one of your salutors. Unfortunately, no matter how many you've managed to capture, you can only pick one salutor action between those of Wiktor - you simply gain a greater variety of options. The core abilities that Wiktor gains access to are set, but players unlock a tremendous number of "upgrades" as they progress through the skill tree. Different upgrades can be assigned to different core abilities to enhance your preferred combat strategy.As you participate in more and more combat encounters, you'll gain a better understanding of attack timing, enemy special abilities & how to disable them using certain salutors, and the focus depletion system. Certain attacks reduce "focus" instead of HP, and if you can deplete an enemy's focus it will cancel their planned action for that turn and give you the opportunity to do a special highly-damaging attack either with Wiktor or one of your salutors.Upon gaining a new salutor, Wiktor will be unable to use it until he visits Rasputin for a hypnosis session. Although these hypnosis sessions have little relevance outside of the story and the way that relationships develop in the game, I found it amazing how Wiktor's face changed from before to after these sessions. Before Wiktor has "tamed" a salutor he appears vividly feverish, and this never ceased to startle me. After these hypnosis sessions, he is more composed and collected.One thing I would feel remiss not to touch on is the idea of a "flaw." While the English word "flaw" has only negative connotations, in  the word "flaw" could be best described as a strong personality trait. Although a strong personality trait can be negative, it can also be positive. There are moments in the game where Wiktor has a choice of whether to "remove" a flaw from another character, and it can be good to keep this gray area in mind. Although many characters can possess these "flaws," only some of these characters have drawn salutors to themselves. As only thaumaturges can perceive and manipulate salutors, when they are attached to other characters they simply intensify the flaw that is already present. This raises an important question, I think - In the game's world, are heinous actions, more often than not, the result of a salutor's influence? Unless we have a thaumaturge in the vicinity, should we hesitate to hold others responsible for their actions?Throughout the game, Wiktor also has the opportunity to "develop" or intensify his initial flaw. This can be done by selecting dialogue choices that lean into the trait in question. However, much of the time I refrained from giving prideful responses (my flaw was pride) because I didn't want to role-play Wiktor as a jackass. The only effect that I noticed from minimizing the number of prideful responses I gave was that I didn't have the option to choose certain prideful responses further into the game. It would've been neat if the attacks from the salutor of pride (Upyr) became more powerful as I developed this trait, but I'm unsure if this was actually the case.Although I certainly have a positive opinion of the game overall, I must say that I didn't appreciate being imprisoned in two separate cutscenes without the ability to fight my capturers and avoid this. Additionally, I have to applaud developer Fool's Theory for creating the most insufferable idiot that I've seen in a game in quite some time (Abaurycy). Although it had story consequences, I interacted with this loser as little as humanly possible in the course of my playthrough. Much like Imelda Staunton's Dolores Umbridge, you have to give credit where credit is due when a writer creates a supremely irritating individual.Lastly, during my playthrough I was given the option to change the spoken language to Polish while retaining English subtitles. This seemed more accurate for the historical period, so I took up developer Fool's Theory on the option. However, this was before I realized that "thank you" in Polish ("dziękuję") sounds eerily similar to a nonsense phrase uttered with regularity by Sacha Baron Cohen's Borat. Therefore, every time someone in the game said "thank you" I'd think of Borat and get somewhat pulled out of the experience.Anyway,  is a fun role-playing game. Although I don't think it will end up being my game of the year, I wouldn't be surprised if it landed in my top 10.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review:
The Thaumaturge is an isometric, story-rich RPG with a unique take on turn-based combat, character development features, and investigation mechanics, facing you with morally ambiguous choices set in a world teeming with mysterious powers and strange ethereal beings called Salutors.

The year is 1905. Warsaw lives under the yoke of imperial Russian tsardom. Its inhabitants constitute a diverse group of different ancestries, views, and beliefs with often conflicting interests: Russian soldiers, Jewish merchants, Polish townspeople, and more. Despite the circumstances, the city is a buzzing metropolis, where one can attend a breathtaking party with the high society, and later get robbed in one of the dark alleys of the Praga district. A city of great hopes and dreams on one hand and dark desires on the other.

In this world, a force that cannot be ignored are Thaumaturges individuals versed in taming spirit-like beings called Salutors, used for manipulation of the temperaments and affinities of other people and even ultimately in combat. The devil is in the detail - only Thaumaturges are fully aware of the Salutors' nature and only they can perceive them in their true essence. Their capability to influence others significantly and demonstrably increases their ability to change the surrounding world - however, Thaumaturgy is a power that should be used with caution.

name: Best Month Ever!
detailed_description: COMING SOON! CHECK OUT OUR OTHER GAMES! AND MORE GAMES! About the Game Take part in a roller coaster of emotions with Louise embarking on a road trip of a lifetime through the late 1960s USA, trying to show her son Mitch how to navigate the often cruel modern world. 👩‍👦 What Does It Take To Be A Mother? Telling good from bad was never easy, all the less when you're a single mum in her late 20s with a clever 8-year-old under your care. Each choice you make in the crucial few moments we all know may change our lives for good in a split of a second, influence what kind of person Mitch turns out to be and what values shall guide him once he becomes his own man. 🧑🏼‍🤝‍🧑🏾 Why Are You Who You Are? Find clues as to why Louise’s life is what it is today, take crucial decisions no other person would be strong enough to stomach, and show Mitch what he needs to see in order for him to become independent, suave, and brave enough to conquer the day. 🔥 Everything Has Consequences Your decisions REALLY matter! To keep track of Mitch’s growth as a person, each choice you make adds positive or negative points to three key statistics: Righteousness, Confidence, and Relations. These influence which type of ending Mitch will reach at the end of the game - there are 9 unique endings in total! 🗺️ Everybody Has Their Story The 1960s were tumultuous in more ways than one - the Summer of Love, the Vietnam War, the survivors and the losers of the great upheaval in history. Canned Heat was “Going Up the Country” while Bob Dylan asked “How does it feel” to have no home and live on the street. Travel across the country and meet a plethora of characters that may help or may dissuade Louise from her goals - including the most controversial groups many thought long gone. 🚗 KEY GAME FEATURES 🚗 A tangible system your dialogue and actions influence directly: Righteousness, Confidence, and Relations 9 Different Endings dependable on your choices in key moments of the game Beautiful, stylized artwork reminiscent of the 1960s era Quick-time events to check your reflexes and feel the adrenaline pumping BEST MONTH EVER! SOUNDTRACK INCLUDED! It'll Be The Best Month Ever! is a complete collection of 29 beautiful, expressive, folk, country and jazz-inspired melodies prepared by the composer Jędrzej Bączyk (Pan Jędras). The stunning, nearly 80-minute original soundtrack is an excellent addition to the narrative adventure game, creating the musical soundscape of the main characters' journey across the 1960s USA.

_childDocuments_.review: The premise was interesting and already gut wrenching to think of but I don't feel that the developers really wanted to make a game centered around what the game proposed it would be. When I heard that Best Month Ever would be a video game centered around a single mother trying to prepare her eight year old son for the cruel world, I imagined nuanced discussions and experiences in which that same mother would be unable to shield her child from what was happening and have to help him understand  it was happening. That the game would be full of experiences, maybe gut wrenching and cruel, and that child would have to grow up faster than they really should have. Instead, I was given a game full of cruel experiences (some of which  could have made cruel for the sake of... character development(?), with no real payoff or explanation for them. Mitch, the eight year old, was never given a single conversation about these cruel things had happened and he never seems to care either.If you're interested at all to see my complete shock and eventual disappointment, as well as the amount of hope I had going into this game, you can see my vod here:
_childDocuments_.name: Best Month Ever!

_childDocuments_.review: Best Month Ever is a narrative-driven choice game, set in 1960’s America and created by Polish developers. It is supposed to be a game revolving around a desperate mother’s choices for her young son, where every decision shapes what kind of adult he becomes… but instead it is a ginormous mismatch of tragic events with no real discussion, choices or character development. This ultimately results in an exaggerated story with no emotional connection.Best Month Ever is a wild ride. When it starts, it does NOT slow down. It is nothing like the store page makes it out to be. This is not a game about a single mother trying to make hard decisions for the betterment of her son. No. This is a game that incorporates every single tragic topic and event it can muster up. Including (light spoilers ahead)   Sounds like A LOT for a four-hour game? Yes, yes, it is. I have nothing against any of these topics being portrayed in games, infact, I think delving into these topics and exploring history is important. However, these topics were simply all just thrown into the game. It felt like each  topic was crafted by a different individual. Nothing flowed, nothing really made sense. It came across as far too exaggerated and fake. The opposite of the emotional narrative the store page made it out to be. The mother, Louise, has to make difficult decisions for her son Mitch. The first one involves trying to get her money that her boss owes her. Players can choose how this is done, but regardless of your choice, she sets her bosses car on FIRE and drives away. All whilst her 8-year-old child is present, and watching. I thought, OK that is a bit odd, I would have liked a choice in that, but I will keep going. Yet, it only gets worse. Louise does completely bizarre things that make no sense. She grabs loaded guns and points them at people, with her child present, when this was not a choice that I made. She also fails to ever speak to her son about anything that is going on. She never has any discussions about the racism Mitch receives, nor about any of her wild antics. The base of the story seems to mainly focus on Mitch’s missing father, and trying to reconnect with Louise’s past. This results in a landslide of difficulties, generally revolving around racial issues. Now, if the game had JUST focused on this, I think it would have been a decent title. But because it throws almost everything else in players’ faces, it is like a thrashing tornado, sending everything into an aimless chaos, and undoing any sort of emotional and impactful message that it was building.Best Month Ever is a point and click game with quite clunky controls. There are very limited hotspots, and it is always blatantly obvious where you need to go, or what you need to interact with in order to proceed. However, the interactables can be quite awkward. Many times, I was clicking on the little white square, but to no avail. The game just seemed to never register my input. Being a narrative driven game, there are also many dialogue choices, but as discussed in the Story section above… these are not integrated effectively and many core decisions can not be altered by players. There are a few QTE events which are very simple, or driving sections which are doubly awkward and difficult to control, but are only a minor element. If these QTE or driving sections are failed, you simply restart until you get it right. Defeating the purpose of a choice or narrative driven game, at least in my view. This leads me to one of my main gripes with the gameplay element of the game, linearity. It felt like I was simply playing along with a set story, not that I was altering it in any way.Every action or decision that Louise makes will impact Mitch’s three attributes. Righteousness, self confidence and relations. After each decision, a symbol will pop up displaying which attribute was increased, or decreased. Most of the time, these made such little sense. For example, the game is very pro-gun, attempting to correctly depict the state of the 60s in the US (in what I assume is a southern state, but I am not sure. I do not recall this being mentioned and although it showed a brief map, my Australian-based geography did not register). I have no issue with these topics,  but it seems to go completely overboard with this as well. Every single time the 8-year-old boy would for some reason, pick up a gun and aim it at multiple people, I would scold him (if  given the option) and instruct to put the weapon down. This resulted in him losing self-confidence and gain righteousness? I do not understand how trying to get a child to not comfortably pick up weapons and aim them at people will result in a loss of confidence, but OK. Louise’s character is ridiculous, blowing up cars and whatnot, but there are no ramifications for  her or the boy’s actions. Even when she murders people. It is not mentioned. This is one of the core reasons why this game has no emotional impact nor credibility, despite attempting to convey such serious topics.I realise the review is quite abrasive, but there is no redeeming element in the visuals either. The artstyle is rather blocky, but almost similar to TellTale’s comic style. Characters have no details on their faces, and the environments are rather lackluster too. It is not bad, but it is nothing to positively comment on, it is just rather dull.In contrast, the audio was pleasant. The backing soundtrack  was soothing along the many car rides and conversations with the characters. The characters are all voiced, and are generally to a high standard. 4 hours. Player choice (untested with a controller, but I imagine the minimal driving sections would be much smoother). Yes, to achieve all 9 endings.The most accurate way to describe the story of Best Month Ever is to describe it as a completely disorderly and wild journey. It encompasses far too many topics, more than its short playtime can handle, and as a result, it does not fully delve into any of them. The choices have little consequence, with the more significant choices being preset. Ultimately resulting in the game feeling extremely linear and limiting. Overall, I do not recommend this title, but for those narrative lovers who are still curious, I advise to wait for a hefty sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Best Month Ever!

_childDocuments_.review: This one was a very tight call because I don't believe this is a bad game and I sense there will be people who love this game and for the first hour I was really enjoying it. Unfortunately I hit a point where I realised my choices didn't really make a difference apart from the end of game cutscene. I even deliberately failed one of the quicktimes events to see if it would change anything and no, I just got put back in to try it again (this time without even having a timer). The story itself is interesting and there were times where I felt for the characters but too many over the top events occurred for me to still find it a believable story.
_childDocuments_.name: Best Month Ever!

_childDocuments_.review: A solid attempt from a Polish team that unfortunately misses the mark. TLDR: I bought this game on sale for under $8, and even then, I don't recommend it. You can see a lot of passion went into the story and the idea for the game is great, but the controls are really wonky, its attempts to confront racism are clumsy, and the dialogue is often bizarre. More detailed explanation below.1. Racism: There are scenes that attempt to address racism in America, while other scenes seem to reinforce harmful stereotypes about Black Americans. Racism in the game is cartoonish -- everything is overt and no subtler signs of racism are seen or addressed. There's no discussion of segregation, despite this being only 5 years after segregation, so even the child, Mitch, should remember that a few years ago he couldn't go into the same spaces as his mother. There are "crazy old Black women" on stoops, there are Black men that talk in the "massa drawl," and of course our White savior, Louise, is always the one to set things right, from saving a failing Black strip club to freeing a lynching victim from the KKK. But don't worry, there's racism against Native Americans too! There's a whole chapter where a Native American man (no tribal explanation, no explanation of culture) is looking for a wild horse and then heals your son with a peyote vision quest which is.... extremely offensive and not how that works. For a game that specifically picked this time period and specifically wants to talk about racism, it really drops the ball.2. Language - Since the game's script is all translated from Polish, many pieces of dialogue are written with strange word order/phrasing. Additionally, you can hear Polish accents very clearly in many of the voice over actors. Could the team have fixed both of these problems easily by setting this story in a Pennsylvania Dutch community, a Texas German community, an Amish community, many rural communities in the Midwest, or any of the micro Polish communities throughout the northeast? Yep! Unfortunately, they want to hit all the quintessential American locations, so we're going to California, New Mexico, and Louisiana.One of the things that really annoyed me was that they kept bleeping the n word. My opinion is that if you're going to write a story about racism set in 1969 America, and you're going to write White characters who frequently say the n word in your script, then you need to have the balls to say the word. Bleeping it feels like such a cop out. Don't pick the time period, the topic, and the word if you're too scared to say it.Additionally, the men in the game seem to only use the c word to insult women (I don't know if there's a single"♥♥♥♥♥" in the game). Again, I think this is because it was translated by someone who doesn't speak English as their first language and isn't American, since they don't realize the the c word is seen in America (at least during this time period) as the most offensive word you can use for a woman. No one seems to be offended at all when the c word is thrown around. 3. Clumsy Controls - The controls are clumsy and characters frequently get caught on scenery. Almost everything is point and click in a 3D world with depth, which works terribly when your clicks are misinterpreted. These point and click scenes are broken up by the occasional WASD driving simulator, which is truly awful every time you have to do it and should have been scrapped from the game.4. The Illusion of Choice - For a game about choices, there's no way to get off the track you're on. The priest has to die -- will you kill him or will someone else? You have to cross this bridge, even if you don't want to and the game has implied you shouldn't. You have to go with the man -- whether you say something evasive or the truth. There is a story, and there's 2-3 ways to respond to each event, but the story will be going the way it's supposed to go, no matter what you do. You are also frequently given nonsense tasks to do (hide, collect fireflies, draw constellations, find some rope, find a weapon, etc.), which I think is done to give you some sense of control, but failing to get those things or failing to do it in time just restarts the section. There are no consequences, the story doesn't change, it just restarts until you do what the game wants.

_childDocuments_.review: Best Month Ever is, for me, quite a mixed bag. To my knowledge, it's the first major video game release from Warsaw Film School, a cinematic arts college. The result, perhaps unsurprisingly, is most successful when it's being like a film, and least successful when it's being like a game.The central premise of Best Month Ever is that you are a single mother Louise travelling across the rural 1960s US with your son Mitch. A number of significant events are encountered, and how you decide to behave as a parent will shape who your son becomes. Interactions are frequently violent, and cover a number of serious themes including sexual abuse and racism.The writing, voice acting, and shots used throughout are really good. The characters are believable, and it makes sense that these formative experiences will affect Mitch in later life. There is a really nice touch where Louise will be reminded of scenes from her past via flashback, juxtaposing her formative experiences alongside her son's. The music and sound effects are subtle, but also very effective, helping the environments feel very real. In short, everything you might expect a film school to be good at, Best Month Ever smashes.Sadly, much of the aspects that make this a game aren't done quite so well. Gameplay is reminiscent of Fahrenheit and the later Telltale games. Dialogue choices have an impact on your son's personality traits, there are lots of "click on the item to progress" style tasks, and quick time events. These last two types of interaction have no actual impact on the game, at all. When clicking on items to progress, there's often many objects on screen, but only a single one is even interactable, making any player interaction seem a bit redundant. With quicktime events, it's not like the story plays out differently if you mess up - you just have to redo the event.The dialogue choices are really the main gameplay mechanic, and it's a good concept, but I don't think it's pulled off very successfully. Oftentimes it wasn't clear to me what the options even meant, as they can be reduced to single words, and sometimes I would pick an option and Louise's delivery didn't really match what I intended to get across. I played through the game trying to maximise Mitch's confidence and social skills, while minimising his respect for authority. I thought this would be an interesting path, but the result didn't really match what I'd expect from those traits (either good or bad) so that was disappointing.Overall, I don't think Best Month Ever is a bad game, and I can easily imagine lots of people loving this game. There is a lot of good stuff in here, but none of it is really on the game side. I still enjoyed it enough to play through once, but found the drawbacks too frustrating to recommend it to others.

_childDocuments_.review: OMG This was a totally amazing game! You know those reviews when people say they cannot understand anyone else's negative reviews? Well I'm using that card now for this game! It really isn't a walking sim or movie. It's definitely a game. The closest I can compare it to is Road 96, but instead of branching narratives, it seems a bit more linear, but definitely not claustrophobic or as if choices don't matter, because I believe they do. It's an unbelievably rich adventure that takes you across part of the country by car, truck, on foot and even... well I won't spoil it. But you meet dozens of rich interesting characters, each with their own personalities. Someone mentioned the dialog being an issue, but it couldn't possibly be any more natural. It seems less like a script, and more like real life. The main female character definitely always says the right things, even when they're wrong lol trust me you'll understand what I mean once you play it. There are a few action sequences and I really wish there were more. The hotspot is a bit wonky at the very beginning but you quickly get used to it. The game does a great job of immersing you in the moment of the story. For example, one chapter on a farm, you kind of felt something was a bit off with the owners. The characters mention at, but you kind of knew it before they said it. That's not easy for games to do, make you feel what the characters are feeling! Bravo!! I literally could not stop playing because I had to know what was going to happen next! And the game is never boring because it throws you into so many situations on this Road Trip "vacation" Adventure! Where else can you go Fishing, Dance at a burlesque club, Rob a gas station and do Peyote in the desert?!! That's pretty incredible right! Sure there are some serious moments, but the game never lets you dwell long enough to be too emotional about it because there's always something new and fresh around every corner, highway and plot twist n turn. By the end, it kind of really makes you think about life and family, and that's definitely a good thing. The graphics are beautiful, the sound and music is too, the voice acting is EXCELLENT and you can tell this game is a real labor of love from the team that created it. If you're into crazy adventures, like being surprised and want to be immersed in truly excellent story telling, then you're in for one hell of a wild ride!

_childDocuments_.review: The game was fun, but far from perfect. I'd say it's worth in the $5 to $10 range.It's a very puzzle-light point and click adventure game, comparable to TellTale's The Wolf Among us in terms of mechanics. Unfortunately, the "hot spots" that you're supposed to click on are unreasonably small, and only activate when you're near the object in question.Let's say you want to talk to the two men sitting at the table at the diner. In most other point and click adventure games, the hotspot would be any part of the body of those men, and possibly even the table itself -- an area consisting of maybe 250 pixels by 100 pixels (on a 1920x1080 screen). In this game, the hotspot is a small diamond overlayed on top of the two gentlemen, about 25 by 25 pixels. Later on, there are quick time events where you need to click on a moving hotspot quickly before "something bad" happens, and it's pretty frustrating when the hotspots are so small.It's also weird that the hotspots are not active until you're near the relevant object. Let's say you want to enter the diner. There's a white hotspot diamond drawn over the door of the dinner, but if you click on that hotspot, nothing will happen. Instead, you need to click on the floor next to the door to cause your character to walk over to the door. Once you're near the door, you can then click on the white diamond to actually open the door. This is in contrast to almost every other point and click adventure game I've played where if you try to perform an action on an object that's too far away, the character will automatically walk up to the object first, and then perform the action.The puzzles are basically non-existent. You'll occasionally encounter a locked door, and the solution will be to pick up the key from a desk before trying to open the door. That's basically the level of puzzles you can expect from this game.The premise is very interesting. You have a white mother who has some undisclosed illness that means she only has a short time left to live. She has to find a new home and guardian for her black eight year old child. I mention the races of the character because racial tensions and outright racism is a reoccurring theme in the game's narrative. I applaud the game for being willing to explore topics that other games tend to shy away from.That said, the writing falters here and there, and the voice acting is just plain bad. Still, narrative wise, the premise itself is interesting enough to get you to keep playing to find out what will happen next.This is a "choices matter" type game, but it does occasionally (albeit rarely) commit the number one sin in those type of games: presenting choices that the player does not understand. A great example of that is a scene where a man is sexually harassing you. You can either "hot revenge" or "cold revenge". There's no context as to what these choices mean. I chose "cold revenge" because it reminded me of the idiom "revenge is a dish best serve cold", and what happened was... well, I would not have described it as "cold" nor as "revenge", and I still have no idea what would have happened if I had picked "hot revenge" instead. Most of the choices are well telegraphed, though: You know exactly what the implications are of the options being presented to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Thanks to Klabater for providing me with a copy to review Best Month Ever!Best Month Ever! starts with a well-narrated prologue, where the player is introduced to the choices system. Our son Mitch has 3 stats, Righteousness, Confidence, and Relations. Your actions as Louise, his mother influence the ending of the game. There are 9 endings. I wish these choices we make changed some parts of the story, but unfortunately, they don't. It's similar to Telltale's game design in terms of how much your actions matter. The game has good voice acting and decent sound design. The scenario gets repetitive often though. You find some help, but then things get messed up by events that do not affect the mother-child relationship other than Mitch seeing what his mother has to do for him. Which is fun at times, when things get extremely quick. The game takes too long with useless scenes till the epilogue but rushes out the story absurdly swiftly in the final chapter. There is replayability, to see other endings or grab a few missing achievements. To conclude, Best Month Ever! is a decent adventure game that has an appropriate playtime that does not drag but has nothing special for me to recommend it.Follow My Curator Page:

_childDocuments_.review: I’m glad I played this game.  It’s still kind of sitting with me right now.  I think the game quality is very good.  I really wish the game was longer.  I wish there was more at the end to wrap things up completely and I wish there were longer breaks between each disaster.  The subject matter is serious and could be triggering for people.  Imagine every kind of bad thing that could happen to a woman and/or a black child in 1960s America, mostly in the South.  It all happens (and maybe more) in this game.  It was kind of like Life is Strange on steroids, but with only maybe a quarter of the length of LiS.  So bad things kept hitting with less time for good things in between.  I also wish that there were some actions in the game that I had a choice on and did not have to do.  But those actions were ones the developers wanted you to take to further the journey, so okay.  That said, I think the game was beautifully done and I am happy to have experienced it.

_childDocuments_.review: I first learned about this game, when I stumbled upon a pre-release trailer, and a playthrough of the first location. The premise of the story in itself is quite intriguing: A terminally-ill, single mom is looking for a future home for her 8-year old, mixed-race son, in racially-prejudiced 1960s America. Even though it's not a type of game I usually play, that short story introduction was enough to pique my interest. I've been waiting for the release ever since.And boy, did it deliver! _childDocuments_.review: Best Month Ever is a graphic adventure that follows the story of Louise, a young single mother who’s taking care of her eight-years-old son, Mitch. Afflicted by an incurable illness, Louise decides to take her son on a road trip across post-Vietnam America to find him a home for when she will no longer be around. Like in a Telltale game, Louise (and sometimes Mitch too) will be presented with a different set of choices that will determine what kind of man her son will grow up to be. The story is narrated by an unseen adult Mitch, who comments on his mother’s though decisions and the obstacles they had to overcome during their journey.You will need to check your son’s three attributes when making choices: Righteousness, which determines Mitch’s probability to follow (or not) the rules, Confidence (about himself when doing something) and Relations which affects how he behaves in front of others. Each choice will add positive or negative points to these stats that will lead you to one of 9 different endings. While there is an effective illusion of choices, most of them won’t change much the story structure, except for the ones that will affect your son’s attributes. There are some occasional quick time events too, but sadly nothing happens if you fail them; no extra scene, game over or anything, which makes these QTEs quite useless.The narrative premise is certainly interesting, but there is a general lack of interactivity through the different environments that you will visit. Sometimes you will be able to take a closer look at some items, but nothing more, with a slow-paced gameplay that is entirely based on dialogues. Voice acting is good enough, but it’s often too slow and you have to wait for the characters to fully say their lines even if you’ve already read the text, which unfortunately can’t be skipped. Some may argue that Quantic Dream, Telltale and others don’t allow you to skip text in their games either.  But they have their own ways of keeping you engaged in the conversation, using cinematic cutscenes and techniques, while in much more static 2D scenarios the choice of skipping dialogues is preferable, and teams like Night School Studio, for example, already do that.Visually the game looks quite good, with colorful cel-shaded environments and characters. Performance-wise there are still some hiccups, like longer loading times between chapters and occasional frame drops even below the 20s, despite the scenes being rather small and simple.What I think is the main problem here is that the game focuses too much on dealing with sensitive topics such as racism, pedophilia and others, presenting generic stereotypes and situations only to enforce its morals on these topics and not because of some kind of well-written and intriguing storyline. It’s basically a cruel, but superficial, vision of a black and white world. Soon enough the story loses track and, instead of focusing on Mitch’s growth, it shifts to a dying mother’s personal drama and her last (crazy) things to do. And even then, after events that would be traumatic for any child, the mother doesn’t have a single conversation with her son about what really happened. Some of the characters you encounter often feel like they were forced to appear down your path, with multiple situations being out of your hands despite the choices you previously made. At the end, you are passively experiencing a game in the only way it can be interpreted, which seems more like sitting in a class and listening to the teacher’s lecture.At its core, Best Month Ever! has some very genuine ideas and the concept of a road trip with your son during ‘60s America is certainly intriguing. Yet the game continuously enforces vague stereotypes throughout the game only to prove its point regarding different social arguments. The choices you make that should define Mitch’s behavior are constantly belittled by some more story-driven moments that collide with what you have previously chosen and the way you wanted to educate your son.

_childDocuments_.review: While the idea is great, and there's serious potential present, there's a certain amount of jank that just keeps pulling me out of the immersion of the story. When it's just a cutscene being a little funky it's fine, I'll appreciate Frank moonwalking out of a certain flashback, but softlocking because I walked through a door not quite far enough despite the cursor not particularly liking the depth in this game just really kills my buzz.Sometimes the non-point and click is also a bit jank, and it's not always clearly communicated which scheme you're using now. And this game sadly also suffers from the fact the choices you make aren't entirely informed and you don't know where they're gonna take it-- in some cases I thought the game had chosen the opposite dialog option for me.Louise and Mitch' actors are really well cast and enjoyable to listen to, the same can't always be said for other smaller performances either through stilted writing or the performance itself. Again, the bones are great, execution not so much. I'd only recommend it on sale for a good deal.

It's about a white woman named Louise, set in the US during 1969, where she must spend as much time as possible with her Black, biracial son Mitch. Louise is dying. Mitch has no idea... her goal is to make her last days, the best month ever and find a care giver for her son.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess it's a matter of opinions but, I didn't really care for the story. It seemed like instead of a mother trying to find the best place for her child, it felt like she was trying to do as much things before she died. I feel bad for the kid; he keeps saying it's the best month ever, but I think it's the more traumatizing lol. The only thing I kinda liked story wise was that my choices did matter, not sure by how much but it does.In terms of actual gameplay it's meh. I didn't realize how sexual and vulgar the game was, which is my fault for not checking but just something to let anybody know if they're interested because I wouldn't have gotten it if I knew. Controls were hard in my opinion; just keep clicking, trying to get them to move. I had it at low graphics at first which sucks, thankfully I could go a little better in quality. Am I glad I finished the game? Yes, I wanted to see the end of the story. Would I play again? Maybe to see the other possible endings for Mitch but that's it. Would I recommend? Mostly no; it looks kind of cool on Tiktok but when you actually play it, you're just thinking how crazy can this game get, and it gets crazier. And not exactly in a good way.
