_childDocuments_.review: If you just watch trailer there may be some points that you may miss and these features make this game much more valuable.First, choices. There is a lot of choices and it matters. Short time, lot to do. In one play you probably missed lot of great encounters. I think replayability value is high.And thanks to rich combat system & small micromanagement mechanics in turf wars (nothing that fancy but still cool) you don’t feel that much repetitive while playing again.I really loved the combat mechanics. I played a lot of beat’em up games and this one is far more better than 99 percents of ‘em. There are lot of combos you can do. U can blindly attack everyone in the street or u can use specific combos to beat different variety of enemies more easily (Maybe there could be some boss fights, it would be awesome)In second part I want to talk about trademarks of this game that I haven’t felt in other games. The world and atmosphere.. The world is cruel, rich and strangely feel very ALIVE. You can interact except the special characters that have interaction pointers above their heads. You can assassinate (not everyone but if you don’t have tips about the man you can just see them and walk away) teach some respect to your rookies, or rack jack some girls when you were drunk or beat some men in streets.Customization in the game is not only a cosmetic choice, it effects the respect you have. I’m not sure when you have higher respect how the world reacts you but in lower respect you can definitely feel it.I don’t know I like just acting cool in this game. Some moves may seem to be useless but i like smoking cigarette, or just walking instead of running.I don't even need to mention about the art style its just awesome, "Kunio kun" type of aesthetics suits the game perfectly.One of the best game i've played in a while

_childDocuments_.review: Fading Afternoon is a game about a man who is steadily getting too old for his line of work. You won't be able to regenerate your health, and it's a race against the clock to get through the game before you get too weak to keep doing what you're doing.Another classic made by Yeo, with multiple endings and failstates. Takes everything done in the Friends of Ringo Ishikawa and does it better. Highly recommended.Adding onto this review now that I have gotten about 10 more hours and getting about four more endings - the story of this game can be heart-wrenching. This game's vibes are immaculate. Once you get the hang of it, it is very rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the type of game where you can set your character to do something mundane, like sitting on a balcony or at a cafe and watching people passing by, while listening to the music, and you don't even have to do anything else to have fun. But it's not just a game of serene contemplation, you have to take action, and the action in this game is very good. A mix of The friends of Ringo Ishikawa beat`em-up battle system and Arrest of a stone Buddha wave-based battles, to me this game is the best of both worlds.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve gotten around 5-6 endings and each playthrough was close to being completely different to the others. I feel like after spending 20 hours in the game I still haven’t even scratched the surface. Fading afternoon is an absolute must play if you enjoy branching story where choices effect everything, extremely immersive gameplay, deep rich mechanics that allow limitless creative freedom, and cozy beat ‘em up action. Friends of Ringo and stone Buddha are both fantastic games but Fading Afternoon really feels like an accumulation of both with a fresh new take mixed in. I can’t see myself ever getting tired of this game and something I will be coming back to very often. For $20 you’re really getting an incredible value considering how many times you can replay it and experience the absolutely gorgeous pixel art & animations by the insanely talented Ueda M, and the overwhelmingly varied amount of backgrounds made by Artem. I’m very grateful this game is getting frequent updates and even new content as time passes and I’m very excited & eager to see how this all turns out in the end. Thank you yeo and the team for such an incredible and unforgettable gaming experience

_childDocuments_.review: Seiji Maruyama is returning to the underworld after 10-year stretch in prison. But it's going to be a very short-lived reunion.Battling with a terminal illness that is robbing him of precious time, Seiji faces the reality of leaving this world all too soon - a world that seems to have already left him behind.When your sun begins to set, will you stoke the last embers of your life into a blaze of glory, or go quietly into that good night?Fading Afternoon is a beat 'em up focused on replayability, time management and small yet surprising details. You spend each day exploring different districts in the city, playing minigames and waging war against rival factions, escalating in an assassination of an area boss. Each day is another move made in writing the conclusion to this legendary Yakuza's tale with his two deadly fists.Combat has you mixing up punches and kicks into various combos, as well as motion-based specials to mix things up a little. Seiji's most powerful tool, however, is a counter that will instantly kill almost every enemy. It is an extremely busted ability that honestly makes many of his other moves obsolete, but if you wanted to throw in a bazooka knnee once in a while for the hell of it, you are free to do so.My only issue with the combat is, unlike basically every other beat 'em up to exist, your attacks will only hit one person at a time, leaving you wide open to getting smacked if you are on the offensive. Many of the game's arenas give you negligible vertical room, so spacing is often not an option to get them to spread out. The bottle boys can be very annoying, and sometimes a bottle will silently fly at you off-screen for a very cheap hit. They can be avoided by parrying at the right time if you are facing it, or by doing the Block + ⬅️⬅️ shuffle if it's coming from behind.Depending on who you run into and how far you push their social links, the tale can take drastic turns. Close friends in one route can be arch enemies in another.While there are several different routes to take with choices as big as murder and as small as where to sit at a restaurant, the end to every road is the end we all will face someday. The game is an effective, sobering reminder that none of us will know every lasting impact we've had on the world.In your absence, you can only hope for what your work will mean to those who were touched by you.(deprecated negative review below)---Only reason why I'm not recommending is because I ran into what seems to be a game-ending bug of a playthrough that trashed hours of progress due to the permadeath nature of the game.The game progresses over several days where you make the most of you're ever dwindling time on Earth. After a certain story beat at the park, every time I tried to go somewhere on the world map the day would immediately end, which fast forwarded me into an inescapable grave. No previous save states for me to roll back to,My first few runs of the game went fine. But having an entire playthrough blown on an unpredictable glitch in a permadeath game has chilled my desire to get back to the starting line.

_childDocuments_.review: Controls and combat are 10/10, but the only thing you really need to know about this game is that there is an entire button devoted to smoking a cigarette. 5% Shenmue,5% Streets of Rage games,10% Ron Gilbert games,15% Yakuza games,15% noir films50% - = A E S T H E T I C  V I B E S = -Great plot and dialogue. Organic, fresh gameplay. Tasty music that makes me think "Yakuza meets Pure Pwnage," which fits because much of the game is spent merely walking around...reppin'. This game is all about the experience, and self-reflection. Most videogames could have been a better movie or book, but Fading Afternoon is a game's game, the interactivity is intrinsic to the way the story unfolds, at all times.

_childDocuments_.review: The name of the game is "it's deeper than it seems" - the more I play it, the more it opens up, the more I love it. This game is so much more than a simple beat-em-up as one my think... You can also say it's a role-playing game, a video novel, a life sim, a rogue-like game or even souls-like game - in a sense it doesn't hold your hand as a player, you're expected to try many things, fail and die over the course of multiple playthroughs, only to eventually get better and become a master of your own fate.My first try was fairly confusing. I wondered from district to district, picking random fights with gangs here and there, struggling with controls and wondering why it only uses half of buttons. I was fairly regular in hospital and struggled to pay in time for my hotel, often spending nights on a bench or in my car. I failed my boss, lost my finger, was kicked out of gang, got drunk in a bar, beaten up by some street thugs and left to die alone in snow... Proper loser's story with a proper miserable conclusion. In my second playthrough I set a goal to reduce my hospital time and really pay attention to the battle system. I'm happy there is the achievement for performing all grappling techniques because it forced me to experiment and understand it properly. I also realised that all thugs have own styles and require different approaches. Once it clicked in me, fights turned from a button mashing experience to an elaborate dance full of wit, finesse and death. When you do things right the system feels very fluid, expressive and extremely satisfying, and when you get punched you can understand why and where you need to improve. I also figured out what to do at the construction site, was saving up for my own place to live, when a casino became available... I lost all money and sent a bullet through my head. In my third playthrough I decided to be a good gang member and really pull my weight. I relentlessly captured territories, tracking area bosses and completing my assignments. By the end I realised there is a method to the area control game and that I've been doing it wrong the whole time. Nonetheless I've managed to corner one of family heads but in a plot twist he got away, I've got betrayed and shot, only to regain consciousness in a pile of dirt at the countryside with 10 max hp... I was furious and wanted vengeance, luckily the game offered me that opportunity. I fought my way into his hideout which was awesome, it required not only a perfect execution, but also learning what to do with bottle-hurling enemies when you don't have the option to sidestep. The guy was waiting for me with a gun - it didn't help him... The ending was absolutely badass, very emotional, I totally loved it.I've done a few more playthroughs since, I'm excited every time as you always find something new. It's fascinating to see seemingly random dialogs and events merging into actual plot lines, even though I have no idea how to pursue half of them yet - the game doesn't tell you what to do exactly, you have to pay attention and figure out things on your own. There are so many endings apparently, so many things to do and characters to build relationship with, you just need time to do all that, but time is exactly what you have in deficit, since your hero is terminally ill and is dying. I usually hate games where you play against the clock, but here it is completely justified, it adds weight to every day you live and every decision you make. The game is totally worth its money. Oh, and it runs great on Steam Deck.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful. For people like me who can get frustrated after failing repeatedly, the controls could really benefit from an overhaul. Also a little bit more info on tutorials. I don't always have much time to learn from failure. I respect and value that approach but when I only have an hour to play and half of it is failing I can sometimes loose my cool. I keep trying because this and Friends of Ringo are works of art but the difficulty of control and available information is very frustrating. I have searched online for help but only full video walkthroughs are available. No quick reference guide or bullet list. Please help me enjoy these games more. I truly love them.After Final update I really have no issues. This is a beautiful story and an enjoyable simulator. Thank you for this truly remarkable memory I will carry with me always like a romantic knife to the heart :)

_childDocuments_.review: I waited to complete the game at 100% (I might have missed something) and 30 hours of gameplay to write this review  - Very enjoyable fighting gameplay with a lot of different moves (punch, kick, guard, combos, chop, takedowns, weapons, etc...) + cool Rumble mode for training and Leaderboard- Gorgeous Pixel art scenery - Reflective and soothing jazz ost that perfectly sets the mood of the story, with some energetic bits at the right time - Immersive Storyline, choices you make have an impact on the rest of your run and there is a lot of different endings. Some hidden dialogues and sidequests to find during your different playthroughs.- lot of side activities and mini games (bar, restaurant, poolroom, baseball practice, fishing, casino, shooting range, etc...)- DETAILS !!! (Take off your jacket, shave your beard, put on sunglasses, Take out your Umbrella in rainy weather ) those details make the difference to be fully immersed in the game. -some little bugs that may break a RUN since there is no manual saving system, it can be frustrating to forego a whole run because of this.-Little to no explanations (I guess it can a Pro as well because you are in full discovery mode but I can admit that it might be a turn off for some) My advice : you are going to mess up, just try, discover and learn from your mistakes. Take in the beauty of the game.- No sound parameters, I would have like to be able to adjust the game sounds.In short, Beat Takeshi's inspired Yakuza storylines , an immersive and beautfiful city (looks like 80's Osaka) and a cool fighting beatem'up gameplay. 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: What does it mean to live, when your life is already over?Fading Afternoon is a game about the shouda-woulda-coulda of life. An old yakuza finally out of jail, coming back to a shadow of a family and an envelope of cash that gives him about a month at a hotel, and a cough that won't go away. It's about Gozuki, a Legend, deciding whether to burn brightly or flicker away in contentment. It's a game about life, and the end of it, and what you leave behind.This game is well worth your time and money. An excellent score, a surprisingly deep and fluid combat system, and a branching narrative meant to be played and replayed to find the answer to why you're still around.

_childDocuments_.review: The thing to keep in mind if you stumbled across this game unaware of the types of games Yeo makes is this: This is an "Art" game. What does that mean? This is a game with a strong theme and concept, and achieving that concept and portraying that theme takes principle over all other parts of the game. What is that theme? Fading. You are a middle aged Yakuza, fresh out of a long prison sentence, and you have a terminal illness. Your character is going to die, that's how this game ends, and if it isn't from gangland warfare, its going to be from sickness. Time is fleeting, and you will not have enough time to do whatever you like, directions are clear, but they are no flashing quest markers, you will have to use your reading comprehension and your power of deduction. This may look like a fun pixel art beat em up, and there is fun, beautiful pixel art, and beat em up action, but this is not a "light" game you play while scrolling passed the dialogue.If that sounds like something you are interested in, Fading Afternoon is an amazing game that fully offers you roleplaying opportunities, not roll d20, thac0 score roleplaying,  but a chance to inhabit a character and play out the role of a middle age Japanese gangster.The structure of this game is most similar to the "Way of the Samurai" games, as it is a relatively short game that is meant to be played multiple times, with you exploring different paths and story lines each time. Maybe one run you are a focused yakuza, attempting to build a criminal empire to stand the test of time after you inevitable passing, taking no prisoners and showing no compassion. Maybe the next you are a gangster with a heart of gold, going easy on your subordinates and sparing your victims. Maybe you try to take power for yourself, maybe you are a loyal solider, maybe you are a fishermen, maybe your are drunk and a gambler. Maybe your are betrayed, maybe you are the one betraying. There are enough twists and paths that in 4 "complete" play throughs I've had completely different stories play out and I've not even focused on fighting the second of the two rival clans yet, let alone work on the various relationships you can build. That being said, this is a story about a gangster, and for the most part you will be fighting other thugs on the streets of Osaka(?).The core of the action is the fighting, it seems simple at first, punch, kicks, block and parry, and throws, and though it may take you a little while to learn the intricacies, once you get a hang of it you really feel like the MC lives up to the reputation of a fearsome yakuza to be respected. Or not, maybe this run you lost your mojo in jail and your repeated defeats will sap the good rep you once had. (notice the roleplaying opportunities here?)What surrounds the fighting is a resource management component. You need to manage you health, defend/capture turf, maintain your rep and keep a roof over your head. This is interesting and gives you a solid reason to acuminate money, and gives real gravity to the gangland promotions you either gain or lose.The visuals of the game are amazing, the music is atmospheric, and the animations are very satisfying. I don't need to write too many things about that, watch a trailers and you'll know if it speaks to you or not.The concept of all this, fading, is what wraps everything together into a coherent package. You will learn quickly that time passes faster than you are ready for, that you have to pick what you can do, have a goal, really get into the mindset of a crook leaving prison "this is my last chance, what do I really want to achieve?" At times it will feel suffocating, and its supposed to feel that way. Embrace the concept, and how it works with the multiple run structure.To complete the review I will leave you with a brief recounting of a run I had, if this sounds interesting to you, give the game a try: I was fresh out of prison, seeing the fallen status of my criminals family, I decided I must restore its honor and power before I fade away. I hit the streets like a daemon,  taking over huge swaths of the city, the yen flow, I have an apartment, luxury sedan, the respect of my youngers and a little brother of my own. I live lavishly in the hostess clubs and the discos. I am forced to make some hard decisions, and I must sacrifice some innocents, and even friends. In the end my peers are all gone, I traded them away for this Yakuza status. I die in bed with a hostess I take home from the club one night. Not by myself, but alone.

_childDocuments_.review: Fading Afternoon hits a lot of the right notes for me.The game is following the beloved ol' tropes of japanese gangster-cinema, particularly the stylings of Takeshi Kitano, and mixes it really well in the context of a neat adventure game. It's sold as a beat 'em up, which isn't false, but I think it's best enjoyed if you treat it as an adventure game. It's about discovery and experimenting, looking at forums to compare notes, and looking for what you think is the right send-off for this dying yakuza-guy. That's not to say the combat is bad, it's actually very fun. It's quick and well animated, the counter-move is busted and makes you understand why Seiji is a big deal after seeing him consecutively wristlock 5 goons. Also, the difficulty increasing as Seiji gets progressively ill is a clever way to raise the stakes. He's the best because he's very skilled, not brawny. By winter I always get that "I'm too old for this boss, I can't do this anymore"-feeling, but like in a good way. The game can be hard but certainly not unreasonable. It even lets you re-try combat on some specific story moments instead of outright killing you. You'll probably feel like you didn't have enough time after your first playthrough but... yeah? You try dying of lung cancer, smart guy, see how you wrap everything up. I'm just kidding, I hope you're healthy. But the main character, regardless of what we do, is pretty obviously a bad guy. We can live through him and maybe even feel for him, but it's not tragic to see him go each time, which I think works very well for this game.  I also appreciate that the game rushes you less than in The friends of Ringo Ishikawa, so if you have the mind to chill out on a bench and light a smoke, there's no pressure. It also fits thematically, as we're playing as a dying man who is definitely lingering more than a teenager whose days of highschool are speeding along. Issues? Eh, I've encountered some bugs but nothing gamebreaking. There are some odd typos and grammatical errors in some of the dialogue, and I've seen some jank when it comes to larger gang fights -like catching a guy 5 feet away in a wristlock. Overall I think it's pretty great.

_childDocuments_.review: Great atmosphere, visuals, soundtrack, etc.But the core gameplay is a bit of a 50/50. On one hand, it's cool to have a game that's meant to be replayed with multiple endings to explore. On the other, the game doesn't really respect your time and you end up spending a lot of it repeating some of the fundamental aspects. One great example is that there is an ending where you do end up very wealthy, but you can't bring this wealth to your next playthroughs like you normally can (by putting money in your bag and dropping it off).It's a very small detail but one would think the item would be designed specifically for this kind of situation, where you've achieved the grandest ending and are rewarded for it.Still, despite many frustrations and never really liking the combat controls, it would be tough for me to not recommend this game. It's worth checking out and is a unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. It is VERY replayable; has an engaging, multiple-ending story; satisfactory and cool-looking beat em up combat; and layers upon layers to its characters and world.Despite this, i cant recommend it just like that. First, you need to be patient with it. Your first 2 runs you probably wont be able to understand much, as you dont really know what to do or where to go. Just, let it flow, try to get the knack of the combat, go to the disco, or to have a chat with your boss, or dont, and go take over as much districts as you can. Sooner than you think you'll find yourself immersed in one of the many storylines.But, beware, this isnt a regular game. Youre a yakuza, just not in a romanticided way. You may have some reputation, but, fresh out of prison and into a decaying family, youre nothing more than a bottom feeder, living day to day in a hotel. Of course you can step up your game and get a house, a cool car and even a girlfriend, but, you also have cancer. You have limited time on this Earth and you gotta use your time well. This is reflected in the game by losing max health every week.As a final note, i'll add: you probably will get bad endings the first 2-3 tries. Dont get frustrated, there are many guides available by the community to ease your experience and help you understand the game better. Besides, what did you expect? The yakuza life isnt about cool fights and life lasting friendships. Everyone is looking for themselves, and theres no top of the mountain for you to get on.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a lovely style and soundtrack. I've spent a bit over 15 hours playing so far and I still haven't seen much of it as far as different routes to go on since there are many different paths the game can take you on. _childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: Fading Afternoon exists as a game that goes beyond the simple fun of the game play loop and basic combat mechanics. It intertwines each and every moment to make the game feel alive and immersive. Yeo is not afraid to take unorthodox and complex strategies to game design, and he forgoes things such as constant action prompts, clear story paths, and excessive reminders about objectives that are popular among many other game designers in order to further the artistry and heighten the experience rather than just the base gameplay. Though that is not to discredit the combat itself, as it is exceptional and unique in this genre. In no other 2D action game have I felt the connection of each attack as directly as I do here. The main character, Seiji Maruyama, is an older, dying yakuza, so while he is slow all of his attacks pack an immense punch to the bitter end. When in combat, Seiji never feels underpowered since he has all moves unlocked from the beginning, and therefore it is up to the player to effectively employ said skills. The sense of powerlessness in the game comes through the story, and how little time and power Seiji has to get things done. It is entirely up to you to decide what happens, but all the same, things will end, and it is a pleasure to see all the ways that can play out.[TL:DR - 10/10 have patience and accept the game's experience, and the rest will come easy]
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: Fading Afternoon is pretty good and has a lot of replay value, so its short length is not a negative thing. I like the concept of the game and the execution is pretty decent too, as there is beauty to be found even in the cruelest moments of the protagonist's life. The fighting can get a little repetitive when the enemy gangs keep retaking the same spots over and over again (and you have to free them up) - but that's not too much of an issue given the fact that the game makes the fights look cool with a Japanese-Yakuza themed action. And each run is fairly short anyway as the game has an unseen time limit with the protagonist getting sick.The depth in the game is surprising for something that is 2D - because these days, beat 'em ups are normally playing it very safe for the most part as experimentation can turn out to be negative. Fading Afternoon takes risks and shows that the developer is someone with passion and vision for game development - regardless of whether or not we always agree with his design choices. And that allows this game to have many features and alternate routes that make it an immersive experience.I know that the developer disagrees with any and all criticisms about the game - but I am positive that I am not insane about the control scheme being unnecessarily cluttered. There are tons of buttons on a keyboard and a gamepad, and more mechanically complex games exist in the world that manage to make controls better to use. The developer can easily make this game control better by separating some of the keys and reassigning them to better spots. Every action does not have to be controlled by one of two keys in a slightly different order. The soundtrack deserves to be on Spotify (although someone did create a playlist of what's already available there, god bless you) and I think many people would buy it if it was sold separately on the game's Store page. All in all, I think this is a game between 7.5-8/10 and can easily be a 9 or even 10 if the developer applies some constructive criticism into making the game feel less clunky. The control scheme is manageable, but far from ideal for a game in the 21st century. It's not an unfixable kind of jank if the developer wanted to improve upon it, so it sadly takes away a few points for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: I've been eagerly anticipating Fading Afternoon for years, but I don't think I realized just how much work yeo put into this game until my seventh playthrough.I ran through bouts of frustration initially, whether it was not knowing how to trigger an event, bugs, trying to beat the clock as my characters health deteriorated day by day. Sometimes I felt like I was just done with the game, but within half an hour I was back at it plugging away.Everything is so complex and obfuscated. It's unclear what your real objectives are and there are so many options. Choosing to take a certain gang's territory, who you interact with and how, how you spend your time as the main character waits for his impending death to an undisclosed illness. Who you chose to kill and what choices you make that will ultimately lead to your assassination.  This is probably the best open world game I've ever played. Everything feels so meaningful and full of life, even while it's so stoic and endlessly violent.The combat is perfect. Any fan of 2D beat-em-ups has a feast of options waiting for them. Endlessly reversing, stealing weapons, takedown grappling everything. Initially the bottle throwing enemies were a source of frustration, but dodging those was a snap by my fifth playthrough. Near the end the throwing guy was my real enemy, but the real fun of it is how all the different enemy types combine as they're randomly running out. Certain areas are either belt scrolling, a single plane or alternating between the two, requiring very different tactics. My favorite technique was grabbing guys and using them as body shields against gunmen. After 34 hours I know there's still more to be seen here. yeo put so much time and effort into this game, I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm absolutely enamored with the worlds that Yeo creates, and Fading Afternoon is no exception. The best way I can describe it is as a thematic bookend to their previous work, The Friends of Ringo Ishikawa. You play as Seiji Maruyama, a yakuza fresh out of jail. From the outset, the player prompts themselves to think of this as a mythic Kiryu Kazama character as they speak with their aniki, Azuma-san. But you learn very quickly that the story of what family controls what part of the city is not, in fact, what the game is about. Without getting into spoilers, Fading Afternoon is about how a person acts when the end is upon them. It's not something anyone talks about, but the way Yeo carefully used game mechanics to make you feel the immense weight on Seiji's shoulders - the way you walk through all these familiar areas of town without any run button, watching strangers living their lives, seeing couples at the disco embracing in a slow trance, the slow comprehension that the most human relationships Seiji has are all transactional...this is a truly beautiful work, and I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a "Choose Your Own Adventure" book without being forced to choose between only 1 or 2 options at each decision. I Love the concept. There are things that could make it better, but what game doesn't have that? It's about 2 to 2 and a half hours long, but there are many paths, and endings to explore. So, if you want to play it like a beat em up with different story lines to find and figure out, treat it as such... There are some guides, and Youtube videos if you have a hard time, but once you understand that you need to follow a logical path, you will look for the clues and make your own. If Visual Novels were more like this, I'd be more into them.

_childDocuments_.review: Spent a whole day (24h) playing this and still havent got all the endings.Edit: I've got to write more about how to get more of this game after some reviews.PLAY IT ON EASY MODE. It is there for a reason. First of all, you don't need to overcommit to fights as less men come to fight you. Fighting mechanics are not only fun but also repetetive. Spamming X and Z whole fight is not so fun. Thats why fighting against Harada is difficult for many players. Instead of spamming, try to fight intentionally. FAIL SOME MISSIONS INTENTIONALLY. You may encounter interesting paths.PAY ATTENTION TO SOME NPCS. for example Eri (won't describe her so you can find her yourself)USE YOUR ACTION POINTS WISELY. Days or Weeks as in the game, end quick after visiting 3 locations. If you stay in hotel you can walk down to restaurant without losing an action point, or if you stay in 10Million worth of home, you can refill your pistol. Triggered cutscenes spend action points. Don't waste your pistol as it takes only 7 bullets and needs a whole action point to take it back. You may use them on shateis. You may see some achievements like Kill Azuma or Ando. you can either check steam pages to discover the paths or try to explore the game. Depends on what you prefer.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to review the game, since there isn't much you can compare it to. The pixel art, the game vibe, the city and amount of things you can do are simply unparalleled. _childDocuments_.review: This is a "where the hell am I supposed to go" game, times a thousand.  Nothing is explained.  The combat is extremely frustrating, with waves of enemies taking forever to get through.  There isn't enough time in an in-game day to do more than a couple of things. _childDocuments_.review: Fading Afternoon is an epic battle of self discipline and will to continue to fight through life. This game reminds us to slow down and appreciate the simple pleasures in life. It's a digital escape from the hustle and bustle of the real world, a place where you can unwind and recharge. If you're looking for a game that will leave you feeling refreshed and rejuvenated, Fading Afternoon is the perfect choice. The fight scenes. Now, I'm no expert in the art of fisticuffs, but I've seen my fair share of video game brawls. According to the snippets of reviews and discussions, the combat in "Fading Afternoon" seems to be a mixed bag. Some players find it repetitive, while others appreciate the strategic nuances and cinematic flair.As for the gambling aspect, it appears that you can make some extra yen by hitting up the loan sharks or trying your luck at the casino. Just remember, kids, gambling is a risky business, and you might end up losing more than you bargained for. But hey, if you're feeling lucky, go for it!So, to sum it up, "Fading Afternoon" offers a variety of activities to keep you entertained, from beating up rival gangs to trying your hand at the tables. Just don't forget to brush up on your combat skills and manage your finances wisely, or you might find yourself sleeping in your car instead of a cozy hotel room.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

Don't smoke too much after the game tho cuz you might want to

_childDocuments_.review: I ended up doing three runs in one sitting, reaching the end of the time limit twice. The combat loop gets really repetitive, really quickly, and the characters don't really seem to have strong arcs like they did in The Friends of Ringo Ishikawa — things just sort of happen in response to the player's actions, where the world and characters feel kind of static and as though they lack agency compared to the world-shaping power of the player. In simpler terms, it feels like a combat/monopoly simulator with consequences, and less like a coherent story with characters — case in point, on one of my runs, I did not focus on attacking specific factions and basically no story ended up occuring, despite Seiji spending every day fighting and capturing districts.Overall, this has Yeo's usual stylistics, good pixel art, and expanded and improved combat system, etc... but it doesn't really leave an impact on me like their first work.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: As of March 2024, Fading Afternoon is in a 99% bug free state. The main reasoning against this game is no more. If you like streets of rage style of combat and more slice of life, atmospheric games like Stardew Valley, then you need to get both this game and The Friends of Ringo Ishikawa. This developer has magic in his hands, and it's a crying shame that these games are as overlooked as they are. With all that said, If you are not an adult or at least in the transitional period between teenager and adult, hold off on these games until you are older. I'm not telling you that you shouldn't play these games because they have violence or drug use, but these games get very melancholic and introspective, and give you a lot of time to sit back and think about the events that unfold and the feelings that those events make you feel, and I don't think a young teenager or kid is going to quite have the same amount of appreciation for those more subtle and laid back approaches to emotional storytelling. If you are the target demographic however, PLAY THESE GAMES! SUPPORT THIS DEVELOPER!

_childDocuments_.review: It's rough around the edges and hostile to first-time players, but this is truly a work of art.I think most people will find this game to be quite captivating, providing they start playing by knowing a few key things. Learning the systems and controls is a big hurdle, but is well worth your time.In Fading Afternoon, you play as a character whose maximum health deteriorates gradually over the course of a playthrough. Several of the given locations that you have access to are random every time, and the decisions you make, the order in which you do things, and failing to complete tasks will all impact your playthrough and how your game ends. As such, this game is worth playing multiple times, and it should be noted that the "easy" mode is very much recommended for beginners.The controls are very obtuse, and brake a lot of tried-and-true conventions, but they can be mastered, and ultimately give you a unique experience that most games would not attempt.It's easy enough to see from the screenshots that the visuals are just gorgeous. However, playing it and seeing it in motion, feeling the seasons, weather, and time-of-day change as you explore lovingly detailed spaces is really special. The music also sets an incredibly sombre tone, and is mostly jazzy instrumental tunes. This is the best game soundtrack I've heard in a long time, and it eases the pain of the games' repetitious mechanics.It's worth playing this game just to stare at the artwork and listen to the music, but the core gameplay is also very engaging.The combat controls are pretty nuanced, but you can get pretty far by just button-mashing and accidentally discovering combos. There are a nice selection of enemy types and although the way weapons (knives, swords, guns) function was frustrating to me for a long time, I do think they are implemented correctly because they never trivialize fights.Genre-wise, this game threads a needle between beat-em-up and management sim. Your time will be spent fairly evenly between killing thugs, and exploring the game world/experiencing the story. Given the main character's increasing weakness over time, how you spend your time and money has a huge impact on the story. You'll fall in love, you'll meet old friends, you'll build an empire and waste time shooting pool and playing baseball. You'll start growing a beard, gamble away your money and wake up on a bench wondering how it got this bad, then retreat to the countryside to end your own life. You'll have a cigarette on your balcony and get lost in thought, you'll get a massage and hit the sauna. You'll get drunk, you'll buy a house, you'll fish until the sun sets.You'll dream about your younger years when you had more stamina. You'll be backstabbed, you'll fail your boss, you'll lose your fancy sunglasses when they get knocked off in a fight; this game has it all.I personally experienced a few bugs but never had a crash or anything that softlocked my game or forced me  to start a new save. The game's structure is fairly complex so admittedly, failing enough tasks in the game means starting over fresh is the best option.To summarize, it's a beautiful game that's not very approachable, but I'm so glad I gave it a chance. If you ever find yourself complaining that most games are too generic in this era of gaming, you owe it to yourself to try Fading Afternoon.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: To cut to the chase, Seiji the PC, (a Yakuza fresh out of prison) is dying of a terminal illness, and has precious little time left. How he lives his last few months is up to you.Having very little to lose allows Seiji to be dangerous AF, and regardless of which path you end up following, there will be lots of ass kicking and assassinations. And there are multiple threads to follow.P.S.: The apartment next to the Pawn Shop is ass. _childDocuments_.review: you are a middle aged Yakuza named Seiji who just got out of jail. You are sick with a disease that is slowly killing you. You get weaker every single day. What will you do with your remaining life? Do you protect your aniki's interests and take turfs from rival groups? Do you take in your own underling and create your own gang? Just remember, whatever your choose, the disease you have is incurable.The more I play this game, the more I was surprised at how many choices/plot lines you can pursue. All the decisions you make impact Seigi's destiny.The music soundtrack is amazing in this game, I really hope they will release an album. If you enjoy Japanese themed games like Yakuza, Way of Samurai series, you'll love this game.The game needs some more fine tuning and bug fixes. Sometimes I get knife locked, combo locked by enemies without chance to escape. And I keep experiencing a bug where the character automatically walks to the right side of the screen where I have to completely exit the game to fix. Hopefully the devs can fix these issues up, then this game will be perfect.A shiny 7.9/10 game. I can fully recommend this once quality of life and bug fixes are fully implemented. But even without them, as you can see from my play hours, this is a fun game to play.So, again, knowing that you are dying, what will you do, with your remaining life?

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to unpack here.  TLDR: It's good.In broad strokes, Fading Afternoon is a time management game with quite a lot of fighting.The core brawling is well-executed.  Using only the direction pad and two buttons (Hands/feet), you can execute a variety of combos and defensive maneuvers.  The animation is top notch, and really sells the moves.  There are fifteen-ish different enemies, and their composition mixes up by faction and area.  Each has its own behavior pattern, to include weapons.  In the default difficulty, the enemy waves get a bit large and repetitive, but setting the difficulty to easy made the pacing more to my liking.Each day/night cycle represents a week, and each area transition advances time.  Your main activities are territory-based gang warfare and building social relationships by chatting with characters.  There are also a series of time and relationship-based story missions that come up from time to time, usually forcing you directly into them at the start of the day.  Adding a sense of urgency to the process is the protagonists failing health.  Each week passed reduces maximum health, and you will have to choose which goals and plots you pursue in a given playthrough.The characters and story themselves are somewhat sparse, but believable and portrayed well.  If anything, I would've liked more story sequences and less daily grind in between for pacing.  Superb art, animations, and music do a great job telling the story with minimalist text dialogue.  Expect a lot of honor, revenge, cynicism, and duty.One accessibility drawback is that the game does not explain systems to you.  There's a lot of trial and error, going places you don't need to go and doing things that don't advance the story.  Once you figure out how the game works, the story unfolds more naturally.  Based on how you spend your time and who you ally with, the story plays out in a number of different ways.  Each ending is somewhat unceremonious, and invites the player to assess for themselves whether the outcome is good or bad.  Strong story, replayability, and silky smooth combat make Fading Afternoon my favorite brawler to date.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: Fading Afternoon is a great game. It has some weird mechanics, like 1 day being 1 week, also some other things are pretty confusing. There are some bugs, but I haven't come across any game breaking ones. The game is really short, but there are multiple endings and the replayability is pretty good. I recommend this game 100%.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: 2D Yakuza. If you played Ringo its like an easier to understand version of that game. Thing still aren't really explained so there are some hard learned lessons. There are some stages where it is hard to tell where the paths are. For example the first house you can buy has stairs to go down but it is oddly difficulty to line the character up correctly to go down the stairs. The combat is solid and there is even an arena mode. A surprising amount of moves as well. Has martial arts, grappling, swords, knives, and guns. The map is pretty big and expands after certain events so there are a lot of locations to visit. Great soundtrack as well. The game auto saves whenever you enter a room. I experienced one crash but did not lose any progress since it saved when I entered the room. Well worth the wait and the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Fading Afternoon

_childDocuments_.review: A really great game. As always Ueda M. and Artem Belov made a really great job with the graphics. The choice of musics perfectly fits each location and scene.The gameplay loop is really cool and money management feels rewarding.The only thing that I don't like is the fact that the main character has a disease that reduces his health everyday, it kind of breaks the gameplay loop and forces the player to restart the game again and again, making him play the same scenes. It also makes it that every time you choose a location where there is not a story progression flag, you are punished, because you'll end up with the same "bad" ending.Overall a really great game with an awesome atmosphere and aesthetic, but the game is not perfect and would be even better with a way to regain max health.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly excellent piece of modern art.  10/10 for sure.  The combat takes some practice, thankfully there is a practice arena.  once you learn the pace of the fights, you can make some beautifully smooth action sequences.  This game is just so stylish, it's a pixel art, slice-of-life anime.   The devs did an amazing job.

_childDocuments_.review: A Masterpiece Worth Every SecondWith over 300 hours spent on Persona 5 and its Royal edition on my PS4, buying the PC version was the perfect excuse to dive back into this masterpiece once again. Because Persona 5 Royal isn’t just a game; it’s a complete experience. The way gameplay, story, and battle mechanics intertwine so smoothly and seamlessly is unique, setting a new standard for the genre.One of the game's biggest triumphs is its ability to blend various gameplay mechanics harmoniously, keeping an experience that spans over 50 hours from ever feeling monotonous. There's always something to improve, a goal to pursue. Whether it's enhancing relationships, leveling up skills, or managing time, the game creates an environment where every choice has real weight on the story and the bonds you create. And those bonds are truly special: each character has a unique, deeply crafted story. There are no unnecessary characters; each one has an impact on the narrative.Relationships and the romance system fit perfectly into the game’s universe. Everything feels so natural that, along the journey, you end up forming real connections with the characters. And the battle structure? The difficulty is masterfully balanced, providing an engaging challenge curve. The ability to customize builds and exploit weaknesses makes combat strategic and dynamic, adding even more replayability. For those seeking a greater challenge, simply increasing the difficulty is enough—the game rises to the occasion.Persona 5 Royal is, without a doubt, an experience that deserves to be lived multiple times. The freedom of choice and the richness of different routes make every new playthrough as exciting as the first. It's more than a game; it's art.

_childDocuments_.review: God I've waited so long for this and I can't express how much I LOVE the game.I'm now in a committed relationship with P5R. If you played any Persona Game before, you'll know you like it.The comic-inspired aesthetics are such a joy to behold, the voice acting is ON POINT again (talking about English VA, Japanese is probably top notch, too) and so far I have nobody whose voice I despise hearing (looking at P4G's Teddy here). I have yet to find a dialogue I want to skip through. Also there's tons of things to do - hard to decide sometimes how I want to spend my free time in game! And I'm still discovering new areas. I like the level design, too. I'm about to get into the third heist now and the first two felt very unique from one another. The stealth-and-ambush mechanic makes fights so much better. Compared to P4G, there's only one part so far that's random generated "labyrinth" styled levels and that's not one of the "main" dungeons/palaces but the place where you go for smaller requests and stuff. And even that's not a pain to get through. I don't know, there's lots to say about the game and why it's good and so far I haven't found anything that left me with a bitter aftertaste. I just love it.If you haven't already, you should give it a shot. And even if you played P5 in its vanilla version, Royal seems to add enough to give you some nice surprises and even some QoL changes.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing and beating this game felt like the anime equivalent of picking up One Piece. Did Luffy find the One Piece yet?GAMEPLAY: 4.5/5The gameplay of Persona 5 Royal encompasses... quite a lot, actually. The game is a mix of a slice of life simulator (playing through almost every calendar date of an entire year), a visual novel where all you have to do is focus on the story, and classic jrpg action where you raid palaces in the metaverse, stylishly fighting enemies in turn based combat. As most of the game is story-driven, there's not too much to say about the gameplay apart from free time, and entering palaces/Mementos. One quip I had with free time was hanging out with confidants - the occasional extra filler hangout required to bond further with someone and get a new cut-scene felt largely unnecessary given the abundance of activities you could do elsewhere in the game. Apart from that, spending time with confidants was definitely a highlight of free time, with how real and developed most of the Persona cast feel.The palaces in the game felt great. Kamoshida's castle admittedly gives the game a bit of a slow start with the introduction of the Metaverse, but the game only goes up from there. By the time you get to Madarame's flashy and golden museum, you really feel like as the player, you're on a HEIST and it's going down in style. The palaces following the theme of the seven deadly sins was a cute touch, especially considering that the game was all about stealing evil hearts. The ambience and atmosphere of the palaces also drastically differed (in a good way!), from cyber city outer space, pyramids, and a casino. The puzzles typically reflected the theme of the palace as well, keeping the raids feeling different and fun throughout the game. Combat felt moreorless like your typical jrpg, with default attacks, guarding, and special skills. The gun being a secondary option to a default swing made for some interesting management decisions in terms of palace raids and SP spent, and physical attack skills taking away your HP instead of SP was a fun mechanic to juggle with as well. Similar to how turn based combats tend to have "ultimate" abiltiies, P5R has "showtimes" and "all out attacks," featuring special cinematic attack animations. They're silly, cool, and leave you with a smile on your face. Balancing in the game felt just about right (I played on hard mode), and if I ever felt underleveled, I never had to grind for long to make up for it. Before I move on from palaces though - Okumura's boss fight was NOT it. The gimmicks were annoying, and felt punishing to the player for simply not being leveled up enough instead of encouraging strategy, given the time limit of wiping out mobs in one turn. Also, I wanted to square up with Okumura himself, not his goons. Grrrr. Every other boss fight gets a pass, though! Finally, the movement in the game felt a bit awkward at times. Like, you try to walk up to an npc to talk to them and overshoot a little, and have to re-adjust kind of awkward. It wasn't rough enough to take away from the gameplay, but making it a bit smoother would definitely make the game feel even better!NARRATIVE: 5/5For a game that's 100+ hours and largely story driven, I'm sure glad that Persona 5's story is TOP TIER. Woo! Honestly, all I have to say about this section is 'congrats to Persona 5 Royal for being the only video game to have Futaba Sakura.' Jokes aside, the character writing in this game is amazing. Some characters just feel so real and relatable, making any down time in the game to spend time with the cast a treat, instead of a chore. Even the less interesting characters like Ryuji, as forgettable as he is, is undeniably a bro. I found it so funny how Yusuke would claim he's not a pervert, and yet all the perverted dialogue options in his hangouts boosted your friendship the most. Futaba is undeniably best girl, and the game spoils you by including her in Sojiro's hangout storyline too (which is downright touching). I need to throw in that Goro Akechi is a hilarious character. No I will not be giving context. Just trust me on this one (source: dude trust me). Persona 5 manages to tackle a lot of serious and heartfelt issues in a wholesome and satisfactory way, instead of being overly clichéd and cringe. Having a likeable cast in a game like this is so important, and the end result is a game that feels like it's spoiling you for being as long as it is. Considering the sizeable number of confidants and party members as well, there's bound to be someone you like or connect with to some extent. The plot has a clear beginning and end, and has its fair shares of twists and turns. While some plot twists are all but expected (I won't be going into spoilers here), how exactly everything unfolds and plays out is usually where the story line delivers when it gets predictable. My favourite antagonist is easily the last one in the game (in the true ending). The complexity of the final villain in terms of their motivations and what their stance was on justice and the "greater good" felt refreshing and set apart from everyone else that came before them, and actually makes you want to pause and think for a moment if they really are the bad guy. Brilliant. I've heard before from people that have played P5R that they got depressed after beating the game, because it felt like they were leaving behind the friends that they made along the way. High praise that's honestly deserved, and speaks volumes of the world building and likeability of the character writing.GRAPHICS: 5/5It's one of those games that make you feel cool just for playing the game. The animation you get for ambushing an opponent? Getting behind them  on their shoulders, ripping off their mask? Kinda hot, if you ask me. HAHA. Character design and art are amazing, and the proof is that Futaba has glasses. The general aesthetic of the game is clean and pleasing, and a lot of touches to the art (including the white/black squares in the font) matches the theme of the Phantom Thieves. Plus points for creativity! The game always looks great to look at, minus that one enemy that looks like. Um. Anyways. P5R also adds animated anime-style story cutscenes, and they were all amazing as well! The game art design also pays attention to the personalities of the cast. One of my favourite examples is when the gang is sitting around together. Ryuji would be manspreading (LOL), Ann sitting up on the table, Makoto sitting like the prim and proper lady that she is, Yusuke standing around, Futaba lying down on her stomach... all these subtle touches to the art really shows how much care and thought has been put into this game, outside of the plot and gameplay.SOUNDTRACK: 5/5Chances are, you've heard Persona music before, even if you've never heard of or played the game series before. The music is iconic, catchy, and good. The music always gets the atmosphere juuust right, while being fun and engaging. About to re-enter someone's palace to steal their heart? You're about to feel real cool for it. Something sad is happening? Prepare for the music to make you depressed. The Persona soundtrack has surprisingly good diversity as well, flexibly allowing the music to enhance the game experience. What more could you ask for in a game soundtrack? As well, the voice acting for the entire cast is great, and suits the characters they represent. I can only imagine that the voice actor for Goro Akechi must've had a lot of fun ;)OVERALL: 5/5Persona 5 Royal is a phenomenal JRPG that sets a high standard for future games to come. Sure, the game is long, but considering how good the game is across the entirety of its length... it's a gift. You get over 100 hours of an immersive world with a diverse cast, in an emotional and cool rollercoaster of a game. If that doesn't sound fun to you, I recommend going on a merry-go-round instead. I'm sure you'll come around!

_childDocuments_.review: I must truthfully admit that I’m not an avid fan of JRPGs; and my first introduction into the Persona series through P4G was mediocre at best because at the time I thought of Persona as a glorified dating sim/visual novel. Thankfully, P5R has proved me to be dead wrong with its charming style, enthralling story and the most amazing soundtrack I’ve heard in a while.Now that I’ve finally finished the game with all achievements, the whole experience felt like an extremely emotional roller coaster. After getting off this ride, I felt both immense joy and bittersweetness: Happy because I was able to acompany the Phantom Thieves to the end of their journey, watching the characters grow and develop as a proud parent watching their children; Bittersweet because the ride is finally over and I would never be able to experience it for the first time again.Now it sounds pretty weird to begin a review about an RPG with its OST but the music in this game is truly phenomenal. The game has a track for pretty much every activity you do and all of them are bangers. From strolling around the city and socializing with people, to ambushing and beating up your enemies; from working hard on your final exams, to going all out on the final bosses; all of the tracks in this game is truly unique, catchy and memorable. So much so that I will definitely continue to listen to the OST long after finishing this game. I would even consider recommending people try this game out for its music alone; and after the music has drawn you in:I find this aspect hard to review without risking major spoilers, so I will try to keep it to a minimum. You take on the role of a typical anime/manga high school protagonist nicknamed Joker, transfering to a new town after a false accusation. He awakens to a power that allows him to tap into the subconscious minds of other people in a place dubbed the Metaverse. Over the course of one year in-game, he forms bonds with various characters as well as made new teammates who accompanied him as the Phantom Thieves – using their special powers to steal malicious intents from the hearts of evil adults. Now as for the rest of the story and its intricacies in character development, I wholeheartedly believe that it will be much more enjoyable for you to discover as you play the game.P5R’s gameplay is essentially broken into 2 main parts: The socialization/life simulation part and the actual combat RPG stuffs. For the life sim part, you get to hang around time, discover a surprising amount of activities to do and socialize with an ensemble of endearing cast (most of them at least ahem). It’s tough to list all of the activities available but just to name a few: going to the movie theater, training at the gym, reading books, going on dates and hangouts, etc.; all of which will ultimately help boost your power in the combat part of the game. Since time is limited throughout the entire game, you’d have to learn to balance these activities in an optimal way, or just go wild and have fun enjoying the city.On the other hand, the combat part mostly takes place in the metaverse where the Phantom Thieves will go on heists to steal people’s hearts and deal with evil shadows and Personas along the way. In a traditional turn-based JRPG fashion, you, your teammates and the enemies will take turns duking it out. Also similar to typical turn-based JRPGs, you will have access to normal attacks, ranged attacks, special skills and items to defeat your foes. Honestly the combat in this game is so stylish that even though it is a bit grindy, I still enjoy the flashy moves after hours into the game. On occasion you can also negotiate and convince the enemies’ Personas into joining your crew, adding new skills to your arsenal. People also draw comparision between the Persona-collecting in this game to that of a Pokemon game.Now, being a JRPG, it also has its fair share of cheesy and cliché moments. But ultimately, it didn’t bother me one bit; and I think it even added to the charm. The game also provides fan service in the form of allowing a highschooler to date adults, including a teacher, which is questionable at best. Good old Japanese fan service I guess.Persona 5 is truly a masterpiece in my opinion and it easily made my personal top 5 games of all time. I’m so glad I listened to the memes and gave this game a chance. Came for the music and memes, stayed for pretty much everything the game offered.

_childDocuments_.review: A year on from finishing Persona 4 Golden, here I am with about 90 hours logged into Persona 5 Royal as the ending credits roll. Much like the previous review, I’m a little perplexed as to how to even begin this review. Simply put, Persona 5 Royal is a stone cold classic JRPG, and easily ranks amongst the best that’s out there. I do have a few misgivings, but it’s been phenomenal.For the uninitiated, Persona 5 Royal as an RPG mixes several elements together: turn-based battles that rely on elemental weaknesses, monster summoning/collecting (the titular Personas), dungeon crawling and a social link system with the in-game characters. The core game play wont be unfamiliar to anyone who has played a JRPG before, but the focus on elemental weaknesses and the role of social links are central features in this game. Most of your party has set elemental affinities, but you are able to switch between an ever-increasing range of Personas to adapt to this spell element-driven system. As the game progresses, mastery of this system, which allows you or enemies to get '1 more' attack by using with the right spell becomes a crucial component. Building further upon the foundation of Persona 4 Golden, social links are a key component of P5R and are a significant chunk of the game. In between story events, you have the option each day to interact with members of your party and other major NPCs of the world. There's also a fairly faithful recreation of a wide range of areas in Tokyo as a backdrop to this, some of it freely explorable. Each party member and major NPC has a sub-story that ultimately enriches the overall plot and has extra gameplay-related bonuses for completing all ten ranks for each character. This additional layer adds depth to the plot and ends with giving access to the strongest Persona summons as compensation. In the process of my run (including Royal’s extra ending), I completed all but a handful of these, even if some were due to the skin of my teeth due to time limits. The game also rewards players for these links by giving passive bonuses that enhance any future new game plus attempts.The narrative of Persona 5 Royal focuses on the seedy underbelly of Tokyo society and a series of increasingly high stakes heists. Your character awakens to the use of Personas, which sets off a string of events that leads to the creation of the Phantom Thieves, a supernaturally powerful group that can change hearts. Part slice of life, part science fiction, part crime drama and part social commentary, it’s an interesting mix in many ways. I’d argue that this leans more on a philosophical and sociopolitical angle than its predecessor, and a range of social issues in modern Japanese society, ranging from structured hierarchical harassment, dog-eat-dog mentalities, corruption, mob mentalities and even populism are addressed as part of this. Each major villain has an arc that features a specific dungeon with a theme, and it’s a little like watching a season of anime each time – which of course also gives you the ability to take a break and come back to the game when you’re ready. It’s a broader mix than Persona 4 Golden, but an intriguing one. Again, I recommend looking up a spoiler-free guide for the True Ending requirements, for your best possible first-time experience.New to this entry is Mementos, a secondary and evolving randomised dungeon that serves as both a means to gain more battle experience and Personas, and explore smaller stories as part of this. Mementos eventually ties into the main storyline, but for a lengthy game, it also presents a very important feature: cutting down on grinding. As you progress through this special dungeon (which can be accessed for most the game), you gain the ability to add passive buffs that improve the amount of experience points, money and items you gain from items. Better still, the cat-bus-based (yes, I said cat-bus) navigation of the area also allows you to run down lower-level enemies, skipping the need for a battle. By the end of the game, Mementos was giving me a 200% EXP boost and helped greatly in preparing me for the late game challenges. As someone who can be starved for time, this was a welcome and gameplay-based addition.Much like its predecessor, the soundtrack and aesthetic look of Persona 5 Royal are absolutely fantastic. Who’d have thought that a JRPG soundtrack using jazz, blues, R&B, and even disco elements would be so memorable and effective. The UI and transitional screens of the game have also been heavily stylised, which is absolutely gorgeous. My only major criticisms of Persona 5 Royal is that it’s beginning to test the limits of some of the features of this franchise by overdoing and overdelivering. It’s a fairly reasonable criticism that Persona 5 Royal has a bit too much dialogue, and can become like playing a high-end visual novel for an hour or more at some points. Likewise, some of the puzzles in dungeons… get a bit grating by the end. There are some really neat and inventive ones, but some, like the colour-mixing puzzle in the game’s final area, grew to be tedious and kind of frustrating. These are only small marks on an otherwise fantastic game.I played Persona 5 Royal in about four blocks, correlating with some quieter times, breaks and holidays, and in many ways, it’s a game where you can binge an arc and set it down for a while, only to return later. The game also offers a handy story recap, should you need it.If you’re into JRPGs and Persona 5 Royal is on your radar, it’s a must-play. Just be ready for the time investment.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 is, without a doubt, one of the most unique and impactful games I’ve ever played and easily my number 1 game. From the start, it pulls you into an unforgettable world—a stylish, Tokyo-inspired city where you balance life as a high school student and a "Phantom Thief," fighting against society's corruption. The story is captivating, exploring themes of justice, rebellion, and the power of friendship in a way that feels meaningful without being heavy-handed.One of the most impressive aspects of Persona 5 is its art style. Everything has a bold, high-energy look, from the character designs to the menus, giving the game a vibe that’s entirely its own. The soundtrack is also phenomenal, mixing jazz and rock to create tracks that make everything from battles to exploration feel exciting. Each tune has such personality that it stays with you even after you turn off the game.But what really makes Persona 5 special is its cast of characters. As you play, you build relationships with each member of the Phantom Thieves, along with other “Confidants” who add depth and skills to your journey. These aren’t just side characters—they each have their own struggles, motivations, and growth arcs, which makes them feel genuinely real. By the end, you feel like you know them as well as your own friends, and you want to see each one succeed.The combat system is also fantastic. It's turn-based but with a ton of strategy built in, and every fight feels fast-paced and intense. You can exploit enemy weaknesses, pull off All-Out Attacks, and summon powerful “Personas” that add a whole layer of tactics. It keeps you engaged while rewarding you for thinking strategically, which is rare to find in RPGs of this style.My first playthrough lasted just shy of about 200 hours of gameplay, Persona 5 is a long ride, but every moment feels worthwhile. The combination of a deep story, relatable characters, and a stylish world makes it stand out from any other game out there. If you love games with a great narrative and want something that challenges you to think and feel, Persona 5 is a must-play experience that will leave a lasting impact.

Recommended for any gaming fan to try this game at least once, if you hate it never play a JRPG ever again, it doesn't get better than this. Persona 5 is definitely one of the games of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 is my first Persona game and it's probably the best JRPG game I've played in a long time and has an enormous replay value. I spent my whole winter and spring holiday to finish this game and wow I loved it. It certainly made me realize I missed something during my high school time. Like the rest of us.Persona 5 Royal is not for everyone. It's heavily narrative driven and has a lot of dialogue which can be a dealbreaker for some people who wants non-stop gameplay.You go by almost every single day in a year, living the student life but also trying to change the society for the better when you awaken your Persona powers. There is so much you can do when you're not at school preparing for exams, playing with friends or clearing palaces. You can self improve your social skills by studying, watching movies, books or exercising which is crucial if you wanna improve your relationship with your crush or your friends. Which is highly recommendable as strong relationships will also make your palace clearing and boss fights go more easier.With Royal you have a few new characters. A new party member and a new teacher at your school who's also one of my favorite characters.I was surprised how very well written the story and the characters is. There are times when I feel like I wanna skip dialogue because it's either just boring talk or fillers. But it makes me want to learn more about the characters, their backstory and motivations. Without going into spoilers I found it really entertaining how some of the characters grows as the story progresses. Oh right, they call it for character development! Your party members are of course the type of friends you can never get irl, which makes them so great and the time you spend together are really fun and there's always something new with them going on.The voices in both languages are really good, although I personally preferred Japanese voices. A tip though, time is limited and not everyone is available every day so you might feel some time pressure at the end of the game, but don't worry. Focus on improving your social stats as you gonna need to max out all of them if you wanna max out your relationship with various characters. Be prepared that by the end of the game you won't have time to max out all characters as there are plenty of other stuff you need to do. So pick your favorites on who you wanna be a best friend with or go on a date with. I recommend getting high levels with the Shogi girl and your blonde short tempered friend as you will get some abilities that makes fights go slightly easier. It really is up to you on who you wanna focus on.It is turn-based combat which throws some people off. But the way it's designed is really fun. Every character, friend, foe have weaknesses and strong points such as Ice, Fire, Wind, Holy, etc and knowing your enemies weak points makes battles more fun and smooth. I liked the baton pass system when you attack one enemy with their weakness, you pass your action to your next party member to do the same thing until all enemies are stunned and you go can go for a All-Out-Attack.The music is a real banger. Which is probably one of the most praised things about Persona 5. You're gonna hear the same combat music again and again. Oddly I never once became tired of it and it's very weird but the more I listened and the further I progressed it just got better and better until the point I started to listen to some of the tracks on the train when I'm off to school myself. I live in Tokyo irl and whoa it was immersive!? Anyway, the music and vocals are pretty good and they fit so well with game's atmosphere. I started to really appreciate the music when I was running up to defeat the first boss and just turned the volume up because damn!!For those who played the base game.Just to say this, the new Royal content starts reaaallly late. Right after December which can be a bummer for people who are interested the new red haired character and gotta spend around  hours to get to the new story. I really liked having her in my party and her Showtime with  was really really cool which is such a shame she doesn't  But I also wanna recommend this to players who also have only finished the base game. If you thought the base game ending was cool, you haven't seen the new ending with the new palace. And the new palace and it's story is my number one favorite out of all of them.For those who like JRPG's I really really recommend this game. It's a very long game which makes the money worth it and even if you might have spent over 100 hours, you might feel like you want 100 more hours.There's no shame in looking into guides if you need guidance or want to be more proficient with your time. But refrain from reading about characters until you finished the game as you might face some spoilers.Enjoy

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to explain how poorly designed this game is. It's as if all of the game design of the past 15 years has been ignored.The game has some qualities ; interesting story, great music, fun art style and some humor and self awareness.But everything else is just a nightmare. It's a 100 hour long power point presentation.The game is linear, but tries to make itself seem like it isn't. Every dialogue or decision is littered with false choices or interactivity. The map shows all the point of interest, shops, exits and entrances but will not let you interact with any of them until the story says its time.The game and combat is littered with animations and small cutscenes...it's litterally probably 30-40% of the actual play time taken.Combat has little to no strategy. Once you get past a few fights, everything dies pretty quickly, and using the weaknesses, all-ins and other various special abilities is longer than just attacking twice...since the animation is quicker.At this point, i'm just stubbornly finishing the game out of spite, but its hard to imagine this isnt a game from the warl 2000s. 80$ is ridiculous considering this is a glorified newgrounds flash dating sim.

_childDocuments_.review: Is there anything of value left to be said about Persona 5? It is a game so ubiquitous and genre-defining that it created legions of fans that have never played the series and introduced a significant amount of people to the genre of Jazz music. Joker even made it into Smash, a move that wins the "Biggest misdirection of 2019" award. Love it or hate it, Persona is a household name for JRPG fans and will line the pockets of lousy video essayists on YouTube for years to come. Surely Atlus, a company famed for their rational and intelligent business decision-making would never release their Holy Grail on other consoles, but here we are in 2023, 26 years after the release of the first Persona. It is a time where mentioning you played Persona 3 incurs responses calling you a  "geriatric boomer" and vocal Shin Megami Tensei fans are better known for bloviating than completing a job application. It's almost certain then that a PC port of a game made by a Japanese developer would have issues. After all, Capcom, Square, Koei, and Bandai have a poor track record  but P5R rises above all doubt. Its performance is smoother than Ryuji and Ann's brain. Not once in my nearly 150 hours did I encounter a bug, and known issues have been quashed like low level shadows by responsive patch updates.I could wax poetic about how P5R actually makes turn-based combat fun, how the pacing issues of the last act of the base game are remedied with the new content, or how the aesthetics and stylish presentation makes most UX designers look like they work with an Etch A Sketch. But you already knew that. It's Persona 5, baby.

_childDocuments_.review: An all time great story. Persona 5 touches upon moral concepts that I have not seen in a video game. The seven deadly sins and heavenly virtues are heavily woven into the story. There are strong contrasts between sins and virtues, and Persona 5 showcases the affects that they have on the characters that embody sin and virtue.Most of the characters are memorable and relatable. It is often enjoyable to see character growth throughout the story. Building character relationships offers a lot of character insights, but it often done so through reading text on screen, as opposed to voiced dialogue. When there is voiced dialogue, it is often quite well versed and written. From strong heart string emotions being plucked to comedic relief, this game made me feel as if the characters were believable. Only downside to the game is Mementos. Basically a grind dungeon that makes me turn my brain off. If Mementos was left to a singular dungeon, it would have been much more enjoyable and made the game hours shorter. Potential downside is the length of the game, which is roughly one hundred hours. At times the game could have been sped up some without much impact to the story.Persona 5 will make you ask ethical questions throughout the course of the game, and I believe it has made me reconsider many important moral assumptions I have had prior. 10/10
