_childDocuments_.review: I *really* wanted to love this game. The art style is adorable, I love repairs and small repair-like tasks (as performed well in this game) and most of the characters have at least some level of depth and charm in some manner.However, the negatives outweigh those. - Many of the mechanics (Especially travel) are painstakingly repetitive and time-consuming (And I'm referring to the "fast travel" mechanics, some of which are necessary)- The inventory, in my experience at least, was impossible to keep uncluttered - Anything new you receive gets slapped in the middle section, and you need so many items on you at any given moment, which the space doesn't account for.- The game holds your hand far too tightly - Anything that may take a brief second for a child to realise is specifically stated, and anything beyond that is practically drawn out for you in a pretty picture, which takes a long time, and if you're not careful you could accidentally have it repeat on you, which is frustrating.- The movement is imprecise, which is usually a very minor thing, but still undeniably annoying- The story - vague spoiler: All in all, there were clearly some amazing ideas, but the writing lets itself down, and the game just lacks the basic level of polish expected from anything other than a free game, in just too many areas.

_childDocuments_.review: is an excellent top-down space adventure in a world where humans got spliced with animal genes, first as a novelty, then convenience, as fur protects them from the cold caused by climate change (so they got the other end of the stick). it's also a world that still uses tapes and other old-timey things, so it appealed to me on multiple levels (the furry stuff not so much, though I like  and such as much as anybody).as a member of , you're tasked with fixing whatever needs fixing, as well as eating pudding. you're on the way to your next job and after crash-landing, you find yourself in a desert, among a bunch of robots who don't take kindly to others doing their fixing. there are also pirates who don't take kindly to others stealing their loot. after a certain amount they show up and presumably take some of your items, but I never found out, as radios let you reset the counters. not even sure why this mechanic is necessary, but at least it's not a timer, just a minor annoyance.there's a log for conversations, jobs and other to-do items, a database with lore and inventory, including a handy filter to find the right tool for the job, though I never used it. you can find all sorts of items in different regions (natives, as in robots, can help with directions) and everything has certain properties (e.g. a coin will be flat, round and metal), revealed by oracles for free, though donations are welcome. items also have a tier from 1 to 5, which decides what kind of fixing they can do, so as another example, instead of a screwdriver you can use a coin. tier also determines what you can get for them from traders, obviously won't get tier 3 for some tier 1 junk., can't use the same coin as a replacement screwdriver forever, so it's necessary to keep looking for stuff via jobs and other places. , but they reset daily and even get removed from your accepted jobs if not finished by midnight. I found this a bit excessive, as meaningless as these jobs are. also job boards are entirely optional, as you can walk up to an item in a settlement and start fixing. oh, and I wasn't kidding about pudding either,  as well, much to my satisfaction. not only do you get to eat all sorts of intergalactic delicacies, but robots reveal secrets while you're munching.soon enough you get  to get around faster, it even has a hotkey to summon it, a tiny bit more believable than making a horse appear anywhere by whistling. and somewhat less so when you learn it doesn't need fuel, but . no energy, stamina, health, hunger or other nonsense. there's a clock and an , but no need to sleep if you don't want to. all it does is it bypasses darkness, which makes exploration harder and more frustrating, but not impossible., but not every settlement has them and they have to be activated first (and fixed, but only in the first area for some reason). the problem is, , and by the time they're online, the other method also kicks in (after visiting 2/3 of the locations), and then might as well use that, as it works with every visited place and that way the  can be avoided.I mentioned good old tapes already. turns out, they're used for recording memories in fixfox-world and they're playable. as in, you can play them to play through other people's memories. neat. there's other stuff to find and do in this crazy place, like unexpected shortcuts, more functionality for some of your equipment, building giant robots, and so on. the primary objective is to get off the planet, so you'll eventually leave the desert behind for literally greener pastures. of course, going back to earlier locations is possible and necessary.it's  but if you don't pay attention, you might get stuck for a bit. I love the conveyors around warehouses, you'll be going around them a lot and this makes those puzzles a lot quicker. the game also often offers a teleport to the next story location to save time. . there are 4 robots, 3 of them with 4 parts each, 4 beacons to place all over the place, then 4 more, then another 4, etc.honestly, . the sidekick's constant 'watch out for monsters that don't exist' lines got old really fast (plenty of memorable-in-a-good-way characters though), , and here's the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying thing: . 'overworlds' get wiped, only the new places of already visited locations will be shown, with the close-up maps intact. there is absolutely no reason for it and once near the beginning was fine, surprise, whatever, but . uncovered the whole map? well, ♥♥♥♥ you then, start over. ridiculous, even if there's not much to see or do outside settlements and you'll be using fast travel as soon as it's available anyway. still, . but mostly work as they should out of the box, a mixture of mouse and keyboard with cursor and scroll sensitivity settings, or gamepad if you so desire. my only (minor) beef is that there can't be any alternatives, so only one set of keys to move, one button to do a specific action, etc. with excellent pixel graphics and great space-country, electronic, chiptune and other types of music.  too. separate volumes, resolutions, windowed mode, v-sync, framerate limiter, and best of all, : size, speed, dyslexic font, automatic/manual progress, typewriter effect and text effect toggles. there's also a dominant hand and pronoun setting., as it should be. well, you can't save while eating or driving, but good enough. manual saving is a bit weird, done by picking up a tape on the save screen and inserting it at the top of the screen. it only shows the current location and playtime, plus mouseover says how long ago the save happened. no overwrite confirmation, but the way it works makes it harder to accidentally save over something. and don't worry about read-only chapter autosaves taking up precious save slots, as once the first page is filled, a new one opens with more.there's plenty more to say about the game, but  and find out the rest. despite some annoyances it's  that just keeps on going and going every time you think it's gonna be over. a mixed blessing due to some repetitive elements, but I really enjoyed my time with it, couldn't wait to continue playing.

_childDocuments_.review: FixFox, an underrated gem.I wasn't exactly sure what I was getting myself into when I first booted FixFox, all I knew was that I was going to be playing as a fox and I'd be repairing stuff. Now find four parts for a big robot again.  Now activate four nodes for a search again.  Now find four parts for a big robot again.  I'm not even joking. _childDocuments_.review: Is this a good game? Yes.Is it a game for me? No.Am I recommending it? HELL YES! It's cute as hell, really plays well, and this dev deserves your money.I just can't stomach the constant "reset to zero" mechanics disregarding the actual warning count.A game that lies to me about how risky something is is a game I can't play, essentially. "Pirates arriving in 9 stashes" for example and they show up after I check 3-4 stashes instead so I lose all items I've found so far that are needed to progress the story instantly ruins the game for me. _childDocuments_.review: (9/10)Extremely cute and highly stylized 'tinker' game where you roam a lifeless (but full of androids) planet and slowly patch together a narrative of how things got to be the the way they are by way of using postage stamps, bananas, feather dusters, and anything else you can find as tools to kludge repairs to anything broken you can find.The graphics are pretty stand-out for this kind of game, extremely stylized characters and a vertical top down (not isometric) perspective you rarely see in games these days.  Things are mostly full of pixels but you get some pretty cool gradients and color lighting effects.  Everything feels comfortable as a retro throwback game from the future or future looking game from the past, and I really did enjoy finding each new area and the new weird tools and things they would fix.One of the other highlights is the musical score which is twangy and sentimental and can pull at your heart strings just a bit in all the right ways.  Really I can't underscore enough how pleasant and just overall enjoyable every song in the game is, especially as you ride between old semi-abandoned towns having a little folksy guitar backing you up and setting the mood was really perfect.None of the puzzle elements were too hard, and really the main reason to keep going is to find out the story of how things got to be the way they are in the game, which definitely gets a lot weirder than you would expect.  The moment to moment play is still enjoyable as well and you can just have fun puttering around in the remote wastes, finding old trash you will turn in to the tools of your trade.

_childDocuments_.review: If you come for a story, and stay for the cuteness, you'll have a good time. Don't expect any complicated puzzles or things that'll make you think too hard. In fact, it handholds you through everything, even after you've learned it. Some of the puzzles require you to keep a store of 'decorated' items, and it seems you don't really need all the things you get. In fact, you even get a way to bypass the puzzles later if you want. At that point, it's likely a good thing since you'll probably have gotten tired of the same puzzles and solution methods.Overall though, it's not too tedious, and seems well paced for a story. Enough variability in where you go and what you get, that it never gets too old too quickly. Depending on how close you pay attention, you may figure out the ending before you get there. But it's still a rewarding and cute along the way. My biggest complaint is that the Fix Fox has no tail. Sadness.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where I feel like I'm on the fence leaning towards one side because I want to like it but there's so many things that just make it worse than the things that make it interesting or fun. Then the more I think about it the more I start to hate this game because it just kinda ruins itself. On one hand I like the aesthetic and like the idea of these kinds of games where you fiddle with things like a puzzler as the main gameplay aspect but on the other hand there's so many things that just ruin the experience that have nothing to do with the actually enjoyable parts. Even then the parts that are enjoyable become excessively repetitive almost instantaneously. The game is about this silent protagonist fox that you can select the gender for that has no weight on the game at all but if that's a detail you like then its there, be a he, she, or they. You're a SPACR employee and your whole job is you're sent out to fix things but it's implied you're bad at your job because you focus on old tech more than new tech so you're more like a completely useless specialist that just so happens to be perfect for this exact job which sends you to a far off planet in an attempt to fix a beacon. The main selling point of this game is two things: the fiddly puzzle aspect itself where you're given an interface and tasks to do and you've gotta use whatever tools suit the situation to do them, and the quirky tv screen headed robot characters that constantly love to make comments and such at almost every turn until you have a very specific task to do and then they almost never say anything because the game is waiting for you to complete those tasks to move the story along. Immediately there are major problems with both of these and honestly it really is a fault at the game's core with how it was designed. The fixing part of this game is interesting at first but then after the first 30 minutes of gameplay, maybe up to an hour depending on how fast you go through dialogue and try to get to the game part of the game, you'll immediately notice that you've essentially played the entire game right out the gate. Even when you progress the story to get to other areas the new places maybe add one or two new things at best and otherwise are just the same things over and over again. Dust this, unscrew that, tape up these wires, etc. This game has like 5 tiers of tool types and none of them matter because all that matters is that you've got a ton of coins and spatulas to unscrew screws, as well as bandaids and postage stamps to tape up whatever needs to be taped up. Collecting all these items for the 50th time in a row from stashes that take like 3 to 5 seconds to tell you that you got 1 or 2 items becomes a major slog after a point where you wish it would just instantly grab the items and just instantly tell you that you got a bandaid, or some scrap metal, but instead you just sit there and watch some flashy stuff as each item is given their own collection screen for the millionth time despite you already having 5, 10, 20 of it already. Thats one major issue I have with all these quirky characters and the gameplay itself. It really likes to drag on excessively so. It's to the point that the game gives you within the first couple hours of the game MULTIPLE fast travel options. You start out on foot, then you get a bike, at some point you unlock these underground teleport points that 90% of the time are barely better simply holding a direction because theres so many of them that they always teleport you to the closest one (that can be 10 meters away, it could be 50 meters away, and they're omnidirectional so you have to activate them from the direction you want to go to, its weird and dumb honestly), you get a fast travel taxi option that'll take you to places you've been but only if you've unlocked enough of the map to allow it, you even get access to a zipline that, like the fast travel taxi option, will only work if you've been to said places that allow the zipline. If it wasn't apparent the maps are absurdly huge and like filled with absolutely NOTHING but space to waste your time. The characters like to talk a lot and depending on what they're talking about the scenes can play out really slowly, sometimes they chime in every 10 steps because you're progressing through a puzzle thats basically walking down a hallway, and they constantly handhold you because there are no quest markers so if they didn't you'd probably forget where the heck you're supposed to go or do. This combined with overly flashy things that do nothing but waste your time to try and distract you with pretty lights or effects just ultimately pads the game's time. I've only got 5 hours into this game and I feel like 4 of those hours have just spent traveling from point A to point B while multiple characters just talk at me because you are a silent protag and don't actually say or do anything other than fix stuff in complete silence. I feel like I could ramble on and on in circles about how much time this game wastes with pointless traveling and dialogue to a story that is mildly interesting at best and completely boring at worst only to get to puzzles that the game either holds your hand at every single individual step (go through that vent, wow this is a hallway with no other way to go but through it, hey look its a door, wow this door went here, hey look at that panel, that panel doesnt work so we should go here instead) or is the exact same fixing mechanic that has no variation at all and your inventory just becomes like 50 coins and 50 bandaids and a bunch of other junk you hold onto because you might need an acid or oil once every 10 fixes or something. I really wanted to like this game but the more I play it the more I honestly feel like I'm just doing literally nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: Normally, I'm not one to write reviews. I feel like it's an endless swamp of other people also yelling about things you most likely have very little interest in. But this game struck me in a way very few games have before. It truly feels like it left an impact on me, and I'll think about this game for a good long while. It's a fun sci-fi adventure, where you run around as a fox, which is absolutely worth bonus points. This game does so much so right, and it left me with chills at the end. All I really want to say is this; to the very small team who worked on this, it was an absolute blast, from start to finish, it's something I won't soon forget. And to the two people who actually read reviews; don't sleep on Fixfox. It's a beautiful game.

_childDocuments_.review: You play as Vix, a SPACR employee on the verge of getting fired for poor performance. The management is willing to give you one last chance – a risky mission to a faraway planet called Karamel, to fix the beacon base and re-establish communications. Despite the hangups of your hypochondriac AI companion and your history with radiation sickness, you set off on your deep-space voyage,  unaware that you'll have to fix more than just a few broken machines to get back home.So... Yeah, I just got tricked into playing a visual novel.This game advertises itself as a puzzle/adventure game, but almost all the “puzzles” are braindead easy, serving only as padding to pace out the story beats. Even with the main “fixing stuff” mechanic, the only difficulty you’ll encounter is “Oops, your inventory doesn’t have the right material to finish this job, time to backtrack to who-knows-where!”The gameplay is a muddled mess. It introduces about 20 different gameplay elements, and then proceeds to do nothing profound or compelling with any of them over the game’s 12-hour runtime. The overworld feels like a soulless randomly-generated junkyard of obstacles filled with copy-and-paste robot NPCs. Loot collection is a nothing sandwich of the same few repeating items. There are even about 5 redundant kinds of fast travel. (I once found myself hopping around to activate fast travel points – by using a different type of fast travel to hop between them. I really had to stop for a moment and ask myself what I was doing!)Looking back, I think I had more fun discovering all the quirky gameplay elements for the first time, which felt fitting for the game’s offbeat, Undertale-like sense of humor. Unfortunately, about 3 hours in, the game runs out of new ideas to show off, and it becomes an absolute chore to spend the rest of the game retreading things you’ve already seen. Still, I almost don't want to describe too much. I feel like it hits harder if you go in with no expectations.One thing I absolutely must criticize, however: the game-breaking bugs. I ran into, no joke, about 20 softlocks while playing through normally. There seems to be an issue with the “delivery drones” mechanic where they will get stuck somewhere offscreen and never finish the delivery, freezing the camera in place forever. If you’re in the ideal mentality for the game – a fox mechanic who solves problems – you might find some workarounds for a few of the softlocks. (After some experimentation, I found you can unfreeze the camera by using your sleeping bag!) Other bugs, such as one which fades the screen to black forever, have no workaround except for Alt+F4 and hoping there was an autosave recently. It’s really quite awful. Aside from the gameplay? Graphics are serviceable, but nothing special. Music is catchy, and Vix has a fantastic leitmotif that works its way into many other tracks. But the writing… yeah, it’s kind of phenomenal. I have some major respect for whoever wrote the scenario and dialogue. A good VN is one that goes for the emotional jugular, and FixFox masterfully hit home, at least to me, on at least a half-dozen occasions. Again, I’m not going to spoil too much, but you can expect a quirky, heartwarming story about AI ethics, unfixable problems, and acceptance. As a puzzle-adventure game, I’d rate this a 2 / 10 – pretty much all “gameplay” was abysmal. But as a visual novel, I’d say it hit a 7 / 10 on the scale of emotional heights. And because of that, I’m highly recommending it. And to the dev, I say: I really want to see another game from you, and I challenge you to make a really compelling puzzle game to go along with the story next time. I get the feeling you can do much better than this. (Achievement hunters: Enjoy the story, put up with the dull gameplay, and it’s a simple and straightforward 100% in 10-12 hours.)
_childDocuments_.name: FixFox

_childDocuments_.review: FixFox tries. It begins its magic act by telling you: look, here are all the ingredients for a game that will leave a permanent mark on you. A wonderful promise... but then it turns out it forgot to start the fire under its cauldron, the magic circle is sloppy and uneven, and the candles have gone out. So it runs out of mana roughly a third in.What is left, then? An okay game that's a little shallow, which I'm only recommending because it at least manages to make you really care about the characters. And the repair system is really fun. I just wish it was more robust and puzzle-like; when the magic wears out, you realise it's just a fetch quest combined with "square block in square hole". Wait, so you're recommending it or not? - I'm sure you ask. Yes, but just barely. I'll go over why, if you'd like.The very first scene in the game is a fun and heartfelt skit which explains to you how the repair system works, and establishes your relationship with Tin, your toolbox; you even get to eat a wholesome lunch. Makes you feel this happy warmth like in Wandersong, or Garden Story. This great feeling persists for quite a while.There are many things to fix, which require different kinds of breakable tools. Collecting stuff you need, trading for it, preparing for all contingencies and then fixing stuff to make people (and the devices themselves) happy - it's fun, and it promises to get more complex and involved as the game progresses.Also, everyone is so nice. Most characters in the game are robots, but that doesn't get in the way of making you feel all warm and fuzzy inside. Okay. So in order to fix the thing, you need to get this thing. Where is this thing? You need to ask NPCs. All of them interchangeable. There are so many. A faceless crowd. Okay, we got the info, let's go there. Let's traverse the wasteland. The empty, repeating, uninteresting wasteland. Oh, wow, we reached a settlement. It's different, but essentially the same. Here's the thing we needed. Now we gotta go back...Oh, okay. So it turns out we need to go to different places to set up plot devices. Cool, cool. More wasteland. Okay, done. New region? Nice. More stuff to fix. More tools. Wait, this isn't that much different. What's even the point. Oh, more plot? Cool! Let's see...What? I need to set up plot devices again? And this time with some weird puzzles? Oh man, this is not fun. Okay, I'll do this, and then we get to progress with the plot......to get more travelling, more fetch quests, more plot devices. This is starting to get really old. And now I need to do what feels like mandatory side-quests to even be able to set the up the plot devices? I don't really care that much... oh well.By then, all faults of the game are laid bare. The interchangeable NPCs. The repeating dialogue. The fake complexity of the repair system. Oh yeah: there are certain tools which have some interesting properties, f. ex. "stick". But as far as I know, the stick property never, ever gets used. Then, there are some fun puzzles in which you need to assign things according to a given category, but there's like five of them, and then they repeat. Multiple tools to achieve multiple things, and yet almost every device has the same fault. And so on. You get the picture.The plot is also a little strange. The game goes through a lot of effort to justify why people look like furries - great stuff by the way - and then puts you into a world full of robots with human faces. The pacing is also a little slow and uneven. And finally, towards the end there are some weird elements that feel not very thought over. The ending in particular has left me a little dumbfounded. Don't worry, it's all okay, just... weird, is all.In spite of all this, the game is still enjoyable to play. It's no masterpiece, but fixing stuff really put a smile on my face. There are moments when that magic feeling returns, and it makes it all worth it. In particular, this game gets an award for doing the best genderfluid protagonist. The game asks you for your pronoun in the beginning. He/she/they. Classic. A lot of games do that; but I feel like it becomes meaningless since the visual design of the characters is pretty clearly skewed towards a specific gender. Worst case, you'll please nobody; the character won't be male, or female, or even NB. Vix, on the other hand, is designed in such a way that they can believably be any gender you wish. It just works. A minor gripe I got is that the game has a quite American flavour - you have good ol' Murican farmers, apple pie, a country fair and banjo music. There's also something about the dialogue that feels American. And yet, the dev is from Czechia. I feel like we Europeans can do better than become a third-rate copy of an already omnipresent culture, and perhaps use elements from our own, often underrepresented regions.With all that said, I still recommend this game. If nothing else, it's very unique - and I hope that its formula will spread, and we'll get more games like FixFox. It could be better, sure. But it's still a pleasant experience for what it is. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: It's an ok game. It's a sort of open world top down point and click game. There are 2 main problems: for one the game is basically just tutorials. You can play this for hours and it will still introduce new mechanics with their tutorial. At some point you are supposed to stop adding new mechanics and instead expand on the existing ones. The other is the randomization. Every now and then the map is reshuffled and things are in new places which is annoying but what is totally unacceptable is that the repair jobs are also randomized. So I was fixing the zipline but needed blue glow to actually do it. So I travel to the edge of the world to get blue glow but when I come back I see that the modules have changed and now I needed a brush instead...

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to say this, but this game feels... bland and flat.It tries to offer many different gameplay systems, but fails at nearly all of them.I won't write a complete breakdown here since honestly I'd like to not spend too much time on this, so here are all the points I wrote down during my time playing it.- Main story is quite OK (but the only thing that kept me playing just to see the outcome)- Sub-plot about the 4 metacorp AIs is pretty interesting and evokes some actual thoughts about ethics, I also liked that their subjects got pretty "dark"- Anthropomorphic characters as a central story element. Who would have thought, a furry liking "furry" games, that's also one of the reasons it pains me to give it a negative review... but otherwise I would not be truthful to myself- The "Data" tab (basically an expanding encyclopedia for all the things and characters you found in the game) and Dialogue "Log" tab are both nice features to have- Zero-G sections in and around space stations were cool- The music is nice (but gets a tad repetitive ingame)- The art and artstyle: It's... functional. But nothing to write home about.Pretty shader effects or other eye candy are not present. The textures look rather blurry and flat.Myself being someone that can only script/program some small stuff but has no knack for art, I can relate to that however.I wouldn't be able to do any better honestly without years and years of practice, so I'd say this point is neutral.- Most dialogue feels to forcedly quirky- Robot characters (i.e. about 99% of characters) feel dull and look ridiculous and kinda boring- Camera is often much too zoomed in while on foot or follows your character in very weird ways, obscuring what you actually want to look at (although that's somewhat rare fortunately)- Repair mechanics with "random" items had me intrigued at the beginning but it is very under-utilized and too simple in the long run. Before too long your inventory will be cluttered with everything you ever need, which is less than you might think. For every repair option there's maybe 2-3 different items you'll be using all the time.- Traders are utterly useless, in all the cases where I tried using them because I needed something, they were out of stock...- "Pirates" and "Order" faction system has no real impact because the alert counters can just be reset all the time, this also lead to the situation where I never needed to use any of the stickers or puzzle items, so I don't even know what they would be doing. I suppose they kept both factions off your "valueable" items if they did get ahold of you (which never happens)- Item identification seems shoehorned in. Why do I need to consult an "Oracle" to know that a stone is heavy or an apple is round?- Too many useless movement systems, I never used Zipline stations or "Underbolts" or whatever they were called, since by that point the best transportation system is already much better and available everywhere- Main gameplay is too repetitive, everything feels like a chore and unrewarding including the "puzzles" like the frequent visits to junkyards or installing scanning nodes, which leads all of it to lose it's steam pretty early in- Periodical "world scramble" after story events, basically reshuffling the randomized sectors of the world, which is completely pointless- The character running got a stamina system only towards the end of the game, before that you could run endlessly (not that it was particularly fast in the first place). This is story related but doesn't really add anything of value other than to annoy.- There were multiple points in the game where I either zoned out or almost fell asleep, there also were multiple occasions where I just quit for the day to play another game just because there was another set of repetitive main story tasks (before the interesting stuff happens) I didn't feel like doing.All this combined leads to a game that feels "flat" all around with it's core gameplay, which is a fatal mistake. A game must have a satisfying and rewarding main gameplay loop, which is absent here.It led me to force myself to play through it just to see what the ending was.Slight spoiler alert: Ending is not too great and is one of a few common tropes.More spoilery, it's this trope: The potential this game had with it's setting would be great, but is sadly not acted upon very much.If there is ever a FixFox 2, I'd like to see many of the negative points reworked in meaningful ways, then it could be a genuinely cool experience.But as it stands for now, I cannot with good conscience give this a recommendation sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: ~12h 1/10 1 You don't need a guide No No No No No No No No difficulty setting, there are no enemies NoFixFox is a lovely topdown game with an addictive loop of finding items, repairing stuff and so finding bigger items and fixing bigger stuff. You'll find an awesome story in Fixfox which I really enjoyed and it was also lovely that you helpful abilities later on in the game so you don't have to go look for the early items again when they break. This game gripped me from the moment I started playing. I enjoy games in which you fix things (especially Assemble with Care) and clean stuff. IRL I hate it, but in games, it feels so satisfying! I also love how you get more and more tools to make the inconveniences easier later on, and how from very early on you can track easily where to go for the next objective. I never felt lost, always had a goal to work toward, and always was invested in the story and how this world became what it is! At one point I got a bit bored with fixing stuff, as the game mechanic kinda stays the same, but gladly soon after that feeling came up, the game gave an option to make it easier to fix things. That was the right timing to get that upgrade! Another thing I struggled with is that I picked up way too many items and my inventory always was a mess. Some sort of "sort function" would have been helpful, but this is completely my fault as I'm the typical gamer who picks up and carries everything. When you're playing this, know that you don't have to pick up everything! The achievements in FixFox are very straightforward. Almost all of them are story-related, none are missable because you can replay a chapter and the only chapter you have to make a choice between 2 things for the achievements is in the last chapter (which is only a few minutes long). There are achievements for picking up items from holes on the map and for wild jobs, know that you'll get already a lot by just playing the game without focusing on those. I would recommend doing a wild job when you come by one while going through the main story. Small note: you have to fix those wild jobs manually to let them count toward the achievement. Bonus points for the dev to add trackers to the achievements, so you can see how far you are with those achievements. All in all, Fixfox is a lovely game, with no real cons for me. Lovely story with an awesome gameplay loop and just so much fun!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game extensively I can really recommend it! It is the kind of game I have long been looking for: something to clear without violence or fighting, without rushing, something I can sink in after a long day at work - without difficult puzzles or constant challenges. A lot to read about relatable characters, heartfelt stories of people missing their friends or their past. Or bringing sheep in to the cinema, oh my god this game can really make you laugh! I wish there were more games like this. The graphics - as conceived - are really great, and the soundtrack is so amazing we had to purchase it so we could play it at home on repeat. You can even choose which gender your character will have. The only thing that let me a bit down was the ending, yeah I was also expecting something else. Still this game really needs more love. Hope the developer will make another one soon! =)If you're tired of constant challenges and want some chill and love, this is your game! <3
_childDocuments_.name: FixFox

_childDocuments_.review: FixFox is a pretty good game! It has a nice art style and music that I quite enjoyed listening to the entire way through. FixFox has a lot of love behind it. Sadly, there are a couple faults that do hold this game back from being a truly great game. As stated much by other people, FixFox is quite repetitive. Even within the story, it has you doing the same tasks over and over. Not that any of it is difficult or even annoying, just rather mundane by the redundancy. Even the core gameplay loop got repetitive because each 'new' mechanic are always a tiny variation of what you already know.Another point of contention is that the central gameplay loop of fixing things does not vary a whole lot throughout the game and gives no challenge whatsoever. Since it is a cozy game, having no challenge is completely expected. However, the lack of problem-solving in fixing machines on a foreign planet gives no sense of real impact. You don't feel like you're ever truly fixing anything, so even by the end, the gameplay loop feels rather meaningless.With both of my critiques, this game was still a ton of fun, and I did enjoy going through it to completion! I recommend this game if you do want a cozy game that has a strong story and interesting aesthetics. I wager it is worth the price, it's worth supporting indie devs anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: FixFox

_childDocuments_.review: FixFox is a fun if disappointing game. It's a game with a pretty fun premise, an engaging gameplay loop, and characters that I rather enjoyed, but I was disappointed with where it took the premise, how much the game seemed scared of its own gameplay and did what it could to keep the player from having to do it, and how much the characters were kind of shoehorned into various forms of social commentary.There's not really any side content, everything you can do off the main story is just half minute repair jobs that are randomly generated and exist just to convert materials into other materials.I had a good time with FixFox and if you have a few days to kill and want to play as a pixelated fox going around exploring and fixing machinery, I recommend it. Just don't go into it expecting much out of the story or gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: FixFox

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an amazing treasure found in a Steam Next Fest event for those who searched through variety of genres. The description and screenshots does give you some context, but it barely scratches the surface... the experience you get in-game is unmatched.The overall feel of the game is nicely done with a few things such as sporting a cute theme while casting a diverse set of memorable characters in a vibrant sci-fi theme, putting little to no pressure on the player for stress-free casual gameplay, and unique mechanics (and yes, that includes the inventory system, which intregates flawlessly into core gameplay)! You'll also love the soundtrack composed by Aleix Ramon as most of the tracks gives off gentle vibes while still being in place, while fitting the scenery as needed.While the game isn't perfect since I did get lost a few times, and couldn't figure out how to make quest waypoints reappear for reminder purposes, it doesn't stop the fact that this game is well crafted with fine details to be found as you play.It makes me quite happy to see a game made by a small team with passion and love. For that reason, I would like to thank the people working at Rendlike for this gem, it's worth every penny.I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys adventure games, especially without a discount. You'll love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird game, because it's not bad per se, but it has a lot of weird choices throughout. At first it was cool, you go around the place doing little jobs and progressing the story, but eventually the missions for the main quest start to repeat over and over again, its just the same thing, several times: - Find some weird clue, but you need to activate 4 places in the map to have more range on the radars or something- you find the places, activate the mindcarts, return and find something orbiting the planet - Inspect some sort of abandoned spaceship or station, find another clue that leads you to another map- Find something random that needs a specific giant robot - Go through the map finding the pieces of the giant robot in junkyards- Assemble giant robot, unblock the next part, and find another weird clue- repeat several times through the gameThis loops at least 4 times, and each time you spend 2 hours aprox doing all of this. While this happens, you read a lot of long and boring dialogs that have little to do with the main story, find hundreds of objects in the wild, avoid pointless pirates and the other dudes that take objects from you if you repair too many things (Which is a pointless mechanic because i only got caught once after i had a 10 minutes cinematic and forgot the amount of things i found before), travel giant empty spaces with generic npcs (They all have the same dialog options), useless traders ( i wasn't able to trade a single thing in the entire game, they were all empty), repair things that let you fast travel from one place to the other (which, again, it's pointless because you already have the drones that do a better job at fast travel, and they don't require fixing), use vending machines that only give you coins and bandaids (which are the most predominant objects in the entire game), and sometimes you eat something while an npc talks to you about random things. Another complain i have its the journal, which is pointless because they usually explain the next part of the quest in a massive wall of dialog and if you don't play attention, you are bassically lost in this limbo because the journal its super vague. At first, i just travelled around the planet repairing stuff because i didn't notice the next mission in the journal, which wasn't explained at all and i wasn't sure what was i supposed to be doing next. Besides all of this, i found several bugs that made me reset the game because the screen was locked and didn't follow the character. Also, eventually you don't even need to repair broken objects or even collect stuff, they just give things for free, BUT, weirdly, you loose the ability to run for too long, because now you are sick and you get tired faster (???)Overall, this game is just not good. The art is okey, and the gameplay has a lot of potential, but its riddled with weird choices, its unbalanced, pointless, buggy, boring, repetitive, sometimes tedious, it offers no challenge whatsoever, and almost all of the characters are annoying, except Vix, the main character, because he doesn't talk at all. Massive downer, it looked fun at first, but became an marathon of patience.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a good story and outstanding cinematography. I played the demo of this a while back and was happy that I was able to pick up right where I left off on launch day. Really love all the robots and the camera work is outstanding! _childDocuments_.review: I picked up FixFox during the 2023 summer sale. I would recommend this game but I will couch my recommendation.While I put in 20ish hours playing this game, as I like to poke around in games, if I was to replay the game I know it would take 12-14 hours to complete. In talking about this game with my teens, the best way I described it was that it was a novice/beginner puzzle game. This is a game I would use to introduce a younger child to the concepts of puzzle games. It provides all the skills that a new player would need to get into these kind of games. For very experienced puzzle game players this game will come across as too 'on the rails'. It is a very liner story with some bouncing around between areas to acquire components/resources to complete tasks. The story is good, as long as you are not expecting anything too grand. A line from the game's launch trailer says, "Go on a peaceful journey," and that is what this game is, a peaceful journey.For a one man studio this is a well done game and it was worth the price of admission to become a Spacr.

_childDocuments_.review: Really charming and cozy game with a story that... takes some turns, in an interesting and maybe slightly less cozy way. And the gameplay is real chill but engaging, exploring the various zones, fixing stuff with makeshift tools, solving puzzles, it's got a compelling gameplay loop that doesn't ever get stale. I will say there's a bit of a mechanic pileup going on - three of the four giant mechs basically work exactly the same as far as puzzles are concerned, and there's like, three different methods of fast travel where one of them is useless the moment you unlock it but e h h more options are better than less options, I guess! I'm also not 100% sure how I feel about the ending but it's... interesting. I don't really have many criticisms in general though, there's just a lot to like here and I can't say I've ever played a game quite like it either, hope this doesn't go overlooked.

_childDocuments_.review: Very tentative recommendation. What's sold as a cute and charming game about fixing stuff and making friends gradually loses steam--the puzzles are all very similar and repetitious, they don't get any harder or more interesting as the game progresses, collecting improvised tools with different properties is an interesting premise but never really explored--and is eventually almost completely discarded in favor of a linear VN where you occasionally have to poke at stuff. The story itself is pretty interesting, essentially a cautionary tale about rampant ai born from mass consumerism with a healthy dose of full-blown transhumanism. There's a lot to like here idea-wise, but unfortunately it just doesn't coalesce with the gameplay quite as well as you'd hope. So while it does deliver on the promise of a chill, friend-fixing adventure, the satisfaction of fixing *everything* in a meaningful way, through gameplay, isn't quite there.Mechanically, it feels like a missed opportunity, but still worth a try if the vibe seems appealing.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to explain, but I quite enjoyed FixFox. I think it charmed me. If you're gonna like the game, I think you're going to like it for the style and the writing. The gameplay is cute with some fun ideas, but it gets same-y very often. Lots of repetition. If you're cool with casual games that are a lot of the same thing over and over, you can enjoy this game. There were several bugs I encountered. When doing certain actions, if you tried to do something else too fast, the game would softlock. This, I suspect, is due to the game never leaving the animation state for the first action. This prevents screen movement and limits other certain commands. Most of the time this can be fixed by saving, quitting to menu, and reloading. A few times this did softlock me where I couldn't save and I lost some progress. The ending won't be for everyone, as it uses a trope that is kind of controversial. I didn't mind it too much since there *were* some hints here and there. I binged through this game 100% in 10 hours. It's very much not a perfect game, but it's one I enjoyed. It left me wishing for some more, but it was impressive for a pretty much one-man project. I'll be interested to see what comes from Rendlike next.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice story all around.  While simple the fix puzzles are fun.  I like the idea you lose your main tools and have to find substitutes. You get these tunnels for your scooter, to jump over mountains as you search but it feels more like a fix of the map generator. _childDocuments_.review: TL/DR: Don't be fooled by the cute little demo, the style is accurate but the gameplay quickly becomes annoying. Maybe in a more engaging game I'd be more frustrated and work harder to find a solution.  But it's just.....meh.  Otherwise, they're mechanics that don't make too much sense (why in some cases do you have to put things in containers one at a time, but others they go in or out all at once?), badly explained or just don't seem to work (if you have 1 stash until pirates come, do they come at that one or after?  And sometimes the count reset doesn't work, the pirates come next time anyway), or are just irritating (if I have 6 of a tool that fulfills the function, just let me automatically use it, don't make me go into the inventory, select it, push it out, use it, manually unequip it, etc.)   And both the pirates and Tools order coming and randomly stealing some amount of my stuff has only happened a few times, 2 of which were scripted, and it's already not scary or exciting or making me engaged by trying to outwit the count or anything, it's just ANNOYING.  And I'm already wanting all the little cute animations that happen EVERY TIME I do anything to stop and let me move on, the story is already going too slow. _childDocuments_.review: I read some good reviews, so I had high expectations, but I give a 3/5. Just to balance the Over-Hype.Fixfox works hard to give a nod to the nostalgia of computing in the 70's. You will love the memories it brings back. It lifts a lot of the console gadgetry experience of yore and brings it into the game, but sadly I think it's lost on the younger target audience. It has an adult underlying theme too, also lost on younger audiences. Fixfox is not as polished as the games we played on those 8-bit consoles were. And although it has that cool 8-bit graphics look to it and very slick animations, it's really not as finished as it could be. However Fixfox is still really a great game for young kids to play. Because if you have played as many games as I have, it's just more of the same, click click click until your fingers get tired. Kids love that kind of stuff though.There are many tiny inconsistencies that you only notice when you look for them, like how the rotating gantry puzzle to get to Baizy the computer stays rotated after the "unspliced" escapes from the cryopod, the gantry stays rotated. How did the unspliced human you just defrosted get out of the room??? Why not add a small puzzle so that Vix has to turn the gantry around again? Tiny little things like this broke the otherwise pretty plausible realism for me. Loot caches for example are another breaker, there are just too many of them...is nice and smooth, it builds your knowledge in lessons and you kind of level up as you go along in terms of interactions you can do, and kinds of tools you are allowed to use. There is none of the mouse jankiness that retro games have. Okay, so the puzzles are nice and kids will enjoy them, but if you are not a kid anymore, then the repeated delays between dialogs, and having to click all the time will drive you nuts. Especially that one when you have to go to sleep at night, it's just a delay, no need to make it an annoying wait for the lights to dim. The puzzles are not really enough, and boredom will set in in the very much samey maps which are quite small really. Because lets face it, it's a very simple game and you are free to explore the tiny maps for as long as you like between quests. Dialog feels stilted, almost as if they tried to dumb it down for a younger audience. On the plus side, it has a lot of story and culture. There are space pirates, there are space nerds, and both are little evil, but in a nice way. There is an underlying humans versus machines thing going on, and that is very very well done I have to say, even the unspliced "smoothface" versus "furface" hinting at racial divides being so artificial is a great thought provoker. I for example can see the pirates and the tool nerds in modern society as Democrats and Republicans in a way. There is un-mined gold in the storyline. I felt like I was Buck Rogers in the 25th century carrying a paranoid doctor Theopolis about. I think kids will love gathering the parts of the back story, I just wish they wrote a nicer dialog presentation system and got someone to write more actual "lore". The flyer the pirates hand out just fails to cut it as actual lore. That would definitely have played to the more senior players like myself too. Especially if the script was more edgy and dark. Although that might be my age colouring my perception. The character development and denizens you have to interact with, are unfortunately all a little bit of tin, literally. I like the positive "try to help" theme of the story; especially how even someone inept, but with a good heart will end up being more help than hindrance in the long run. Something this world sorely needs.You can choose to be nice and help lots of people, but doing so has no greater a reward than if all you do is fix one machine per game-day or if you fix four or five. This is not really a choices-matter game like I had hoped. If you are over 16 years old, this game will bore you, and if you are younger, then the really well executed 8-bit era feel will be lost on you anyway, so I cannot grasp who this game was targeted at. Which is a pity, because if the dialogues were energised a bit more, then this would be a killer.Personally, I did enjoy the game, and if you did too, check out some of these

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and original idea weighed down by clunky mechanics and time wasters. Have fun constantly traveling to reset two different "doom counters", or have your inventory stolen. Travel to the nearest hub to get it identified. Travel through a dead wasteland that constantly puts up roadblocks in your way, forcing you to traverse around them. Can't have you going somewhere fast, after all. And while you do that, you'll have to constantly jump off and on your speeder, accompanied by an animation that prohibits input while it's playing. Why get of? Scavenging, of course. Which also presents the loot in an animation prohibting movement. Fun for the first two times, after that you'll be button mashing hoping to be able to skip it. _childDocuments_.review: It's a cute concept, and the art and story are charming, but ultimately I found it unsatisfying.Most of the "puzzles" are really fetch-quests for collectibles: You need a specific type of tool in order to do whatever arbitrary thing is required to fix this gadget. Some of them make sense, such as "Cut power, fix this wire, then restore power" or "unscrew this module to clean off the dust from the fans". But others are complete nonsense, probably intended to be funny but not very amusing to me, such as "feed the robot mouth a specific flavor of glowing goop" or "tape the robot mouth shut so it will stop jabbering". Because you need so many tools of various different types (and each one is typically only good for a few uses before it breaks; they don't make stuff like they used to, I guess!), most of the effort is actually spent gathering tools, and then manually sorting through your toolbox to find the tools you've gathered (because it is presented as a physical space with stuff stacked on top of each other, which is sort of neat in theory, but also means you can't sort, filter, or search for anything---it's like a real toolbox, ). There are a few actual puzzles that require some problem-solving, but they are relatively few and also not especially interesting.The characters are delightful, the setting is intriguing, and the story about the history of AI and furmods is compelling, but in order to get this story you need to slog through a huge number of these totally arbitrary repair quests. "Repairing" things is the core gameplay loop, but it doesn't feel at all like repairing things or solving problems. It feels like getting a list of tools you need, then following arbitrary nonsense instructions with those tools. The world map keeps randomly changing at each story milestone, which is both annoying from a gameplay perspective and immersion-breaking from a story perspective. (It also seems difficult to code... so, uh,  What is the upside here!?) If the tectonics on this planet are that volatile, earthquakes and lava should have wiped us all out by now. Maybe they were trying to artificially extend the "exploration" part of the game---but exploration isn't fun when you're just trying to figure out where that same stupid town wandered off to this time.If you like the idea of traveling long distances to scour a randomly-rearranging world for coins, band-aids, postage stamps, and spatulas, then using them to complete random, arbitrary sequences of tasks that often involve utter nonsense, you might enjoy . But me, I gave it a few hours and ultimately just got bored.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad leaving this review because I can tell this game is a labor of love. I wish the developer the best, but I have to be honest in expressing my dissatisfaction with this game. Bear in mind I did not complete the game and instead refunded it, though from what I understand I made it around half the game's playtime before giving up so I think I gave it a fair shake.I picked up FixFox for $5 during the Anthrofest sale. I have to say I think $5 is about the right price for the game as opposed to its normal $15 asking price, but even the discount was not enough to get me to put more than a few hours into the game. Here's why.Putting it bluntly, the game has nothing to keep me interested. It is weak in both narrative and gameplay, at least in my opinion. Normally a game weak in one department makes up for it by being strong in the other, but FixFox fails in both.I will say the gameplay is definitely the worst of the two. In my 3 hours of playtime, the vast majority of my time was spent traversing an empty, largely non-interactive open world picking up garbage which I used to solve menial, uninteresting puzzles. To be more specific, the core gameplay loop revolves around you fixing broken machines. To do so, you need "tools", which are mostly improvised items you use to jury-rig a fix that you get through looting, trading, or skyrim style radiant quests. Yes that is about as mind numbing as it sounds. The kind of puzzles you solve are extremely simple and worse than that, repetitive. Within the first few fixes, I had seen every problem the game threw at me for the first 3 chapters. I cannot emphasize enough how boring it is to just slap a bandaid on a broken wire or unscrew a panel to solve the same logic puzzle over... and over... and over again.Gameplay aside, I am not a fan of the writing either. To be fair I think the worldbuilding and storytelling is serviceable, but I was turned off immediately by the character writing, or lack thereof. As a silent protagonist, the main character doesn't meaningfully contribute anything to character interactions, but their AI toolbox buddy sure does. I imagine this won't be inherently true for everyone, but I found Tin to be extremely annoying. His personality was grating and his attempts at being quirky and funny all fell flat, and seeing as he is constantly talking in lieu of the main character, this is a problem. He is also the vehicle through which the player is handheld through a lot of the early game, which given how trivial the puzzles were was completely unnecessary, and is made even more annoying that way. I genuinely think the game would be far more tolerable if Tin was absent and the main character was effectively a mute, a more genuine blank slate for the player to insert themselves into, rather than eye-rolling every time Tin mentions to be careful about SpAcE vAmPiRes.Aside from Tin, most of the other characters I encountered in my time were fairly generic robots that served a single purpose within the narrative, then immediately became brick walls after. Many will not even talk to you again after they fulfill this purpose. This had me completely disinterested in the world since, despite having an interesting premise, I didn't feel attached to anyone in it.I do feel there are good ideas at play here, but they have all been poorly realized. Overall the caliber of writing and gameplay might lend themselves well to a younger person just beginning to explore gaming, but I think anyone who's fully developed and has played other titles in the same genre will find this game uninteresting. TLDR: The gameplay is boring and the characters aren't interesting. I couldn't get past the 3 hour mark. There are better chill games out there, go play those instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there, fellow furries and gamers! It's your friendly alpha male ice wolf, Kiba Snowpaw, straight from the icy realm of HowlStrom. Today, I’m diving into , a delightful indie game that's been warming hearts across the galaxy. Using everyday items like coins and bandages to fix machines adds a quirky twist that's both amusing and inventive.Developed by Rendlike and published by Joystick Ventures,  is a passion project from solo developer Jaroslav Meloun. Inspired by a visit to the Peace Memorial in Hiroshima and a personal vow to create non-violent games, Meloun crafted a game that emphasizes kindness and friendship. The game’s music was composed by Aleix Ramon, and the key art was created by Jana Kilianová, adding to the game's wholesome and creative atmosphere.  offers a mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and item management. The chiptune soundtrack complements the game's lighthearted tone, making the experience even more enjoyable. While the main story is linear, the game’s charm and numerous side activities offer plenty of reasons to revisit. Collecting all the different tools and experiencing the various interactions with the planet's inhabitants add layers of depth to the game.-  The protagonist, a space mechanic with a passion for fixing things and a kind heart. The combination of exploration, puzzle-solving, and narrative keeps the gameplay engaging and varied. leaves a lasting impression with its heartwarming story, charming characters, and innovative gameplay. The game's emphasis on kindness and non-violence offers a refreshing change from the typical action-heavy titles, making it a standout experience.The hook of  lies in its unique premise of a space mechanic using everyday items to fix machines. The thesis revolves around the themes of friendship, ingenuity, and the power of kindness. Every puzzle solved and every friendship forged reinforces these themes, making for a deeply satisfying experience.- Unique and charming gameplay mechanics.- Heartwarming story and characters.- Beautiful pixel art and engaging soundtrack.- High replay value with various side activities.- Some puzzles can become repetitive over time.- The linear nature of the main story might not appeal to all players.- Occasional navigation issues with the scooter and map. As an ice wolf with a love for heartwarming tales,  was a delightful journey. The game’s blend of exploration, puzzle-solving, and storytelling kept me engaged from start to finish. The unique use of everyday items for repairs and the charming interactions with robot characters were definite highlights. The game's art and music added to the overall immersive experience. The occasional repetition in puzzles and some minor navigation issues were the only drawbacks in an otherwise stellar game. is a gem in the indie game world. While it shares the charm and creativity of these titles, its focus on non-violent problem-solving and friendship sets it apart. is a delightful and heartwarming adventure that’s perfect for gamers looking for a unique and wholesome experience. The "moral of the story" can be a bit heavy-handed sometimes.  But I overall enjoyed it...except the ending CHEESED ME OFF.  Maybe just, stop playing the game the MOMENT the planetary jumpgate activates, save yourself from knowing the official ending.SPOILERSSPOILERSSPOILERSOk, so I strongly dislike that it ended with it all being a dream, "sorta maybe".  Even if it seems kinda clever in retrospect, like haha, dream tapes amirite?  :|  But no.  It invalidates whatever meaning the story had, making it yet another level fake-er, for whatever that's worth.  Not even real in its own fictional setting. _childDocuments_.review: Initially very cute and interesting, setting up some potentially fun and tricky mechanics. But the game constantly undoes everything it throws at you. It feels like there was a bunch of great ideas and as development went along the developers became scared of how the game played even though under the surface there IS a fun game. Examples: - 2 groups that will steal items from you after you do certain actions. Sounds fun, something to be wary of. However you can ensure the groups only steal their favorite things (stickers and puzzles) by having them in your inventory. The game THROWS these items at you constantly so the stealing things will never be a worry, but also resets the counter constantly so I only encountered the groups once in the entire game and my inventory was brimming with items to keep them away. - An interesting fast travel system you have to fix that sends you to designated points. Before I even got a chance to fix it the game throws an instantaneous fast travel system at you that negates the other one by being more efficient and brings you literally everywhere instead of designated points.  These and other things make the game more tedious than fun. There's no challenge. Every puzzle is the same. I got to the fourth round of junkyard puzzles and just had to stop because any joy of surprise or discovery was totally gone. I've never experienced a game that felt terrified of itself before.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unexpected game - going in, one might expect a goofy-colored soft drink, but it's more like taking in an entire holiday feast through a straw. It is a game about how brokenness is a matter of state, but fixing is a matter of action. It is a game about the transitional nature of data and self. It is a game about passing along knowledge and improving things by tiny yet measurable increments. It is a game about unification - both the collection of things that make people, and the collection of people that make up a group. It is a game about growing, with both its regrets and its joys, and the fact that some homes are given, while some homes are made.What does it mean to "consume" something, to use a hammer to drive nails until it can no longer function, or to eliminate food and augment the body? Can the act of healing a wounded hand improve other parts as well? Where do the influences of what is hated, and what is loved, come from... and how should we tend to each?B for innovation and simple but fairly compelling gameplay, A for story and writing, A++ for "freakishly in-depth epiphanies were not expected on this road, would epiphany again."

It's opened up, and led me to different regions and tasks.  And while on one side you could call these things predictable, they're also innovative at times, but fundamentally, they're also fun.Nothing is too taxing, nothing requires a faq to be open, and if something can't be solved, you can normally figure it out with very little effort.  As I play this game, I'm amazed how polished it seems for just one person to create, and for that it can only be praised.  No crashes, no janking Ux, just a game doing what it's supposed to do.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a game that I had found through one of the Steam Next Fest events prior to its release.  A demo had been released at that point, and while I didn't love it immediately upon opening up the game, it was one that grew on me fairly quickly.  This is one of the few games that I ended up purchasing on release day since it had stuck with me so much.Your character, Vix, is a genderfluid fox-human accompanied by a backpack loaded with an AI that works as an astronaut / mechanic for a space program.  From there you get a mission to fix a beacon and start your first mission clear on the other side of the universe.  There are no people on this planet, only androids and the AI metas that accompanied you there, and no way to get a signal out to Earth.  From there, Vix has to get the signals up and running, though there are several other factors that end up being at play.I loved the artstyle of the game from the moment I opened the demo, though I did not really enjoy the execution.  I'm not a huge fan of bird's-eye view games, so finding that this game used that was ever so slightly off-putting.  However, the design of the game itself did win me over, with the cute designs of the bots down to each unique location on the map.  I loved all the emoticons that each character would give, from the loading circle on their faces, to the floating hearts.  Many of them even had quirks that made them different from the others, like their love for ice cream, or their flock of sheep, many even had a passion for cooking (many of the meals I would love to try in reality)!  Now the soundtrack wasn't something I was necessarily fond of, and its monotony sometimes grew tiresome, but it was a very calming and relaxed tone for a majority of it.  Of course, there was different music for the driving points of the story, but the traveling music was similar enough to each other I did eventually grow old of listening to it.The biggest reasons that I stayed with this game for so long were how the repairs were made and the storyline itself.  As a computer tech, I loved seeing how unique it was being able to fix technology using quarters and bananas and toothbrushes.  The further into the game, the harder some of the repairs would be.  They added in scent-bots and taste-bots that were sometimes needed for repairs.  You could have a honey-dipped cookie, a ketchup-dipped pepper, or a jasmine-scented feather duster.  Every area gave you a different mechanic that would follow you for the remainder of the game which I thought was unique.  Now the storyline was one that I really enjoyed.  While the game started as a simple "you have to fix something to gather data" it became something much heavier.  You learn about different topics that relate to our reality through Medico, Lexico, Nutriko, and Naviko.  Each has a compelling story warning us about issues we currently deal with and the consequences of their actions.  You learn about how the opinions of others can traumatize and hurt others, and how the cards dealt in life can cause some people to take drastic measures.  It kept my attention, though I did fall out of playing it for a few months and found my love for this game again recently.  I absolutely would play this game again for the storyline itself.My biggest issue with the game other than it being a bird's-eye view game was the difficulty in regathering information.  You as the player really need to pay attention to the dialogue of the game so you know where your next direction is.  My biggest piece of advice is pay the most attention when you are eating meals prepared for you.  The bots that give you the food give you valuable information that will help you get out of binds.  There were a few different times where I got stuck and wasn't sure where to move forwards from since there is no way to reread the information provided to you.  There is no dialogue log that saves that information, nor can you speak to the bot that gave you that information again.  Please please please make sure you notate whatever tips and tricks the game hands to you because you will use it.  Other than that one issue, I absolutely loved the game and would highly recommend playing it if given the chance.  The game has content to keep everyone happy for hours, and all of the achievements are achievable for those that are completionists.  This game is worth every penny I spend for it, and I am so glad I was able to finally finish this game and learn the story.

I call that good game design.Overall, I found FixFox a very enjoyable game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Short Version:Furry solves racism with the power of mechanical engineering.The Long Version:While I am fairly mixed when it comes to this game, I'd say I would recommend it. Some people say the story was "ruined" by the ending, and it was "all over the place", but really all of it connected in a meaningful way. Not to say you need to be some kind of philosophy major to get it but you do need to read the dialogue. I do however agree with the repetitiveness. Most of the game was doing 4 things, and then doing another 4 things. It could definitely be better than that, but really that's the only problem I see with it, besides the fact that the repairs don't necessarily get harder in higher tiers, they just require special tools. I feel like higher tier repairs should have more things to do on them to make them harder. The maps shuffling and cluttered inventory are only moderate inconveniences, that are only magnified by your laziness. The game gives you the option to sort your inventory however you wish, and if it's cluttered, that's kind of your fault. The map shuffling offers to make going back and looking for things more interesting than just going to the same map and going to the same spots. But with all this said, I enjoyed playing it. I think others might enjoy it to. Not every game will be perfect. Every game will have a bad review. Every game will have a flaw. To say these flaws mean you should "stay away from this game" is  Whether you enjoy the game or not is up to YOU, not some random person on the internet.

_childDocuments_.review: it's the future. we've become a spacefaring civilisation. everyone is a robot or a furry now, for very important plot reasons. you're Vix, a fox-human tasked with fixing a disconnected beacon on the planet KR84-M3L "Karamel."in the marketing for the game, Vix is given she/her pronouns, but you actually explicitly choose between he, she, and they pronouns at the beginning of the game. you even choose whether you're left- or right-handed, which affects the cursor in the UI.this game is one of the most cozy and wholesome games I've ever played.at a low level, you run around the planet fixing random machines with a variety of "tools" found hidden in the ground or gifted in exchange for fixing people's machines. there are some rather nice puzzles sprinkled around the map that are fun, but not too hard.at a high level, you're travelling the planet and exploring its secrets in an effort to reconnect it with the outside world. you learn more about the main character Vix, your AI companion Tin, the "metacorporations" at your employer SPACR, and multiple other interesting characters who you'll meet throughout the game.I'd describe the setting as a "dyst-hope-ia," in the sense that it takes place in a future where people have experienced extreme hardship and tragedy, but manage to live happily regardless. the story is extremely well-written and even hours after finishing it, I can't stop thinking about it.I don't want to say anything specific to avoid spoilers, but treat this as a soft content warning: the game is about fixing, but not just like, toasters and lamps. by the end, I cried so hard my face hurt, but I say that in an extremely positive way.the game is relatively short, and you could finish it in a long weekend. I cannot recommend it enough
_childDocuments_.name: FixFox

_childDocuments_.review: It is a very cute game, even if I couldn't help but think of it more as FixCorgi due to the way the main character looks in game (no tail, not very fox-faced, more tan then red).  It reminds me a little of SpiritFarer, in that it's one of those games where you travel around and perform more or less the same task over and over again.  Unlike SpiritFarer, there is no base building aspect at all; it is sort of like, drive around, collect items, then use those items to solve problems.However, unlike some of those games, this game steadily unlocks things that make your life easier.  For example, there are many different fast travel options, and towards the end of the game, you get options to auto-solve puzzles and auto-collect goodies.  As you go forward in the game, the repetative nature of the game play is made milder by the enhancements you get, and they do try their best to make the last few puzzles a bit more interesting within the limits of the game engine.Also, while there is a lot of going back and forth between locations, the developers wisely give you the option to basically teleport back when the story wants you to return back to base.  A lot of games don't do this kind of thing, and make the back and forth incredibly tedious (I'm looking at Rustler for example).  The developers behind FixFox do a really good job at minimizing the tedium in what could easily be a tedious game if done incorrectly, and it's something I rarely see.  I really commend them for it!All the while, it's got an interesting story and a lot to dig into story-wise in general.  Overall, I'd say it's worth playing if you'd like a chill game, I'd buy it full price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting little project.  Quaint, homey, very very niche.I'd say if you're queer, trans, aspiring cyborg or splicer or both, posthuman, heck even furry in general to an extent:  THIS STORY IS SPECIFICALLY FOR YOU.  If not, play it anyway!  You might discover a few things about yourself. ;3  The ending might be a bit polarizing, but it's the kind of thing that gets you thinking, in a good way.The gameplay?  Very cute and simple and straightforward, basically exploration and puzzles.  My only complaint is that it's generally very, VERY easy and the mid-game drags a fair bit (particularly as you start learning the AIs' backstories).Were it a AA studio like the one behind Slime Rancher, I'd question why they couldn't tighten up that part just a bit.  But for a single-dev project, this is amazing.
