_childDocuments_.review: If you have not played the mod or the original 2013 release of The Stanley Parable… boy, do I envy you. But anyway, this game is a story exploration title, that is well aware that it’s a game. Back when the genre of these story exploration titles (aka “walking simulators”) was appearing, The Stanley Parable was a fresh take on the idea, where the interactivity of the game, the ideas of “choice” and “free will”, and the relationship of a creator with the audience and its creation were central. Everything that you do (well, mostly) has some sort of an in-game reaction and many things lead to unexpected “endings” in this otherwise never-ending experience.Ultra Deluxe builds on top of the already existing structure, exploring even more variations, more topics and providing the developers themselves to have the game tell about the experience of making and releasing the game. And it’s fantastic, funny and a bit sad at times, with good memorable moments and a lot of things that still feel fresh. Though, I have to warn that if this is your first experience with The Stanley Parable, I’d avoid the “new content” until you’ve played the game a few times.Or even play this after you’ve played the original. This new version, while having “more”, doesn’t fully “supersede” the original release. A few elements were tweaked, the wonderful original demo version (that is a unique game in itself) is not included… Unless, it’s hidden under many layers of other stuff, as this game loves to do occasionally. So there’s still a case to get the original, if you haven’t. Though, only this version is available on so many different platforms, thanks to the engine switch.I wish I could sound super excited, because The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is a blast. It’s just that I’ve played the original versions so much and currently have so many things to worry about, that the new release isn’t getting me as mesmerized as I would be without the prior experience with the old releases. Still, this might be different for you, even if you’ve played the old versions. And if you’ve never experienced The Stanley Parable before – most definitely play it now.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the review of a game called The Stanley Parable, and while I'd love to write the whole review as if I were the narrator, I lack the ingenuity and wit to do so, which is why I'll stop now, and proceed with a proper review. So, what is The Stanley Parable, you might be asking? Well, it's a game about choice... Wait a minute, didn't I do this already? Ah, right, this is not the review of The Stanley Parable, as I'm proud to introduce the updated and renovated Ultra Deluxe Review for The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe!And what can I say about such an Ultra Deluxe version? Well, pretty much the same things I said about the original game, so I'll keep some copy-pasted paragraphs, rewrite them here and there, and hope people don't notice it (even though I'm saying what I'm gonna do!).Anyway, what is The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe? The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is a first person game, and one of the earliest walking simulators. I've been a fan of this game (or is it a franchise now?) since its original mod release, and it's been great seeing it evolve over the years, first with the original Steam release, and now with Ultra Deluxe. The story remains largely unchanged from the previous entries, and it's rather simple, or complex, depending on your choices. The game basically tells the story of Stanley, or Employee 427, who worked in an office. One day, he discovers that all his coworkers have disappeared, and thus decides to explore the office building in search of answers. As he moves through the office, he reaches the game's core: the two doors. A simple concept, choosing left or right, that this game manages to explore in incredible depth. With Ultra Deluxe, even more choices and endings have been added, even endings that affect other endings, and what could be considered a "true" ending.All throughout the game, there's a secondary character, the Narrator. As his name implies, he's the one narrating the story, and thus, guiding Stanley's (and the player's) actions. However, going back to the two doors mentioned above, the player can choose to ignore the Narrator and figuratively wrestle with him for control of the story, the more you progress through the game, the more options that begin to show up, leading to a great deal of replayability as you try to get all the different endings. All this accompanied by the Narrator's hilarious dialogue.The writing is superb, and I can't state this with enough emphasis; while the only speaking character is the Narrator, as mentioned above, almost all his dialogue is hilarious, though there are some somber moments here and there. In Ultra Deluxe, the dialogue has been expanded a whole lot, with even more somber moments and times of reflection; the "true" ending I mentioned above is a particular favourite of mine. Visually speaking, it looks pretty good, and it manages to keep the look of the original despite moving from Source to Unity. There's several new environments to explore, and they all look beautiful. Gameplay wise, it's very simple: you walk and interact with certain objects; as it is a very heavily story-driven game, there's not much else to do, no fancy shooting or parkour sections, but they aren't needed. Finally, the soundtrack, while minimalistic, serves its purpose well.All in all, I can say I definitely recommend this game. Saying too much about it would spoil it, which is why I won't extend this review more than I have to.

_childDocuments_.review: I get the appeal for this game for people, I think. I might be wrong considering people like this game for different reasons. Which is okay.The game's' all about making choices, The game's centered about making choices. but they're mostly making only obvious choices. I thought because this game's centered about choices, it'd feel personal or something. Like the 'little' things you do affect the bigger story, or the concept of butterfly effect or karma would be used in the game, But no, not really. I played this completely blind because I didn't play the OG stanley parable. And when I explored things that doesn't feel obvious to explore, it never really rewards you with anything. And because I played the game completely blind, because I didn't know what the game is all about other than making choices, I didn't know what I was supposed to do. I guess it's because in video games nowdays, there's a lot of choices that you can obey or disobey. People like disobeying things so the game's all centered about that concept. But when I played the game this game, I felt like the "obeying orders and disobeying orders" thing FEELS like obeying orders. Both of them. Because the game is about choices and basically tells you to do BOTH the obeying order and the disobeying order. Making me feel like i had to double disobey it by exploring places around the room or something because I thought there'd be a secret in other play that the game might take notice.Which is why I ended up always trying to interact with objects like turning all pc's off or interacting with this and that and so far the only thing i've ever achieved, and the only thing that has rewarded to me this was the door achievement. And even though the achievement itself is meant to be a funny easter egg for people, because I have an unclear way of playing the game, I thought the game would be littered with THAT kind of easter eggs in other places, only to discover the fact that, no, so far, I've only encountered the door (and the keypad if you enter quick enough before the narrator tells you the keypad's number code) as the only really choices that feel invisible or personalized. Meaning I've spent more hours actually just exploring for nothing than the obvious things to do, actually progressing.Anyways, it's just a personal experience of this game. _childDocuments_.review: Skip to the end for less extensive review.The Stanley Parable isn't just a game, it's an experience that redefines what interactive storytelling can achieve. From the moment you step into Stanley's shoes, you're plunged into a world where every choice feels significant, yet delightfully absurd. This game isn't about winning or losing. It's about exploring the myriad paths life can take, and it's executed with such brilliance that it keeps you hooked from start to finish.What makes The Stanley Parable stand out is its uncanny ability to blend humor with deep philosophical insights. As you wander through the empty office, guided by the ever-present narrator, you quickly realize this game is a commentary on choice and free will. The narrator's witty and often sarcastic remarks add a layer of comedy that never detracts from the profound questions the game poses. Instead, it enhances them, making each decision you face feel both hilarious and significant.One of the most striking aspects of The Stanley Parable is its ability to make you reflect on your own life. The game subtly pushes you to question the nature of your choices. Are you really in control? Or are you merely following a predetermined path? It's a question that lingers long after you’ve put down the controller. The game masterfully uses its simple office setting and minimalist design to focus your attention on the narrative and the choices you make, creating an introspective experience that's rare in the world of gaming.The Stanley Parable is a triumph in interactive storytelling. It’s a game that makes you laugh, think, and question everything you know about games and life itself. It's a refreshing reminder that video games can be art, capable of delivering profound messages in ways that are both entertaining and enlightening. For anyone seeking a game that offers more than just an escape, The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is an absolute must-play. Its not just a game, it's a journey into the heart of choice, consequence, and the human condition.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Whether or not you should buy this game. A choice. A or B. And as with any choice, there are multiple decisions. At the end of every decision, there's a viewport you can use to look back and decide if you made the right choice. Is this yet another shoveled out the door remake or rerelease of a popular game purely to give more money to the developers? It can't be, the developers of the Stanley Parable wouldn't do that. If I want to replace a game cameo with  TWO new game cameos, if I want to add a bucket, then the Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe will have all the buckets and collectibles that I want it to have.End of story.

_childDocuments_.review: My name is Phantasmagoria. P-h-a-n-t-a-s-m-a-g-o-r-i-a.Brief synopsis of the joke:This is a joke about the game "Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. The very first choice of Stanley Parable is between two doors. The narrator clearly states "When Stanley came to a set of open doors, he entered the door on his left." If Stanley goes through the right door despite that, plus knowing it wasn't the correct way, he would be subverting expectations. The joke is Stanley reviewing the game on Steam, in which he presses "no" on the question "Do you recommend this game?", even thought he would, indeed, recommend it, since he enjoyed it and played it for hours; thus subverting the expectations once again. He thinks, "Just like the time I went through the right door!", this thought pointing out the similarity. You are supposed to laugh after the thought is delivered.P-h-a-n-t-a-s-m-a-g-o-r-i-aStanley opened Steam to review the game Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. He read the question "Do you recommend the game?" Stanley clicked on "no" despite the fact that he enjoyed the game and played it for hours. He thought "Just like the time I went through the right door!"The Survey1. What did you like the most about the joke?2. Did you enjoy the delivery of the joke?3. Do you have a bucket with you right now?4. Did you predict the punchline?5. Is your name Jim?6. How effective is this joke to be used against your political enemies to silence them?7. Do you have a bucket with you right now?8. If you were a hypothetical real person named Rupert, would you invent a machine that eliminates food shortages across the world to make life better for all people, or spend years of hard work forgetting how to read?9. Is this comment a bucket?10. Do you have a bucket with you right now?11. Is your name Jim?12. How many choices do you make in a day?13. Did you enjoy the delivery of the joke?14. Are you a bucket?15. Am I a bucket?16. What is a bucket?17. How effective is this joke to be used against your political enemies to silence them?18. Was the broom closet ending your favourite?19. Did you enjoy the delivery of the joke?

_childDocuments_.review: Did you know that the developer of this game was nearly sued for plagiarising "The Stanley Parable (2012)"? Tragically, the lawyers found the plagiarism, and... The jig was up. You would be rather hard-pressed to find another game that took more jigs.That's not all, however. Also in The Stanley Parable’s credits is a writer, Dan Pinchbeck. We can guess that Pinchbeck, presumably not knowing he was plagiarising, signed off the game's credits. Tragically, at least Pinchbeck is is now a much better writer. Perhaps this will inspire him to be the next Brian Fargo (creator of Wasteland 2).Unlike Wasteland 2, however, this game uses the name "The Stanley Parable Ultra Duluxe", a completely unrelated game which was made for a cheap license and a short time frame in 1989 by Interplay, which later sold the rights to Crows Crows Crows and went on to make Wasteland 3.

_childDocuments_.review: if you've never played the Stanley Parable at all before, I do highly highly recommend this. This review is more for those who have been anticipating new content from those who've played the original.On reconsideration from a previous review, Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe is a good game. Disappointment from many fans is what I would expect, especially given the price tag and build up. The Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe has something to say, mainly one thing, despite all of it's fluff in between. The fluff is hilarious, but beyond "insightful" commentary on AAA games that definitely have never been said before, I do resonate a lot with the main theme of Stanley Parable. It's a good game overall, one of my favorites, but it leans a bit too heavy into what it's trying to say, pretending to be something it's not. This would not be a problem, if it weren't at the expense of the player. Playing through the new endings, I felt cheated even if parts of it were funny, and was upset at my wasted $25. Genuinely, the best way to play this game is to wait for it to drop at $15 if you don't have the base game, or buy it at any price if you're going into this completely blind.I would not recommend completely disregarding this game beyond these requirements. I would recommend it if you know what you're getting into (though only through the general premise and not specific content) and want to enjoy the game regardless, with graphics that really are stunning.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you play video games?Oh, well, yeah, I guess it was a stupid question. After all, you’re here, aren’t you? Asking the reviews if you should or shouldn’t buy the game, just so you can know if your money will be well-spent should you decide to buy it.What’s your favorite game?Mine’s Skylanders: Superchargers, personally just for its balance of humor and difficulty. But what’s your favorite? Is it Half-Life? Among Us? The Sims? Why is that your favorite? Does it challenge you? Does it make you feel like you’ve accomplished? Does it make you laugh? Do you play it with your friends? Does it make them laugh? Have you beaten it? Have your friends beaten it? Do you feel like a loser because all of your friends have beaten it and you haven’t? Has this self-rejection led to you placing an unhealthy level of self-worth in accomplishing the game’s preset goal? Is the game your friend? Is it your enemy? Have you fallen asleep while playing it? Did you dream of playing it while you were asleep? Did you wake up only to realize you were still dreaming? Are you dreaming right now? Are you still reading these questions? Does it let you make choices? Are those choices good? Are they bad? Do good and bad choices depend on the situation? Do those choices make you feel like you’re in control? If you do feel in control, why? Don’t you know that no matter what choice you made, the developers knew you might make it and planned accordingly? Don’t you know that every choice you make in that game has a preset outcome and you’re just choosing a door and seeing if there’s a million dollars or a hungry tiger behind it? Don’t you realize that you can’t control what’s behind those doors? Don’t you realize that they could just put a tiger behind both doors just for the sake of giving you the finger? Can you win the game? Can you lose it? What’s the difference? Why are broom closets so darned soothing?!But of course, I digress. In this game, you play Stanley, a man whose skill set is limited to waking and pushing buttons. A man who finds two doors and can only walk through one. A man with choices.Do you play video games? Well, then, definitely consider playing this one. And get ready to ask yourself some questions.

_childDocuments_.review: ...but they didn't understand that the game was never meant to be funny! It was meant to have a point! It was meant to speak to the human condition! "But where are the jokes? Where are the jokes?" they bemoaned, they screamed. They gnashed their teeth and said "Entertain us!" It wasn't enough. They had to leave a pathetic little thumbs-down review and make all of their pitiful demands.But then, "He's talking too much," they said! First he didn't entertain us, now he won't shut up! It's the inconsistency! It's the lack of accountability! It's the unwillingness to examine with an uncompromising heart the words they are speaking into the world! As though there were no consequences to someone's lack of cohesion in their examination of others! But of course absolutely anyone can leave a review, so here's what we get! We get these demands that seek everything, and are accountable to nothing!We get these demands that say "Ohh, there should be a skip button! You should be able to freeze Stanley in place, while the Narrator sits there forever and ever! We want all of this in the new Stanley Parable! We demand it!" And then, because it was said, because it was spoken, now it simply has to happen! The most immediate desires, every single thing demanded by every person at every moment in time, if someone wants it then it's a crime not to bring it into being!Have we been given to indulging every fleeting whim for no reason other than to do so? Yes! Yes! It seems that this is now the world we live in! It seems that we are a people living in such bleakness and discomfort with ourselves that our entertainment is now our lives! It has come to represent us! It absolutely must speak to who we are as people!Because otherwise, without our entertainment, we have nothing! Without entertainment we would have to face inward toward the cruel bleakness inside of ourselves. We would turn to look at our deeper nature and find a resounding emptiness gazing back with unyielding aggression. And so - so because of this - we require that our amusements and our play things and our flights of fancy be so impossibly captivating that they consume all of our attention, turn our heads completely away from the bleakness! In effect, we have demanded that our entertainment be the collapse of ourselves! What a pitiful reflection of humanity these entertainments are! What a shameful mirror to the human spirit they project!I'm not mad. I'm not mad about any of this. I'm at peace with it. I am the calm center of gravity around which these perversions hurl themselves. I am a waypoint for reasonable and collected discourse. They're the ones that are mad! They're the ones who couldn't stand the idea of me using my game to try to say something! Maybe they were just jealous of me?Yes...yes, of course. They've been jealous of me this whole time! They are mired in fear and insecurity, and cannot help but attempt to tear me down. What a sad state of affairs. When you read these reviews now you can see it. You can taste the bitter resentment. And my, how good does it feel now to speak truth to these words! To finally allow these thoughts out! Contained and managed for so long, neutered and sterilized! At last I am free to truly think, to feel!It must be that they were so discontent with themselves, they couldn't help but leave a negative review on Steam. Perhaps it says far more about them than it ever did about me. Perhaps the state of their psychological being was in such tatters, and my constitution and willpower are so ironclad in comparison, perhaps it was this state that they saw some outlet in which to tear me down!This, you can see, is clearly why they felt the need to expect the game be funny. That it be filled with yuks, and whimsical humor. That it amuse them endlessly from start to finish.

If it didn't require so many runs with that bucket it may have been enjoyable, its a joke that gets old really really quickly.Basically this game is far too on the nose in writing and execution: it's gameplay was boring this time (since we know now where everything is, unlike the first game which was a genuine adventure), and it's message is on a topic that's not really in the realm of the original. Where the first game talked about narratives and how our expectations can be destroyed and leave us confused, this was accomplished by doing just that in an engaging way, Ultra Deluxe tries to do something similar. Except in this case its making a subpar sequel.There's a lesson in letting go in all of this that's not so much apparent until the end but the method of getting there has been done better elsewhere.Speaking of which, this game is a lot like how people saw Omori: the core message of the game was best represented by a small portion of the game. Except the "boring" bits of a Omori were still engaging with things to do discover, and characterization of the cast in someway, or at least a reflection of how the main characters saw his friends. The boring bits of Ultra Deluxe are how Stanley really really really likes a bucket.An Additional 6 hours later, and the only benefit I see is when i redownload the game the graphics options are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent addition to the great original thought provoking work of art that would forever change the narrative in video games as a whole. I cannot display in mere words how the original screwed with my mind as a teenager growing up when thoughts could still be thoughts and you weren't afraid to think for the sole purpose of having thoughts. I love the narrator and can't imagine a world without the relationship between him, Stanley, and you. This game expands upon exactly what the original intended to do along with keeping the original game included with some refreshed and enhanced textures. Despite any of the 10/10 of demeaning thumbs down reviews, The Stanley Parable is my favorite example of literature and art in a video game and I hope you find the same meaning I have in this narrative.P.S. If your name is Jim there's a special secret for you in the special content.

_childDocuments_.review: Just know that this is NOT a joke review, nor will I be providing spoilers of any sort. Everything can be taken seriously and trusted, since I know there is some BS and misinformation going as far as what the "game is really about".First, just to get this out of the way, if you've played the Stanley parable and you want to know how much new stuff is present? Well do you remember how much the original had? This version has a little over double the content if I had to estimate, and thankfully there is a way to skip right to the new stuff.Alright, to everyone else: The Stanley parable is a meta-narrative comedy. I won't go into too much details for fear of spoiler, as the plot and happenings of this game are everything with this game.However, without spoilers I will say this game can get a little creepy, has a few tense moments and such. But let's be clear,  alright? There are no real jumpscares unless you are high (and everything scares you when you are high), nothing worthy of such anyway. One or two things that might creep you out momentarily, but that's it. And its only momentary. The game is supposed to be funny, and for the most part it certainly is.Minor spoiler for those who are getting unnerved when playing or watching the game, still vague but here to reassure you a little:Still a great game, had more than a few laughs, worth getting for sure if you have a good sense of humor, particularly the British kind.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I felt unsure about this new version, but the more I played, the more I was made aware of a mighty bucket's worth of new content for veteran players of the 2013 version. (thanks for the discount to veterans, and reasonable regional pricing, too!)There's quite a lot to search for, if you have the patience to comb through repeating many steps to experiment with the alterations. For new players, it's practically an infinite hole's worth of content.If you never played the 2013 release before, this is even more worth of your time. If you already did, it's a bit repetitive and tiresome in some areas (if you remember most of it, like I did) but still quite enjoyable, witty and thoughtful - just not as intoxicating as the first time (though the bonus item for veterans helps spice up the classic scenes and endings). Would've been welcome to have a bit more new content and more of the cutting room floor content - it's a bit lacking. Writing and narration is still top notch, though. The title doesn't lie, this is indeed an ultra deluxe version of The Stanley Parable. There's quite a few bugs right now (had to lower my resolution and turn v-sync on to engage on the phone ending with the "veteran" item in hand, otherwise no prompts appeared... and a few other problems - I imagine these will be ironed out very soon).If I had to nitpick - I kinda wish there was a skip button to skip some of the narrator's ramblings. Maybe next game?Now, off to get the 10 year achievement legitimately. Forget about that tuesday one, though. You guys are crazy.

I was an enormous fan of the first game, I spoke very fondly of it and I was very excited about the new game. The possibility of having a new "Stanley The Parable" experience was such a delight, but as soon as I reached the bucket part I understood that the developers were not interested in making a new game. I wouldn't recommend this game for fans that have completed the first one, and remember it as it was yesterday they played it. For you it will feel grindy, for you it will feel lazy.but for new players, go ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: To be very honest, this game was a massive snoozefest. I had never heard of it and decided to buy it due to the very positive reviews it had been getting. One of the featured reviews in the game trailer said "Do not read any reviews 10/10", and maybe I took that too literally. I bought the game fully expecting it to be a trippy puzzle-esque game, but was horribly disappointed. This game ended up being an attempt at a whitty, narrator driven, walking simulator with no love given to actual gameplay. I understand the message that was being conveyed and I think it's clever, but that does not make up for the astronomical level of mega-bored I was while trying my hardest to become intrigued. It's a clever concept, but unfortunately that is the only positive note I have on the matter.

_childDocuments_.review: A skip button really would change everything. It's too bad the only "skip button" in the game is bad-faith gimmick just as annoying as everything else.Does this game have anything interesting to say? Well get comfortable and listen to EVERY. SINGLE. THING. You think got the joke? F*** you! It's 15 more seconds AT LEAST before this one is done. Just pray the next bit doesn't go on for 5 do-nothing minutes.The narration/writing honestly feels hostile to the player's time. It's like a bitter teacher telling you "Class is over when I SAY so" even when you're ready to move on.Imagine that you're free to skip the boring bits. Well, then it's YOUR fault when you miss something import- THAT WOULD BE FINE!!! In fact, missing something important would be a great way to regain my attention after steadily losing it for the last half hour.Would you see a comedian who made everyone clap after each joke else he'd never finish or leave the stage? That's this game. There is NOTHING to do while he talks. Honestly the new content belongs back in 2013 when this approach was still novel.

_childDocuments_.review: As expected, it's just the original Stanley Parable game plus more. The "more" isn't too special, though, and probably less than you would think, some of the endings were really just weird or lame, lacking in creativity and charm unlike the original endings. They just didn't really know what to do with it, I guess. Might be more fun for new players but for a returning player it's just kinda disappointing and a silly use of 6 hours of my time(but a use nonetheless, which I'm always looking for something to do). So buy it if you want the original game + more or are some kind of completionist. But the original game is... probably cheaper... and just a more authentic experience, so. That's my review. -Finley

_childDocuments_.review: A very funny game with multiple great endings/story lines. I dreamt of playing this game for a while now and I must say, it was worth the dreaming. The ironic speeches and the witty banter from the narrator is amazing and made me laugh multiple times. I am sad that other games by these people haven't been seen as much and I am sure that they are great too. (I haven't played them either). This game made me feel like I was in a choose your own adventure book as the decisions you were allowed to make made me feel curious and adventurous. Some people may not like it due to "excessive commentary" but that is just one of the reasons I enjoy this game and is one of the key components of the game. This was a 10/10 experience that I would kill to play again if I had forgotten about everything that ensued when playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely pathetic excuse for a re-release. Nothing more than a pathetic corporate cash grab, with barely any meaningful new content added. Truly a disgrace to the original masterpiece that was The Stanley Parable. Even though I think every game is terrible compared to The Stanley Parable, this one was especially bad. A complete bastardization of what used to be the perfect video game.

_childDocuments_.review: Has 2 or 3 great sequences on par with the original Stanley Parable and Beginner's guide featuring great environments and gags, but the new content then quickly devolves into you repeating endings from the original game centering around a single joke that gets old fast. Always happy to have more Stanley Parable but I can't see how this took so long or why I'd drop 16 bucks on it.

People would ask why I would jump so and I could, finally, after all these years, say that I, (username), were to be jumping for joy! Such a long time I had gone, looking at the joy that was stuck up there, the top shelf that I in my small stature could almost-reach-but-not-quite. Then, for a few moments, I had achieved it. _childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe actually does expand on the original game and is worth the 10 extra bucks (although to be honest I just got it from the 2023 winter sale). Yet The Stanley Parable 2 just added a bucket and some figurines and some of the features they promised like the Jim button were missing. If I were to pick one it would be The Stanley Parable 3: The Desert of Pencil because that one fixed the Test Achievement issue.(In all seriousness, from someone who has never played the original game before, Ultra Deluxe is the same game but actually makes it somewhat funnier and gives it even more secrets like, SPOILERS,  But if you want to buy the original because you think, from some of the reviews say, that UD is lacklustre or because it's cheap or because of the GMOD assets, then go for it.)

_childDocuments_.review: It's time to get serious, Stanley. no jokes, no games. Outside of this room I might be more tolerant of those things, but now we're in the room. Which is why I'm subjecting you to the most serious punishment I can think of: One hundred, billion, trillion years standing here in the serious room. Perhaps after that we can talk about the severity of your actions and whether you've learned anything, but until then, serious room. GO.

I had learned to love this version of the game instead of the previous. I also appreciate the fact that they took my review into consideration and put a skip button in. It made the game complete.

_childDocuments_.review: The New Content for The Stanley Parable was Unexpected, I thought it's gonna have  and i even thought there's gonna be a True Ending where Stanley breaks the loop () and then actually free'd from the building . but despite all of that, Ultra Deluxe is a Good Expansion to the 2013 version. it's interesting seeing more stuff that actually funny while at the same time, made good lessons about our lives, the real world and even game development as a whole (which is what this game was actually about according to one of the endings). since AFAIK this recent version is a send-off to Stanley, The Narrator and The Entire Series, i guess it's just for the best. Superhot did the same thing with Mind Control Delete (sort of, if you count "Superhot JP" which idk if that new game would ever come out) so it's understandable that we'll be move on from playing this game and remembering the moments of what The Stanley Parable gave us (unless we'll gonna not play again until 10 years later for getting the "Super Go Outside" Achivement....yes, really), i'll give this game a 8/10 for still a Good Expansion.

_childDocuments_.review: I morally have to give this a recommend, don't get me wrong! Amazing game, I absolutely love it and plan to get that "Play for the entire duration of a Tuesday" achievement and play the baby route in full during that time! But MY GOD. it HURTS to go against the narrator sometimes. I don't know if maybe it's me over-analyzing the story and the game but I realized maybe in my- I'd say 14th run of the game? The Narrator, despite his name, actually has no control over the story whatsoever. He's more of an influence, or rather an occurrence. The Narrator has no power unless you, the player, do something, and even then you can ignore his attempts at power or flat out override it. Even other characters in the game like The Adventure Line (tm) and The Curator have more power over The Narrators own game than him. I want nothing more than to give The Narrator a hug and listen to his stories and follow his script to a T.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying I enjoy the type of humor in this game. Sadly, there are a few short comings for me to consider this a worthy sequel.First off, this is basically just the Stanley Parable, except you get slightly different endings, because you carried a bucket, meaning there aren't really any new rooms to visit.The game pokes fun at people asking for a skip button, while I really would have preferred having one since my save data got deleted (likely a problem with Steam sync not the devs' fault) and this is not the kind of game that you want to have to replay for multiple hours again, since the jokes don't change.There was no visible visual overhaul or improvements to the game engine. For instance, I managed to clip myself out of bounds once in a way that surely wasn't intended (there was no narration and you kept falling.)This game sadly seems like an easy way for the devs to re-monetize the success of the original game. If you want to buy it, at least wait until it is significantely discounted, because this game is not worth the full price.

Even if I'll only play it for about 20 minutes in a day, there's no telling how those 20 minutes will be spent.Though, one thing is for sure; Those 20 minutes will be worthwhile.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:TLDR: If you own the original, don't bother with this one. If you don't, you could buy the original for cheaper and get pretty much the same experience, though the new edition does have some accessibility features that are always nice to have.Alright, I need to talk about this. I'm going to preface this Yelling At The Wind Session with the fact that I love the original Stanley Parable. If you haven't played the game before, you can play this one. There's no harm in it. The Ultra Deluxe (which I'm just going to call UD now) keeps the original game intact (minus the console and an old bug which is an unfortunate loss, but this whole game's a cash grab so I'll save my complaints for later), so you'll be fine if this is your first playthrough. The lack of saves is really, really dumb in the Ultra Deluxe though. Of all the features, removing this one was a stupid idea (unless I'm missing something).Spoilers for The Stanley Parable and Ultra Deluxe in this review. With all that being said, I'd say that UD does very little to improve over the original's ideas.I respect their decision to not do the same thing again, but I can't help but feel the new ideas presented are all so unlikable. I'll get to that later, but first I need to cover what makes the original so good.I've always loved the original game's ideas- I even played the original mod version with all the Half-Life 2 assets and it's great! You can see how the ideas evolved into the retail game and it's really charming to see. The original had a very good thesis statement, mainly one of how a player's actions affect a game. The important thing is that the concept is played moderately seriously thoughout the entire game. If you don't take the game seriously (a.k.a going for the "evil" route where you just play Minecraft or Portal or HL2), it seems to laugh with you until the end; if you're power-hungry (in the "take over the machine" route) the narrator takes control. Every ending in the game seems to point to your character dying except for the (purposefully unsatisfying, as noted by the original author commentary) "good" ending; a lot of the endings are contradictory (on purpose); sometimes the narrator is real, sometimes he's not; Stanley is crazy, Stanley is rational, Stanley is insane, this is (not) a game... The contrast between all the endings and the fact that they are all supposed to coexist creates a very interesting game. The fact that, even when it acknowledges it's a video game, it takes itself moderately seriously is what's so interesting. It has good reason to- most of the endings involve serious topics.For example, take the Zen ending, my favorite ending. Initially, it seems like the end truly is the beautiful atmosphere with swirly lights, but then you notice the door on the side. Going through, you are given a choice: do you stay with the narrator (and perhaps close the game, satisfied with the end here), or do you take your own life in order to "achieve a true ending" or simply to hurt the narrator? The game proposes an idea of "how far are you willing to go to truly win?", one of its many ideas on control, and by forcing the player to kill themselves in order to simply get an ending (which refers to the cylical nature of the game), it perfectly shows how the player's control can affect the world (the narrator here). You could say this for nearly every ending in the game that isn't a joke one, but even one like the glitch one (where you jump out the window) says something about "breaking the game" and notes that the player does not have nearly as much control as they think they do. I could go on for a lot longer about how The Stanley Parable is very well tuned and all the endings have a purpose and all that but this review is getting long and I haven't even covered the new content...With all that being said, let's cover the new content of UD. The main content comes from a couple endings, the first of which... pokes fun at the gaming industry. This is an alright thing to do (the whole gaming industry could use a laugh or two, even if it's been laughed at to no end already), but the way it does it is by doing the . I guess it's fine if satire indulges in its sources' concepts, as this game does for laughs, but when that's all the game does, why even bother? Why re-release a game that was about something entirely different in order to poke fun at something we've all laughed at a thousand times over? Why charge $20 for it? Is the fact that the game does it under the guise of satire make a lazy re-release okay? None of the jokes are inherently original either- jokes about lazy implementations of ideas, collectibles, day one patches... it's all old. The game also talks about dealing with criticism, showing the narrator as somewhat narcissistic (as shown by some of the endings in the original) which is fine, but it's just played up for laughs. Nothing interesting's being said other than the narrator can't take criticism well, which... okay. (We knew that already.) My main issue with the game is that everything just  to be a joke. Every new ending ends in a joke, I swear. Maybe I'm just exaggerating, but when every ending is trying to be funny, especially when there's maybe two jokes that land in the new content, nothing feels genuine. It all feels so insincere.While yes, the original game had its moments with humor, UD acts like this was the only reason people played the original. All the contrast between the endings with some being humorous but most being kinda depressing (usually ending in the player dying) is gone. With the bucket, every ending becomes a punchline. Some of them get close to something- the ending where the narrator becomes jealous of the bucket is kinda-sad-kinda-funny and it could be interesting to see the narrator feel replaced by an inanimate object but then they add sexual tension because... funny? Why?? The ending where the narrator can't let go of the past is also a good idea to explore. Companies cashing in on their old products because they know it'll sell and gamers buying it because they can't let go of old ideas is a very real concept. The problem is that all the idea is deflated by the narrator "introducing a new character" and then having the sorta-semi-ironic line of "I miss the friend we just made" is just... it doesn't feel right seeing as everything else is so jokey. The entire concept of befriending an inanimate object could be cool too, but it doesn't use it more than a punchline 90% of the time which is beyond frustrating. Everything has to be a joke in this! The original was funny, sure, buy why can't this game just be serious for a second? Along with this, the game feels much worse about droning on about nothing despite realizing the issue in the game! (The review says that the narrator is talkative so you make the entire game drag every joke out three times longer! Genius!) It could be because a lot of the content is less interesting and more irritating, causing the game to drag, but opening the game with a "Set the time" thing that ends up dragging on and on and on... it's annoying, simply put.With the change in the gaming industry and the decade difference between the original and UD, the vision of the original has been lost. Change is good- a rehash wouldn't be interesting, and while a change could've been good for the pseduo-sequel, it's a very poor change. I don't know what happened, but the struggle, the paradoxical nature, the interesting parts of the original are all mostly gone, and any potentially interesting idea is usually stifled by some stupid gag.To sum up my thoughts...Original review:Stop trying to be funny!---Note: I think that "I'm doney with the funny" bit is what inspired this review. Genuinely one of the worst things I've experienced in a game. The original was a little on-the-nose but it was moderately grounded and still works today.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is just okay. To preface this, I love the original, its great. It is genuinely one of the best games I've played. But this?It ain't it.The new endings are built entirely off the original game. There is new content, and some jokes that are actually funny, but that's it. It is trying to make a statement about video game sequels, but in doing so, it just becomes what it mocks. It's like ,"Oooo here is a thing that other games do, and now we have it! Isn't that so much fun?"Breaking the fourth wall and acknowledging what things you are adding to the game are annoying doesn't make you doing it any more fun or interesting.This next part talks about a specific part of the game, so if you want to experience this game for yourself, don't read it.This game, all and all, just isn't great. This game is 25 dollars, and realistically it should just be a 5 dollar DLC. The game doesn't try to expand on what made the original so great, but just piggyback off of it's success. If you want to experience the game for yourself, just go and play the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Stanley Parable was one of the first games that a lot of gamers got to experience meta-narrative driven game. Perhaps now a lot of games (particularly indie ones) have elaborated on 4th wall breaking mechanics in their games similarly to this which may dampen the experience for people who have never played this game before,  but I find it still holds up wonderfully well.   The new content is great (and ominous), and it is very fun checking out the older content as well since you may be surprised by some of the updates they made to reflect it. Playing this has made me excited over the idea of these creators one day working on writing another game (or book if I'm going to be honest with myself) discussing autonomy and trans humanism.

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable was a landmark of 2013- it lambasted and parodied the gaming landscape of the day. Without giving too much away (as I am sure some people reading this have still not played the original), The Stanley Parable was, at it's core, about challenging the illusions of choice in game design. To that end- and, because the original game still exists in a mostly untouched capacity (with a few minor updates), The Stanley Parable still contains everything it once did, even if the message no longer hits as well- because, unlike in 2013, there is some meaningful choice in video games of the 2022 era. That is where the Ultra Deluxe version comes in. It once again has a statement to say about the games industry (which I think you can probably guess from the trailer), and it does so in a way that, if you enjoyed the 2013 release of The Stanley Parable, will probably be meaningful to you. Plus, I think you get a discount on this version anyway.If you never played The Stanley Parable, buy this version. If you have played The Stanley Parable, buy this version.

_childDocuments_.review: From the ashes of depravity, rises the phoenix of quality. How else to describe the Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe?Such a revolutionary step forward in the lineage of one of the most beloved video game properties of all time. The additions and changes made to this expansion will surely resonate in the history of all media.It is perhaps true to say, that no mistakes are forever etched in stone, for the stone that the Stanley Parable is carved has itself been transmuted offering a message of hope to those who have ever erred in their judgment. You are not beyond redemption, you may change, and you may become more...so much more than you were before.If there is any message to be taken from The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe, it is this: What a fortune, a privilege, a joy it is to have had such an experience. It leaves me hopeful that as a community, as a world there is time for us to become our greatest selves. As great as we ever could dream of in our wildest, most ambitious visions for a brighter future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tricky review for me because the original Stanley Parable stood out as a unique and interesting game with a fun set of mechanics to hunt out every plausible branching path of a what appears to be a simple story. It has interesting and funny narration that keeps you thinking and all sorts of unique twists and turns, if you've not played the game before it's extremely novel which is part of it's strong suit. If you happened to have never played the original game then get Ultra Deluxe for sure, it's worth the money.For people who already own the original and only care about the new content I think it's a much harder sell. Part of this is due to how the content is handled and part of it is an intrinsic problem with revisiting a novel idea and trying to capture that novel experience and re-imagine it, it's an inherently hard thing to do. I won't give any specific plot spoilers, but I will speak broadly about the new content for those who want to know what they're getting themselves in for and if it's worth buying. The game starts as normal and you progress as you normally would a few iterations before eventually a new path/door opens up to start the new content. This branches off through a linear meta narrative that breaks the 4th wall about the indtroduction of the Ultra Deluxe version, it's kind of like an on rails intro that passes through commentary about the reception of the original by the press and public, and then a trip down memory lane. Then you're set free in a more open area to learn about what new mechanics to expect. Once that section is complete you're dumped back into the original world which is largely the same as before, but with minor differences. With these new mechanics you can experience alternate endings to most of the originals which are often little more than just different narratives, but are sometimes completely different.The problem is there's no real novelty here, if you remember most of the routes it's just kinda ticking off a list of re-doing everything just to see how it differs from the original. The narration is slightly different and the endings are a bit different but it's a spin on an existing theme. There is another collectables mechanic which itself has it's own meta narrative about collectables in video games. It's very introspective and self referential, but the dialogue is almost what you'd predict from a game like this that is trying hard to be clever, it's bit cliche. I found myself unsurprised by the narration.Overall I do recommend it if you're a Stanley Parable fan, if you can get the launch deal bonus + original owners discount it comes out at about £13. For me quickly speed running 90% of the original endings, and then going on to do 90% of the new content was just shy of 5 hours. If you were expecting more of the same then you'll probably be a bit disappointed, there's no new branching paths off the original with new content to explore, there are lots of new areas but most of those are on rails linear narratives reflecting on the original, so it lacks the same kind of novelty the original had.

_childDocuments_.review: (MM/DD/YY)After replaying, I've decided to change my stance on the Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. I've grown a lot as a person over the last two years; the game is excellent. The old content is here, which is wonderful, but the new content is something completely different. I wouldn't call this the Deluxe version of the game; it's more of a new game entirely, separate from the original Stanley Parable, that's deeply interwoven with an old one. The marketing of this game primed me for something different than what I was expecting, and that tainted my expectations.With that said, the best way to enjoy the game isn't actually to seek everything; that's what made me get sick on some aspects when I first played it. Not to mention I suffered from Gamer Brain; this game is priced more as a movie than a game.For archival's sake, I'm going to leave my old review up that had a thumbs down. The amount of content in this game is straight up not worth $25. Sure, the writing is fantastic, and that's the main selling point. While it is a fun game, it is not $25 of fun packed into four hours, as it is a $10 game at best. This is an apples to orange comparison, but Undertale is priced at $10 and contains just as amazing writing, not to mention that when you aren't engaged with its writing, it has its own gameplay loop that keeps you invested with its battle system.The original being $15 was already pushing it content-wise, but $25 for this game is honestly outrageous. The new stuff isn't even particularly high-quality, and a lot of the content is ported from the old game with a lot of broken lighting. It isn't a remake by any means, and honestly looks worse in many aspects than the original. If this is the joke of Ultra Deluxe, Crows Crows Crows clearly fails to understand what the developers find funny is not what the consumer finds funny.I also need to mention the control options are god-awful. You cannot set your mouse sensitivity to a precise decimal number, and even if you set it to 0, it still is very, very high,  if you use high DPI on the daily. Also, the game doesn't remember your rebound controls. I had to consistently and repeatedly set Left Shift to crouch on start up every single time, as using left ctrl to do so is awful and uncomfortable for me. It also doesn't allow you to rebind to mouse buttons, as I usually set Mouse5, a side mouse button, to crouch.  My opinions are blatantly in the minority, and I would hate to ruin the enjoyment of the game just because I go against the popular opinion. So stop reading now, unless you're looking for an in-depth look into my hatred of one of the new additions, plus mentions of a few other major things. If you're willing to accidentally read things though, then skip to the  beyond these paragraphs.You still here? Alright, your fault for learning about my hatred of The Bucket, and why The Bucket is a perfect mascot for this game's missed potential. If The Bucket was simply a gag for the New Content areas, fine, it'd be a great joke. Even if it appeared in the main game as just something a bit extra, like a very minor gag every time you pick it up, that'd be fine too. The issue is that The Bucket is a cop-out for writing new and interesting endings, as it just rehashes the old endings with "but you have a bucket now." Sure, many of the endings are  different than their non-bucket counterparts, with one of my personal favorites being one where you kill the bucket, but when you realize that the entire joke is that you have a calming and soothing bucket with you on the normal endings, it gets stale. Too much effort was put into the bucket, and I feel it really hampered the quality of the game. I would've much preferred if The Bucket was cut and put into the museum; the development resources the bucket took could've lead to more interesting areas. Not to mention that some of the bucket endings  to have choice, but in reality, there is no significant difference between the two. There are funny moments with the bucket, and they definitely are funny at first. But I noticed I started to laugh less and less with each Bucket ending I got, as the joke got stale. It isn't a running gag; it is an ordinary gag forcefully put on stage against its will repeatedly, and you can feel its silent plea to be taken off stage more and more every time it goes on. The Bucket is the perfect example of when an idea goes too far and becomes too expansive.To conclude this rant, The Bucket feels like an incredibly lazy way to add new content. Ultra Deluxe had so much potential to expand the original humor of the original, while still being able to modernize it. One of the greatest strengths of this game is how explorable the game is; it always felt like there were more secrets to be discovered. More endings to achieve. More secrets to uncover. Ultra Deluxe only keeps that feeling for people who have never played the original; instead of more content, it is the same content with a different coat of paint, sometimes literally. The game of the Stanley Parable is that of exploration and figuring out where you haven't been; when you take that away, it's just a movie, except you're the one who moves the protagonist in a predetermined path. And the second half of the movie is same as the first half, but with The Bucket. - I'm done ranting now. I tried to make it more coherent; if I failed, oh well. Anyways, the actual conclusion:My thoughts on the game as a whole is that, while I still ended up being a fan of the game, the thing I ranted on and on about is still too big to sway my opinion into the red. I cannot recommend it, as while I enjoyed the game a lot, I didn't enjoy it enough to where it was worth $25. The only reason I didn't feel like I got scammed is because I got the game at a somewhat reasonable $15, as I owned the original. It is yet another mediocre remaster of an old game that looks a bit worse than the original. My final thoughts are is the same as my : Wait for a sale if you really want to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this are the reason why I wish Steam had an option for Mixed reviews, instead of forcing you to pick between either a thumbs up or a thumbs down.Because while I do think TSP Ultra Deluxe has a fair deal of good moments and clearly had a lot of effort put into it, I also think that ultimately, all this new content comes across as pointless and derivative, resulting in a game that feels bloated and unsure of what it's supposed to be doing, compared to the simplicity of the original release. The fact that I can't tell whether this is supposed to be the point or not makes this feeling all the more apparent.TSP Ultra Deluxe is basically the original game, with new content tacked onto it and with some graphical enhancements here and there (mostly better lighting in a few places). I think a major point of disappointment for me is the fact that, while the game does have quite a few new ENDINGS, it has very few new PATHS. I counted I think 4 new paths (one of which I'm not sure if it's bugged or supposed to be so... nonexistent), everything else is reusing the existing paths, all centered around the gag of "the same thing, BUT NOW WITH !!!". This is not at all what I expected when the trailers claimed to have new endings. I expected those new endings to come from new paths cleverly snuck into the existing environment of the game (like the aforementioned four), not... this.Considering the elaborate joke of the "" ending, I can't help but wonder if this is supposed to be intentional. A riff on how all those remakes and remasters lately are very pointless and either add very little or add stuff that dilutes the original experience. But, well, even if that was the intention, TSP Ultra Deluxe still commits that very mistake it's supposedly mocking, it just does so "ironically". If I smash my head with a hammer and say I'm doing it ironically, it doesn't change the fact that I'm smashing my head with a hammer, now does it?This is basically what TSP Ultra Deluxe comes across to me. A supposed parody that doesn't really know what it's trying to do, and feels bloated and unfocused as a result. And while I admit the game gave me a good 6 hours of looking around and curiously checking out the new content, in the end it left me feeling confused and disappointed. And that feeling is why I'm ultimately leaning more towards a thumbs down, since that's probably not a good feeling to have.

_childDocuments_.review: The year is 2032. I'm wandering and scavenging in the wasteland. I come across a familiar looking home, it's eroded and caved in. Checking inside, i find a broken but all too familiar old computer laying in the rubble. I try to turn it on, but most of its parts are fried, long out of working order. I carefully remove the hard drive and stuff it in my backpack. I must take this home as soon as possible. I make my way back up the old highway, fighting my way back through the hordes of sentient killer self-driving teslas, crypto-bandits, and mutants to get back to the haven city of New Shreveport, and wait at the outer wall while the guards check me over to make sure im not radioactive and let me in. The moment I'm inside I take off running up to my friend Wizard Kieth's shack and asking xer to restore this hard drive. I plug it into the beeping Windows 69 generator-powered sludge-cooled holoscreen terminal and boot it up. A familiar scent wafts into the air as I log into my steam that's still up somehow and launch The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. the console text that always shows up at the start of the game appears once more, but it says "Oh thank God. You finally found me. Thank you." in the corner i see "Achievement Unlocked: Super Go Outside". my eyes well up with tears and I smile for the first time since before this damn war began.

_childDocuments_.review: Stanley Parable begins as a promising game, offering an enjoyable experience at first. However, after a few hours, the repetitive gameplay —despite the variety in commentary—started to feel tedious to me. In fact, it became boring. I admit, since the game is widely loved, I felt hesitant to share this opinion, fearing backlash.Still, I couldn’t fully enjoy it. That said, there were moments of genuine fun, particularly the segment featuring the 'infinite hole' (or at least, that’s how it’s described). Moreover some endings are truly well-crafted. Yet, I can’t help but feel the game is slightly overrated and receives more praise than it truly deserves. It’s by no means a bad game, but I found myself forcing myself to keep playing, mainly due to its popularity. While I wanted to enjoy it as much as others seem to, I think the reviews inflate its appeal a bit too much.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Update: allowing comments. I feel comfortable handing constructive criticism having played this kind of games for 10+ years.CCC also happens to make some of the best marketing campaigns out there. The first email they sent out was a joke about how they would simply include a one terabyte file cabinet texture and be done with it. Typical CCC humor of course, but the seed was planted. If you're not familiar with the world of remakes, the de-facto 'go to' remake in terms of walking sim is Observer: System Redux (O:SR). When OSR released a remake of their title, they produced a game which graphics . OSR added raytracing, added 4k textures, the works. It looks photorealistic in parts, and is competitive with some of the Unreal 5 footage - seriously - go play it. Evidently that's no reason to buy the game a second time, but it gave a new generation of player or simply people who missed out on the first release a chance to experience something truly 'incredible' visually. So a lot of walking sim fans started asking for these remakes. Dear Esther got a makeover, and so on. Time for The Stanley Parable and ... they release a v1.5 of the game with a lot of new content and tons of inside jokes, but the graphics are only marginally better than the original. Hell, in the 'infinite hole' section, SUW is broken. So one has to ask: what gives?As I mentioned, the expectation where set wrong, just like countless titles before. Developers aren't careful with words in general, and when they get as insanely creative as CCC can be, this can be dangerous. Personally, I don't regret buying the remake - I love the company AND the game - even at 50 bucks i would have bought it. But I'm a minority of super-fans. And quite frankly, seeing 'my' community bashing people because the graphics  of a 2022 remake are 'oh-hum' at best and frankly no better than the original in some places, makes me sad.We had all the reason to expect incredible graphics. CCC even jokes about this in-game, it's done well, it's done tastefully, but they still joke about the lack of RT and whatnot to explain their design decision. This will rub a lot of people the wrong way. There's another problem - it's no big secret the 'magic' of the SP is its multiple endings - and how difficult they are to get. Yet reaching out these various endings (13+4+0.5 that I counted so far) give you achievement whatsoever. There's no way to know if you've seen everything, or only a fraction of the game. The new version makes this worse - take the'confusion' ending for example - with the new item at your disposal, you can interrupt it, and miss out of the actual confusion ending. I did the math, you can repeat that ending 'progress' until the very end, then terminate it abruptly only to have redo it all over again and nothing will come of it except the waste of 15 + minutes. Again here i expected better - maybe a better branching mechanism when the game sense you are trying to break it to prevent such annoying , wasteful 'loops'.Then, you have what i call the 'useless' repeats. For example, in the new 'is this a bucket' section, you will be tempted to play it twice - but in reality, your choices make no impact to what the narrator concludes, even if you answer correctly every time. Highly frustrating.And let me tell you- there are GREAT parts you won't want to miss. Your only recourse is therefore to play the game while following an online guide, which sucks.The original was brilliant but as this 'v.1.5' demonstrate, it could benefit from more polish, more content... more everything. The truth is that not everyone will want to do a full replay of a game just to get a very slightly different ending that's NOT recorded anywhere, and that's a CORE issue that this reboot DOES NOT address.Very few people, for example, will want to get the 'zending'. The game knows this, jokes about it by adding a new narration if you hold an object, but still, to this date, lack that sense of meaningful purpose to the journey beyond the initial question of choice and predetermination. Ultimately: the truth is the Stanley Parable is a game about listening to the most narration ('story") possible, and sometimes succeeds at making you feel okay about a decision (the window jump) and sometimes, not at all.Fore example, few people, again, will want to spend several hours trying to understand if the 'sound you hear when you bring a phone near a speaker' emitted by a specific object in the game is a hint to a hidden room or just there for fun. Well let me tell you because I did spend these hours: it's just a sound effect in there, for fun. The game has TONS of these little hints: element only seen through windows, seemingly entire gameplay 'just a hop' away in a game where you can't jump. Finally, some paths can be locked forever until you hard reset the game - including the Epilogue, which is ironically the 'big pay off' for this game. This one, I had to watch on Youtube, because I didn't feel like spending 2h+ for 3 minutes (if that) of new content. This is not a game for everyone. Heck, some people just listen to the mp3 files from the folder.  Anyways... ultimately, they could have recompiled with a newer engine , added a few lights and call it a day like Dear Esther did, so I'm still giving this a thumbs up - it outdoes the original and its still a MUST HAVE title. However, please stop bashing people who expected way better graphics - I did too.

_childDocuments_.review: 2845:  Reporting===============With an uncompromising heart I write:  "From the ashes of depravity rises the phoenix of quality."  I'd like to thank in advance the Skip Button suggester that stole literally minutes of my life away.  The Jim button was funny.  Let's nominate this game for The Most Enjoyable Bucket in a Video Game (what that's not a thing???  Who'd have guessed?).  Please do visit the Mostly Infinite Hole.============= End Tongue In Cheek ==============================================Gawd, all the things I hate about story games wrapped up in an annoying (albeit under the watchful (and often funny) eye  of a FANTASTIC Narrator) package.  Running around endless corridors, finding nothing and zero clues.  Not being able to interact with anything.  Jim Cricket it only cost me $25.00 to be annoyed.  Game design so good it was bad.  If I ever feel the need to be tortured for a couple of hours straight I'll be sure to load this game up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an incredible addition to the original. Being almost 10 years old, I think it was about time we saw some new additions. The humor and wit of all the new endings is just great. Revisiting the old endings and getting to experience this stupidly funny story is awesome as well. The only gripe I kind of have is it being $25. For basically the same game with 4 hours of new content, I wish it was more like 15-20$ but it's fine honestly. I like supporting them as a company.The new storyline is funny and adds lots of good jokes to laugh at. I like that the bucket lets you redo all of the old endings with a slightly new twist. I also really appreciated them changing the Portal and Minecraft to 2 new games. Some people have been upset about the change, but its been a long time and I like the inclusion of new gags for them.All in all, great game. I recommend it a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: After thinking about it enough I can't help but feel like this game is an actual malicious joke at the player's expense. like i mean literally intended as such. We love getting all metanarrativey don't we folks! thats why we love the stanley parable! We love exploring the players relationship with the game and story! Well this expansion really takes it to the next level. What if we made a game about making a bad game, but here's the kicker, the game is actually just the bad game we were talking about! Wow that is just so quirky. its a game so meta that the experience of purchasing and playing the game is actually part of the bit! Me wasting my money is the punchline! I'm the cringe ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for buying the nostalgia bait cashgrab! i get it crowsx3, i really do get it, thank you for the good lesson. what was i expecting from this? the original covered its subject matter pretty exhaustively, what could be meaningfully added? I will say I did actually enjoy some parts of the new content, but mostly under the assumption it was actually going somewhere eventually. In particular the infinite tunnel was a highlight. But then the rest of the game is just the original game but with a bucket. as if the game was designed to make someone write a sentence like that in a negative review. sure, it's a funny sentence, i guess i'll fulfill my role in this big meta joke of a game. Like they wanted to read a review like this and laugh at me for wasting my money. None of the bucket dialogue is funny. No, it didn't get old, i was immediately over it a couple minutes into my first bucket run once i understood what was happening. The whole point of the joke in the first place is how stupid it would be to include, and it wasn't really that funny then. but then to actually commit to it simply can't be interpreted in any other way as '♥♥♥♥ you'. the only other option is that they genuinely thought it was hilarious and i think i might respect that less than just trying to scam people.edit: after thinking about it a bit more some final thoughts. The reason this game is so annoying is that it clearly isn't a low effort cash grab. i guess that's why it feels so malicious in nature, there's obvious effort here, it just wasn't put towards something actually enjoyable to play. so much time spent writing and recording bucket dialogue. i've seen some real advanced thinkers who love to tout that this game has over double the amount of content as the original. pretty funny considering the game itself makes fun of this idea when the narrator mentions if quantity was all that mattered he could just start reading off the dictionary. Anything you can criticize this game for it can just solemnly shake its head and say 'you just don't get it. i was doing it on purpose! that was the point!' as it smugly jerks itself off in the middle of a street. My review of Ultra Deluxe: The video game equivalent of watching someone jerk off to a video of themselves jerking off. and (after watching the epilogue online) the whole point of it all was that he doesn't care if you liked it or not, he's gonna jerk off for his own sake. while charging you money for it and advertising the experience as a interpretive dance flash mob.

_childDocuments_.review: How else to describe The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe?Such a revolutionary step forward in the lineage of one of the most beloved video game properties of all time! The additions and changes made to this expansion will surely resonate in the annals of the history of all media ever made. It is perhaps true to say that no mistakes are forever etched in stone, for the stone into which The Stanley Parable was carved has itself been transmuted, offering a message of hope to those who have ever erred in their judgement. You are not beyond redemption. You may change, and you may become more, so much more than you were before.If there is any message to be taken from The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe, it is this...What a fortune, a privilege, a joy it is to have had such an experience. It leaves me hopeful that as a community--as a world--there is time for us to become our greatest selves. As great as we ever could dream of in our wildest, most ambitious visions for a brighter future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Dear Narrator,Dear "The Stanley Parable" -Team,Dear Gamers,I just was really amazed by this new content ending!I'll try to write a review without a spoiler for people who enjoy the beautiful art of storytelling just like I do!Therefore let me quickly explain what I think art is!Art is not about using the right colors or words to create or describe something! But it also is exactly about that!It's not just about you liking or admiring a piece of art... It's about embracing the love and creativity of the artist with your soul and heart and mind...Art can be anything as long as it's created with love and effort!Even if it's only the picture for your mom which you drew as a child!Don't be afraid to show your art to others!If they dislike it they just might not be able to see or understand it the way you do!Don't let them drag you down!Be proud of your creation!Or as I like to rhyme:"Art holds the key to the heart which creates art!"In other words:"The end is never the end is never the end is loading"Thank you for your beautiful work "The Stanley Parable" -Team!Looking forward to discover more content!10/10Kind regardsMax

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game about art and why people create art and consume art. It's a game about games. It's a game about nostalgia. It's a game about modern games with broken features, collectibles, and iterative/gimmicky "new content", which the bucket is a metaphor of. It's a game about cheap re-releases of games. It's a game about greed and the video game industry. It's a game about humans clinging on to the past and wanting sequels of things. It's a game about Stanley.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally do not understand people saying that the game is not enjoyable for players of the original Stanley Parable. I knew every single ending from the previous game, and I found this new iteration to be a blast. Sure, it's not going to be as fun as it would be if you have never played The Stanley Parable before, but for $30, honestly I'd say it's worth it. The endings that it did include I found to be funny, entertaining, and even really suspenseful at times. There is a pretty good amount of new content for you to explore, and a lot of the older endings have new twists to them. I won't go into any specifics, as spoiling this game COMPLETELY ruins the experience, but seriously, it's still an extremely enjoyable game, even if you have played the original. If you haven't ever played the original, definitely buy this game, you won't regret it. If you have, it's a bit more complicated. You may find the new content to be lacking, or like me, really truly enjoy every single bit of it. You really just need to give it a chance. (Also the graphics are better, so yeah.)

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a game named The Stanley Parable. Released in 2013, the Stanley Parable was a branching-path walking simulator with a wacky story, a comedic tone, great funny writing, deep meta-commentary about choice in games and choice in general, and one small issue: it didn’t end properly. Since it was based on both branching narrative paths  repetition (the latter allowing the exploration of the former), it couldn’t so much end as it petered out, as the player just sort of stopped finding new things and didn’t feel like rummaging through story lines he had already heard before, in hope for a few more funny voice lines or easter eggs. This is where The Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe comes in because it is an expansion of the original.But how do you expand on something that, to someone who is still familiar enough with it, will already have become a bit repetitive? You can’t just make your audience look again through a lot of stuff that they have already decided once was not worth looking through again. So, with a few exceptions, you delineate very clearly between old stuff and new stuff, so that the people who already know all the old stuff know where to find the new: Even the paths that you redo, you redo in such a way that it is very clear how to get the old and how the new version. Walk through the door like you’re used to, you get the ending you’re used to. Walk through the same door with the newly added bucket in your hand, get a unique bucket-based ending. Simple. Fun to navigate.This approach bears one issue, though. The new stuff feels a little extraneous. But here’s the kicker: since the game is so meta and so self-aware and so full of fun commentary, better yet: since that’s the entire point, you can make this expansion pack / sequel  expansion packs and sequels. About how to add something new to something old. About marketing based on nostalgia. About hype in the games industry. You still have extraneous features, but really what you have is extraneous features as ironic commentary  extraneous features and a sequel  how unnecessary sequels are.Whether this solves the problem is a matter of personal priorities. If you personally believe that it is worth it to pay 20 bucks for a piece of art that (in a really cool, funny, and well-written way mind you) is pointedly  its own pointlessness, then this game was made for you. If not, you might be left with a slightly sour aftertaste, because the drawback of art that (again, very entertainingly) keeps telling you that it is meaningless, is that you could end up believing it. And then your meta-commentary about a waste of money just feels like an actual waste of money.Personally, I had fun with it.
