_childDocuments_.review: The Expanse is one of my favourite sci-fi TV shows from the last few years, and I’d even argue that its the most underrated show because it didn’t seem to get much mainstream attention.If you’re not familiar with it, basically its set in the 24th century, where Humans live on Earth and Mars. There’s lots of political tension and conflict between those planets, and a third faction called Belters who live on space stations and mining colonies, with much of the show focused on the discovery of , and how each faction want to use it for their own agendas.This game is a prequel to the TV show, and features two playable characters who had supporting roles. The main five episodes feature Camina Drummer, a belter starship captain, and the bonus DLC episode features Chrisjen Avasarala, a high ranking diplomat working for Earth’s United Nations.If you’ve ever played a Telltale game, you’ll be familiar with the gameplay, which mostly involves the player making dialogue choices during conversations with NPCs to advance the story, and basic QTE combat scenes. There are also some sections where you’ll explore starship interiors to find items to solve basic puzzles, while avoiding combat drone sensors.The main reason I’ve given this a negative review is because the story is just kind of boring. Compared to the best Telltale games (Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us, Borderlands, Batman, Guardians of the Galaxy) the pace of the story is really slow. A couple of interesting things happened in episode three, but those plot threads didn’t really get a satisfying payoff in later episodes. At 6 hours, The Expanse is also significantly shorter than most other Telltale games.Your choices can have an impact on the story – mostly whether the other crew members live or die – but unfortunately I didn’t actually like any of those characters, so I didn’t really care one way or the other. They weren’t interesting, and I felt like a couple of them were overly aggressive and disrespectful towards Drummer, who is actually their commanding officer.Probably the best thing I can say about this game is that the texture quality and character animations are an improvement over previous Telltale games. I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate and the controls worked fine on my xbox 360 gamepad.Unfortunately I can’t really recommend the game, unless you’re specifically a fan of Camina Drummer, in which case you might find something to enjoy on a deep sale.I wouldn’t say no to a sequel focused on the Rocinante because I liked every member of that crew in the TV show, but the story would also need to have a much bigger scale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re looking for some screenshots  to view all the ones I took for this game.For those unfamiliar with The Expanse, here’s a small rundown. In the somewhat-distant future, humanity expanded to colonize the solar system, using vessels and technologies that belong to the ‘hard sci-fi’ category. That means no warp drives, force fields, phasers or lightsabers; everything is as down-to-earth, no pun intended, and scientifically-feasible as it can be, with our current understanding of the universe, at least. Space travel is still dangerous, laborious and exhausting - as it should be. Inter-faction conflicts between a united Earth, Mars independentists and the remote Belt regularly ensue, threatening to break a fragile peace.In all this, you’ll play as Camina Drummer, a hard-ass officer currently employed by disgraced ex-UNN officer Cox, on a clandestine salvage ship. With her being one of the prominent characters of the TV series, an entire spin-off wasn’t a bad idea, as long as they got it right. Well, in the end they didn’t. You have to understand Camina is a gritty, tough-as-nails Belter officer that went through Hell and back in her life, did unspeakable things and lived to tell the tale, with all the psychological consequences. Telltale, instead, decided to water down Camina’s grit and character, which leads to her acting like, and saying things that, she normally wouldn’t in the original source materials. Basically, she’s more of a crybaby and of a weakling compared to the series or novels - and it shows, especially later on. She’s still pretty badass, but nowhere near as much as she -should- be.The roster of side-characters encompassing her adventures is fine, but that’s the problem - it’s nothing more than that. There will be only minor appearances of characters involved in the TV series, exceptions made for Drummer herself, so if you’re waiting for your favorite one to pop up at some point, that’s not going to happen. Be that as it may, save for Khan, the ship’s pilot, and perhaps Virgil the crew medic, no other character feels remotely memorable. The ‘main villain’, if we want to call them that, is especially cheesy and unremarkable. Very few of said characters show any growth during the events that transpire, and most feel one-sided.Speaking of the setting, it’s an overall excellent rendition of the original material. From the interior of ships, tools, equipment, weapons - to the different mannerisms and ways of speaking of Belters, Martians and Earthers, everything has been transposed with minute attention to detail. Unfortunately, there isn’t any space for introductions to said setting, or any reference material like a codex or lore files, to help those unfamiliar with the TV series understand more of what they’re looking at. I would say that seeing the TV show is sort of a prerequisite for complete understanding of the events. Said events will be exciting at first, but get toned-down and less exciting as the adventure goes on. An attempt to make things spicy again is made during the last chapter, however it also misses the mark with its execution. The finale is more of a non-ending that leaves many questions - if that’s by design or laziness, we’ll never know.Each level is linear, and unfolds in more, or less, open environments depending on the situation. In some cases you’ll be exploring derelict ships in an open-world environment with multiple paths and optional locations, while in other cases you’ll simply have a linear path forward, as expected from a narrative adventure. There will be optional interactions and items to collect in each stage, which might lead to different interactions later on. For instance, finding a lost hacking device early on might prove to be useful later - sadly, the number of such interactions is limited compared to the actual number of items you’ll find, most of which serve as nothing more than achievement-related collectibles. There won’t be any real, major ‘secret’ to speak of, but surely there will be hidden side-areas sometimes with extra lore bits or side-quest items you can then give to specific characters. Exploration feels interesting, and is often encompassed by Camina’s radio chatter with the crew, or her own personal comments about the situation.There’s a limited degree of interaction with the environment: you’ll have to pick up or use specific objects as customary in this genre, while everything else will remain static for the most part. Certain sections have a bit more action, which either are about evading enemy detection with clever movement, or performing very forgiving quick-time events so fight, shoot, take cover and so forth. Failing any of these action sequences often means death, and restarting from the frequent auto-checkpoints. In some cases, it feels like dialogues or interactions are excessively forced towards a certain spectrum of actions, without giving players more freedom of choice - this is particularly true on the romance section, where you’re basically forced to romance a certain character and admit to love them anyways, even if you might not want to because, you know, it’s a choice-based game.

_childDocuments_.review: Walowda, fo pensa sasa! Mi pensa im gut, gut, imim na wé to:The Expanse: A Telltale Series da blast imalowda onto screens, invitin' to to pensa into da gritty lifes na Beltalowda before da events na diye iconic sci-fi show. Da game ta set a few years before da firs' season na show, un im pensa da helm as Camina Drummer, da fiercely loyal XO na scavengin' vessel, Artemis. Cara Gee, who embodies Drummer in da show, do da same ting ere, infusin' every line wit da character's mark blend na pragmatism un a likit vulnerability.Telltale's signature narrative style shines offering new insights into Drummer's backstory and the Belter world, weaving a gripping tale of political intrigue, crew loyalty, and the ever-present struggle for survival in the harsh expanse of space. The episodic format keeps the tension ratcheted up, leaving you desperate to see what unfolds next after each cliffhanger ending.Choices, glorious choices, milowda! The Expanse throws some gut-wrenching decisions your way. From navigating delicate political alliances to determining the fate of your crewmates, every choice carries weight and shapes Drummer's story. The replayability is high, as different choices lead to significantly different outcomes. However, while the choices are impactful, some might find the illusion of influence slightly limited, as certain plot points remain unchanged regardless of decisions.Beyond the gripping narrative, the world-building is stellar. Telltale crafts a lived-in, believable Belter society, where the grime and desperation are palpable. Claustrophobic ship interiors, vast stretches of zero-g environments, and the ever-present looming shadow of oppressive governments come alive through detailed environments and immersive sound design.Some might lament the lack of the series' signature space combat, but the focus on character interaction and exploration pays off handsomely. The zero-g traversal mechanic, where you propel yourself through ships and stations with your trusty tether gun, adds a unique layer of dynamism to exploration.Graphically, the game is a visual treat, capturing the gritty and futuristic aesthetics of The Expanse's world, now in the upgraded Unreal engine. The character models are impressively detailed, and the environments are immersive, transporting you right into the heart of the solar system's political intrigue and conflict.The soundtrack is atmospheric and perfectly complements the game's tone. Of course, the gorgeous title sequence from the TV show is here too - Clinton Shorter’s ethereal music blends perfectly with Lisbeth Scott’s haunting voice.  Voice acting is another area where the game shines. The cast delivers powerful performances that bring the characters to life, enhancing the emotional impact of the story. The writing is top-notch, maintaining the complex themes and tone of the original series, and the dialogue is sharp and engaging. But it isn't without its flaws. Technical hiccups like occasional frame rate dips and lip-syncing issues can be immersion-breaking. The Telltale formula, while tried and true, can feel a bit predictable at times. And let's be honest, five episodes feel like a tease when you're hooked on Drummer's story.Despite its rather minor stumbles, this is a must-play for fans of the show and narrative-driven adventures alike. It's a thrilling space odyssey that respects its source material, brimming with tough choices, gut-wrenching moments, and a badass Belter captain at the helm. The game's ability to immerse you in the politically charged world of The Expanse, coupled with its strong storytelling and character development, makes it a standout title in the Telltale lineup.If you're looking for a story that will stay with you long after the credits roll, set your course for .Just remember, beratna, every choice has consequences. Choose wisely. Sasa ke, pili kopeng, sa-sa

_childDocuments_.review: There’s Lesbian astronauts, ‘nuff said.A true beltalowda wouldn't hesitate to press the purchase button, sa sa ke?Let me start by saying that both the show and the book series this game is based on are fu*king excellent. It’s easily one of my favorite shows, period. This game doesn’t even begin to scratch the surface of the universe. It’s a blend of noir, hard sci-fi, political intrigue, war, and more. It largely keeps the science as realistic as the story really allows and it does so to some pretty great effect. It feels plausible in a way few space operas do.The first season starts a little slow, not bad in any way just slow, it has a lot of world building and character introductions to fit in, but once it kicks in… it fu*king flies. They adapted everything but the last 3 books because of a massive time jump that pretty much makes it a new show but it does complete its main arch and dangles a little more if they ever get the chance for a sequel series.I honestly can’t recommend it enough. The game does a nice job of introducing you to Drummer, a fan favorite character, but doesn’t open up too much with the overall plot of the show/books which I’m thankful for because it’s a wild ride that goes places you won’t expect and plays with genres in very fun ways. Love how the series has come full circle, since originally, even before books, The Expanse was prototyped as a tabletop RPG.As a big fan of the show though, I can say with confidence the game is very true to the atmosphere of it. The game feels like another season of the show. I really enjoyed it, hearing the theme tune play from the main menu made me a little emotional. They really nailed the look and feel of The Expanse universe and it was a genuine thrill playing the protagonist. I teared up a few times. It's hard to tell whether it would be appreciated as much for those who don't have the knowledge of the lore, but I still think it’s a very solid story. If you want to enjoy the game more, just watch the show before playing the game, it's a masterpiece and you will learn a lot about this universe. You’ll gain a deeper appreciation for some of what happens in the game and some of the characters who show up. Gameplay is a big leap, way more interaction which was lacking in later Telltale Games. There is not a massive time spent with your crew but I still came away thinking it was a very dynamic group. The episodes are short but only if you aren't one for exploring. I must have put over an hour into the wreckage exploration alone. When I first went out into it, I was overwhelmed with how open it was and how small it made me feel, they did a fantastic job at creating that feeling visually. And I just love Maya and Drummer together. Fantastic lesbian relationship. It’s a bit slow at times - mostly because a game can rarely be as fast/dynamic as an actual movie/TV series - but the tone is perfect. Solid writing and dialogue, great exploration (the zero-g section was amazing) and good characters. There’s some hard choices that (potentially) have a ton of impact like whether or not to space a traitor, and side quests that might end up having a major effect or not on the story, which is much different from Telltale’s old formula.I thought the star of the show in the game was the exploration. I really liked all the characters as well, but the exploration is what really felt straight up out of the show to me. I don’t think the novelty of that ever wore off for me. I also really liked the ending between episodes as it reminded me of how the show would always end episodes with really interesting hooks. Again I think anyone could pick up the game and enjoy it, that said... I think at the absolute minimum to get the most out of the game you should read a quick worldbuilding recap just so you know the generic factions, state of the galaxy etc. The game very much expects you to know specific terms and what each faction is. I wouldn't say it'll make or break the experience but it's just good to know exactly what is what.Overall it's definitely worth it but just know it's more like an interactive novel/movie vs a game. Personally I love these types of games. Detroit Almost Human, Until Dawn, The Quarry, Dark Pictures Anthology are some of my favourites. It’s the perfect kind of game for me - slow, meditative, exploration-heavy, story-heavy. If you like things to DO in a game, it’ll be boring. But if you’re looking to explore ships and watch the show while looking for easter eggs etc. It’s perfect. Yeah it always leaves a bad taste in my mouth when exclusivity ends and I support it. It's like they can get away with it. Saying that... I like Telltale, I like the Expanse and I wanted to play this game. I hate that I’m weak like that, but there’s a DLC about Avasarala with a warning about how much she swears, as a big simp of her how could I say no to that?!Buy it and enjoy it beratna, soon you won’t be no inya but a proud beltalowda.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Love it but...and it's a big but.I DO NOT RECOMMEND this game to those that have not watched the series or are not into Drummer as a character. This story is quite narrow in scope and is starring a lesser main character of the story. Drummer is my favorite character in the series, but I believe there is quite a bit those that haven't been properly introduced to her and the main story who will not understand. Her discovery is mind-blowingly significant, actually. You're not going to know that if you've not watched the show. It's the entire reason for the main story and all major conflicts! So before playing, if you like sci-fi, do yourself a favor and watch the series. It nods to real science, the story and characters are gripping and it will completely immerse you. So of course, that said, Drummer is an exceptionally charismatic and complex character. Playing her story is incredible - to me. But, I think a lot of people that don't know any better are going to be bored. I think this was a failure on the part of the writers. Providing a prologue to the story even in text format, would have gone a long way in helping people get invested and understand the story, why what she discovers is so huge, and even want to check out the books and (one of my top 5 all-time-faves Sci Fi) television series. Unfortunate, really.Also, it's just too damn short, like all Telltale Games, tbh. I don't know if I'm being unreasonable, however. It take a LOT of development and art hours to go into video games. On the flipside it takes players minutes to eat content that took months to make by many, many on the dev team.Ending on a positive note: I liked the story a lot. The designers did a terrific job giving the player a pretty good idea of what it is like to live in zero g, where the floor isn't always the floor, but the walls and ceilings of buildings and ships are for walking with mag boots too. Because, in zero g, "up" is is at most relative and at least, meaningless.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you watch the Expanse? Did you enjoy it? Well boy howdy, have I got a game for you. You play as Camina Drummer and Chrisjen Avasarala (Archangel DLC), and both of their show actors (Cara Gee and Shohreh Aghdashloo, respectively) reprise their roles as voice actors, and it sounds goooood. Camina is a vulnerable, but proven badass, and Chrisjen just oozes charisma, even as she's threatening to cut someone's  off. And yes, you can insult people while playing as Avasarala. She's just as visceral as her show incarnation and it's very funny. A lot of negative reviews are about the gaming being 'boring', and I get that and all; but this game felt exactly like the show. Slow when it needed to be, sometimes very slow, but when action kicked off it was tense and never felt out of place. People can die with the wrong decisions, characters will alter their opinion of you on how you handle stuff, and at no point did any of it feel like wasted time or filler. Give it a shot. If you like TellTale's previous catalog of games, you'll feel right at home in this one. Just hope you brought some hull seals with you!

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings shame to The Expanse IP. It is lazy, short, incomplete, and feels like it was made by interns.From a gameplay perspective:- The quicktime events seemingly do nothing and you can progress despite completely failing them.- Arbitrary interactions with objects will progress the story despite secondary objectives being incomplete, apparently failing them and impacting the story. - Zero G movement mechanics are buggy and not at all realistic- Obvious opportunities for 3rd person shooter mechanics, or other minigames are replaced with shallow quicktime events.In summary, the game leans heavily on the story, which might be fine if the story was compelling. _childDocuments_.review: FANTASTIC! Everything I could want in a Telltale version of Drummer's story before "the Expanse". Even if you have not seen the TV series, or read the books,  but are a fan of Telltale Games' work, you will likely enjoy this game.First of all I cannot BELIEVE the people complaining about the quick time events as combat in this game.  Standard Telltale Games stuff.   Nothing new or different here.  These games are narrative driven,  and "choices have consequences" driven.  Have been since the Walking Dead (also great games) days.   Please don't buy these games expecting them to be something they NEVER were and NEVER claimed to be.  I've loved the Drummer character since her intro in the TV series.  Cara Gee (returning to voice) brings such life, such steely grit and determination surrounding a moral core of dedication to her fellow Belters and empathy for all,  I can't believe she has not been nominated for any gaming awards. It is a great disservice to her and this game. This is the story of Drummer before she hooks up with visionary and redeemed UN figure, now OPA leader, Fred Johnson. Filled with memorable characters that I quickly became attached to (even the "bad guy" was likeable in her own way!) the story is engrossing in a way that it seems to fly WAY too quickly by.The art direction is gorgeous.  The "click" of your mag boots and hiss of your jet pack really does a great job of immersing you into a world without gravity.  Without going into detail for worry of spoilers, there are times when emptiness and a dwindling oxygen supply transport you into the story, as Drummer.  Just fantastic writing, sound, and environments.I literally am hard pressed to find something negative about this game in order to present a balanced review.I only hope we see more of this character or at least, more of The Expanse from Telltale (Amos -- HINT HINT)

_childDocuments_.review: Definitively worth it if you're a Drummerhead like myself, and a good narrative game besides. I don't think you'll like it as much if you're not a fan of exploring 3D spaces, The Expanse in all of its wonderful diverse semi-realistic sci-fi, or the best of the original Telltale games but if none of those scare you away then you'll find a good story where you don't need to know anything or even have read the books or watched the show to have a good experience.The sound and visual design stand out - its slightly stylized, the visuals, but a lot of the audio is straight ripped from the show. I didn't expect to hear the show's theme song when I booted up the game nor the signature kathunk of magboots but its all there.Overall it feels like the pilot to a prequel TV show, and I mean that in all the best ways. Left me wanting more but ultimately satisfied with its larger connections to the show, even if there were one too many for my personal taste.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played a Telltale game before--until this one involving The Expanse, generally I've not been interested in the settings nor the gameplay.However, as an interactive story in a setting and with both characters and actors (Cara Gee) that I enjoy, I found this game entertaining and exactly what I expected. The story within fits The Expanse extraordinarily well and Drummer (Gee) is well written and acted. The choices seem appropriate. It's very much a choose-you-own-adventure style of book, if you recall those from decade past; and there are lot of optional bits to choose. Plus there is some exploration, without timers, which I always appreciate.The graphics and audio are suitable; certainly without surprise. Performance is good and without glitches or crashes--there is not a lot of complexity to the mechanics, so this is a low-bar. I enjoyed the EVA and exploration segments--I have a SpaceMouse, yes the 6-DoF gizmo like they used for the Rocinante controls in the show, which was fun to use and a bit meta.The game is short: 8 hours for the main game. So it's hard to say it's a good value; I usually look for a better value proposition. But what with the forum trolls and anti-EGS children, I figured I should not wait for a sale and just get about enjoying the story and setting.I would not recommend the Archangle DLC. It has little of what is good about the main game, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: For a game that needs to court fans of an existing series, and meet their expectations head-on, delivering a minimally-acceptable product is still an achievement. To tackle a goal that large without generalized failure requires a great deal of competency and effort... but once acknowledged, that leaves us with a much weedier question: even in all its humility and hard work, is it something that you'll want to give several hours over to? Telltale's Expanse is respectful of the source material, particularly in flavor text and dialog. It does pretty well here, and it's also done in arguably the most important area. Plus, if the environmental artists aren't fans of the series, well... you could've fooled me, because the environments do a great service to the scale of the setting. But when it's time to contrive gameplay segments to challenge the player, the "Hard Sci-Fi" setting's cold, merciless practicality gets benched pretty often. Stuff like your enemies flooding 40 recon drones into a hallway so they can loop back and forth along 20ft tracks and make you dodge the (highly visible) laser cones. Segments like this are firmly on the Mario side of videogaming, and with one of the series' central themes being how narrow the margins are when you try to survive the frightening efficiency of future tech, it's... pretty distracting when an enemy needs to rely on a bay's worth of roombas to scour a couple of hallways for a human-size target on a ship less than half a kilometer away. If we're going to pretend shipboard sensors can't accomplish this without extended presence, then it'd at least be way cooler to play cat and mouse with one respectable piloted probe instead of dozens of "avoid me" drones.Now, it is a game. We can understand that these sequences exist for variety, and that breaks from the setting are forgivable if they keep the core of the experience from getting too sleepy... but in that case, it's also really important that the sequences don't overstay their welcome. Once you hit one, odds are it's going to be a focus on a singular mechanic that intensifies over time, and it may not take long to discover that if you trigger a game-over screen, you're probably starting the entire thing over... including the training-wheel section at the beginning. Considering that the tasks aren't especially absorbing or tense, you may find that arriving with at the next apparent action section fills you with resignation before you even know what the assignment is.Oh well, it's a Telltale Game. It's my first one, but I know by reputation that I'm signing up for the story and characters more than anything else. On this point, it does deliver some high points, such as the first time you thaw the proverbial ice with your pilot... but these peaks stand in unavoidable contrast to the valleys that surround them.The two brothers on your crew are a great example, because throughout the first act, you'll see a lot of them. And while you do learn a fair bit about their on-paper characteristics, it's surprising that neither of them is made out to be particularly plausible, or even likable for that matter. One's a pixar protagonist whose childlike innocence is tempered by chronic clumsiness; the other is a ruthless cokehead, and despite being a volatile prick, you're told that he's the more reliable of the two.Despite those tropes being fertile ground for fleshing out a believable character, that potential doesn't deploy into anything much deeper or more relatable during my playtime. I never broke the sense that they exist only as a philosophical litmus test for the player to weigh in on later: "if you could only pick one quality in a subordinate, would you favor their character, or their performance"? You might think it's unfair for me to assess this without completing the game, but I've seen these guys appear out of nowhere to catch barrels, make quips, and squabble for a couple of hours, and I remember my exposure to them more than anyone else on the crew: despite this, I'm not-at-all holding my breath for whatever it's building up to, and it's hard not to notice the absence of tension for their fates. I've seen a hundred fictional characters die to make a dramatic point, and these guys haven't graduated from "plot device with a pulse" despite a dozen opportunities to give us a glimpse at personhood.Most characters fare the same way (including the aforementioned pilot) until their designated moment of drama where they reveal more of themselves, but if you're allowed to wait long enough for that moment to appear, a lot of interest can leak away and create sinkholes under the desire to know more. Especially if a lot of that time waiting, is spent with the same characters you're waiting on.So, the core experience of "story" never sinks to poor quality, and there are moments where it shines; but it's also told pretty economically, and for me, the truly engaging moments were pretty distant from each other. It definitely falls short of that classic-Bioware quality of "I'll use my gun to plunge every toilet on the station it takes me to the next story beat", which isn't much less than what you'd need to outweigh the action sequences bundled in here and create a holistically Great game.Overall, I find Telltale's Expanse impossible to condemn, because it's made with a lot of respect and it seems to be doing everything within its power to achieve quality. But as far as endorsements go, my sales pitch for the game can't do much more than help you navigate the caveats and see if it's right for you. Personally, I'm unsure if I'll complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed and finished every Tell Tale game I've ever played, which is most of them. But this one has so much tedious 'game-play' where you're searching in third person for items instead of progressing the story. Is ANYONE playing these games to walk around slowly and click on stuff? We're here to choose responses and enjoy the story. The last straw was an awful point where you have to float around and hide from robots that insta-kill you. Why? So unbelievably lame. At best these are mildly annoying time wasters, and at worst they're frustrating enough to kill motivation to continue. I'm part of the latter and I don't recommend this absolute miss.

_childDocuments_.review: Eh.. not Telltale's finest work.  If you've never seen the Expanse show completely, you will be lost with the background lore.  The game's plot is very linear and there's only a couple major decisions (which doesn't affect the plot very much).  Once you've played through once, you've seen the whole game.  The "puzzles" are repetitive and extremely simple.  Unskippable dialog often blocks progress until it finishes, even if the dialog has been heard already.  The dialog to interaction pacing is all off.  They kept the episode format, but dropped the breaks between episodes so it just throws you in to the next episode with no recap.  Each episode is only an hour long, which is half of what it should be at minimum.  The bonus DLC was just alright.  4/10.   Telltale, take notes from Detroit on how to make a story game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Expanse: A Telltale Series is a gripping narrative-driven game that will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish. As a fan of the hit sci-fi series, I was excited to see it come to life in this interactive format, and I was not disappointed.The first thing that stands out about this game is the stunning graphics. The attention to detail is remarkable, and the familiar landscapes and characters from the show are rendered beautifully. The music and sound effects also add to the immersive experience, making you feel like you are a part of the world of The Expanse.One of the best aspects of the game is the decision-making element. As with other Telltale games, your choices and actions have consequences, and they can greatly impact the story and characters. This adds a layer of intrigue and excitement as you never know what will happen next and how it will affect the outcome.The storytelling in this game is top-notch. The writers have managed to capture the essence of The Expanse and have created a new story that stays true to the source material. The dialogue is well-written, and the characters are brought to life with their unique personalities and motivations. As a player, you feel invested in their journeys and can't help but root for them.I also appreciated the puzzle-solving aspects of the game. They were challenging enough to keep me engaged, but not too difficult to become frustrating. They added a nice break from the intense decision-making moments and helped to flesh out the gameplay.My only criticism of the game would be its length. As a Telltale game, it falls on the shorter side, with around 6-8 hours of gameplay. However, the quality of the story and characters makes up for it, and I found myself replaying the game to explore different paths and see how my decisions could change the outcome.Overall, The Expanse: A Telltale Series is a must-play for any fan of the series. It captures the essence of the show perfectly and adds a unique interactive element that will keep you engaged until the very end. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a thrilling and immersive storytelling experience.

_childDocuments_.review: It's ok.  It was fun to play a Telltale game again after so long.  Lot's of floating around in a space suit which is pretty fun.  Lot's of scavenging which seems fun at the time, but I'm not sure actually did anything or effected the game in any ways in retrospect.  Most of the "game" aspects of the game were very minimal, with some simple puzzles and quicktime events.  Voice acting and story was good, really liked a few of the side characters and enjoyed interacting with them.  My biggest gripe is that I wrapped up the base game and the DLC in about 6 1/2 hours. _childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant addition to the Expanse lore and story. It adds depth and complexity to existing characters. With that being said some aspects of the story might be lost on you if you are new to the Expanse. As expected the game moves a little bit away from other Telltale games, with perhaps the overall story being a bit more linear than you might expect in previous titles. Despite this, I think it innovates in a lot more ways, with excellent writing, visuals and music. Crucially it does feel like your choices matter within that story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the TV show and Telltale games, I enjoyed this game.However I would not recommend this game to anyone who has not at least watched the first season or two of the TV show. Although this game takes place prior to the events of the show, this game does not introduce anyone who is unfamiliar with the Expanse universe to any of the factions / politics / characters. Someone going into this game blind without having watched the show will likely find this game confusing and likely get bored.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game but short. I suggest buying this game during a sale to get your money's worth. The script and writing was well done. _childDocuments_.review: 4/10This game is very boring. Neither the story, the gameplay or the environments pull me in and after the short experience (the game is around 6 hours long) I felt nothing. It looks alright, plays alright and sounds alright (apart from two instances where a voiceline peaks, which is very sloppy). The rest is just so dull that I cannot recommend this game. However, there are a few reasons as to why certain people might enjoy it.Let me start by noting that I have no previous knowledge about The Expanse. I have not read the books, not seen the TV-show, nothing. This obviously makes my experience with this game worse than it would be for an experienced fan, but when it comes to similar games developed or published by Telltale, this is the only one which made me feel this negative about it. I played Tales From the Borderlands without having played any of the Borderlands-games and enjoyed it, I played Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series without having read any of the books or seen the TV-show and I enjoyed that game a lot and I played Back to the Future: The Game while only having vague memories of the first film as a child and I enjoyed that as well. Those games presented a world and characters that, while tying in to existing media, presented a story that stood on its own and did not rely entirely on external knowledge of the IP. This game does, and it does not stand on its own.This story serves as a backstory for one of the big characters in the books and TV-show, Camina Drummer. She works as an XO (some kind of second-in-command) on a ship tasked with doing a salvage-job. We follow Camina and her small crew as the salvage-job turns into something slightly bigger. It could be a lot bigger, but as someone who does not have knowledge about the universe outside of what the game provides, I do not understand the larger consequeces that certain actions would have. However, certain situations ARE life or death for the crew, and that is obviously important. Or they would be, if the characters were likeable or interesting. Most of them are rather unpleasant, presenting an attitude and demeanour that almost instantly makes me not care for their well-being. They are also not given the proper time or care in order for them to grow much, and mostly ends up where we met them (unless they die, of course, but for me it APPEARED rather obvious how to act in order to save those who could be saved). Camina herself suffers from prequel-armor, where the player KNOWS that she cannot die, because she exists in later media. All tension and suspense around her well-being are thus null and void and she serves as a vessel for how the player wants to interact their environment rather than the destiny of the protagonist. This is not bad in itself, but is terrible in the context of this "choices matter"-game in which some choices (too obviously) do not matter.That is really all that is needed to say here, otherwise the game is fine. It just has so many obvious flaws (and for me a very dull story) that I cannot recommend it. If you are a fan of the IP you certainly might feel otherwise, and I suggest you read other reviews that help you form an opinion on whether or not this game is worth your time and money. Still, some critique stands, regardless of whether or not you are a fan. I hope that later games published by Telltale will get more care in order to stand on their own.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Telltale Games and I love the Life Is Strange Series (which developer Deck 9 has been working on in recent years). This should have been a good collaboration, but the end product is practically worthless.The most obvious flaw is that the game is only about 5-6 hours long. This is a game that was originally priced at $40. This is half the length of a typical Telltale or LiS game and double the cost of what those used to be. Even if you justify that original $40 asking price based on the newer game engine and (hopefully) better working conditions, that doesn't fix the rest of the game's flaws.For a Telltale game, there are basically very few choices to make. In fact, with how short the episodes are, you pretty much get a cut-to-black, see ya next time after every main choice when the episodes wrap up an hour in.Another huge issue is that the game is oftentimes a walking sim instead of a narrative game. You'll spend more of each chapter floating alone through the space ship than you will talking to other characters or doing anything else. It's just filler of moving around finding collectibles to stretch out the episodes to an hour because, somehow, they didn't even really have 5 hours worth of story to tell. The zero gravity movement is kinda neat at first but becomes boring very quickly. But don't worry, they put in two whole puzzles for you to solve with little-to-no-effort to help shake things up.It's also worth stating that the story has pretty much no value unless you're a fan of The Expanse already, which I am not. I felt no connection to these characters and a lot of the dialogue involves characters using terms from the show without any sort of context or even a glossary for newcomers. Contrast that with past Telltale games where (imo) you can easily enjoy the story and characters even if you don't know the IP beforehand.By the third episode if not sooner, I had pretty much come to the conclusion that I was unhappy with this game. I saw it through to the end, but despite how short the game is, the finale 2-3 hours felt like a drag because I was just ready for it to be over.I really want Telltale's comeback to succeed, but this collab with Deck 9 just wasn't it. And with Wolf Among Us 2 still in limbo, things are looking pretty grim.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes I played the game and yes I beat the game in 6 hours. The entire time I legit felt like the things you collected early on in the game would matter by the end of the game but literally nothing matters in this game. No matter what you choose or do the story will rail on in the same direction. Some characters can die yes, but it's extremely bland and almost like it was made for an 8 year old with no critical thinking skills. I got an achievement for "dodging the drones" when I literally just flew straight and didn't even attempt to dodge them. Brain-dead is an understatement when it comes to problem solving6 hours of game play and the ONLY thing I did was like 6 or 7 quick time events and make entirely inconsequential decisions. The ambiance is good cause it makes you feel alone in space and the story isn't necessarily bad. It just feels like this should be the first game the company made and not the newest game. Why in the hell did they make me pick up the magnetic boots for Khan in chapter 2? Why did I get the medicine for Arlen? Why did I literally do anything in the game except walk/float forward?If you wanna float through a story and enjoy the Expanse I guess you'll like it, but it has "Telltale" in the title so if you're thinking it's going to feel even remotely like Wolf Among Us or any other game they've done...you are going to be very very disappointed. It feels like a decision making game for children minus the very few moments of violence. Nothing you do matters. Watch the game on youtube and you'll have played the game pretty much.You are essentially playing a walking simulator in a visual novel. There is no "exploration" like the tag says and I have literally no idea why "RPG" is in the tag. There's no leveling up or stats involved at all. I'm not kidding when I say you will be just listening to unskippable dialogue every 5-10 seconds and just going to your next objective. There is no feeling of failure either in this game. It holds your hand and practically plays itself. The QTE's are just a snoozefest.

Unfortunately, The Expanse: A Telltale Series lacks the life-or-death, world-changing consequences that make the show so watchable and enjoyable. As a prequel, the story needs more real stakes, and it may have been better with an original character.Using the original voice actors was a nice touch; however, not all actors are voice actors. The performances don't match their brilliant on-screen roles.The Expanse: A Telltale Series is a rainy-day game for fans. _childDocuments_.review: Hm... This negative review is a difficult one to give, because I've loved most everything Telltale has done, from The Walking Dead, to Tales from the Borderlands, to even their original stuff like The Wolf Among Us. And with their recent-ish return, I was particularly excited to get back into new Telltale stories. But unfortunately, this one just lacks depth and intrigue to keep you interested, like most of their past works do. I have not watched the main series this game stems from, but neither did I for The Walking Dead. Telltale is more than capable of making stories that capture you, whether or not you know the material the story's derived from, so it was a little disappointing that I still felt pretty uninvested and disinterested in the story/game by the time I completed the final episode. It's not all bad though, so let's highlight a bit.The Good:The Bad:In conclusion, there are more negative and generally disappointing takeaways here than I would have expected from Telltale. While the graphics and visuals have improved, and the voice acting continues to be top tier, only having two (often undesirable) choices in a Telltale game feels like an extreme level of regression. And I really don't like saying that because I love Telltale and their ability to make engaging, engrossing stories that are customized a bit to the way you play, how you choose to act, what you say, etc. Many Telltale games have stuck with me for years. But unfortunately, I get the feeling I'll hardly remember much from this one aside from how bare-bones and entrapping it felt. And how annoying it is to have a single, inescapable romance constantly thrown at you.Oh well. Staying hopeful for the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult game to rate without spoilers.  Chances are that I played the first Telltale Walking Dead game before you were born.  Thus, my expectations may be different than someone more contemporary.Of course you should play it, especially when on sale.  The Expanse is a beautiful episode set in that narrative universe, desperately on rails with little input from the player.  The characters are well designed, and the environments are immersive.  Scavenging is fun.  The cut-scenes can get very long, and the developers did not see fit to allow dialogue slipping, so the thought of additional play-throughs feels tedious.  There is no rewind option.The quick-time events barely deserve the description.  They are so slow they are impossible to fail.  What has happened to innovation and building on the works of earlier games?  So much gameplay feels rehashed and regurgitated.  Shenmue had better QTEs on the Dreamcast.  Oh man, now that was a game.  I miss my VMU.I loved Telltale's Batmans, Borderlands and Game of Thrones.  Some decisions in Game of Thrones left me feeling torn, sometimes nauseated-- I still think about them.  When I finished GoT on a to-be-continued only to learn that there would never be a follow-up, well... I was depressed for days.The decisions in The Expanse are almost inconsequential, you can just mash a button. The narrative for this game isn't terribly compelling, since it occurs completely out of context from the rest of the solar system and human culture.  It doesn't even feel like it matters.  The game is over and now I move on.But of course you should play it, especially when on sale.  New experiences are essential, even if disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: I needed this. After start-stop-ing several games in order to try to get into the groove of one, I spun up  with a vague hope that the game lives up to the excellency of the source material. And while it only tells a very small prequel side story about one of the series' most iconic and likable characters, the game did manage to do what I hoped it would.It is hard to put into words how much The Expanse means to me -- first and foremost its TV series, as I haven't yet read the books (I have all nine of them and I swear I will start them tonight). The atmosphere, the  right , the characters (as flawed as they can be), it just resonates with me so well. I personally rate it even higher than 2000s  or the best episodes of Picard's Star Trek, all of which I love.The game manages to tap into all the same atmosphere of the TV series and rekindle the same kinds of feelings playing it as I had watching it. That is the best compliment I can give. Yes, it is mostly a walking simulator with a few choices that can feel artificial for someone not invested in the universe or the characters -- but I was invested. I searched nooks and crannies for salvage, which allowed me to make the right choices for the best ending and it felt great. I loved the early episode's space walk sections, as small they might have been, they felt completely right. The third episode was the highlight, with the mystery and creepiness of the abandoned mining station and the discovery of what happened to its inhabitents. The last two episodes were very linear and driven by choices you make along the way, but it was still fine.I could play a game for dozens of hours, just salvaging or adventuring in space with a small crew that banters and looks out for each other, if the universe and atmosphere is just right, and Telltale did a great job capturing the Expanse universe and making it feel right.Overall it was excellent for me, as I am a huge fan of the show and its characters and this type of science fiction in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Mouse settings are completely frustrating. For goodness' sake, just use RAW MOUSE INPUT. There's no need for a fancy mouse reading code; just utilize the readout WINDOWS PROVIDES, for crying out loud.They even went ahead and implemented Mouse DECELERATION. Who in their right mind comes up with BS like this? Seriously? PC gamers for well over 30 years have despised the idea of mouse acceleration. While it has its place, most people don't use it, so naturally, make it an option. The folks over at Deck Nine, though, did something even better – try moving your mouse fast, and it's going to get capped and slowed down. And it's not an option that's set in stone.And just for that, I won't recommend it. It just doesn't make any sense that out of all the people who worked on this game, nobody had the bright idea to put this in as an option, something that nobody even thought about."But you should use a controller" some random guy about to comment.No, they made the game for PC, meaning they have to provide controls for the game usable BY a mouse and keyboard. And it's not like the gameplay is there to pick up the slack either, with some floating about and interacting with a few things, and solving some 'puzzles' that have no stakes or challenge. And whilst Camina was a pretty cool character, it was strange putting us in control of her when she's already been portrayed on screen and in the books, and thus canonically established. _childDocuments_.review: The good first. The strong point of this game is its cast of characters.  is already famous as a TV series for the compelling personalities it has butting heads in its episodes, and the new ones added in this game feel like they fit right in. Khan and Toussaint are such good presences that it almost feels like they were written by completely different writers than everyone else. I cannot say enough good things about those two, and about the protagonist, Drummer, who was without a doubt an excellent choice for the focus of the whole thing. I hope we see Cara Gee in a lot more things.In terms of gameplay it's nothing to write home about, and the limited scope of budget is definitely showing. At multiple points I felt like connective scenes and clarifications were missing, and most major decisions don't branch out into significant story alternatives. The exploration and scavenging minigames are... *there*, and they do make you feel like a proper beltalowda eking out an existence in the ass-end of the universe... but they don't add much to the narrative. No use is ever made out of the random scavenged items you find, apart from filling out a collectibles counter. It feels like some of the budget for these sections could have been put to better use making more story.The one section where the exploration pays off as a concept is the midway, Episode 4. To say more would be spoilers, but suffice it to say that they could have done more with that concept, and they might have arrived at a much more compelling gameplay.I played this game out of nostalgia after the TV show ended. It definitely scratched that itch. The bonus episode, , ended in a genuinely emotionally affecting manner, and was generally the high point of the entire game for me. But I'd credit that to Shoreh Aghdashloo's spectacular voice acting than anything else.7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a wonderfully enjoyable experience.PROS:Characters had well developed personalities, that you as the player will genuinely care about. Action scenes are quick time events, that are not punishing but still instil tension.Story is well written that is not confusing or weak. Impact-full moments hit hard and were a great experience.NEGATIVES:Some of the exploring became slightly tedious at times. Wasn't intolerable though.Some of the space battle effects looked a little underwhelming at times.SUMMARY:A great experience that I would recommend to those looking for an immersive story to enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game but it's just not my cup of tea - I've played for just over an hour (73  mins) and I just can't see myself going any further.  Ultimately you follow a pre-determined storyline and make several choices that - presumably - will have consequences later.  But the game is slow... very slow.  Walking is slow, flying is slow, and clicking around walls/icons is slow - it's mindless.I'd rather just watch the TV version of this.  I didn't feel engaged at all.And at the end of the first chapter, you've given a "grade" or "score" on how well you make your choices... huh?  Who is playing the game?  Me, or the developers?I wanted to love this game - The Expanse is the best hard sci-fi that we've had in the last 10-20 years.  But the game plays like a really slow mixture of Call of Duty (fixed story, just futzing around until the next cut-scene) and Mass Effect (choices that have very little overall effect on gameplay - from what little I could bring myself to play).
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: As an Expanse super fan, having watched the series and read the books, I was happy to see it  getting a game adaptation, especially from a studio like TellTale, which prioritizes storytelling above all else, so it is with a heavy heart that I say this was a story barely worth telling, with choices that felt empty and that have almost no impact whatsoever.The best content in this game are things like The Mausoleum, but it is just a location with an interesting background and visuals that help with this Universe's world-building.Frankly, as much as I like Cara Gee and the expanse, there was no need to tie this with the main events of the Expanse if the story was this small and limited, I would have preferred an entirely new spin-off story in the past. The characters were relatively shallow and unexplored, and the chapters of this story barely 30% the size of what I would consider to be an acceptable old TellTale game chapter.As much as I love the Expanse, this is a game that I can't recommend, and it worries me about The Wolf Among Us sequel, and any future TellTale project, if this is the new standard for this studio.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend this only to existing fans of the adapted property, and only on a 50% sale while skipping the DLC. The lack of budget has clearly impacted the length and overall quality of the game, though this may not be completely detrimental for those already invested enough. I hope that this is not indicative of what we can expect from The Wolf Among Us 2, which is still in production. While most decisions are not at all impactful, some do have unforeseen consequences that may determine one to replay the game. If not today or tomorrow, then maybe at some point in the future. Improved when compared with the old TTG graphics, though I can't say how relevant the comparison is; the company  bought some time after filing for bankruptcy, so the developers are most likely new. In any case, moving away from the cel-shaded aesthetic was a good decision (at least for the purpose of adapting The Expanse). Very impressive, visually. They make up for the very linear level design. Getting some of the cast from the TV show to do the voice acting is a huge plus. On the other hand, this makes some of the internal monologue seem a bit out of character at times. If there's one problem I have with the cast is that they picked a younger person to voice an older character and it's very grating. Which is unfortunate because that's also one of the better written characters in the game. Quite lengthy and well animated. The space battles in particular remind me of the TV show. One of the most idiotic decisions that a publisher can take. No matter the payout, this exclusivity harms both game sales and discoverability in the long run. I didn't even know this game came out on Steam until after a few months in which I had forgotten it even existed. About half as long as older TTG games, but asking the same price. I wouldn't buy it unless it's at least 50% off. Moreover, the reduced amount of time you get to spend with the characters prevents you from getting invested in the story. This is also a factor that directly impacts the value of the game. The game comes with a separately priced DLC. Honestly, it's not worth the money. It's very limited in scope, and I'd go so far as to even call it a lazy cash grab. It mostly consists of you being locked up in a room and making phone calls (the devs didn't even bother animating some video calls at that). Braindead easy. They were jammed in just in order for the game to conform to the old TTG formula. Most times there's not even any consequence to messing them up. The game doesn't provide a proper introduction into the universe that it's based on. This reinforces the argument that it was made specifically for existing fans (of the books or TV show) and prevents it for having a larger appeal, like The Wolf Among Us had, despite most people never even hearing of Fables beforehand. Leaving consequences of said choices aside, you only get 2 or sometimes (rarely) 3 to pick from. This is very disappointing but it was probably a budgetary constraint.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: ...meh. Not a bad a game by any means, especially standalone. Unfortunately its attention to detail is no where near the level of the phenomenal series it is based on, and my suspension of disbelief was difficult enough to maintain that I cannot recommend Telltale's interpretation as an Expanse game. The unnecessary inclusion of Julie Mao as a side character in the plot, the Protomolecule as a generic McGuffin to be forgotten until it reappears with no mention of the incidents in the game, and the lack of attention to the set design of the series (most glaringly, some the wrecks that are explored in game are oriented with the decks parallel to the direction of thrust, rather than in the "skyscraper" layout described in the novels and shown in the show) make this a jarringly sloppy interpretation of the show and novels, despite good character development and some interesting details.The DLC is actually quite good, and fills in details regarding some of Avasarala's past that went unaddressed in the series (rather than inventing new story details from contrivance). For the current price of the game, however, I don't think it's worth getting just for the DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I have really mixed feelings about this game... I bought it due to my love for The Walking Dead series and The Wolf Among Us hoping for improvement not only in graphics, but also in gameplay, the importance of the choices, complexity of relations and the whole story. Now, after I finished all 5 chapters, I feel REALLY dissapointed. First of all, the main story is ok. Just ok. For me "ok" means same as "meh". There were very few crucial, important choices and when there were some, I didn't find them hard, challenging and making me question my conscience. I didn't connect with the story. The chapters were too short, the crew also wasn't so engaging and likeable. I found this game really boring at times. There were some easy QTE actions, some flying in the cosmos, but no actual shooting. This game seemed really hollow and empty to me. It was the better looking game from Telltale, but regressed in every other aspect.The next big problem of this game is that characters use a specific language in their conversations but I can't even check what does it actually mean in some ingame dictionary f.e. There was only one note in the beginning, but it didn't go to my inventory...For me the most important part of these type of games is being excited about the story and I was really bored most of the time :/ Walking through same areas, boring hollow spaceships where nothing is happening. I don't know if the team wanted to potray the series as close as it can be (I don't know nothing about it, so the game is the whole universe for me), but it's still a game and it had way too less twists and interesting moments to call it a great game, which I would like to replay in the future.However, the graphics are amazing <3 I can't say nothing wrong about the presence of "The Expanse".I have to give it 6/10 and I really hope that "The Wolf Among Us 2" will be much more entertaining and impactful.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved The Expanse. Enjoyed the books. Enjoyed the TV show. Now I've enjoyed the game too.Is it a great game, though? Not really. It's not a bad game, but a lot of its appeal is that the show did a speed run in the last season and it felt like we didn't get to spend enough time with the best character who was, of course, Camina Drummer. How awesome to have a whole game featuring Drummer, right? Well, yes, it would be if the story was compelling. But the story tries to fit itself between a couple of episodes in the show, and you know how it's all going to turn out, so there isn't really much suspense. None of the choices feel like they have an impact, because we know the macguffin is not going to change the balance of power, otherwise we would've seen that in the show.It also doesn't help that they've given Drummer a love interest with whom she has no chemistry. There is a lot more chemistry between Drummer and her pilot - or Drummer and her piratical antagonist - than the improbably scrawny ex-marine she's paired up with here. When the TV show already gave us the baddest ass marine that there is - Draper - you got a high bar to clear, and Castillo does not clear it.You spend a lot of the game floating around space hulks filled with corpses but no bad guys, as if the developers desperately wanted to build a horror game but realized halfway through that they couldn't introduce aliens into a pre-existing universe. It all feels very austere and empty, missing the political complexity and human warmth of the show. The best parts are the conversations with your crew, when they don't involve relationship melodrama. Maybe the romance could've worked if they had picked a softer main character, but softening Drummer in this way didn't come across as authentic to me.However, it's still The Expanse. It's still sci-fi. The DLC features a day in the life of Avasarala, who was probably the breakout star from the TV show, and that has all of the political intrigue and maneuvering that you could want from a short story set in this universe. So if you are a fan, it's worth buying. If you are not a fan... Eh, there's better Telltale games out there, like Tales from the Borderlands. On the Deck Nine side, this is not as bad as Life is Strange: True Colors, but it's not gonna make you feel things like Before the Storm did. Mediocre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: This is alright but I do not recommend at full price.  I recommend this heavily for fans of The Expanse or story driven games.The Good: Easily digestible story with a focus on visuals during scenes which are beautiful.  The freedom of exploration in space is nice allowing the player to miss items they feel could be key for another play-through.  The diverse dialogue options also allow for repeatability with moral/perspective changes.  Players looking for a re-playable movie game will enjoy this and other Telltale titles.The Bad: Weak world building.  The universe of The Expanse is not fully fleshed out in the main game and even through data logs as pieces of the world building is left in the dialogue hinting on generally only one type of point of view.  Knowledge of The Expanse outside of this game helps.  Also lacking in character depth as much as other Telltale titles for some characters.Edit: After playing episode Archangel, it fills in some of the world building that I found weak in the main game.  This is episode is too compact with little exploration but is necessary to understand the world more.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I love the Expanse, I love Telltale Games, I jumped on it as soon as I saw they had come together to make this game, and I've loved every second of it.  I've had great experiences with other Telltale games, but I would play 10 games set in this universe if they were all this good.  Originally the DLC content seemed like it wouldn't be very interesting, while still intriguing because I love the character it is set around, but halfway through the game I decided I'm definitely buying it and playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Picks a cool character from the show and tells her prequel story to the series. Keep in mind this isn't really a game (you can totally ignore the gameplay, the minigames and such), more an immersive story telling kind of thing, and with that out of the way it works quite well, using some of the original cast as voice actors, the original music/score: If you enjoyed the series you will enjoy this.Quite short ~4h, so ideally buy this on discount.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished The Expanse: A Telltale Series. Got it on sale yesterday. I say it's worth $20. What it accomplishes in about 6 hours of gameplay is solid. Cara Gee reprises her role as Camina Drummer in a a prequel that sets up the story we know and love. There are also just enough branches to the story to tempt me to play through again and make different choices. But to be clear, it's a walking simulator with the occasional QTE, none of which were too hard. And I found it a bit too short. Would have liked 1 or 2 more chapters that resemble the best ones in the existing story, but what's there serves the plot well.I enjoyed the voice acting. The one thing that put me off was that Jared Harris didn't return to voice Anderson Dawes. I assume he is so expensive and could probably sue imitators of his particularly distinctive voice that the stand in opted for close-but-not-quite. That said, the character is definitely true to form, and that's what matters.Each chapter ends with the trademark Telltale scorecard comparing your choices to other players'. I'm always pleasantly surprised when I take a major story beat against the grain. I like this feature and have thoughts about it.As a story in The Expanse setting, I give it a 10 out of 10. As a Telltale game a 7 or 8 because it's short. As a gamelike-form-of-entertainment, you either like walking simulators or you don't. I do, so, yes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this on sale, probably the best way to do it. I enjoyed the nostalgia of the game as a huge fan of the books and show. Fab to ride with Drummer, a much loved character, so perfectly voiced by the original Cara Gee. Not so much game as story adventure, which is fine, with progression and outcomes dependent on your decisions. You can spin through it pretty quickly if you just complete the main objectives, or extend play by investigating all areas and following side missions. Quite tame and gently paced overall but enjoyable none the less. No manual save option so don't abandon play mid chapter until you see the autosave symbol!
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I think I got to Chapter 3 before I just couldn't anymore.Its trying, but its a "video game" first and The Expanse second. You don't need to waste my time with contrived "avoid the laser" sequences. I bought a story-driven game. PDCs NEVER worked that way in the movie or book. It's like this all over, the established logic of the show is only there until there's a "game segment" that has to contradict it in order to justify its existence. If I wanted a stealth action game, I would've bought a stealth action game. If I wanted a game about item collection I would've bought a platformer. I bought a story-driven game based on established IP, why is that being compromised to provide half-assed chunks of other games I didn't buy?

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a mega-fan of the Expanse, you'll get some enjoyment. The setting is beautifully realized, and it is fun walking/flying around interiors that could have been ripped right out of the universe.The characters are just ok. The story has potential but fizzles and doesn't say anything of much importance for the characters or the setting. But most damning, the gameplay is boring, mostly walking around empty ships looking for interactables to get voice lines from. Action scenes are painful quick time events that begged for a simplistic shooting gallery minigame instead. And the choices you make lack the reactivity that make Telltale games worth playing. _childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those times I really wish Steam had a "Thumb sideways" review...Are you a fan of The Expanse and you just want to live in the world for a few more hours? This game is *GREAT* for just sitting and enjoying the atmosphere and story. Two thumbs way up.If that's not you though, then you will probably not enjoy this. It doesn't have much really in the way of gameplay, there was I think exactly 1 interesting/challenging puzzle, and it really expects you to understand the world of The Expanse.So overall: It Depends. *I* enjoyed it. I do wish it had more, you know, game. But as far as walking simulators go it was well done, it played well on my Steam Deck, and as a major Expanse fan I quite enjoyed the story. It took 7.5 hours to get through the entire game + DLC. I'll probably play again later, after I've forgotten some of it, to try and get the last few achievements, but there really isn't a *TON* of game here either, so waiting for the sale isn't a bad plan. But once again, despite my general thumbs-down for most players, if you love The Expanse and you just want the story: Two thumbs way up!
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give Telltale a thumbs up and Deck Nine a thumbs down.  Telltale did a wonderful job, per usual.  This was also the best looking Telltale game I've ever seen.  The mechanics of the game were fun - they did a superb job on the maneuvering and magnetic boots.  And as always it was an absolute pleasure to see your choices compared to others.  So why can't I thumb this up?  THE STORY WAS AWFUL.  Full disclosure, I never read the books or saw the actual show, but Good Grief it was BORING and laughable.  It was hard to take anything seriously.  While some of the accents were interesting, there were just certain segments where it was a joke the things that were happening.  The illuminati eye and the pedo-triangle symbol showing up hand in hand put the stamp of idiocy on this, the characters almost entirely being females with throat cancer sounding voices and the ceaseless message of anti-male propaganda was a bore.  The characters, even the ones that seemed interesting, never went beyond a little toe dip in the pool of development.  Instead, the dialogue devoted to quips and sass against men.  I am so sick of these ideologies flooding entertainment when instead we could've had some good story telling.  You can have a bad-a** female character - one who even shows up men - without converting the entire story to nothing more than that shtick.  By the end I sincerely could not care any more who lived or died.  The cast was awful.  Even with great voice acting, the characters were just so..... UGH.  There were segments of the game where you had literally nothing to do for upwards of 5 minutes but sit and listen.  I think in total I might've pressed 20 buttons through all 5 chapters.  I really would love to see Wolf Among Us 2 than this hot garbage story.  Sincerely, my life would've been better not having toiled through this.  This game, the story, the writing, was just too bad to give this a thumbs up.  I will never play this again, or any future expansions beyond Archangel which I bought with it, unfortunately.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I have really enjoyed the game (for the most part) through the first four episodes. Eps 1-3 were great, however the game comes to a screeching halt in episode 4. It's a long, boring slog. I couldn't wait for it to end. Thankfully it appears to pick up again in episode 5. But overall, I like the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Well, it was really good - but really short. If you like the show this is a great game and you'll understand the lore. If you don't know the lore, it's still a fantastic story, and will serve as a wonderful introduction to the series.My problem with this game is that it's $25 for 5 hours of gameplay, seems like a real stretch right now. Maybe get it on sale but I'd BARELY recommend it at this price with the amount of content.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to hit this with the thumbs up, but my review is actually mixed.If I had not already been a huge Expanse nerd, this would have been a down-thumb.  I've read the books, watched the show, so of course I wanted to gobble this up as well.  However, this is a terrible game if you're looking for a one-off.The characters are largely one-dimensional; this is where prior knowledge of the Expanse universe comes into play.  Even the characters that are truly one-dimensional are uplifted by prior experience with the universe.  A Belter isn't just a Belter once you've experienced Belter culture across an entire novel series and a six season show.As for gameplay; it's Telltale.  It's basically a movie, you just have to walk sometimes.  Fun for some folks, horrible for others.  Stacked against classics like The Walking Dead - this measures short.  However, if you're a fan of the Expanse universe, then it's a pretty nice trip down memory lane, some extra info prior to the story that currently exists, and an enjoyable experience.  For context, I just beat the game in 5.4 hours.  It did leave me regretting some decisions and wondering about the outcome of others, so the writing is definitely decent, as expected from Telltale.  All in all this seems like it may have been a junior dev project that got greenlit; there just isn't enough there.Will also caution gamepad users that this game, despite saying it's best enjoyed with a controller (and believe me it really is) is seemingly very hostile towards gamepads.  Mine worked throughout, but I constantly dealt with my glyph prompts having seizures and throwing out keyboard bindings.  The frequency of the stutter was enough that it made it pretty hard to figure out which button I was meant to be pressing sometimes, mainly during QTEs.  I did my due diligence researching this bug and found a couple of promising posts but they were always about a similar-enough-but-different issue, so I never did discover a fix.All in all - 6/10, 10/10 if you're already an Expanse fan.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: I was so excited for this game. It would be the first Telltale game I played blind (everything else I watched YouTubers play first). Maybe I wasn't the target audience for this game and that's fine.However, I do wish I asked for a refund when I had the chance. I wasn't invested in the story at all and got motion sick from the game play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: Very very very awesome telltale title, I felt like difficulty was a bit too easy but outside of that it was nice to see that your decisions really matter and that the slightest thing will have consequences into the future!10/10 would recommend playing this, it's a classic Telltale game through and through and tickles that need for more The Expanse content
_childDocuments_.name: The Expanse: A Telltale Series

_childDocuments_.review: If you were a fan of the TV series, you'll love this game just for it's story and the fact that it stays true to the series.
