_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Yet another "remaster" that has enshittified a beloved classic and neutered it. If you REAAAALLY want this, try and wait for 90% off sale. Otherwise avoid it. If you want a truly remastered(ish) Crysis, I would suggest firing up original one with Tactical Expansion Mod, awailable here: For optimizing original to run on newer hardware, refer to PC Gaming Wiki here: Pros: Newer CryEngine (3, I think) gives you better graphics, and nominally better optimizations: but I haven't seen much difference between original's maxed out and Remaster's High setting graphics.Onslaught Level gives you as initial spawn tank with infinite main cannon ammo, unlike original where it was limited to 25-30 shells, if I remember correctly.Achivements, maybe, due to most of them being tied to story progression, with only about 5 or 6 referring to various gameplay and physics shenanigans. And most of those are achiveable on first playtrough. For Achievement hunters, do not expect to sweat too much if you want to get them all.Cons: EVERYTHING ELSE.  Mods? ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gone.Multiplayer? ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gone.Warhead expansion pack/sidestory? DOUBLE ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gone. Seriously, you only get first Crysis, and it is playable trough in 6-8 hours, I have about 8.5 hours of game time at writing this, and had made a playtrough on Medium while suffering from cold, so thus was not at 100%. Sound: some details are better, as well as audio cues about suit status being more prominent, but other are at same exact level as original.AI: braindead idiots, with occasional wallhacking spots of "briliance". (I also play Star Citizen, game based on heavily modified Cryengine off-fork and even with SC's servers running badly, AI there is still miles better and more lethal that here.)UI: worse. Older players may remember how you could choose between different colors for HUD and menus, and EVEYRTHING would be adjusted for color. Well, not in this remaster. Original's Olive Drab Green still remains strong in game and on menus.I also noticed stutterings, mostly on Assault and Onslaught levels, ones that are massively sprawling and stretch for kilometers. SO, my guess is, the game has not been nearly as well optimized and it should have been. Closing: I only bought this because it was on 90% sale, and I still feel ripped off. Remaster that is more of a sloppily done port to newer hardware and OS rather than proper remaster. Think long and hard if you really would like to buy one.

_childDocuments_.review: Crysis Remastered looks better and runs better than the original games in everyway, especially with the raytracing features turned on. However, due to being made from the PS3/Xbox360 console port instead of the original PC release, the Remastered version has a few shortcomings and missing features but it is not enough to hamper the gameplay experience. What does hamper the gameplay experience however was the plethora of new bugs and glitches found in this version that did not exist in the original 2007 release nor the console ports. Although these can be fixed the  mod by , it is disappointing that the game has stopped receiving official updates.What's more disappointing however is the lack of the multiplayer and full scale mod support that the original got, which offer players a tonnes of replayability and variety of user made content and modes both online and singleplayer. Resulting in an overall short experience that can be completed in under 10 hours without much replayability. I've 100% the game and got all achievements within 9 hours.Overall, Crysis Remastered looks impressive and play as well as the original, bar the new bugs and glitches. It's a game I can wholeheartedly recommend and well worth experiencing again even if you've played the original. But without the modding capability the original has, Crysis Remastered feels lacking when compared to the 2007 release.

_childDocuments_.review: Can it run Crysis, the term has been renewed. That is the short version.Considering this is a remaster, not an entire remake. It will on that setting, demand an RTX 3080 or better to run, at least in 4k.The original was released in 2007, running the second iteration of CryEngine.A piece of gaming history.What has changed, considering it's a remaster it still uses the original game's assets. Like all remasters do.What has been added:*Higher Draw Distance LOD, would be the most noticeable.*Completely new lighting techniques, including Ray Tracing. Your GPU doesn't even need to support it, it's built into the engine itself. While the game offers some basic extension to it, turned on by a simple checkbox.*Tesselation on more objects such as rocks, mainly is where you will notice it.*Texture resolution on assets, some are even remodeled from scratch.*Sound samples, mainly on guns and they way they sound.* Ray Tracing light effects, you can run this effect in this game even without an RTX enabled GPU. It's embedded in the engine's software according to Linus Tech. Also here the minuses begin, it's demanding. A lot!* Quality of Life improvements to the controls. The control scheme is taken from Crysis 2 and 3, and gives you easier access to the nano suit. However if you preferred the original game's controls, you can still go back to that. Other QoL stuff is the intuitive toggle function on certain actions such as aim down sight and crouch. The original game locked ADS to toggle and crouch to hold and you could not change that. This point is probably the only reason I would recommend the remaster over the original. That and this remaster IS very good looking if you can afford to turn up the graphics settings.-Shaders, makes the game look like a cartoon. It's not celshading thankfully. Everything is just too green, too lush. Where the original showed moonlight on the palm leaves, here they simply look... unreal. You can easily mod this however.-HDR, but absolutely gives nothing for it. We're not talking anything remotely HDR10 here. It's like they forgot that HDR supports 10bit color depth but all the assets are still 8bit. Games that supports W11 HDR enhancement looks better using it than this game does with official HDR support.-Again Texture resolution, apparently or obviously resolution doesn't always mean sharper. Some look even worse than the original, like parts of trees, even the nano suits in some places like the helmet. Faces of the main characters? Generic NPC's look better now than the main cast of the game.-Shadows, they simply shimmer all over the place now a lot of the time. Most likely to the in game Ray Tracing lighting. When it works, it looks great, but it often does not.-Vegetation, as beautiful it looks on picture, once you're in the game you may notice how static they are. Trees and brushes no longer moves in the wind, no longer do you or NPC displace vegetation in the same realistic manner, nor does the brushwork hide you effectively as they did in the original game.Also the animations on them seem to be locked at a very low frame rate whenever displacement does occur.Game does support DLSS! For those with an nVidia card who wants to enjoy this title in 4k. You will need that turned on. Or simply install the original and run it in 4k with ease. It demands about 4GB V-RAM (Which is one of those reasons it never ran well at all on older machines when the original came out, most cards sported about 256-512MB at best back then, but then the target resolution was 1024x768, not even 1920x1080 widescreen, 4k was a dream far far away nobody had probably even thought of being a possibility in video gaming back then)The original Crysis runs very well on modern machines from the last 6 years or so. A GTX 1080 can run it in 4k. This remaster however, not so much.I was running this remaster with an RTX 3080, on an Intel machine 10th Gen i9 10900k, 32 GB of DDR4 RAM at 3000MHz XMP and from an M.2 Drive. Still PCI-X gen 3.0 but... on "Can it run Crysis" settings with DLSS on Quality I get about 40-50 frames per second, in 4k. A stable 60 if I run on Very High. With experimental RTX effects and HDR turned on. This for comparison is about the same I get from Cyberpunk 2077 with Ray tracing turned on and reflections on Psycho and with DLSS on Auto. (Not Quality setting for DLSS it becomes unplayable in 4k for some reason on nVidia cards now when everything else is maxed out, except maybe on a 4090 and is thus the pinnacle on hardware demanding PC games currently, despite even this remasters release trying to clearly be mainly intended to take that back) Either way I guess it's safe to say my machine can run Crysis =)This though is from a remaster of a game that have much smaller levels and was made in 2007.Does it look good? Yes, is it indeed does, but it still feels like an old game even visually. You can tell it is a remaster, not a remake.Don't buy this if you are just looking for a good game to enjoy, unless it's on sale, otherwise I would go for the original version. Because it was great as a game and still is!Especially on Delta difficulty where you really had to think and plan before you acted. Even on easy it was difficult to go full Leroy Jenkins, but on Delta it truly shines.Only buy this version if you want to push your new hardware to the max or are interested in getting the Steam Achievements. Though you can also buy this version of the game on Epic Store depending who has the better prices for the moment.The best part of this release however, it's an EA owned IP, but doesn't require neither Origin nor EA Play third party applications or accounts to run. It does blow a bit of fresh air into an old but fondly remembered title that is indeed a very important part of PC Gaming History.Crysis. A title that pushed boundaries of video game fidelity, in fact CryTek, just like Epic has always been about that and the simplicity to use their engines for video game creation. This particular title was definitely a big reason why other video games started looking much better than before. It was and still is a great showcase what games can look like, and I mean even games made today! 13 years later. This version, is sadly a bit generic. Adds things you will most likely not notice all that much, unless you run a comparison of them next to each other. If you want a showcase of RTX effects, even Minecraft and Quake II RTX does a much better job of doing that, or I recommend Cyberpunk 2077 or Watch Dogs Legion to best enjoy that as a tech demonstration.I would buy this remaster only for the Benchmark, "Can it run Crysis" hence the other title comparisons, and the Steam Achievements. Otherwise, the original release will do you just as well.You should also know there are MASSIVE differences in the game play when using the sequels mechanics. They were better the first time around I felt, even if they caused you to think before you acted more.Also the AI is MUCH better at spotting you in the remastered version, even on Delta, making the game immensely harder than the original release.And last but not least, the original did not use checkpoints or constrain you to to them, the original uses the old fashioned manual saving system and relied on that. The remaster does not offer this, it is a MUCH harder game than the original in comparison. Even on easier difficulties.Another last minute negative thing: The expansion for the original, Warhead, is NOT included in this release.Though Warhead was also standalone, you do not need the original game to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Even if you've never played it, as a PC gamer you've undoubtedly heard the phrase "Can It Run Crysis". The first installment in the trilogy is a great shooter but it lacks the refinement and polish of the 2nd and 3rd titles. Playing all 3 back to back, you'll notice an inherent clunky aspect to the original. Not that it doesn't have it's charm and appeal but it lacks the smooth power solider power fantasy the sequels provide. The narrative leaves a bit to be desired, often times a bit generic and campy. The remastered version performs excellent on modern hardware.

_childDocuments_.review: You can still buy the original Crysis by searching for Crysis Warhead, then selecting Crysis Maximum Edition. You can also buy it from gog[], if Crytek decide to pull it from Steam completely. If you're keen on the remaster's visual improvements there's a mod that improves the original's visual fidelity beyond those of the remaster, giving it 4K textures, global illumination, screen-space ambient occlusion, real-time reflections, tessellation, volumetric clouds, and so on.As many of you know, Crysis Remastered is a PC port of a console port of the original Crysis. Destructibility has been scaled down. Physics are worse. Performance is worse. Quick saves have been removed. Difficulty is lower; enemies do less damage and hit less frequently. The most damning thing about the remaster is that the gameplay has been changed significantly from the original game. Certain suit modes have become tied to actions, such as speed with sprint and jump with strength. Furthermore, you suit mode can't be changed while in vehicles (I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loved ghosting past enemies—they'd know I was there, but they wouldn't know where in the vehicle I was).The original Crysis was hard by design. By making you select suit modes on the fly, you had to think when planning out and enacting combat situations. The remaster takes away a lot of this and Crysis plays more like an action game rather than an immersive sim. I died a lot going through the same levels in the original Crysis, but those deaths made me consider the inadequacies of my play style. I breezed through the first thirty minutes of Crysis Remastered without a sweat. This is not necessarily a bad thing, because it is still enjoyable, and there's no fault in enjoying a breezy game. What's unforgivable, however, is that Crytek has tried to hide the original game as much as possible, rewriting the experience of Crysis to conform more with its successors, Crysis 2 and 3. As I said earlier, the first felt like an immersive sim, where you necessarily had to discover new ways of playing the game through experimentation. Mapping suit functions to actions streamlines this process of experimentation, and I think it's an incredibly sad thing to do. The richness of the original game is lost.You can read more about my thoughts on the original Crysis here, as well as ways to make it perform well on modern PCs.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, this is a tough one. Did it give me a nostalgia? Yes.Do I like the game? Yes.Would I recommend it full price? Never. This is a half-assed remaster so you should pay a half assed price for it. Get it on at least a 50% sale (or in the remastered trilogy bundle when on sale)My main gripes with the game are: Who the f* playtests those games? I just can't believe how fast the mouse sensitivity is at the absolute minimum.(at 800dpi) I had to configure the slider myself via an autoexec file to make the mouse feel like it's not on crack.After fixing the FOV and the sensitivity for the main game - the vehicle aiming is just absolutely unusable. It's WAYYYY too slow. Like I'd use my whole mousepad area for the damn camera in-game to barely move 10 degrees, and playing on DELTA difficulty, it was IMPOSSIBLE to kill those enemies in the sky with the anti-aircraft vehicle or whatever that thing is. I had to get out of it and use other guns to do what I was supposed to do in a vehicle. Like genuinely this makes me question if the devs responsible for the mouse controls even playtested this. Like, did they just make it somewhat work and decided "eh, whatever that's good enough"???How does the game just go from sonic aiming to turtle mode in vehicles? Can't it just strike a balance somewhere in the middle? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.Second: The performance is...good-ish? But I'd still expect better. On a 3080+Ryzen 9 5900x I was getting about 80-160 fps, perhaps with rare drops into the 70's, that's running max settings, apart from object detail, which was set to high. Running at 1440p with DLSS on quality. Graphics: Objectively it looks better in places, the draw distance is better, the lighting is better, the reflections are good. However the faces of characters look really bad here, I'm even going to say they were better in the original. The caves just look terrible here, the volumetric lights are gone. Gameplay: The game is easy once you understand what it wants from you, however it doesn't always make sense. It's not fair. Your AR bullets would rarely go where you aim because of bullet spread, so unless you have a gauss rifle or a precision rifle (aka sniper), then you're way better off sneaking up to enemies in cloak mode then killing them. Now this would be okay if only the enemies ALSO had this bullet spread, but no, they can mow me down like they're shooting a fully automatic sniper rifle with no recoil. Sometimes the game would glitch and your cloak wouldn't even work. Like I was cloaked behind cover far away from a tank, I walked all the way to the other side of a road and the second I see the tank I'm dead, WHILE CLOAKED. Other times I can't even see the enemies cause they're on the other side of the map, yet they can see me perfectly fine. This just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ruins the "predator" vibe you're supposed to have with that suit (at least on the delta difficulty), because the enemies just have the best eyesight in the world, you hide, cloak walk around them faaaaaar away, the second you uncloak (if you're not in the bushes) you're spotted. OH, and why the hell remove the ability to manually save? It's now a checkpoint based saving system. TL;DROkay-ish graphical improvements, performance is good but not amazing, gameplay is the same old crap with a few improvements but also a few drawbacks compared to the OG. AND WHAT THE F IS WRONG WITH THAT MOUSE SENSITIVITY??? If you wanna play it, go for it, buy it on sale, the game is GOOD, but don't expect a fully polished game.6.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the "Crysis-Remaster Edition" together with "Hunt Showdown" for roundabout 30€(~34,92USD). I played through the whole game on "Delta" (Highest Difficulty). I played it for ~10H in 3 sessions.By default, you get a suit more similar to "Crysis 2". An easier to control suit with less versatility. It is perfect for console players, but if you're using a mouse and Keyboard i highly recommend switching to the more versatile "Classic" Nanosuit.Options -> Game options Tick "Classic Nanosuit"(Don't forget to Click Apply, if you just press ESC afterwards your changes will not be applied)For newcomers having problems with the Classic suit just remember:M3+Mouse Forward = Speed (A movement as if you would engage)M3+Mouse Backward = Cloak (A movements as if you would retreat)M3+Mouse Right = Strength (Imagine a Knight, Sword in the Right hand)M3+Mouse Left = Armor (Imagine a Knight, Shield in the Left hand)The default controls of the remastered edition could be described as very "Creative".Like Putting lean left and right on T and H or changing fire mode on 5.I highly recommend changing the controls to something similar to the original.I use the Classic nanosuit with these control changes:Q/E - Lean left/rightH - Change GrenadeC - Fire Mode (I put it on C instead of X because i have big hands)X  - Customization MenuSTRG - CrouchT - Melee(Certain Objects like toilet brushes can be used as melee weapons.)If you change your Grenade through the Grenade-Selection-Window and left click, you will throw the selected grenade;  in my case a smoke. Afterwards the grenade display in the HUD changed from frags to smokes. Up to this point everything is working as intended.The smoke grenades were still displayed as the "active" grenade in my HUD. I was quite surprised when I intended to throw a smoke under myself to cover my retreat, but got blasted into space instead. It does not matter which grenade you have selected, if you press G and are in possession of a frag, a frag will be thrown.For some things you have to hold the key, just pressing it wont work. I repeatedly pressed F like a madman until I realized that I had to hold F to exchange my SCAR for a Shotgun.If you aim at a person who is on your side, you get a red X and your gun won't fire. This includes dead friendlies. The "Gunlock" hitbox is bigger than the actual hitbox of the entity. If you sit manually on a friendly tank you cannot openfire since you are sitting inside the gunlock-box. On the Aircraft Carrier I often could not shoot at the enemy, because my dead teammates were triggering the "Gunlock" making the end boss fight very frustrating.Ohh the Alien Trooper is right in front of you tearing through your HP? Sorry, I can't let you attack it because somewhere in that direction is a dead body that theoretically could get hit. Oops, you're dead. Thanks game!The AI in general seems to be more perceptive, you are no longer a ghost when activating "Cloak" mid combat. Also even when invisible the AI will notice you when you get too close; I noticed that the hard way when I tried to sneak past an ATV (Jeep) and the gunner unloaded his MG right into my face.The only annoying part is that they seem to "Lock On" and sometimes see through brush. Once they are (Red)alerted to your presence they do not care how many bushes, trees, fences, etc. are between you and them, they'll shoot at you with pinpoint accuracy. On the other hand, if they're still yellow, they are sometimes stupidly blind.If I recall correctly, the AI navigation inside the Cryengine is mostly done with "Forbidden Area" and "Navigation Area". The First one just prevents the AI from stepping inside the zone, the second is made for precise Navigation, where the AI can only move from and to placed navigation points and can only enter and leave the zone through placed entry markers. The Navigation Area appears to be not working. The AI is walking against walls, gets stuck in buildings.In the original Crysis game where invisible AI-behavior markers where the Enemy AI would perform certain actions like smoking or repairing something. Most of these Objects do not work. I noticed it when the guy who is usually relieving himself next to an explosive barrel was missing in the first level.The "spawning" of enemy AI is done through Flowgraph. Something happens like entering an area and then an AI Entity is switched from Disable to Enable and it pops into the world.This leads to some enemies standing around in a pose that looks like someone pulled the Plug. Like at the end of level 2 some of the patrolstaff stood on a rock, armes straight down, with their FY71 attached to their right hand, staring into the jungle. In the original the boats in the first level were spotting you quite fast. They may have been a bit annoying but they were definitely a threat. The Boats in the remake are no longer the Hawks of the original, instead they are completely blind. In the 1st Level, I killed the first boat's gunner from the Jammer position and destroyed the second boat with the MG of an ATV(Jeep) from a beach near the KVA Command Post. In both cases the Boats did NOT return fire.The battle tanks in the 5th map only fight back if you drive close to them, a few foot soldiers of that map just run past the player, not even attacking when you shoot at them.In the original I remember a surge of helicopters getting in my way. There were so many of them that they were absolutely annoying. But in the remaster, there were only a few of them, I'm not sure if they were removed or the AI just couldn't find their way anymore.The Alien Scouts(Flying Tentacle Monster) didn't use their Secondary attack even once(Charge Attack, firing an explosive projectile). The Alien Troopers(The little jumpy ones) had trouble moving in the Aircraft Carrier, sometimes being unable to attack.I might be wrong, but the damage dealt by throwing objects seems to have been nerfed. This is a good thing. One Shotting the NVA-General with a Box was kind of a balacebreaker.I don't remember if it was the same in the original but incoming fire comes with Camerashakes and other effects. It makes returning fire more difficult, I like that.In the Cryengine, The Roads are drawn with a Pathtool and then plastered onto the map like a decal. But it seems a few of them are floating.

_childDocuments_.review: I kinda can't believe how people made a big deal about the mangled baby resulting from a freaky threesome between CoD, Half Life and Halo back in the day. Cry Engine was and is still impressive to look at yes, but without decent boss and level design all you end up with is some semi-enjoyable moments in a sandbox-ish island at the first half and just unprecedented and almost completely un-enjoyable chaotic warfare at the latter half of the game. Like, I couldn't even enjoy the supersuit abilities because of weirdly unresponsive controls. Additionally, couldn't even use most of the cool abilities because the game does a rather terrible job of explaining them anyways and sometimes they outright don't work for some reason, albeit excluding some very basic ones. Then I also think the game fails to deliver the whole supersuit aspect as well since you frequently go from feeling like you are the single most feeble being on earth at one moment to feeling like the indestructable super soldier the next, depending on what the game decides at any given moment. While I inititally thought there would be certain upgrades that could fix that uneven dynamic at the early stages of the game, it turned out that that wasn't the case unfortunately. So yeah, I am still surprised about how this (or at least the original) is considered a  according to many people and critics alike because I think it is way too scuffed be put on any all-timers lists.To summerize, when I decided to play this the main thing that worried me was the optimization but the game was supposed to be a grade-a classic so it'd worth the hassle in theory, yet after some minor tweakings to get the game running smoothly on my medium level system I just ended up getting frustrated with the game itself instead. I did encounter some glitches here and there but nothing game breaking; catching some dude t-posing out of the corner of my eye was the worst it got honestly and sadly I learned to tolerate stuff like that thanks to the state of modern gaming. At the end of the day even though I don't really recommend it, I know there can be certain people who can overlook its issues and enjoy it and with that I'll just say that while you won't lose anything particular by passing on it, if you got it as a part of the Remastered Trilogy bundle as I did, you can safely give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing Crysis back in the day and being blown away. I've had an absolute blast coming back to it years later but ran into a game breaking bug near the end. There's an on-rails section where an NPC is driving while you shoot, but he crashes the car instantly killing me at exactly the same corner every time. I tried many things to get past the problem: restarting the level, changing arbitrary settings, verifying files and even moving the game's install directory but the bug persisted. As a last resort I decided to uninstall the game and re-download it. Turns out the game doesn't support could saves so I've lost all my progress. I probably should have checked but that's the last straw for me. I'm not playing all the way to the end again knowing that I might just get stuck  anyway. A real shame as I was really enjoying the remaster and it holds up remarkably well so many years after the original release. I don't think this bug is particularly common, as there's not many people talking about it online so your mileage may vary (FYI I was playing on Deck) but I can't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great title. Shockingly advanced for a game made in 2007, and a good remaster to boot. Running into enemies with speed mode is great fun, grabbing and throwing them is hilarious, and it's especially great to just say '♥♥♥♥ shooting' and chuck a big box at a North Korean soldier. Not one crash for me, not one bit of lag either, even on "Can It Run Crysis?" (actual in-game setting btw).  In 2007, how advanced some of the mechanics are would've blown my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mind. Holds up surprisingly well, even with the occasional physics bug.

_childDocuments_.review: 1. Game play (3/5): Its average, Running and shooting seems fine. Power jumps feels weird, cannot influence the movement once you are in the air. Vehicles and Air plane (VTOL) were fun.2. Story (4/5): Story was short, took about 8 hours to finish on Hard diff. Well though out story considering it was meant to be the first of the 3 instalments. Also paints a good picture of whats to come in the next games.3. Enemies (2/5): AI is so bad in this game. They give you suit that can go invisible but the moment you shoot someone, everyone gets alerted. No point playing stealth. Plus they cant figure out where the bullets are coming from, so if you are shooting far enough from them, they act so dumb and search stupidly.4. Music (?/5): Honestly I dont remember whether there was any music or not. So even there was, it means that is was unnoticeable.5. Graphics (3/5): Even tho its a graphical remastered, it feels a little aged. I played on ultra with mid level ray-tracing. Sometimes NPC faces were like they melted down or something. _childDocuments_.review: The controls for both controller and kb/m feel too clunky, the performance is not that great (I thought they fixed taht but I guess not), the guns feel weak against human enemies (also headshots are very inconsistent), the game's open world feels too gimmicky since there's almost nothing in between objectives except for maybe an enemy patrol or two, and the suit drains your energy way too fast which is annoying because you're mainly going to use super speed to reach your objectives. I find Crysis 2 to be the better game because that game's performance is far better, the levels may have been more linear but it still gave you freedom to approach those levels any way you preferred (like the Halo games except now you can also use stealth), the controls felt great and the game made you feel like an action hero when fighting against humans but then became challenging when you had to fight against the aliens.

_childDocuments_.review: Dumb, action packed fun in a similar vein to Command and Conqueror: Renegades, after never really playing the original past the first couple levels, I went into the game relatively blind and after people had hyped it up so much in the past, I was underwhelmed in some ways. The game has problems in that, you don't necessarily feel like a super soldier, you feel like a normal squishy soldier with the odd buff here or there for a couple seconds at most.The Nano Suit is at its worst here, it has next to no energy, meaning you take 4-5 shots and your armour depletes, you sprint for 5~ seconds and your energy depletes, you do anything but crouch whilst using invisibility cloak, your energy depletes after a couple seconds.The game suffers in my opinion with a lacklustre second half since the aliens that show up are much less fun to fight than the North Koreans and there is lots of jank from 2007 you have come to expect. In saying that though, I enjoyed the majority of my time with this game and beating up conscripted soldiers in a super suit is really, really fun. I really feel like the game would have been better if it expanded upon the power trip and made you near unstoppable on normal difficulties whilst throwing more enemies at you. Another thing, that some people might like and some people might not, it's got a very open level design, this translates into sprinting past entire objectives the majority of the time since the sandbox isn't enjoyable enough that you should take every single fight. This game would have worked better in a much more linear hallway shooter style and thats what the rest of the trilogy turns into for the most part.The story and dialogue is pretty damn corny, like Transformers (2007) levels of corny but if you embrace that, it's all the more enjoyable, overall I would recommend it but I suspect Crysis 2 and 3 are the better of the bunch.You want guarantees, buy a toaster - Admiral R. Morrison (2020)

_childDocuments_.review: I don't generally play lots of fps games and the ones I play I never play multi or hard modes. so it is a casual perspective if you will. the game took around 9 hours instead of 5 shown here as my internet died halfway. the game is old and it shows in many places textures load in front of your eyes optimization is garbage and much more such problems. _childDocuments_.review: Realising that you aren't supposed to ghost your way through levels like Metal Gear but instead use the cloak to hunt your enemies like the predator turned this game from one I could never enjoy as a kid to one of the best FPS experiences I've ever had in my life. everything just improves once you figure out the intended uses for the mechanics.It's also so fantastic that the levels essentially just give you a semi-open world, an objective, and lets you loose to figure things out however YOU want. after properly playing through this game multiple times and 100%-ing it I came to the awful realisation that there's nothing else like it out there. of course there is the third act to talk about but I didn't really find it all that bad, sure it's nothing in comparison to Act 1's predator game play or Act 2's Halo-like vehicle segment power trip but it isn't garbage like I've seen some people say about it; It can be a bit of fun to doom marine your way through a bunch of alien scum.Anyways play this game please.

_childDocuments_.review: It's I, Starscream, once again, to share my recent experience with Crysis Remastered on my new OLED TV. Previously, I extolled its virtues, but alas, after this recent encounter, my opinion has shifted.The original game was akin to wearing a golden armor, reminiscent of my legendary exploits in the Transformers episode, The Golden Lagoon. However, what I've noticed in this remastered version are not upgrades but downgrades. The lack of plant physics is appalling. In the old game, you could interact with foliage, pushing plants aside as you moved through them. Now? You simply clip through them like a malfunctioning Decepticon.And the nighttime, supposed to be an immersive experience with ray tracing, falls utterly short. Instead of darkness, the night is as bright as an energon cube, ruining the tension the original game offered. The flashlight no longer serves its purpose, leaving me disappointed and vexed, much like Megatron after a failed conquest.In conclusion, Crysis Remastered on my new OLED TV is a letdown. It's like encountering a malfunctioning Seeker in the midst of battle. The downgrades from the original, particularly in plant physics and the lack of darkness in the night, have soured the experience. I'd have to give this version a Starscream-revoked rating of , purely due to these disappointing deviations from the original game's immersion and mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: By now, this game has been data mined like crazy, and there are plenty of guides and strategies to min-max your monsters, and play in the most "efficient" way possible.  But for me, the most fun I had playing this game, was as a 13 year old kid, going in to it blind with no help from the internet, and figuring things out on my own.  I spent a good chunk of my summer after 8th grade trying to unlock the Dragon and Henger monsters in MR1, and the sense of accomplishment and joy I had when I finally spawned them remains unequaled in my gaming life.

_childDocuments_.review: MR2 is literally my favourite Psone game of all time.But does it hold up to modern scrutiny?Kind of.The story is essentially non-existent. You are a rancher of monsters, you raise them, fight them, breed them, and (if you see fit to) sell them.The human characters are equally lacklustre, but they are not why you play this game.Music is passable as is sound design in general(although some of the remastered sounds actually seem worse?). The battle sounds have some satisfying moments (Zuums “Millionbites” attack is so crunchy, I never get tired of hearing it). Graphically its middling. The monsters themselves look good even though many lost some extra features from MR1 (Pinkeyes “wings” for example). The backgrounds are basic and often low res. The battle stages are equally simple.But this is a game about battling monsters not exploring rich detailed worlds so…First up the star of the show, the monsters. From telekinetic eyeballs to farting baboons, all the way through to good old fashioned dragons. There's something here for everyone and if you cant find a species you like then seriously what's wrong with you?They are well animated, full of personality, and each offer subtly differing training obstacles for the player (what works for a Dragon may not necessarily work for a Hare).Unlocking them all is a pain but save scumming is nothing to ashamed of in a game like this.(There's only so many times a monster can miss the turn-off in an expedition or die right before a special tournament a person can stand before losing their mind)Oh yeah...Monsters have perma death. Once its dead its dead, no phoenix downs or revives here. The best you can do is reload and cryogenically freeze your charge before they snuff it thus allowing you time to try and decide the best course of action (Combine it? Defrost it for important fights? Send it on a suicidal expedition to acquire a rare item?)Second the meat and potatoes of the gameplay Breeding and Battling. As this game is closer to a horse breeding simulator than it is to Pokemon, you can forget about camping out in the tall grass fighting pigeons, raising monsters is all about optimising training, diet, and battle schedules. At first you’ll struggle to have a monster capable of living out even half of its lifespan, as you stumble through semi-hidden mechanics like stress and fatigue, desperately trying to squeeze that last training session you need to stand a chance in the next tournament…But stick with it, experiment, learn and soon you’ll be running a boxing boot camp for velociraptors. You’ll forget what a stressed monster even looks like.Battling is an odd but compelling affair. Fights occur in real time and monsters can attack from 4 different ranges depending on their learnt techniques and costing “Guts” as a resource, meaning it often feels more like a beat em up than an RPG. The majority of traditional RPG strategies will work for these battles (Tanking, glass cannons, resource control etc etc) but they are limited to the capabilities of the monster species and the individual attributes of each monster itself (Some species are much easier to train as glass cannons and other species lack the techniques to starve the opponent of resources).Breeding is also a bit of a misleading term. Monsters in MR2 are not bred in any physical sense but are in fact combined magically in a lab to produce offspring at the cost of both parents existence.The combining system is a rabbit hole itself with pages and pages of guides and forums breaking down parental compatibility, combination item use, and selective breeding through generations. Its overwhelmingly in depth stuff but well worth a browse if you’re planning on raising the perfect beast.Overall this game is and will likely always be my favourite Psone game.Its core gameplay loop is easy to learn difficult to master.Its premise is casual but its depths are hardcore.Its understandable why it doesn’t (And didn’t ) appeal to either crowd when one balks at challenge and the other loses interest in ease. Still awesome. Still ranching. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I picked a cool monster. It looked awesome. I gave it the best treatment. It beat the A-Rank leagues. I tried to beat S-Rank but it grew old after 3 years. It was about to die. I froze it. I will combine it later to create the best. monster. ever. period.I picked another monster that complimented the stats of the first monster for combining, but It looked like a pervert in a gimp suit. It drank. It smoked. It constantly spat at the floor when I told it off. I told myself it would make good cannon fodder for the next monster, but my hatred grew in time. The amount of care I gave it was slowly slipping. Letting it get old faster would mean a new monster sooner I told myself. But it just wouldn't grow old. It made it to 6 years and it was still going strong. It developed amazing stats. It learned an absurd move that never missed and always laid down the hurt. And then it demolished the end game leagues without breaking a sweat. And before I realised what was happening, there it was. The credits screen rolling. and my fat gimp monster immortalised on the end game content congratulations screen. This is my legacy now. Just a trainer who dreamed big and ended up as a fat alcoholic gimp's ♥♥♥♥♥.No I said. This won't be the end. I'll freeze this gimp and make that cool monster. I'll combine them and make a new monster. Better. Faster. Stronger. And then, there it was. Reborn. Gimp Jr. I wanted to reload the game. But his stats were undeniable. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you where a fan of the game back on the PSX and PS2, then this game is for you. It has everything you loved and some quality of life improvements that make it quick to jump in and have fun.Value: A+ To do everything there is to do in each games takes about 20 hours each. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher was a quite memorable game for me back in my childhood. Seeing MR 1&2 DX comes back again brings me a good rush of nostalgia, and with it also a sense of duty to "finish" the game that my child-self failed to do. The game is mainly about training and raising a monster with the goal of achieving better ranks than before. Each monster is unique, and there are many different kinds of monster for you to see and experience. Back then, the unique appeal of monster rancher is that you can pop your CDs into PSX and the game will generate a monster based on your CDs. Now it changed into you choosing a song from the in-game database list which consist of approximately 664,909 titles that you can choose. However, don't expect the monster variety level to reach pokemon and digimon since this is a 25 years old PSX game. To note, MR2DX also support "slating" your MR1DX monsters, which is using your MR1DX frozen monsters to "import" them into MR2DX (this does not delete the monster used to slate in MR1DX).After you have yourself a monster, the only things left is to train, care, and bond with your monster. On the surface this sounds easy enough, but monster have "fatigue" and "stress" that you have to watch out for that the game only scarcely gives you info about it. Too much stress and fatigue can makes your monster run away from you and it also makes them grow old faster. Hence, we need to care our monster. You can combine your monster with other monster to create a new breed of monster which will inherit the parent stats, which completes the cycle of breeding and raising monster. Training your monster increase their status, and sending your monster into training (MR1DX) or Errantry (MR2DX) can help them acquire new techniques to use in the arena. With your monster trained and grown up, you can battle other monsters to win gold and reach higher ranks. In a battle, you can give your monster "advice" which is essentially you controlling your monster, or you can just sit back and watch as your monster battle by itself through AI. You can also battle others through Vs match but sadly Player vs Player is limited to the switch version, the steam version only has CPU vs CPU or Player vs CPU. MR 1&2 DX is a polished version of the PSX version of the game with bugfixes and hidden easter eggs for you to see. However, that is also the negatives about the game, as this is only a "remaster" of the old PSX games. So you can see that the graphics are of an ancient PSX as well as the content itself is limited to the era itself. Other notable things: - The game has a fast forward feature that is only accesible from the menu, which can be accessed whenever you are.- The game does not have a volume dial, there is only ON and OFF for the sound, and the music volume is crancked on to the MAX so take care of your volume and ear when playing the game (Edit: use  to tune down the volume, but still this doesn't bring volume dial to the game)- As a port, Keyboard-mouse support is kinda off but the controller support is betterAll in all, MR 1&2 DX is a good monster raising sim. Although to be honest this game feels like Koei Tecmo testing waters if the market for monster rancher is still here or not. if Koei Tecmo ever read this, please make a new monster rancher game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: At long last, the classic niche monster raising games return, for a new generation (and old generation) to enjoy!I've long considered this series one of the "Big 3" of Monster Raising Games (i.e. Pokemon, Digimon, and Monster Rancher).So...for those who've never heard of these game(s), in the original PS1 game, you would insert your own music or game CDs, the game would read them, and generate a monster to raise.At your ranch, you feed the monster, train it, battle with it, and enter it in tournaments.That said, I will warn you -- These games are famed for their difficulty. Monsters have a limited lifespan, and your actions can shorten that if you push the monster too hard. They can get stressed and fatigued (both of which are semi-hidden stats).If totally outmatched in a battle, to the point of getting one-hit KO'ed, they can be injured or even outright die.But, these games are charming in their own way, it's always a treat to see what a CD will generate.Now, for this DX remaster, since most PCs (and the Switch) don't have CD drives, Koei-Tecmo have instead included a database of metadata for over 600,000 CDs (including a few important PS1 games).Search for an artist and album you want, and see what comes of it.Sure the graphics are from the PS1-era, but honestly, they hold up surprisingly well in this day and age, especially the monsters themselves.If you want fun games, two games that won't hold your hand and actually will give you a challenge, then this game bundle is for you.-----Q: "I've played Pokemon. How does this compare to that?"A: "I like Pokemon, too. So... imagine a Pokemon game where you own a ranch. Instead of walking around and catching what you find, you go to a shrine and pick a CD, and are handed the monster inside.You train the monster through drills, and have unlimited tournaments/battles for money and items.Oh, and the monster will eventually grow old and die, leading to you generating a new one. (Assuming you don't combine two monsters into a new hybrid).And instead of a gym challenge, there's no hard endgoal.This will be somewhat easy in some regards...but that disguises the true difficulty. It's not hard to get to a meager C rank. But to get to the world-class S Rank (where the endgoals are)... that's gonna take true skill from you. So imagine a Pokemon game where beating the first few gyms is fairly simple... and then the kid gloves come off and the game gets brutal, to the point facing the champion requires tons of effort and tears, after dozens of hours of work.And lastly, instead of separately buying two versions of the same game...here, you instead are buying the game, and its sequel, in one neat package."-------As I said, these two games are difficult, but fun, and rather unique, in my opinion.Very important to remember: This includes TWO GAMES in one.So for $30, that effectively makes both games $15. And each game has dozens of hours of things to do. Well worth their price tags, even for these older games.So, do you like a game that you definitely are not going to blast through in a week (or even a month)?Do you like getting two long games for a mere $15 a piece?Do you like a game that's not afraid to kick your rear and punish you for making bad choices?Do you just want to enjoy a fine slice of monster-raising history, maybe even raise an adorable Moochi?If you said yes to any of these, then yes, I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Been having a spectacular time with this game. I had a blast making an int based monster line and a Mock made it all the way to the hall of fame. This definitely brings back all the feels from when I first played the game. But then I made the mistake of looking up some helpful hints for unlocking some monsters, which led to some helpful hints for training, which in turn ran me down the route to max stats with a Gen1 monster. I have done it to two Gen1 monsters and reached hall of fame super fast. To me, it is glaringly poor design if you can spam nearly any Gen1 monster and hall of fame it in a few hours. What more is there to expect from a game made more than 20 years ago? I spoiled the game for myself by looking behind the smoke and mirrors. It has instead just become a math problem.I would still recommend this game to anyone, but go in blind. Don't look up anything. Don't go searching for the most meta way to train. It turned what could have been a very enjoyable experience into a repeatable 4 hour math problem. If they end up re-releasing Monster Rancher 3, you bet I will buy it. And I will take the lessons learned from this and go in blind.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of Monster Rancher 2, I have played the game for countless hours back in the day on PSX and via emulation.This review doesn't take MR1 into account as I don't have any experience with that game.This is a *somewhat* lazy port of MR2...The new HD monster textures are done via AI Upscaling, which although they look nicer in most respects I wish that Koei Tecmo spent a little more time giving the monsters the care and attention that they deserve! A lot of the backgrounds don't much different from the 1999 version which is a shame.The font looks a lot nicer and the loading times are much better.There isn't a skip feature on the training anymore which is a somewhat baffling change imo. There is a Fast Forward feature that can be enabled in the options but I haven't had time to play around with this.Thankfully there have been some nice QOL changes to the game, such as Colt letting you know EVERY time when a monster reaches its Prime stage rather than once ever in the entire game. The enemy AI has been updated so they fight more naturally and a plethora of other bug fixes.It looks like Koei Tecmo are still fixing bugs and tweaking the game so I'm hoping there will be some more slight improvements along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: I appreciate this childhood favourite being made available on modern hardware but it's too clunky a port for me to enjoy.The good:- It loads quickly and runs smoothly.- Although you can't generate monsters from your physical CD collection anymore, the in-game CD database is a nice way to replicate the experience of popping in your favourite album and seeing what monster comes out of it.The so-so:- As far as I can tell, the visual assets are exactly as they were presented in the original games and have not been rebuilt or remastered in any way. This isn't a bad thing in and of itself, but they were designed to be viewed on a CRT at lower resolutions and to be honest they don't look great on a modern display.- The remastered soundtrack is pretty cool, though I'm not sure what the need for it was - you can turn the original back on in the options menu and it sounds great.The bad:- The game doesn't control very well on mouse and keyboard at all. You can technically do everything with just the mouse but nothing about this feels intuitive and battles are downright clumsy.- The new UI elements were clearly designed for touch controls, which makes this PC version feel a bit like a mobile port.- You can turn the sound master ON of OFF but you can't adjust the volume of individual aspects and you can't turn music off while leaving SFX on. Either you have the music on full blast or you play the game on mute.All in all, a bit disappointing. They've made it run on PC but they haven't made it click. I wonder if it feels any better on Nintendo Switch?

_childDocuments_.review: Old, fun pet sim with battles that allow either hands-off watching your monster do the dumbest ♥♥♥♥ in its roster on end or micro-managing its every move and getting enraged by the RNG system that makes Blood Bowl's look downright forgiving. I will say they could tweak the settings a bit to let you mute background music (it's so repetitive) and not battle sounds, but instead it's all one big mute or not button. Odd, but fine. Fast Forward option exists, haven't used it.Harkens to a time of challenging (sometimes unfairly so) single player games with no season passes, micro transactions, and some interesting mechanics (scanning your CD collection was really novel) that has long since passed. Haven't touched MR1 DX much at all, MR2 DX is superior and more of what I remember playing. May give it a go sometime later.Game is actually a lot of fun despite the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ RNG, and the DX versions having a built in backlog of discs to generate monsters from is a huge boon and wise choice. Snag it on sale if you aren't sure, but otherwise watch some old VODs of someone playing it and see if it's your speed. I recommend playing it blind your first go around and then look at the guides that have entirely deconstructed the games if that's your speed. Seeing what monsters generated from music CDs I had as a child/teen was something special.

_childDocuments_.review: FINALLY WE GOT IT! FINALLY! MONSTER RANCHER CAME TO STEAM!! MONSTER RANCHER CAME BACK!! Oh, how I've missed my ranch. My monsters. My kinda not-so-bright, but always caring best friend and assistant. I don't know if I can be objective about this game, though. I genuinely love Monster Rancher. I've been waiting with bated breath to come back and make more friends with all the Hares and Bakus!!This monster-raising sim focuses on the intimate week by week training of monsters. If you're looking for a Pokemon clone, this ain't it. It's Tamagotchi with extra steps, and I find it to be not just fun to play but very relaxing despite the difficult learning curve, and general difficulty of the game. You'll learn to love your monsters, and hopefully, they learn to love you in return. After finishing the Pokemon Diamond remake, I find this incredibly refreshing! It isn't an RPG, it's a sim. Having to take my Prince Hare to freeze because I know it's at the end of its lifespan has brought me to tears. I will always miss Luna the Prince Hare. Ranma the Kung Fu Hare. _childDocuments_.review: So, first things first, we have to address the elephant in the room - this is pretty clearly designed as a mobile port of the first two Monster Rancher games. The title screen says "tap to start", the border has virtual buttons that you're expected to use to control the game (using a controller or keyboard just seems to map keys to trigger the virtual buttons), and the new way of summoning monsters is is definitely meant to work with streaming. The virtual buttons would actually be phenomenal with a phone or table screen, but they're really cumbersome to trigger with a mouse - I highly recommend using a controller or spending some time mapping keyboard buttons instead.The change to the summoning system is also a little disappointing, but understandable when you keep in mind that this is effectively a mobile game. The way it works is that the game has a big database of music; you just enter either the artist or album title and it searches it for you. It also has a random option, so you can always fall back to just hitting that and seeing what you get. It's a little sad that you're not actually scanning anything, but makes sense as fewer and fewer files are stored on physical media or even devices themselves these days.The music it has in the database is, admittedly, a little weirdly hit-or-miss. Some of the music I consider a little more obscure in my playlist was found with no issue, including Mal Blum, Math the Band, SALES, and even some rare EPs from the some of the less obscure artists... But then there are some bigger names that just don't appear at all: Mice Parade, Neko Case, and even Juno and Polaris award winning artist Caribou are mysteriously completely absent. It also has an odd habit of sometimes mistaking tracks for albums. This is especially obvious among the works I tried with Justice, whose entries are filled to the brim with track names from the album Cross, but somehow don't include the album Cross.All of that said, if you can get past that weirdness (and it's not that hard to get past, honestly), it's basically straight ports of Monster Rancher 1 &2. They're still some of the most clever and unique monster raiser/battler games out there, they're still very charming and enjoyable - and for that reason I wholly recommend this game if you want to play these games again, or experience the series for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: These two may not be full-on remasters, but an enhanced port available on modern platforms is more than we have already.While I may have been familiar with this series, this would be my first crack at it. And I gotta say, I went in expecting something like Digimon or Pokémon (two games this franchise gets compared to A LOT), but got something completely different. It’s much less a full-on adventure RPG and more so a life simulator RPG.The vast majority of the gameplay is done through menus, where you will be directing training for your monsters, managing a small inventory of goods, and coming up with more monsters. Coming up with a new monster at the shrine is perhaps what this game is best known for. Back in the day, you would have to physically insert music CDs into your PlayStation and hope that the game’s mystery algorithm would spawn a powerful monster from it.The new method is simply looking up an album by name and artist, which I think this is a good workaround to maintain what made the original games unique. It’s always fun to go through your favorite albums and see what monsters spawn from them - my first monster, for example, was a small pixie spawned from Rick Astley’s piano rendition of “Never Gonna GIve You Up”.Anyways, each in-game week acts as a “turn” of sorts, where you give your monster one instruction and pray that it succeeds in doing so - because each monster has its own personality and will sometimes fail or shortcut training. Each time it does succeed though, its stats go up - and that’s basically what these two games revolve around.You will spend hours clicking through training menus and getting these monsters ready for battle, oftentimes repeating the same set of inputs over and over while you wait for your monster to reach a certain stat level. There is stuff to break up this monotony, but I would be lying if I said that the core loop wasn’t tedious.The point of all of this is to win battles, which are NOT menu-based and actually take place in real-time. They’re simple mechanically, but play out VERY fast and you’ll need to know what you’re doing to clear them. Again, there’s a lot of repetition involved because you will be going through a lot of these battles, but seeing training pay off and having your monster one-shot another with a single slap is always satisfying.Despite these seemingly simple training exercises and battles, there is a lot going on under the hood here. Stress levels, loyalty, stat gain modifiers, monster type combinations, lifespans, unique techniques - I could go on. For example, I spent several hours hunting down a specific monster: the stone ape. This required me to reach certain training goals, find a specific item on an expedition map that only opens once per year, and hope for the small chance that combining my ape with my golem would result in the monster I wanted.This process was both a pain and a testament to what makes this game unique - it’s not all just menus, training, and battles. And honestly, I kinda liked it. It is repetitive for sure, but it’s charming in its own way and the hours flew by while I was playing. It is definitely not something I can see myself powering through to the end, but spread out over some months and yeah - I’ll probably end up completing both of these provided I don’t get distracted and spend hours chasing a specific monster like my Stone Ape - but I guess that’s just part of the fun.The PC version comes with a launcher where you can adjust a grand total of three settings: fullscreen toggle, window resolution, and controls. It’s a bare-minimum port, but that’s par for the course from Koei Tecmo. It at least works though - in my many hours of playing, all I had was one crash (there is an auto-save though).Controls are also surprisingly good. I didn’t change any of the defaults and had no issues swapping between controller and keyboard/mouse, depending on what I was feeling at the time. The game has full mouse support and can actually be played entirely using just that - no keyboard necessary.For someone that has never played the series before, Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX is a nice package to have. It ports both titles to modern platforms, enhances their visuals and playability a bit, and stays true to the disc-swapping mechanic of the original with its own unique interpretation. It’s not an easy recommendation to make, but it’s one I might throw out there if you like monster collecting games.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

And let me tell you, they absolutely enjoyed it. I had them pick which songs or artists/bands to try out and see what monsters generated from them, and they liked seeing the dumb and funny designs some of the monsters have. _childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for a hint of life from this series since Monster Rancher 4. Sure it had some iterations on Nintendo DS and Advance but I only ever played the core games in the series. This port is okay, though since it has been around in ROM format for ages for use in emulators it was not exactly a tough ask. Do not let the lack of disc use push you away. Sure it was a part of the game and part of the fun of it but the database system is pretty good. You can search for albums or songs and games as well and if you are lazy about it just hit random and it will just pick one of the 600,000+ items from the database to get you a generated monster, assuming you have unlocked that monster through game play. I have already sunk 11 hours and it has all its charm in the "just one more week, just one more battle" area. This is not a graphic over haul and yes it is a port from a more mobile version of the game though it plays well. Controls can be clunky but can be remapped. I don't like that I cannot skip training scenes (except errantry can still skip those scenes) but since there is a fast forward option that you can toggle in options it does at least blow through the animations quickly. The graphics are not upscaled much if at all. Maybe some smoothing out at best but nothing else. There is the addition of a job game that was only released in the Japanese version but I saw no real point to using it though I did mess with it once. Sound is pretty good, at least in MR2 as it has a remastered soundtrack. I have not hopped into the original game as I have always preferred MR2 over the original. I still like the first one I just prefer 2.Over all I would say that if you are a first time player the graphics are PSOne so don't expect much there. The game play loop is satisfying and there are a ton of guides out there to help learn about the game. I usually just roll with whatever I feel when I train but there are guides out there that can help you create epic monsters in short periods of time, but keep in mind the first go around with a monster you will need to really make money for some of the  techniques to work. For my old heads who have played the game on and off over the years like myself. It has all the charm still, the addicting play loop and the challenge. I have played Monster rancher since the first one released in 1997 here in the states and I always come back. This just makes it easier rather then pulling out the old PSOne or 2 and swapping discs and dealing with long load times. I have the games still and until this released I would often boot them up and play them or at least use an emulator and ROM it. Now that I have it on Steam here and with my Steamdeck eventually arriving I will be able to play this on a whim whenever and not worry about if my memory cards have gone bad or if I lost my save on an emulator. If you are on the fence I feel the hours you can sink into this game are absolutely worth $29.99 and I am sure there will be some future polishing that happens with the game. Who knows, maybe Tecmo will see merit in releasing a new game in the series.TL;DR versionit makes it much easier for me to hop in and out of monster training and the database is actually not bad to use. Graphics are PSOne and audio is remastered in at least MR2, not sure about original. Gameplay loop is still as fun as ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Nostalgia is the greatest component with this release, and boy the nostalgia is real with this one. This is basically a port, so what you remember is what you get. Altho, they have made it possible to play it discless. In the old ones, you could pop music CD's into your Playstation and get new monsters. This is a problem in modern day as most of us don't even have diskdrives. The rest of the game is the standard Tamagatchi/Digimon pet sim with battle mechanics. In this, however, you don't always get to use the move you want. The moves you use all depends in how close or far away the monster is from yours. There's more strategy to these games. You also have to sent your monsters out on adventures to get new moves, which severely cuts their life expectancy, so you need to plan out what you want before hand. Yes, this is an old school spreadsheet game of yore. Each monster has their own hidden stat raises like Pokemon, but with the added twist that they die, like Digimon, so combining them is necessary to get max stats. All in all, this is a great game that holds up today. If you like this series please consider buying this instead of emulating. Money is the only way we're getting another one.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty quick and easy review, this is pretty much MONSTER RANCHER 1 & 2 essentially updated to work on PC // soon to be Switch. If you liked Monster Rancher back in the day and still want to play it, this is def. an easy pickup.The only major change is that instead of disc-swapping for the monsters (which is really fun), you now instead use a virtual catalog and look up different discs that exist in real life, it's much faster and responsive, and there is even a Random button to press and just see what you get which is actually really fun. You can even use a mouse instead of a controller now, and it is quite nice in certain situations.The only other minor change I noticed was that item stacking was a thing, which is nicer visually, but the item limit is still pretty low. Otherwise this game is pretty much exactly as it was when it came out 22 years ago.If you're new to the series, its basically a monster life simulation game, you train up your monster, enter it in tournaments, try to unlock new types of monsters to train and become the master rank. People always compare this game to Pokemon, but other than the fact that you 'collect' monsters its not even close. You primarily focus on one monster at a time, and its a very laid back and relaxing experience most of the time. Train up monsters, fight them in tournaments, send them off on adventures and eventually even combine them together to make more unique monsters and find cool (hidden) combinations or entirely new types of monsters.Highly recommended, classic game.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad port of a beloved title, I sunk a ridiculous amount of time into this game back on the original Playstation, so the issues with this port were glaringly obvious.First off, the audio cannot be adjusted to your liking. I'd love to have the in-game sounds with no music, but this isn't possible, apparently. Keyboard support is also weird. Why can we not just type in names? Controls for the most part are pretty much what you'd expect, it's a menu game everywhere except for battles. As for visuals, they're good enough, the game keeps the original look and style, so it's good for nostalgia.One of the most unique aspects of Monster Rancher was always the ability to create new monsters through reading other discs. In this game, you just look up the artist and track, and hope the game can find what you're looking for. This is fundamentally flawed, as it does not allow you to look up other old games, which did give new monsters in the original, and the system also seems to have trouble even finding artists/tracks that were proven to provide specific breeds. Of the dozen searches I performed of some old favorites, I found two. The others turned up no results. This is unacceptable, as it's literally the cornerstone of this entire franchise. How did they screw this up?The biggest issue for me was the removal of the ability to skip individual training exercises, which was possible in the original. You just start the training, press a button, and boom: you've got your result, whether it's a success or failure. For some reason that I cannot fathom, this was removed, and it's the final nail in the coffin for me. That one little button press saved SO MUCH time during the monotony of training up a fresh monster, as the little video that plays during a training session gets extremely repetitive, very quickly.I loved the original, so much that this port was an instabuy for me purely for the nostalgia, but less than half an hour was more than enough for me to demand a refund. The original was great, even with its various flaws, and this port (while mostly faithful) feels like a huge step backwards. Damn shame, because this could have been great. Instead it just sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, the main real reason this has a negative is purely a lack of a mediocre rating, and it's main thing dragging it down is purely the price. On sale for 10 or maybe 15 it's probably worth it, even if not that great.The main downside listed and stated, are the controls. The key binding menu is horribly clunky and nigh nonsensical, forcing you to use a dropdown menu without letter or input hotkeys and tiny scroll bar so unless you arrow up or down, it can be a huge pain to adjust. Controller keybindings are changed from the PS1 and un-changable, annoying but not deal breaking. Touch screen functionality is a distinct sign this is a mobile port, but it isn't that bad to have it, it doesn't detract from much. This all could be handled better, and hopefully if they bother to do any updates this is one of the first they do.The gameplay seems about normal for vanilla monster rancher, with a small few tweaks like AI attacking under 45 guts but nothing seems broken either. However it is very clunky regardless, there is a "part time job" minigame based on a VMU-like minigame, that pays awfully low amounts and only is accessable on the title screen. Music sometimes cuts out and won't come back. Overall it seems fine, but woefully unpolished and anything added in was an afterthought to say they added more, instead of actual additions and fixes.The new features that I can tell, are as follows: More save slots(But actually less if you factor having multiple/swappable memory cards), listing your total stats, a remastered copy of the soundtrack (toggleable for the classic as well), graphics are a little clearer (but still has that low-render quality wobble), a disc library to search from, a bit easier updated online fighting, faster loading screens, a fast forward mode... and you cannot skip training animations anymore. All said and done, it is not bad, because the games themselves weren't bad. But, ultimately the only thing this game can sell itself on is if you don't have access to this game in any other way, as what is out there is at worst on par, and in some cases superior to this poor port. Nothing was ruined, but nothing to gain unless they start adding more updates. If you get this, get it on sale or if/when they lower the price.

Like they'd somehow make even better monsters, damn... kids are dumb).Anyways... I had my favourite Monster, a plain ole green Dino, I took such good care of it, tried my best to spoil it, give it the best digital life I could, as a dumb kid, thought it was just the tops. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 are classic epics, from a time when games were actually art.This is the director’s cut of the original PS1 titles from the late 90s. Both of these games put you into the shoes of a newly licensed rancher and your job is to raise and train monsters with the goal of becoming the best monster rancher in the world. Unlike in Pokémon, here you focus primarily on a single monster at a time - it’s more about carefully raising your monster, bonding with it, and the choices you make that ultimately determine their success.All in all, Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX are games that will mostly appeal to fans of the originals, but it’s also the most complete version of these games that we’ve ever had. There’s so much depth and complexity here, that if you’re into the concept, there’s a solid chance that you’ll become completely hooked for hundreds of hours. Some slight clunkiness and definite signs of age aside, it’s still clear why so many of us fell in love with these games when they first came out.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who don't know Monster Rancher is a Monster Battling game at heart, more closer to Digimon than Pokemon. The game tasks the player to breed, raise then fight other monsters in arena battles using their monster. Monster Rancher is a long winded game in that your first monster won't be good enough to get to S Rank, no where near close in fact. However that monster will earn you money and can be used to breed better monsters. The ultimate goal of the game is to get S Rank on all four continents. To achieve this you must build up your ranch and your quality of monsters till you can start unlocking better monsters and breeding better monsters by combining powerful monsters together.So how is the port?While there are a few baffling decisions in this port like not being able to skip the drills and the omission of local Vs and Online Vs. and the lack of graphics options other than resolution change, this is a pretty well done port.However on the other side of the coin I would also argue that this is the definitive way to play this game. The in game Disc Database (which replaces using physical CD's in this version) and being able to upload your monster online to compete against other people in Ai vs AI Tourneys is super fun. Also other smaller quality of life changes like being able to freeze more monsters and buy multiple items at the same time as well as now finally being able to unlock the region locked ??? Monsters make this a must have for any die hard Monster Rancher fan.While I hope the developers continue to smooth out some of the small issues I have with this port, all in all as it stands I would currently recommend this port of the  game to anyone who owns a controller as the keyboard controlls are scuffed.

_childDocuments_.review: Of note: This is a port of Monster Farm 1 & 2 with "Rancher DX" tagged onto it.  It is not a port of 1997 & '99 NTSC/PAL Monster Rancher.  That being said...The Good:There are some Quality of life features introduced to the game that have made this quote an enjoyable experience.  Load times are virtually Zero, bulk item purchases, a Fast Forward (FF) mode that speeds the game up 2x across the board, and some upscaling that smooths it out a bit from the original. The game still holds up after so many years, albeit easier since so much time has gone by to learn how the game works, but if you're new to the games, it will still prove just as challenging.  The traditional CD/Shrine system is replaced with an elegant solution that uses a CDDB/List lookup to choose from instead of requiring physical media, and Shrining monsters has never been faster. Overall, the improvements with Load times, play speed have made this a treat to replay, and playing at normal speeds is difficult to revert back to.The OK:There were some bug fixes applied to the game to correct things that were present in the originals, but there are also new bugs introduced.  The Translation was redone, but still contains many errors.  For those unaware, the western games received an additional 100 weeks of lifespan for all monsters, but as this is based on Monster Farm, the original Japanese lifespans are what is used in the game; Not a big deal for experienced players, but could be punishing for brand new players.  Monster Names are pluralized in their "Main" and "Sub" sections for some odd reason, it's weird to look at when it's never been done this way before.The Bad:There are several game-crashing bugs present, a SPD Gains bug (which is arguably fantastic, but still a bug), that as of this writing still have not been fixed nearly a month after the game's release.  Monster Farm 2 had no option to Skip Drill animations, which unfortunately also does not exist in DX either since this was added in the actual NTSC MR2 game and not MF2.  The Online battle menu and user friendliness is clunky and leaves a lot to be desired for a good user experience.The Verdict:Buy the game, Support the franchise, have fun with it.  It has been an absolute joy replaying a commercially supported product again, and seeing so many new players popping up with new or renewed interest.The re-release/port isn't without issue, but For a single player game, this is still great fun and likely a much better experience than on the original console.  For online battles, it allows people to do what used to require a DexDrive or mailing physical memory cards. Even with the clunky online interface, at least it is still an option and can be quite entertaining, and opens the door for people outside of the emulation/modding community to participate in tournaments.

Major ones that I'll mention now are that there's items that will reduce fatigue and stress, but they'll never mention that you should use them even though they make training so much easier, and loyalty caps out at 50 if you spoil your monster. I personally don't like that you gotta be a bit mean to get higher loyalty, but despite that I love the game to bits, enough to buy it again and dive back into all the guides and old sites I used to peruse to calculate a perfect combination of monsters.10/10 would ranch again
