_childDocuments_.review: One of my all time favorites finally gets a PC port!! I've only played the MF2 port since that is the one I grew up with !I have been itching to play MF2 again for quite awhile, so much that I had made a back up of my original game to try and play it on my computer, only to find out the brilliant disc swapping technology doesn't really work. Since I do 99% of my gaming on my PC I was hoping to avoid having to hook up my PS1 with an adapter just to play and I found this!So far I'm having a great time in scratching that itch but there are some things that bother me. As people have noted the controls are definitely made with the intention of touch screen, so using a mouse to navigate training / errantry, then swapping to KB for battles using Q and E to move and K and L to push / attack is quite annoying.Not being able to skip training or errantry cinematics is quite frustrating, so to speed it up I open the menu and enable FF while doing drills, but having to switch off for battles. Speaking of battles...It seems the input during battles can lag severely, I'll get stun locked even while spamming the button to use a skill by a monster due to game ticks I assume. Can be quite frustrating especially going up against the Golem/Golem in C rank that can OHKO your monster.Having no volume control for BGM and SFX is especially frustrating. You either have sound off or on and there's no in between. I enjoy the remastered audio but it's just waaaay too loud.All in all, I do like how they just created a library to pick from when doing disc stones, although it does kind of take the magic away of putting in Spyro the dragon or a Tomba! 2 CD in and finding out what monster it gets. I am enjoying the game besides a few control and system changes. Definitely recommend at least getting on a sale if you enjoy the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of the Monster Rancher series, I was ecstatic to hear about the release of Monster Rancher DX. Having played the first two games, I was curious to see how this modern version would compare.Firstly, the graphics are a significant improvement from the older games. The user interface has also been streamlined, making it much easier to navigate the menus and interact with your monster.However, Monster Rancher DX has managed to keep the nostalgic charm of the original games. The gameplay mechanics remain the same, but with a few modern twists that make it even more enjoyable. The inclusion of online multiplayer is a great addition, allowing you to battle against other players and trade monsters.The game's soundtrack is also worth mentioning. It's a beautiful blend of modern and nostalgic tunes, and it perfectly captures the spirit of the original games while adding new elements that fit the updated graphics and gameplay.Overall, Monster Rancher DX is a fantastic addition to the series. It's a nostalgic trip down memory lane for fans of the first two games, while also being a great entry point for newcomers. I highly recommend it to anyone who wants to relive their childhood memories or experience the joys of monster-raising for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: Both Monster Rancher games are even better than I remembered, granted there’s tons of internet resources nowadays so you can learn about all the things the game never tells you to help you get started. Looking at a guide or two on how to raise your monsters right feels necessary to be able to get them in shape for higher rank tournaments, but knowing what to do is only the tip of the iceberg and applying this knowledge through how you train, feed, rest, and battle with your monster is the hard part.Each monster has its own specialties and personality, so raising different monsters requires slightly different approaches. One monster will make you proud by doing its best every step of the way, while another is a little twerp that will cheat on its training drills, but you can’t really complain because it gets results in tournament. Your relationship with each monster is unique, making every monster you raise special.The port itself is… questionably designed. It’s basically a direct port of the japanese mobile release of the games, so it’s not really designed to be played on computer. For the best controls, use a controller during battles, as these games were originally designed for controllers, and use your mouse everything else, because they apparently forgot to rebind some of the menu items to controller inputs.The port’s addition of a fast forward button is quite welcome, and how they dealt with generating monsters through CDs in the original PS1 versions of the games was quite smart. They simply added a search engine into the game so you can look up any album or PS1 game to create a monster from. The search engine is fairly picky as you have to put in the title or artist name in order if there are multiple words. For example, if you want to look up Perturbator’s “Night Driving Avenger” and you put in “Driving Avenger” it won’t show up, but if you put in “Night”, “Night Driving”, or “Night Driving Avenger” it will be in the results. Some artists and games don’t show up in the search engine for some reason, but most of the time if it doesn’t show up, the engine is being picky about what you were trying to search.If you want a monster raising/battling game and don’t mind PS1 level graphics, Monster Rancher 1 is quite good, but Monster Rancher 2 is amazing. I may be biased by nostalgia, but I can't recommend these games enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Gather round kids, it's story time.Years ago, I played Monster Rancher for the first time. I know, common story so far. I bought this game for nostalgia sake mostly, but I also knew I'd actually have fun with this game for a long while at least. So I played and noticed something different. The game was cleaner, everything is smooth and concise, and the game is just as cute and entertaining as it ever was. Now here's the thing. When I started this game through Steam, I was expecting the same story line as I've played before. Type stuff, get a monster, go a few weeks in and suddenly face and op monster that belongs in the strongest division before you even get to fight a proper tournament. But missing that story line in this game, I looked it up and realized what I used to play was actually Monster Rancher Advance 2 on the Gameboy Advanced.So far, I love the classic game for what it is. While relatively minimal, it's still relaxing and calming to play, Reluctant to play pvp any time soon though since there's people making saves with fully maxed out stats just to never use that monster outside of pvp, otherwise i'd love to try it if i knew there were some way to monitor and balance out the matches (such as only being able to use monsters within certain parameters, such as not allowing a monster to have above a certain level for any stat).Would I recommend this game to newcomers? If you're a fan of pet and resource management games where combat is involved, I would encourage you to at least look into the game and try it out yourself. I will say that it's not for everyone, but keep in mind that you have up to 10 save files. you can save before making crucial or risky decisions, then load back if you get easily frustrated by mistakes or anticipated failures. While it's not photo-realistic or high-end like many new games are, keep in mind that this bundle contains 2 games from the 90s. It is polished, refined, and outstanding in comparison to the respective games of their original system.Keep in mind, you can change the keyboard inputs through the game selection screen. The game works best with either a controller or touch screen inputs, but you can make it convenient on keyboard as well. The default keyboard setting is fairly awkward and annoying to navigate, especially since there is no tutorial or mention of what keys are what once the game is initiated. I think it's unfair to downvote this game when it allows you to customize the controls.

New graphic are awesome with a lot of attention paid to the original game. Scenes all have the fabulous traditional MR1 feel with the classic backgrounds and musics. I love re-spinning monsters I've raised and encountering new ones. I miss the old way of spinning up monster.  It was a large part of the charm. Don't think I even own something w/ a cd drive so don't know how  that method would even be now. The digital database is very convenient. But I have come across a few artists (both esoteric & kinda well known IMHO) that aren't available. Not sure if the catalog will be expanded or not.Have only played Monster Rancher 1 DX so far. In the past, it was the one I enjoyed the most. I love slow growth, farming-esc games where things evolve and learn. MR1 was the first farming game I played so most loved! Would  recommend this game for anyone who loved the anime, or the original game. As well as the slower gaming found from the farming or world building games instead of the high action -- blood, soaked, thrillers. Realistically, anyone looking for high-end action may be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, it's complicated!Did I wait for more than 10 years to play the game on PC? YES!But is it just a mobile port inferior to the console versions? Sadly, also yes, which is a big NO NO for quality...TL;DR:Buy it to show KOEI there is a western market for true Monster Rancher Titles (not those Gameboy Advanced half baked improvs) and that PC players still play it! Maybe we can get future titles and those from PS3 and PS4 that naver made it over here.However, be ready to request a few updates to revive some features lost in the mobile port that originated this product.PROS:- They've made it touch screen compliant and created an entire web database of CDs you can search for the most popular albuns of the back then and almost now. By itself this is far superior to the Gameboy Advanced versions that you could just type anything that didn't make any sense just to get a strong monster!- Now there is online multiplayer to Monster Rancher 1 & 2! A great addition to all of us who moved around and lost direct contact with so many of our friends that used to play the same game.CONS:- Even though the web database is a great idea, I can't find most of my childhood CDs because of midia localization differences or the fact that half of the artists were never internationally famous. That being said, my PC still has an optical drive with support for CD, DVD and Blu-ray, which could be used for the same purpose, but this resource isn't available in game. So I still have the discs and listen to the songs, but can't use my Space Jam Soundtrack disc for example.- Did I mention they made online multiplayer available in the PROS? Yeah, for some reason the local multiplayer disapeared from a game that already had it in the original. Now, as a software developer I can understand hiding the feature from the mobile ports of 2020 as there is no UI that can make a mobile device adequate for local versus matches. What I cannot understand is keeping it unavailable in the PC release when we have Steam Remote Play Together for instance, or maybe people with kids and families that might want to play locally.

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of a 2021 gaming bingo card, Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX being re-released and on Steam was not on it but here we are with the mobile port of Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX. Monster Rancher was an anime and classic game that I spent quite a bit of time watching/playing back in the day and in 2022 it holds up pretty well as an off-screen/play a little bit every day game. Although I can't say Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX is critically a good game, if you have any sort of nostalgia for the series or just love life sim games around monsters, you can't go wrong here.Just know before getting into the game that it is mostly around training your monsters and clicking through menus until you are strong enough to compete in tournaments, unlock new things, and then rinse/repeat. That is partially why I think it works well as a second screen game while playing something else or working. If you like Monster Rancher, mindless clicking, or simulation games there is a chance you will enjoy Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX but just make sure you read some reviews or look at gameplay to understand the amount of menu navigating you have to do to succeed in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX is a creature tamer/collector fighting simulator. Not much story here, you just run a rancher where you raise a monster to fight in tournaments. You get monsters through a very cool game mechanic. Back on the PS1 when you were generating a monster, you used actual CD disks to do it, well they sort of kept that by letting pick from also any song artist and CD possible. You can only train one monster at a time, but thats okay, you invest a lot more into them than you would with a team of monsters. Also, your monster has a lifespan which will live longer or shorter depending on how you rise it. Play through these again reminded me why I like this type of monster tamer games over games like pokemon. Plus you get Monster Rancher 1 and 2 for a really decent price. And I give this a 10/10.Monster Rancher 1 DX: Styx – Pieces of Eight = GolemMonster Rancher 2 DX: Pink Floyd, The Final Cut = Granity

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played the game before, there's some new stuff. Online player vs player, mouse-only and keyboard options (some complain about controller options, I've had no issues with my Xbox controller personally), a Remastered Soundtrack for Monster Rancher 2 (you can switch to the original if you want), and the CD Database which allows you to just type in a Title or Artist of ANY CD (Music, Shows, Video Games, Etc.) and if it was one of the CDs that worked with these two games, its in there and you can just select it and pop a monster out of it. No physical CDs required to play this. Honestly that was the main reason I got it cause while I have the physical copy, it got tiresome swapping CDs in and out. So I switched to the emulator, which limited the types of CDs I could use to PS1 games.There's also a Fast Forward button you can use to double speed the entire game, but apparently they took out the option of being able to skip Training cutscenes for this button. Its not the worst thing but its still a thing.For anyone whose never played and curious about this: this is basically Princess Maker, but instead of raising a girl, you're raising monsters. You can only raise one monster at a time and the goal is to raise a monster so strong that its able to beat all the Ranked Tournaments and become the strongest Monster out there. Train it, battle it, feed it, give it praise and scold it. Also if you're not careful your Monster might get sick, injured, run away, get lost or even die. If it survives all that, it will still eventually need to be retired (basically go to the lab and Freeze it) or just let it die of natural causes.Frozen monsters can be combined and that's how you're expected to get the really "strong" monsters. Combined monsters earn the stats of their parents and can continue to grow stronger. Its not the same as Pokemon; any monster can combine with any other monster. A single combination of monsters can result in one of several different types of monsters.You can also go on Adventures if you get enough Fame through winning battles. You won't get much from Adventures (you'll be lucky to even find 1 item) until you have a certain few stats really high up. Really high. I'm talking 300+. That's the SMALLEST one.This game can be grindy. Some people can beat the game with their first monster. There's tricks and strategies out there. I'm not one of those people. You can control just about every aspect of it. Pretty much everything in the game has some sort of purpose from your training Style to Stress to Weight and even the week of the year you decided to combine your monsters! You can literally manipulate everything into creating the perfect weapon. Or you can treat it like a Tamagotchi and try to raise it as lovingly as possible. Or forcefeed it tablets and torture it until you game over because you ran out of money!Obviously 1 and 2 are different games with 1 being more simplistic: only 3 food options, you earn money during regular training sessions and training animations are 2d pixel graphics. 2 has more overall Quality of Life fixes, like your monster not getting lost while Adventuring or doing Special Training, likes and dislikes become a thing and your monsters earn more points overall during training. It also introduced attacking monsters during Special Training and minigames, which I despise, but at least I can watch my monster wander around a small 3d environment when I'm at the ranch and pretend its my screen background while I take a break.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: If you like monster raising games, this is the one for you! A true classic from the late 90s comes back today and I couldn't be happier!Graphics: Keep in mind this is still a PS1 game and not a full-on remaster, so going by the graphical standards of then, this game looks great! Many bright colors and everything just pops out at you. The monsters you raise all have various striking designs and even many combined sub-breeds (more on that later) stand out on their own while incorporating elements from the two monsters that made it, while having unique features of their own. For example, a Pixie (think a mini succubus) and a Suezo (The yellow eyeball guy)) combine to make a Vanity, which is a yellow Pixie who lost the wings and tail in favor of a mirror-like thing that floats in front of her. It should be noted of course that this is especially true of Monster Rancher 2, as the first game while not ugly by any means, is a lot more simplistic in its aesthetic. However it does get a point for its little sprite cartoons for when your monster works, trains, and rests. All of which are unique to each main breed across any task. In both games (especially 2) you can also simply wait in the main screen and watch your monster do its own thing and just be itself. And these are always full of charm and personalitySound: The music and sound design is top notch and every moment feels like it should, from the entering of a small tournament sounding tense but not necessarily dangerous, to the S-rank top tier tournaments sounding like a major event, to the monster getting sick and feeling incredibly tense in MR1 and unnerving in 2, right down to the actual death sounding depressing as a funeral dirge plays through the process. And the sound effects are equally perfect, as every monster has its own sound bank, as well as a sound bank for general sounds, which allows the game to add to the aforementioned personalities. Dinos/Zuums sound like mini raptors, Suezos sound like comical little guys, and Monols sound mysterious and foreboding while the evil Jokers have all sorts of unnerving laughs and noises as they swing those scythes around. If a hit lands or misses in a tournament, you will hear the audience react to it. There's tons of little details that make the whole experience feel that much more alive. Remember, these are games made back in the late 1990s. This much detail was not a common thing.Gameplay: Hoo boy, these games are DEEP! Not so much the first one (though its certainly got plenty of depth) but ESPPECIALLY the second one. Actually, it might be a little too deep, as there are many mechanics that are hidden from the player that determine a lot of factors. For example, you never really have any helpful indication of how stressed your monster is until its too late. You generally want to focus on a few key stats throughout its life, or if you're going the full competitive experience (Yup, there's actually a competitive scene for this game too!) then you're gonna need to make full use of your money and items to maximize training and minimize rest. Each monster has its own personality. For example, Apes are lazy SOBs who will fight you at every turn to be able to sleep instead of train while Tigers (definitely not a tiger by the way!) are loyal good doggos who always try to perform at their best. Combinations can have aspects of the breeds that make them up influence their personality, there's training courses for new skills, there are many unlockable breeds, the list goes on and on. There's certainly no shortage of things to do in either Monster Rancher game, and while the game gives you a clear goal of win your way up the ranks and clear the major 4 tournaments, the game doesn't really end until you decide it ends. Maybe you want to try raising a new breed or shuffle through the Shrine to see who pops out, or whatnot. You decide where your game ends.Speaking of the Shrine, in the 90s, the game used your actual CDs at home to produce monsters. We're talking ANY CD so this includes those old AOL discs they used to send in the mail every week, your parents' music collection, and even those collector's edition soundtracks you get nowadays! Due to the CD becoming obsolete in favor of digital music, that method is also obsolete, so to compensate we have a music database built into the game itself. This does two great things for the game: First, you won't need to be online in order to use the shrine and reproduce a monster, so no worries of the database being pulled and the game being unplayable. Secondly, it allows anyone access to any monster, which was not possible in the older games since monsters had a sort of rarity system. For example, the Disk breed in MR1 was completely unobtainable for many players as it was not available in any form save unique sub-breeds in two very specific CDs you probably didn't even have. Now you can raise one here!When your monster gets old, you can combine it with another monster to generate a new monster with attributes of the previous games. This uses a system that quite frankly is way too complex for me, but from what I can understand, if you can figure out how exactly it works, you can create some truly broken juggernauts right out of the box with extensive and careful lab combining. They will inherit moves, stats, and even personality traits! There's a lot you can do here and you will always have something you can do.In battle is where things both shine and falter however. The battle system is pretty straightforward: You and your opponent will have one minute to dole out attacks to each other, and whoever has the most hp at the end wins. Different monsters have different guts rates. Guts are spent to use attacks, and recharge over time, with the speed depending on the breed. Bigger, stronger, and flashier attacks consume more guts which can be a killer if it doesn't work out, so you need to be strategic in your use. Of course the fight really begins before the battle, as there is no real protection from fighting an overpowering enemy you can't hope to beat, save for forfeiting before they get to kill (emphasis on KILL) your monster. Good judgment will allow you to pick and choose your fights and clear through tournaments effectively while poor judgment may lead you to a funeral procession. Inversely however, enemies will also use their judgment on you, and may forfeit the match before it begins if your monster is simply too strong for them. The problem with the battle system is the AI simply put is random. Some battles it sluggishly reacts and gives you a free win, while other times it can spam attacks instantly and not give you a chance to breathe. This isn't much a problem in earlier tiers where you can usually weather the storm, but in the lategame where battles tend to be one-hit kill fests, it can kill you before you even got to play the game.Finally, are expeditions. When you get far enough into the game with a monster, you can be invited to partake in an expedition which has you explore desert/volcanic ruins, a jungle, or a tundra. These use your stats differently than battles and are usually a good way to get money, rare items, and even entirely new monster breeds you can't get anywhere else! However your monster needs to be strong, skillful, and intelligent in order to do these well or else the cost in fatigue, stress, and lifespan will simply not be worth it and you won't get far in them. Additionally they need to be strong enough to rank high enough to be invited in the first place. These are however quite fun (when your monster isn't getting lost in MR1) if you need money, making a monster  specialized for these is an excellent way to generate a great burst of cash on hand.Final Verdict: Due to Steam review text limit I can only say this with no further elaboration: Great game. Buy it. 9/10!

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen people say this is a 'Pokemon-like' game and I'm going to say right out; if you go in with that expectation, you'll be disappointed. Monster Rancher is more of a Sim than an RPG where you play as a monster breeder. You raise a monster recruited from a disc, sending it to work jobs so you can pay for items, ranch upgrades and expensive training routines so you can fight in ranked tournament battles to win money and prizes. Your monster can get spoiled, fat, stressed out, injured and even lost. It can even die eventually, either through old age or injury. Eventually you'll also be sending your monster out on expeditions, exploring ruins and even combining them into stronger monsters with the help of items you find out in the world.These are older games and time hasn't been especially kind to the graphics, UI or controls but there's a ton of charm here and seeing DX get a US release gives me hope for the future of a fun and unique series, even if it's just re-releases of the other games.

_childDocuments_.review: Legendary game by a very well-known publisher that is unfortunately not known by many because it was overshadowed at the time by Pokemon, due to their similar nature - likely due to Pokemon's accessibility and ease of use by children, while Monster Rancher is a bit more complicated. Have played hundreds of hours before Steam release, somewhat detailed review inc.Monsters are much more personal in MR, as you only raise one at a time and it grows in size and power before your eyes over time through training (and resting) and battling/gaining tournament rank, until it's eventual death -- having differing potential for stat gains from training and success rates as they age, creating incentive not necessarily to minmax (though you definitely can get into the more hardcore side of MR if that's your preference) but to raise the monster correctly in a way that allows you to progress the furthest or do the most with that particular monster.Monsters come in Main and Sub breeds and can be combined (eg Dino/Dino and Tiger/Tiger makes D/T or T/D depending on first monster chosen) and have 6 different stats. They have Loyalty levels depending on how you treat them (praising or punishing them for things and giving them items/monthly food type) , different and unique moves per monster that each scale with one of two of the stats.. Plenty of room for different builds for different monsters, allowing for nearly infinite replayability.This has been all over the place, but the game is a very easy 10/10, couldn't believe my eyes when I saw that Koei-Tecmo was 'remastering' MR 1+2. If Pokemon or any kind of monster raising/battling/collecting type game holds your interest AT ALL, I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: The CD monster summoning gimmick is probably my favorite part of the game, but it's an all-around solid monster raising game. Growing up one of my friends had Monster Rancher 2 and we used to steal his parents' CDs to summon monsters from and now the game has a database to search for CDs and video games from (which includes recent releases, not just from the late 90s). There's a lot of bands/artists that are omitted and there's usually not every album/single by an artist available (ex. if you search for David Bowie, you won't get every one of his albums) so I'm wondering if they'll update it at some point.Also, there's lots of guides online for the DX versions of MR 1 and 2, because there are subtle differences between these versions and the PS1 originals (some CDs won't summon the exact same monster as they did on the PS1 versions) so keep that in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: GRADE B+. Monster Rancher 1 feels clunky and outdated. But Monster Rancher 2 still holds up and is worth playing. However, like many of these CLASSIC game ports on steam, they just didn't do much to update the game other then some very minor QoL improvements. I would have loved to see A remastered score or updated graphics or maybe some Voice acting would have been amazing, Even something as basic as adding achievements would have given some motivation for me to spend more time revisiting the game.Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX on Steam is a faithful port of the DS versions, offering classic monster raising with no frills. Hatch pixelated pals from a search engine (which is better then switching out a ton of CD's) Train their quirks, and battle for glory in tournaments or take your monsters on adventures and explore the mysteries of the setting. It's a really nice hit of nostalgia for fans, but expect no modern bells like online play or remastered graphics or even something as basic as achievements. it's a little bit sad to see the wasted opportunity to throw a little polish on a classic gem. But Monster Rancher 2 is still pretty great and the price is very friendly, and totally worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Despite being two decades old, this game is just as good as I remembered it. If you like breeding games, you must give this a try.I remember playing this for the first time when I was little. My parents had just bought me and my brother a PS1, and a few games for christmas, this being one of them. Back then, my English was not very good, and my parents weren't exactly interested in our games, so it took me literal years to learn that you could actually use CDs to summon other monsters. Even so, I loved the game from the very beginning.When my brother told me he saw the game on Steam, I didn't hesitate and bought it immediately, and I'm glad to say it hasn't lost its magic. Aside from the title screen music, which I do find quite annoying, the remastered soundtrack was a great touch. I know many aren't that fond of it compared to the original one, but to me, those melodies bring such great memories, and the funeral dirge bgm is honestly amazing with that choir. This game was always fun to me as a kid, but as an adult, I'm simply amazed by how complex it actually can get. Managing stress and fatigue, combination seasonings, drugs, growth stages, all the new things I ignored at that time have pulled me even more than before. I'm quite glad it came back to life.

I know this sounds like a sad excuse for multiplayer, but I can assure you that it is a great addition that players are very welcoming about. There are plenty of tournaments held this way and it's so much fun.- . This is based around the mobile version of Monster Farm 2, so screen aspect ratio and mouse implementation aren't perfect. Not only that, the way you setup the control scheme is the most counterintuitive piece of garbage I've ever seen, which is a drop down menu for every hotkey (without an instant search function). Even worse, the reference is an XBOX controller rather than the keyboard itself... Not even PSX symbols; which would've made more sense, considering that's the one we all remember!- . For starters, every monster has an handicap on their lifespan (-100 weeks, to be precise). Secondly, drills animations are unskippable, making the training process all the more slow and tedious. Lastly, the battles are incredibly harsh if you don't setup the perfect control scheme, which can be troublesome as stated earlier. Otherwise, you'll have to juggle across the screen with your mouse to select orders. That's not optimal... But do you want to know a thing they kept that, instead, should've been revisited? Unlocking new breeds via incredibly obscure and obtuse methods. This was hell back in the day and of course, it still is. You're forced to use a guide in that regard, when the game could simply help you out more with some hints. It is what it is!- . Besides some new, albeit minor features and balancing through-out (which don't get me wrong, are appreciated nonetheless), KOEI TECMO did the bare minimum and the final product is serviceable at best. For example, you could have better antialiasing and the removal of graphical artifacts if you emulated the original PS1 game with the right BIOS/settings, rather than play this port - which is a bit ridiculous.-. A music database is a bit lame when compared to your local files. They could've scanned your .jpgs, .mp3s, .avis and whatnot in order to get those binary codes needed to spawn a new monster. Instead, we got something entirely different. Still, it's not that bad and it could've been way worse. Considering how software houses operate nowadays, it could've been removed.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who lived on Monster Rancher as a kid, I fully admit that I am biased. I know I love this game, but the reasons I love the games are why I think others will love them as well. It's true that the graphics are largely the same as the originals - though it does seem like there's some smoothing, at least, and unlike every attempt at emulation I've made over the years, MR1 doesn't break random layers and the font is actually fully readable. This is what it is - a port of an old game with bugfixes and updates to make up for the lack of CD availability in modern day. It isn't, however, a lazy port; there are legitimate bugs that could stop you from getting unlocks or end up with items stuck in your inventory forever now fixed. There is also more variety added, with boss monsters previously inaccessible now being trainable as well as variations in generation that never existed before. I suppose not removing - or making removable - the phone buttons IS lazy, and they get points docked for that, but the underlying fixes and port in general are still good enough as to warrant a recommend.I truly hope this is KT dipping their toes into the franchise for bringing it back; I would love to see proper ports of 3 and 4, as neither works *quite* right on emulation. It's a rather unique series - most stat sims tend to be buried in dating sims, and having one where you raise and fight monsters is satisfying. It's a niche that needs more entries, and I hope that we get them. Until then though, despite the admittedly dated graphics (although I love the sprites in MR1 still, hah), it's still an extremely solid sim with a LOT of life.One thing I'll say is definitely go into it blind if you're new; looking up optimum training regimens and unlocks will seem extremely daunting at first until you learn how the game works, and it takes away the fun of exploration to have it all laid out in front of you. At least, uh, until you want to unlock beaclons. Screw doing that on your own. It's dumb.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: No resolution options but you have borderless full screen. Works great on Steam Deck, but you'll want to swap 'A' and 'B' buttons in the controller configuration menu for the game before you boot. Maybe wait for a sale. I saw a streamer play this game and wanted to play it for myself from how much fun I saw from the game. Before this remastered re-release happened, I was already looking at playing Monster Rancher 2 on original hardware, however from my experience collecting old video games, Playstation 1 games are one of the 3 main pillars of pain to collect for when you're on a budget as a vast amount of Playstation 1's library is incredibly expensive. Luckily this re-release package deal for not only Monster Rancher 2 exists, but it also includes the first Monster Rancher as well as their respective manuals, but on Koei Tecmo's website...For the most part I played Monster Rancher 2, so a lot of my review will be based around it. First off, if you want to change your resolution, you must go through the launcher which allows you to select which Monster Rancher game you want to play, however the resolution options are the worst I've ever seen. You have a full screen option and only a 854x480 resolution choice (for context, the menu shows a drop down menu for changing the resolution but can't be selected to be changed). That's already egregious, but what's worse is that the startup settings window is stylized as a Windows 2000 application (whether that is good or bad is up to you) and simply shows bare minimum effort was put into this small portion of the game, and although there are no other resolution options, at least when you select for the game to be played in full scree, it is borderless full screen so that's good. These are my gripes with this version of the game and they end here at simply "start up settings menu sucks and is bare bones."I went ahead and also played this version of Monster Rancher 2 on Steam Deck (while also comparing it to the PC version) and I believe MR 1&2 DX is completely Steam Deck compatible. No display issues, no sound quality issues, nothing of real note other than the control scheme for the buttons which they use on PC as well. I recommend swapping A and B around if you're using a Xbox controller or a Switch controller for this game because it seems those inputs are hard coded to be in those positions. Simply swapping them makes playing MR2 a lot more organic. Other than a minor control scheme change, everything plays great! MR 1&2 DX should get a Steam Deck Verified icon at some point in the future unless I've missed something catastrophic that prevents it from getting verified.I want to note one this before finishing this review, and it's the weird icons that are to the left and right sides of the screens while playing either one of the MR games, and doing some bare minimum research, I found that there were mobile ports of the first two Monster Rancher games. I have no idea if the Monster Rancher games used in this re-release are those same mobile ports as those mobile ports are, to my knowledge, Japan exclusives and I cannot find any footage, discussions, or even any screenshots that are floating around the net. I'm not saying that the games used were from mobile builds of the same games, but I want to bring attention that these icons are far too familiar (and also functional) to many other mobile ported games that have on screen press-able buttons. However if anyone has more information about this, please let me know as I'd like to know more whether or not if my assumption is correct or not.

_childDocuments_.review: A monster battling game with a huge emphasis on training and life spans. The monsters are created, grow, age, and combine or die. Combinations inherit statistics, moves, appearance, and other features from their parents. It can be enjoyed casually but there are also a lot of subtle mechanics and strategies that can be explored.This is a steam (and there is a Nintendo Switch) version of one of my all time favorite games. There are enough new graphical and control settings for compatibility and support but extremely true to the original.The monster generation from CDs is performed by searching and selecting from an artist and album list which I've found to be more accessible than the original method.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher is arguably one of the best monster Raising games Ever. If you've played these before, you'll definitely want to play it again!MR is a monster raising game where you try to raise the strongest monster you can, and battle your monster against other monsters in various tournaments raising your fame, and rank. You're goal is to be the ultimate trainer and having your monster win the 4 major tournaments. (Similar to Pokemon's Elite four).Here you feed your monster, train them so they gain STR, SPD, INT, LIF, DEF, SKI. You can also send them to learn new Skills for battling! Or you can send them on explorations to get new items and uncover new secrets! You can also breed monsters by combining and creating hybrids.You'll be sure to enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever played a Monster Rancher game before, you know what to expect here. This is a perfectly serviceable port of Monster Rancher 1&2. It plays well with a controller, fine with mouse controls, and okay with keyboard (though you have to go set the buttons yourself, because the default control scheme is jank). No, the resolution isn't even 1080p, but I'm not playing Monster Rancher for the graphical fidelity. It runs well, it plays well, it works the way I would want it to. I'm very happy with it, and I hope my money helps convince them there's demand for a new Monster Rancher game in the future.If you haven't played a Monster Rancher before, the start's as good of a place to jump in as any! Far from being a Pokemon clone, the series focuses on raising a single monster at a time to be the best it can, retiring it, and fusing it with another monster you've raised to create a mega-powerful super monster. It's fun to see what you'll get from the various CDs you choose to use to create a monster from (now a database rather than actually using physical media, but honestly? I get the same kind of fun out of it). While the gameplay is definitely somewhat repetitive, it also has that just-one-more-month appeal as you schedule, raise and battle through your monster's lifespan.Give it a shot! If you like making numbers go up and battling weird-looking monsters, you'll have a good time.

The main issues I have are the graphics, dialogue, and the sounds. This was a re-release and not a remaster, I know, but I feel like they definitely could have spruced things up a bit more in the graphics department. They also could have put more effort into making sure the dialogue made sense. My biggest gripe, however, is the fact that there isn't a slider to adjust the sound. I'm not sure what they were thinking just using a toggle switch and it's the main thing that I wish could get fixed. I do not need clown music blasting into my ears every time I go to town. Overall, I do really enjoy the games! I have a lot of fun and get really into raising every monster I take back to the ranch. _childDocuments_.review: So i would like to give people a honest review of this vs the ps1 versionLets get the negatives out the way first.First of all this is not a remaster its a port disguised as a remaster this has bothered me when they call this a remaster when in reality the models look as if they just had anti aliasing put up to the max to smooth pixels and made the music HD rather then redoing any of it to a remastered quality.The monster cards looks as if they just copied and pasted from the ps1 version i am assuming they ran out of time launching this and was on crunch time because taking new photos and sticking them on a card for the system to utilise as the new card surely should not that that much effort.The music has a bug where it wont loop properly or change and you will get dead silence in combat kind of destroying the immersion.No remote play that is odd because this game would look as if it would work very well with a remote play even if it was a special one that allowed both players to control their monsters as the online only allows AI control.Okay now onto corrections needed for steam.Steam why is there no multiplayer label this game does have multiplayer also why cant you add to allow it to have remote play literately playing this game is a must have with controllers. Now for the positives.If you love nostalgia your going to love this game as it brings back all those memory's from monster rancher 2 from the good old PS1 era if this game is ever on sale 100% buy it as this game works very nicely on the steam deck.If your craving a monster battler with more complexity compare to like Pokemon for example this game i would even call it the dark souls of monster battlers due to your monster can in fact die if you fail to train it correctly or allow it to be critically hit in battle its the first game where forfeiting is a core mechanic nothing worst then losing your handwork to a critical hit killing your monster out right.Also its the first game i think when it comes to monster training that address the concept of life spans and death that will make you sad when you find out your training routine was too harsh on your buddy and reduced its life span to a fraction of what they should have.Overall if you view this as a port and your more in for the challenge harsh punishments for messing up as well as the reward for succeeding to feel like you accomplished something great i would say give this game a go but if you was expecting a remaster and you don't like the idea you can be punished i would say give this game a pass.

The game is mainly watching unskippable cutscenes to watch your monster's stat numbers go up, fight in tournaments with absurd RNG difficulty, and eventually having to repeat (almost) everything over again once your monster either randomly dies from being knocked out, or hits its age time limit (which this remake makes even worse than the original US releases apparently). It's definitely kinda unique, but it's a slog to play through and apparently there's not really much different as you progress. You can spend ages playing and reading about this game and you still find out something new here and there. _childDocuments_.review: I never played the original as a kid, but I always wanted to. I was excited when I heard that it was being brought to steam, but as mentioned by others it just feels like a mobile port. And a bit of a lazy one at that.The UI is clearly designed for mobile users. Bars and buttons on either side of the screen, and, for some baffling reason, only partial controller support. The buttons on either side of the screen aren't generally mapped to anything on the controller forcing you to use the mouse even when using a controller, which feels like the right way to play old console games, to me, at least.Graphics are what you would expect from a PSX game. Which is either good or bad, depending on your preference, but I would have enjoyed touch ups to the old graphics personally. (They are probably upscaled, maybe they did work on them, but it doesn't seem so to me.)Gameplay is actually pretty fun overall. If you're not into monster raising then obviously you're not going to enjoy this game. But if so, this will scratch an itch. It's grindy as it can be, and unfortunately the game doesn't really give you much info to go on. The internet has your back on that, but if you don't want to keep alt tabbing or reading a guide on a second monitor then you'll probably find it a bit annoying.Personally I don't recommend it, but I do enjoy seeing the classics brought to the modern day. Sadly, this port feels like someone found the source code on an old computer in storage, whipped up a mobile port and then released it on PC and Switch as well. It was close, but it missed the mark in my opinion.Happy Ranching!

_childDocuments_.review: I was transported to a farway planet to a place where monsters rule, I played the game like an Ace now we're in this place to save the monster from the evil Mu!Okay 90's nostalgia aside, this is a great game.. a Tamagotchi for adults. And it is for adults, sexual themes, death, realistic consequences, and a difficult curve that will infuriate you (The grind is real)I recommend this game, but I also recommend knowing what you're getting into.This game will seem familiar to many who remember the cartoon that ran alongside Pokemon on Kids WB.The show gave many false impressions of what the game is like. First of all, know that this is not Pokemon. While the show adopted many themes from Pokemon in order to cash in on its popularity, the game is not a Pokemon ripoff or knockoff in anyway. Outside of it being about monsters fighting, they're nothing alike. (To say Pokemon and Monster Rancher are the same thing because they're about Monster Fights would be like saying Hotel Transylvania and The Lost Boys are the same because they both have Vampires)Pokemon is a child-friendly experience about catching all the pokemon and forming permanent bonds with your favorites.Monster Rancher has you picking out one monster and trying to raise it to be as strong as you can in order to win prizes. Your bond will not be permanent as monsters have limited lifespans. The game will warn you to retire a monster (by freezing it), and major progress will be made by fusing retired monsters together to create stronger monsters.The pacing is rather slow, but the gameplay and grind can be quite addictive.This collection includes two games, the first has 20 monster types, and the second has 38 (17 of the monster types from the first game, and 21 new ones. The rejected monster types are replaced with stand-ins. Doodles are now part of Monolith, Magics are now Bajarals, and Discs are now Nitons, with the latter two having skins based on the monsters they replace)There's not much of a story, just raise the best monster and unlock all the breeds.I recommend this game for anyone who wants to piss away a lot of time while being immersed.It's definitely one of those games that looks boring, but is quite fun if you get sucked in, and hooboy, call this game Kirby cause it will suck you up.Tecmo, please port Monster Rancher 3, 4, and EVO, or better give us Monster Rancher 6!

_childDocuments_.review: . However If you are a fan and didn't want to get a PS1 and/or overpay for a used copy of these games then you'll probably have a great time.  For everyone else, it's too expensive for what feels like a straight port of the PS1 games. They can claim enhanced graphics or whatever but that's generous. It looks exactly like the old versions of FF7 you could buy on Steam. It might be somewhat better in the character models, but the backgrounds are all still awful PS1 textures. I thought I would really miss the CD swapping feature for the Monsters and...I do. But what they have in place works pretty well. I suppose it's about as good as you can get today and I'm ok with that. It does take away that moment of anticipation from the discs though, where you're waiting to see if the physical disk you had contained a "special" monster. I really love Monster Rancher and have fond memories of playing it on the PS1 in college and then playing 3&4 on the PS2. Back in the day when people would come over for parties they would go through my CDs and ask why I had sticky notes on every case with something like "Rabbit/Dino" or "Stupid Plant Caterpillar" written on them. For me it's barely worth the cost just for the nostalgia and I couldn't believe how I still remembered so many of the arena names and the music since it's easily been over 20 years since I fired up MR2.So, it's fun for me but I'm a big fan. My kids (teenagers) wanted to see this game in action as I had told them about it for years and years and they were highly unimpressed. I don't blame them. The graphics and animations make me feel old and poor when I see them. If someone showed this to me and talked about how awesome it is I would think they were out of their mind. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: buy and play if you're a veteran of 1 and 2, or if you're determined to make it all the way through them, otherwise, there are other far more reasonable entries in monster training games to play. this title will remain on my steam list, in my library, because it's an important part of gaming history, but I don't see myself putting any more time into them.I came in to this series at the 4th game, on the PS2. I had not seen, nor played, the first 3 games until this steam port. to begin with, this appears to be a MOBILE port, which doesn't make sense to me, it's an old playstation game why would you port it to mobile and port *that* to PC when playstation 1 emulation is still strong and possible? but that's a comparatively petty issue I have.the larger issue is the lack of a CD reading system, and a lack of a reliable music library to search. I can only assume it wants you to search by *song* titles and band names rather than album like it says ON THE STEAM PAGE. further more, I tried famous albums, I tried famous songs, by well known artists over and over and came up with 0 results EVERY time, finally, I hit the random button and . . . . I'm not even sure most of these bands names are written in english at all, much less who the hell they are.so, using the random option, I finally get a monster for both games and start getting into the game itself, and realize that it's in no way as refined or friendly to new players as the 4th entry is even once you get past the problem of not being able to just rip from CDs you actually have (yes I know, most people no longer have a CD tray on their PC, but you have to accept the HUGE liability with completely removing that and using your OWN library for monster data), and once I have my monster, and  take it to my ranch, I find out about the RNG. both games have what seems, at least at this early stage, to be VERY unfair RNG. be it for the training, or the tournaments the RNG seems entirely stacked against you. And you only earn money from tournaments in 2, and from work and tournaments in 1, and the money that cmes in from work is a TINY sum compared to the ammount for winning a tournament, but good luck winning a tournament.both of which also have a month long hard core training regimen for your monster that has a HUGE pricetag that takes winning at least a D rank tourney to earn, yes, WINNING the tournament because if you win a D rank, you get 1,000 plus some bonus . . . . get second place and you earn about 350. I'm seeing more and more reasons why no one knew about the Monster Rancher games in my childhood until I was in highschool and the 4th game in the series was coming out.

Over all, solid game, pretty nostalgic, could have been better but it's completely functional and serviceable.

_childDocuments_.review: Once more, I crawl out from under my comfortable rock to get a steam badge.At least this review will be an easy one for me, as this just seems to be a mostly accurate re-release of a game I spent literal days of my life not only directly playing, but digging through my father's CD collection in order to create monsters with.  If anything, some degree of my quite varied tastes in music might have stemmed from conversations he and I would have about the various artists whose work I was popping into my PSX.  Coupling that together with the genuine attachment I would feel for these creatures that I would raise from infancy, it actually can reach you on an even more emotional level than something like Pokemon, or even ARK despite the latter's growth mechanics.  These games would make me question how harshly or softly to raise a creature for more than the mere mechanics.  I would actually feel personally -guilty- if I felt I was too strict on a monster, or even wondering if being too lax was actual a detriment to their long term potential, as if they actually cared on some level about how successful they would be in combat.In shorter terms, I would put more thought and care into my relationship with these colorful pixels than I would with peers from school I interacted with every day.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Monster Rancher fan, my play time doesn't calculate all of the save files I've messed around with in the two games in both their original releases and the Japanese Switch port prior to DX's release. This release, in particular, is a very good one (bar one bugged tournament, the New Years Cup in MR2 when played on Fast Forward), featuring many quality of life changes. While lifespan for all of the monsters is still shorter by 100 weeks compared to the original English version, the rest of the changes more than make up for that. This features the Swim Bug fix, 20 freezer spots for monsters, unlimited shrine usage (was limited in base MF1&2 Switch), a fast forward/2x speed mode, the Pocketstation minigame, and works great with the fanmade Advanced Viewer. Now, for a review with previous fans less in mind. Monster Rancher 1 and 2 are raising simulators where each action takes time and has effects on a monster's overall lifespan and disposition. Your goal is to train monsters to fight, unlock other monsters, and, eventually, combine them to make stronger baby monsters to repeat the process. Fights are done in a tournament styled system, all Round Robin in MR1, with an additional Bracket Style introduced in MR2. The battle system typically has a fight running on a 60 second clock (3 minutes in errantry fights) with monsters moving on a 2D plane split into 4 distance types. Each distance has its own techs (moves) a monster can use with its own guts cost. Battles have increased dynamics due to the guts system acting as a cost for attacks, leading to things like guts correction, which make it safer to wait out attacks to make them stronger. The person with the higher percentage of life/HP at the end of the match wins!Over time, you will find out which monsters you prefer raising, what methods are worth using, and which techs are worth spending lifespan over. Monster Rancher 1 feels like Monster Rancher 2's prototype in many ways, but, even there, the cute sprite work makes it worth your while. Now go out there and raise some Worms!

_childDocuments_.review: I was in my early 20s when the first Monster Rancher came out. I spent hundred, if not thousands of hours playing it and its sequel. You can't skip the training animations, the skip feature was from the U.S. release and this is based off of the Japanese one. There seem to be some new monsters and I notice that the monsters you unlock from cd's differ from the old PSX versions, at least some of the unique ones that were attached to certain albums. Thats not really a complaint, just an observation. They did a good job with the upscaling and some modern conveniences. The mouse actually works great for most of the interface although I am still using the controller if I decide to manually fight.I rarely buy games directly from Steam but this really deserves some support. There is a lot of gameplay here. Not a whole lot of main story, work your way up to the top. Its the exploration missions, and little events that pop up and special matches you can aim for that add so much to it. This is a great game that deserves a modern sequel. Between the Monster Rancher series and the Deception series, Tecmo made some of the funnest games with the best replay value during that era. If you liked these in the past, this is probably the best way to play it now if you want to generate a variety of monsters.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a set of old games, from 1997 and 1999 respectively. I tried Monster Rancher 1 and couldn't stand how lacking it was compared to 2, so I can only speak about 2. The biggest difference between the original and this, if my friend that has emulated the game is to be believed, is the overall speed of the game. The cutscenes, the text boxes, and most significantly, the fights. All of these are at least twice as fast as the original. This is a good thing, since the game can get a bit repetitive as you're raising your monster.I highly recommend using a controller, not mouse and keyboard.Pros and cons of the game if you haven't played it before:PROS*It's an ambitious foray into the (then new) Pokemon genre, monster training. The gameplay is not at all close to Pokemon, but that's the closest equivalent I have. There's a great amount of detail, a lot to learn. Many monster types, many moves, many things to unlock.*Your assistant trainer, Colt, has an interesting and dynamic personality. It's going to quickly become clear that this is a Japanese game translated (occasionally awkwardly) into English. But in spite of that, the assistant trainer is memorable and a large part of what makes the game great.CONS*It's an old game and the graphics haven't really been revamped. That might be a shock to you if you haven't seen Playstation 1 era graphics before.*It can get repetitive and you might not know what you're doing at some point. Fortunately, there are plenty of detailed online resources to help.Two resources I can recommend, one new and one old:This is old GameFAQ, originally from 2006 but there have been updates to it since then, the latest of which was in 2019. A lot of detailed and very useful information. I didn't have a great combining result with my CrabSaurian, stats wise, but other than that I have nothing but good things to say about the guide.This is a modern resource of how to unlock each of the (many) locked monsters. That will take a good amount of time if you want to do all of them. The website also has a good many other resources on it, including an in-depth guide on combining monsters  Very, very useful!My guess is you're either going to like the game a lot or not at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely ENTHRALLED to see this port of a childhood favorite make its way overseas.For those finding their way here without former knowledge, Monster Rancher is a game in which you, surprise surprise, raise monsters. Your goal is to claw your way from the bottom to the top ranks, managing your monsters' health and stats as you enter them into tournaments to fight. It's much more about managing stats of one specific creature than other monster-oriented games that were released at the time, and there's a bit of a learning curve it you're jumping in blind. These elements really set it apart and make it feel much more personal than the rest, even without its once iconic method of obtaining your various beasts via real world CDs.The only real disappointment is just how low-effort this port is. It was designed for mobile first and foremost, with touch control buttons on either side of the window at all times, even if you're playing with keyboard/controller. There have been no optimizations to visuals, so you'll sometimes see holes in the models and the like. The games are LOUD, with no option to adjust the volume in-game. The names of the windows are even unchanged from their japanese counterparts. It is the absolute bare minimum, with the only change being to the monster generation system, which was more of a necessity for the games being ported to mobile than anything else. But I'll state again, I'm glad to have gotten a localization of this extremely niche franchise at all. Monster Rancher is a fantastic time, and offers an incredibly unique experience I've never encountered before or since, and I'd highly recommend giving these games a try if they pique your interest! I'd be overjoyed to see these games not only succeed, but also communicate to Koei Tecmo that maybe, just maybe, a new entry in this long dormant franchise would be a worthwhile endeavor.

I was never a fan of later ones, even 4, but this is as great as remembered. Even better with all the community info!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say much about this game, compared to all creature collector game nowadays Monster Rancher 1&2 prob not the best one but If you played the PS version before and you want to dive into nostalgia it's basically the exact same one.I just wish we can cheat to unlock the creatures rightaway for the disc stone feature because a lot of the discs are unavailable to generate.It's an alright port. 3.5/5
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this for a while, I can say this is indeed the best way to play Monster Rancher, at least in my opinion. It's easier to select the moves in battle, since I can just click on them to rotate them. They've added in the region exclusive monsters that were previously unavailable. While some people say these games haven't aged well, I'm not sure what they mean. I first played Monster Rancher 2 back a few years ago, and it's exactly what I always wanted from a Virtual Pet raising type of game, so maybe people just don't like Virtual Pets? I don't know, but I already loved MR2, and it's back better than ever, and I get to play MR1 for the first time ever. I really like the nice little sprite animations in MR1 for training. Overall, I highly recommend if you have any interest in these type of games, I've already put several hours in and didn't even notice!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: More or less the same experience as when I played this on the PS1. Getting new monsters are a lot easier with the new shrine system. It can get monotonous and repetitive, specially if you already know the ins and outs of monster training but I still love it.It could use a volume adjuster. The BGM can drown out any other apps you might have open
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game about 20 years ago and it still holds up to this day. This game is more accessible than ever before and if you want a game that you can play for YEARS get it ASAP. There is no wrong or right way to play this game and is the pinnacle of this series. If you are looking for a game where you can actually get attached to your monster, and not view them as tools get this immediately. The game is rated T, but when released in the US it was E so take the rating with a grain of salt. Dive into the complexity of this game, but beware. You may drown.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: Better than I remember. I still have both PS1 Discs. Loads fast, has not crashed once. Clear audio, smooth port. Works fine with both keyboard and mouse, as well as xbox wireless controller. No issues on my end. the game looks great. 3950x, 32gb, rtx 3080. Thank you for releasing this game. So many memories. I feel emotion again. Bring on the rest of the games. I never played past 1 and 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: Obvious mobile port but haven't noticed any major issues except for you being unable to skip training animations. You can toggle a fast forward function in the menu so effectively it's the same though.As for the games themselves, it's a monster training game with a little more simulator aspects like monster stamina and feeding requirements than your average monster game. It's hardly overbearing though. What really set Monster Rancher apart really was the fact you created monsters from CDs you had laying around the house. The ports effectively can't replicate that so instead you input a song/soundtrack and artist now and it generates a monster based on that. As just an example, I used Linkin Park's Hybird Theory to get a bunny girl. Then I created a demonic Wolf using Gorillaz's Demon Days. It's a fun little way to further personalize your favorite music. As far as I can tell there isn't much new to the ports except an autosave, so for me the purchase was a matter of convenience to access the games with little set up.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: It fills my heart with joy this game came back to life and there are so many people gaming it and streaming it as I post this review!I'm in love with the polished and colorful new textures they've added to the game. I'm in love with the fixed cameras. I'm in love with the recreated orchestra they've used for the classic game sountrack. I love it they added the new job feature, which helps one get additional in-game incomes.The only things the game is lacking of and I would like they to add in future updates, is the compatibility with a PlayStation controller, as well as the "skip" feature for the errantry training stages the original game had.Keep up the good work and thanks again!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I like it, just a port with a few extra features and a very nice search function for generation, my only gripe is that the UI is just the mobile version ported to PC, c'mon, at least put in the minimal effort and allow anyone who plays with a controller or keyboard to toggle off the incredibly distracting mobile sidebar.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I am still playing with MR 1 and won't be starting MR 2 until I get to S rank. This was one of my favorite games when I was a kid. I bought it for the sake of nostalgia but after a few minutes I couldn't put the game down. As you would expect, the graphics is dated as this game was made over 2 decades ago. The combat is simplistic, given they had to work with what they got at that time but is enough to get players to think strategically on which skills to use at the right time. So far, it's worth the $30 and I am just talking about the first game I have yet to get started with MR 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: Glad this game made it's return after so long. Played the original version of the game. And replaying it now gives my old heart a feeling so good i couldn't explain it. So yeah, if you are like me, play it again, treat that nostalgia. If you are new, give this game try, you'll love it for sure. It's one of the best, back then, and still is, even now.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I will never not recommend Monster Rancher. I am very happy to see the series again. The monster generation system is very simple to use, and still exciting without having to dig through everything manually. The game plays pretty smoothly, and the increased speed in training also makes things go a bit faster. I hope that the game will meet it's market goals so that we can see further remasters and perhaps even future games! I hope that you enjoy these games as much as I do!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: To the people that played this game in the past... It is just as you remember it. Some things a little different, like how you get monsters, but otherwise the same classic game is there. It is an absolute blast!To those who have never played it, capturing the magic that those of us who have played it in the past may be a bit difficult. Generating monsters, is still fun, but not nearly the same as rifling through all you're parents CDs trying to find something cool. Combat is basic and at times can be frustrating, there are a lot of mechanics that the game does not really explain. Raising monsters is fun, but once you figure out a solid method, it can become tedious. Is it worth 30 bucks? To fans of the series trying to have fun with the game again, absolutely. To new comers, it can be, but i would recommend watching a video or two just so you know what you are getting into.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game when I was a kid. Playing it again as an adult and you know what.. it still holds up. Super solid monster raising/battling game. You get a monster which you take to your ranch. You feed it, you train it, go on adventures with it, fight in tournaments with it, then it dies, then you cry. After all that then you will take a new monster and do it all again with that one! This game is both very simple and also very complex. There are a TON of under the hood mechanics that you may never even know about unless you really dive into it. But it can also be played casually and you can just look at it like a fun monster raising simulator. Even by modern standards this game is quite fun IMO. As for the quality of the port? It's just ok. It gets the job done and is playable. I would have liked better resolution options or just more options in general but that is probably my biggest issue with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: A Great remaster of the original games. It plays well, and so far has had no crashes, or bugs. Its keybinds are fully customizable, and work on both controller and kb + m. There are also full mouse control should you want to be lazy with that, but those controls are sometimes awkward in a fight. Stick with a controller if possible (it is what the game was designed for). The side buttons shown are neat shortcuts to get to monster data quickly, which can be helpful. I will be playing this game for many hours, even if I am already S rank in 5 hours in Monster Rancher 1. I am hopeful this will bring a resurgence to the franchise, and we get the Monster Rancher 4 remaster that was teased at TGS this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for something from this franchise for over a decade. I'm having a lot of fun. I mostly grew up with MR3, 4, and Evo but my interest in the series started when my cousin showed me MR2. This is my first time playing both 1 & 2 and I'm loving it. Hoping for more remasters, re releases, and above all a brand new game in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Heres the controls for controller aka Ps4/ps5 controller that i've figured out so farbumpers/L1 or R1 : Are to make your monster move left and rightX : Is to cancel or too push a monster back when you and opponent is too closeO: Is to confirm or command a monster to execute an attack (remember your loyalty depends on how successfull they are in executing that attack)The Pros:-Its monster rancher as you'd remember it and it play the same with no performance issues or bugs that i've seen so far-They actually reworked the summoning cd feature and it's kinda impressive cause it's a lot of effort to get real music artist and songs and put it in the game -Its fun as you'd remember and as much as you would expect-you can get op and one shot opponents monsters-has ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ autosaves that are independent from hard saves which are done in the emulations so they (I assume) are separate save types which is really great if the game crashes or power goes out, great feature really appreciate Koei Tecmonintendo could learn a lot from you-Can change screen resolution and keybind, just click options before launching one of the two games.- has boarders to fill black space since this is a ps1 game and tvs were square back then, they also added buttons on these boarders which make me think this is probably on tablets and phones which is fine cause it's the same game with no phones or tablet games ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥The Cons-Theres apparently online, but later on its gonna get ruined by ppl cheating by editing their monsters stats or something which isn't really the game's fault but hey it's gonna happen cause some people really can't handle losing so they gotta cheat to cope-Can't change screen resolution, as atm it's windowed mode and a medium-ish sized the game which sucks-bugged my discord when switching games, which is the games fault but it was something they probably didn't would affect discord and it's a very minor inconvenience

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far in my opinion one of the most underrated franchises of all time and with the remasters fixing some of the most tedious parts of the game it makes it somehow an even more enjoyable experience when it was one of my favorite games to play with my cousins growing up. If you have not played this game I'd highly recommend you do so. It's an experience to never forget.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher 2 was an absolute favourite of mine whilst growing up. I am so happy to be able to play it now as an adult, the nostalgia is crazy! Be aware this is a port of a game from 1999 so the controls are a bit outdated and there is a lot of repetition but if you enjoy games similar to this then it is a must try! The redone soundtrack is a nice addition but everything else other than the monster shrine music selection is the same as the game was. Here's hoping for a new Monster Rancher game soon!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game a ton as a kid, and while I'm really enjoying the game I wish there were a few things that were different.1.) The autosave feature is awesome and saves a ton of time, so other quality of life features like buying multiples of certain items at once would have been a very welcome addition.2.) Sadly as of right now there is no way to skip ahead during training sessions, I think this isn't intentional as you can still skip the cut scenes for errantries, but its something that needs to be looked at regardless.3.) Controller binding and the ability to disable that blinding light that appears whenever you click on something using the mouse would be nice as well.All in all I'm just happy to have this game available, it is nice that the game has been re balanced and some of the bugs have been fixed as well. I love that we have a VS mode online, and I like how they adjusted the Shrine so you can still have some semblance of mystery around getting random monsters. As of right now I'd recommend this to fans of the series, but for a newcomer some of these design choices might seem archaic and time consuming. Hopefully they continue to adjust and patch this.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: The game is well worth the value, and a lot of fun. If you're new to the series and wondering what a "monster rancher" is, well it's really it's own unique game - so if you're imaging some pokemon 1v1 it's much more like 1 on 1 time with your favourite 'mon. I'm so glad it's back and hope this will inspire more games. I played this game extensively as a kid and was worried the remake might not be as great as I remembered, now that I'm coming back with an adult's eyes. Let me tell you - I played 11 hours straight today and it was a blast. The new shrine feature to replace CDs had me spending and hour just searching favourite songs, popular songs and meme songs alone. Its every bit the game I remember with some small QoL improvements. I played with a ps4 controller and apart from some small adjustments the new controls have it was like a time machine into one of the funnest ps1 games that will just eat your time without you noticing!
