_childDocuments_.review: Just popping in here to recommend the heck out of NeverAwake.This is Neotro's latest game. You might remember VRITRA, their previous effort, which was really quite good. This shmup is even better. Rather than go for the typical 5-8 stages of arcade action, NeverAwake has 70+ stages to shoot through. What's interesting is that all of these stages loop indefinitely, with each loop featuring more enemy bullets and higher scoring potential. Now bear in mind that unlike most "survival" games, your score is not recorded if you die. The only way to progress & achieve high scores is to collect 100% souls. Souls drop from most enemies, so depending on your skill-level & playstyle, you can either rush to collect souls, or push your limits to get a great score.In any case, you must be aware of the importance of special weapons. There are a multitude of them to purchase and equip, and they can function as a shotgun, rebounding bullets, or homing lasers. Experiment to find the right special weapon for each stage. Accessories are also important part of your kit, as they can increase your shields, give you more ammo, and add numerous other powers. There's a lot of customization to work with here, allowing players to find a build that works for them. Bear in mind however that aside from the special weapon, all you have to work with is your maneuverability and your main cannon. To put it another way, managing resources is just as important as dodging bullets. If you waste your ammo, it'll spell disaster for you down the line. Accessory slots are also limited. Consider this an opportunity to choose accessories that play to your strengths or cover for your weaknesses.One other very important ability is the dash. There will be multiple instances where an attack simply can't be weaved in-between. This is where the dash comes into play. The player-character is invincible while dashing, but there is some recovery time. It's a powerful move...when used properly. Otherwise, the key to surviving strenuous bullet-spreads is to "lead" them away from yourself. Never settle for merely reacting to what the enemy throws at you. If you don't take the initiative, you'll be overwhelmed and wiped out, especially on the higher loops.Throughout the game, there are several bosses to face. These dastardly and visually intriguing foes have a wide array of attacks. Much like any regular stage, you can focus on gathering souls to end the fight quickly or destroy the boss repeatedly to boost your score. Naturally, successive loops result in bosses that are more aggressive and toss bullets with greater frequency. It's on you the player to manage your special weapon and soul count to achieve a satisfactory score. The last thing you'll want is to destroy a boss multiple times a row, without ever bothering to pick up a single soul. The level of difficulty makes a very significant jump after eight loops, so you don't want to be caught without a means to finish the stage quickly.Like numerous other classic 2D shooters, NeverAwake rewards players who memorize enemy patterns and develop routes. The scoring system mostly relies on surviving multiple loops in a row, and there aren't any convoluted subsystems to account for. Despite the voluminous number of (looping!) stages, the game never feels repetitive or slow. On average, a single stage can take about a minute to complete, provided that you're rushing for 100% souls. In that minute, you'll face not only a solid variety of enemies, but you're also bound to fly into creative problems that require creative solutions. Some stages can involve block pushing or using objects as a shield from deadly lasers. This variety never comes off as gimmicky or takes away from the rest of the game. There's never a point where you'll think "Oh no! It's the block-pushing stage! I absolutely loathe it." Everything comes together wonderfully, adding to the game's identity and appeal.I'd also like to add that the visuals and atmosphere is flat-out superb. There are seven worlds and they're all quite distinct from one another. Each world has their own unique enemies, as well as the aforementioned "creative problems". You'll witness (and destroy) all sorts of nightmarish fiends. The bosses are especially creative and well-realized. There simply is not a weak fight in the game. Also, the boss-battles end quickly enough that fighting them over several loops in a row never becomes frustrating or tiresome. The pacing is absolutely a large part of what keeps this game so engaging. The average play-through can take upwards of four hours, and many more if you're shooting for high-scores and all of the optional content. For a shmup, this could be considered a fairly sizable amount of time. Nevertheless, you always have a goal to strive for, and you're always entertained. Altogether, NeverAwake is one of the strongest entries the shmup genre has seen in quite some time. Its structure and method of progression is unlike most anything else out there, and yet it all works wonderfully. Neotro knew exactly what they wanted to do here and delivered an astounding game. It's a twin-stick shooter that doesn't just require good reflexes, it teaches you the essentials of resource management and positioning. The level of depth on display here is really impressive. It's sure to keep novices and experts glued to their controllers.So yeah. I recommend the heck out of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting take on the loop mechanic commonly seen in arcade STG / SHMUP!The game is basically as hard as you want to make it. So it should prove appealing as much to hardcore players as to casual ones.That being said, base difficulty is surprisingly not that low : expect some serious struggle toward the end of the game.However to compensate, the game regularly unlock equipments based not just on progress but also total numbers of death. So you can still improve no matter how many times you fail (SO NEVAH GIVE UP!!).Special mention to the mesmerizing art direction, and the amazing soundtrack!
_childDocuments_.name: NeverAwake

_childDocuments_.review: NeverAwake is one of the most charming twin-stick shooters available on Steam.The game is an audiovisual tour de force, featuring a Gothic style that almost makes it seem like it was designed by Tim Burton, and an awesome soundtrack that wouldn't be out of place in Plaid's discography.It's a fun, accessible title, with 80+ stages, a steady stream of power-up unlocks (which should help anyone struggling with the difficulty of certain stages, but it also means there's quite a variety of different loadout combinations possible, so veterans will have plenty of ways to maximize their scores), and unusually for the genre, an engaging storyline, even featuring multiple endings.In short, NeverAwake is a worthy addition to the library of anyone who enjoys the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: NeverAwake

_childDocuments_.review: A good twin stick shooter at this price is pretty much an insta-buy from me, as it was here.  I'm getting older and my reflexes are very much dulling, but I'm sill reasonably handy at a SHMUP.  So your experience with the difficulty level may not be the same as mine.But for me this game has such a finely tuned, and enjoyable, difficulty level that seems way more interested in me having fun than beating me over the head until I give up.  Almost like the devs want me to see and experience the entire game. and have a great time along the way  Totally refreshing!I'm up to world 6 and have completed the challenges on the first 2 worlds so there is still quite a bit to do.  But I couldn't carry on without trying to spread the word about how good this game is in pretty much every way.The weapon and accessory swapping is just great at adding depth and making sure constant changes in strategy are rewarded.   The graphics are truly spot on with easy to read bullets and some great patterns.  The levels have great variety in obstacles.  The bosses are never a pain, inventive, plentiful, and gorgeous to look at.  The story is interesting enough but never gets in the way of the action and the music is funky and fits the game nicely.Honestly, if you have any interest in the genre, or curiosity about it, just buy it.  Well done devs this is great work!
_childDocuments_.name: NeverAwake

There's a lot of fun ideas and clever twists throughout — a couple boss patterns even had me shouting "damn it, why didn't we think of that?!?!" out loud.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely stellar game little hidden gem of a game. Easily my favorite twin stick shooter ever, but not a stellar bullet hell until really late into the game. Lots of replay value and bite sized levels makes this easy to pick up and put down in multiple sessions, with the main game taking me about 9 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: NeverAwake

_childDocuments_.review: Having a lot of fun with this. A shooter with a remarkable art style and the level/enemies/bosses design is unique. You play through a whole bunch of levels that you clear by gathering a certain amount 'souls' that drop from enemies. The levels are short and loop around, but each loop the levels get progressively harder (so you typically don't want to wait around). There's a lot of upgrades to unlock as you play through the game, and additional challenges to do.If you're on the fence, there's a demo available.
_childDocuments_.name: NeverAwake

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really fun indie shoot 'em up game! If you like classics like Contra and Gradius & Parodius, or even the more recent Cuphead, you'll like this game! You play through stages, fight bosses, and find out the truth about the protagonist, Rem. The story is mostly given through notes you read as you beat or lose in stages and it's genuinely a emotional plot which I won't spoil. You collect currency as you beat stages and as you either win or lose in stages you unlock new passive abilities to buy and use. My favorite part of the game is the bosses, they're very well done! For the most part most of the game is well-designed, a few sections are a tad hard but most of the game has a fair difficulty such that anyone can beat the game - even I'm not the best at shoot 'em ups but this game was fine for me to beat. The only stage I disliked was the one with drawers? that kept popping in and out, it was very troublesome.And the great thing is that this game will observe if you're losing a lot and will give you specific hints for the stages/boss you're on, and if you keep losing you'll unlock the ability to buy more power-ups to help you out, so someone who struggles more early can buy upgrades earlier, but if you didn't die as much you might unlock them later. The game purposely puts hard enemies and sometimes it's better not to disturb really aggressive enemies.The game has optional stages and you only have to beat one of two of certain stages to progress, so if one stage is too hard then you can skip it and still get to the credits. The final boss was hard but fair and I felt very accomplished after I finished the game and there's good payoff for finishing the game. After you beat the game there's optional challenges in the previous stages you can complete to unlock more content. Overall a very fun indie game, it has great artwork for both the protagonist and enemies, and the bosses are amazing. Definitely one of my favorite shoot 'em ups!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic. Phenomenal soundtrack, excellent variety from top to bottom, great mechanics like soul collecting that open up levels to a variety of ways to play, great visual design, surprisingly chunky amount of content, and a light but touching story. Sans a small handful of cheapshots here and there, I have basically two complaints:1) There's a *heavy* reliance on asking the player to tune the game's difficulty for themselves. It's possible to set up a kit that will afford you almost *20* extra hits on a single stage, which is enough to limp through basically every main challenge in the game without really trying. for what it's *worth* I did tune this to my own needs as best as I could, giving myself more hits after a few tries, but it seems like the game very much does not want you to struggle on the overwhelming majority of its challenges. 2) This is partly a preference for more uplifting endings to stories like this but I really, *really* wish the Route A and Route B endings were swapped. Having Route B, with it's depressing tone, being the last bit of unique Content to play noticeably took the wind out of finishing my playthrough of this game, and I think the narrative context that comes with Route B would have heightened Route A even further. The idea seems to be to give players who are less invested the more satisfying ending without needing to push themselves as hard, but I think the desire for Something Better could have been a great motivator for people to reach that second ending, and I think it would suit the game's theming more effectively to have Route B come first, then route A. It's not really like Route B's that much *harder* than Route A, either? Theta Divine is still the game's hardest main fight, and again, I think it could have been even better than it already was if it had the stakes of Route B behind it. To be clear: I don't think Route B is bad, but having it come *after* Route A feels like it ultimately hurts the message and tone of Route A.These are a *lot* of words to the two things that bothered me about this game but I want to be clear that I have this much to say because I LOVED everything else going on in NeverAwake and it hangs *incredibly* close to being a 10/10 experience. I want many people to play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone. No seriously, everyone.  NeverAwake is my prime example of what the indie gaming scene.....hell what gaming as a whole has to offer. It''s the prime example of a development team taking the genre, understanding it's core principles, and yet evolving it in certain ways to create a unique experience that will stick with you for years to come, while also making you wonder why you hadn't heard of it up to this point. It's criminal that the game hasn't got the attention that it deserves so far, because not only is it line to be my most overlooked game of 2022.....it's probably my favorite game of 2022. The top down shooting is refined thanks to controls that give you the precision that you need, but punishes mistakes with fantastic level and enemy design. Each level feels hand crafted to create a unique experience: twisting gameplay to introduce new things that test your might and will while also being familiar at the same time. Customization of equipment helps refine the way you play, and it's amazing how well the game's pacing and feel from level to level keep you wanting more. Bosses push you to the limit while having replayability, and what the game does masterfully is to make the gameplay seeminglessly transition into the presentation and the story.The visual symbolism is masterful, with representing the horrors of this girls mind while still showing the hope that still exists. Each visual element tells a story that makes you want to dig further, seeing the next diary entry as you play detective in truly what is happening in this world. The music paints a haunting melody while you do this, and the story truly pulls on your heartstrings while allowing for interpretation that's unique to each player that plays it. Really, the only thing that really lags in terms of the game is the options menu: but when everything else is a shining example of what the genre and the gaming world has to offer: it's going to be reasonable to overlook the small flaw.It's a game that puts itself in line with some of my favorite gems in the last 10 years: the VA-11 HALL-A's, the Wandersongs, the Virgo vs the Zodiacs. It's a steal at the price that you'll get it at, and frankly the only reason you should even consider not hitting the buy button is that you want to pick it up on another platform when it hits them eventually. And even then, I'd advise you to double dip. It's that damn good.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend this game.  Great visuals, good music, fun gameplay.  I really like the constant progression you get as the game gives you more and more upgrades. Combining the health upgrades with special attack gain whenever you are struck is pretty unstoppable.  Then add in the health regen every time you hit 33% and 66% and you can steamroll basically every boss by standing in front of them, taking damage and using your special (the special that attacks in a circle works best).  This worked all the way to the final boss.But that said, the game has an autoaim and "oversoul" mode to make the game even easier, so I don't think it's meant to be a super challenging game.  I beat it in about 4 hours (not including the extra challenges), so it's not very long but I think for 20 bucks it's good value.My one gripe is in world 7 when they introduce these walking creatures that take down all your shields in one hit.  They should just deal one damage like everything else.  The game goes from being insanely easy and almost impossible to lose, to fairly difficult.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy a good bullet hell game when it's done right. The likes of Cuphead and a number of Housemarque's games are amongst my favourites. This game however, despite having beautiful graphics, a smooth performance and, at times, a tough and enjoyable gameplay loop, just doesn't quite seem to understand what differentiates good bullet hell and poor bullet hell. The increase in difficulty as you progress is accomplished via cheap shots and wonky new level mechanics (one level in particular requires you to move boxes into place to stop incessant laser beams from hitting you as you move with the screen. Good idea, but awful execution). There's 75% of a good game here, but it does unfortunately get undercut by amateurish and artificial difficulty spikes. The story elements are completely underbaked and presented in a repetitive, text-based way. This isn't really a game genre you go to for narrative, but there seems to be a good idea here for a story underneath the basic way it's presented.  I'd keep my eye on this dev, as they're sure to iron out a lot of the issues that make this game feel unfair in later levels with more experience. If the gameplay and story matched the colourful, child nightmare-esque visuals; this game would be an easy recommendation. As it is, I'd have to say it's probably not worth the plunge money-wise.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique SHMUP that has a surprising amount of levels, but not as much mechanical depth as I was hoping for. Very worth the price for the art style and storytelling alone.Pros+The game's art fills a specific niche of disgusting yet cute, because the enemies all spring from the nightmares of a little girl. They have a sort of dark realism and fantasy elements without going too overboard. This is a plus for me because I like grotesque creatures, but this could be a negative for other people.+Twin-stick controls work really well for this game and are tight and responsive, aside from the dash which I'll mention in the cons.+The game is Difficult, but the upgrade system allows you to give yourself additional protection / beat levels sooner.+Dying actually unlocks things so you're basically encouraged to die and aren't really penalized for it outside of your score resetting.+A lot of levels for a relatively cheap price. The game also gives you extra things to do without overstaying its welcome. Very respectful of the player's time.Cons-The game is occasionally too difficult. Some of the additional challenges will really push you.-Since you have to shoot enemies that come from all sides, the first playthrough of most stages means you will be blindsided by something you could not have seen coming. It's just in the game's nature. It's going to happen. -The base dash is pretty bad. It does give you some i-frames (keyword being SOME) but it feels too janky in that it locks you in recovery frames and doesn't really move you in a natural way. The fact that certain badges add utility to this that involve NOT actually moving is very telling.~Minor nitpick for me, but the game's English translation is not as strong as it could be. There are a lot of diary entries that are written from a little girl's perspective, and they certainly read that way, but some things aren't explained very well and will confuse non-Japanese players.Overall, I think NeverAwake is a solid entry in the genre, an impressive effort for this indie team, and definitely worth picking up! 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review:
A girl who never wakes up. She has been fighting monsters in her dreams...

"NeverAwake" is a nightmarish twin-stick shooter with a unique worldview and original game rules. The girl fights against vegetables, dogs, school friends, and other things she hates. What does the girl see at the end of the battle? And will she be able to wake up?

With over 80 levels, dozens of bosses, and a unique gameplay system that allows players to retry many levels, NeverAwake is suitable for both beginner shooters and experts.

name: The Entropy Centre
detailed_description: ❤️‍🔥Level Editor is HERE❤️‍🔥 Deconstruct time itself with the free level editor update! Design, build and challenge custom levels created by the community with the full toolset used to create The Entropy Centre. About the Game The Entropy Centre is a mind-bending puzzle adventure where you reverse objects through time to overcome seemingly impossible obstacles and conundrums. Manipulate time to your will and solve ingeniously challenging puzzle rooms, each one taking you closer to the heart of a colossal space station in orbit of Earth. An extinction level event has set the world ablaze. You appear to be the last remaining person alive. Mankind’s only hope lies at the core of the Entropy Centre. Meet ASTRA, The Entropy Centre’s most advanced technical marvel. ASTRA is an AI-powered device that can scan an object’s spacetime chronology and move it through the past. Powers include rebuilding collapsing pillars to reheating cups of tea. She’s pretty chill. The truth behind The Entropy Centre’s imminent collapse, and the Earth’s demise, can be found at the heart of this sprawling dangerous facility. But will you accept the unfortunate truth that awaits? Deviously challenging with razor-sharp witty writing and outstanding voice acting performances, The Entropy Centre merges a brilliant puzzle game with an epic adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you enjoy games like Portal 1&2, Antichamber, The Witness, Superliminal, etc. I would recommend you to pick it up (on sale or not is up to you) and give it a play through. Play the demo to get an idea of some of the intro/beginner puzzles.Puzzles: Great, can sometimes be broken by the player (intentional?) and limited by the time you are able to reverse objects. if it is possible, I would want the max to be about 60 sec so that most of my issues with the puzzles would be solved as it would give more player freedom. 30-40 sec (is it ~38.1?) seems a bit short with some of the more complicated puzzles.Story: The Terminal Messages are the main way of conveying context and story to the player. Most conversations that are done between the voiced player character and the companion AI is small talk, jokes, etc. with the main plot line being discussed as things progress. The ending makes sense, gives closure and hope, but it felt underwhelming to me after all the buildup. ENDING SPOILER:; .Game: Some reviews have said "It is Portal but with time." There are some aesthetic similarities (, ), but I would say that similarities end there in my opinion. It is a game that doesn't need the 'Portal" crutch to be enjoyable.Weapon of choice is used really well in most environmental and puzzle based platforming as well as in defense. I enjoyed my time with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Strong recommendation - time-based puzzles in a sci-fi setting with some Portal-like humour, but its the overall vibe and aesthetic that really work for me here. As far as puzzle games go, this one is very accessible and fun, while never truly straining your brain. You have a gun that rewinds time, you position cubes on pressure plates, and as you progress you get different types of cubes to solve different types of puzzles. Once I came to grips with the time rewind mechanic I found I moved through the puzzles quite swiftly (around 5 minutes each puzzle), with the longest duration puzzles being those with big arenas, lots of steps, and precise manipulation of the time rewind (longest puzzle was about 18 minutes). I really vibed with the story and the characters - I'm a sucker for a sci-fi setting with a world ending cataclysm, and a good use of time loops, and The Entropy Centre does a fantastic job with all three. I really enjoyed the visual aesthetic, and the constant reminders of the big cataclysm you are trying to prevent. The ending may not work for everyone but it think it was bold of them to end the story the way they did.The only problem with puzzle games is once you have solved the puzzle there is no real replayability outside of finding all the journal entries. You have to wait years to dump the solutions from your memory but, just like Portal 2, I'll definitely be keen to try this one again in a couple of years time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The Entropy Centre is a really enjoyable first person puzzle game similar to Portal. There are a lot of similar mechanics such as jump pads, light bridge, pressure plates, etc. The main difference is instead of your gun creating portals and you have to use your momentum, your gun will rewind time for objects so they can move across a room without you necessarily carrying them. The story was interesting and the gun talks to you in a much more wholesome way than GlaDOS would talk to you. The one thing I would recommend to the devs for future games is to give people a sort of "hard mode" option. The game itself is relatively easy. The tricky things have massive hints by having squares painted on the floor so you already know where to place certain cubes. That's fine and all but it would be cool if there was a "hard mode" where these painted squares are disabled so you don't have any hints in solving the puzzles.Regardless of that, the puzzles are still fun to solve. I enjoyed solving them all. This is a solid game if you're interested in first person puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start this off by saying I really don't want this to effect the dev so heavily since he is indeed the sole developer, and I understand how much work this must've taken. However, I must look at it as a game from my perspective of how a game should be. First off, I'm not sure if it was marketed as "similar to Portal" or if that was only that one critic's review. I hope it wasn't marketed as such, because it clearly took almost no inspiration from Valvian games at all, besides the most basic cube and button mechanics. The game suffers from the same problem Portal did during initial playtesting; people wondered where the game was because it was just puzzles, so they had to add some main objective and maybe a character to focus on. This does have an objective, but its worth is so poorly emphasized with the expectation of having to rush to fix something when you have 70+ mind-numbingly tedious puzzles to get through and in reality the objective seems so non-chalant in actual seriousness (until it's more clear in the end), considering the way the technology they have works. In addition, if still comparing it to Valvian games, there is little to no interactivity with anything besides the puzzle objects and there are unnecessary invisible barriers in areas where the player exploring would not cause an issue (e.g: bathroom stalls [yes, I know, bad example]). What can be interacted with by the Entropy Device (referred to henceforth as "ASTRA") is so few and far between they felt the need to give a highlight, which removes any possibility of mystery and absolutely shows you exactly how little you can affect the game world from the start. In reality, this is great for unassuming players, but for immersion, this does not help () If you're hoping for Valve-quality, well look again at the fact that there is  developer. I do believe many things could've been improved with just a little more time spent, as you'll read... There are several other things, but I have no room to type it. Basically, please playtest your game.Others have already mentioned the unnecessary precision needed, the "combat" sections being abysmal, the irritating backtracking of it all, and the entropy recording time being too short. The story is okay, the ending is decent. The writing is definitely cringey sometimes and I see no reason to become attached to the characters, but it's fine. The music is okay. The seemingly endless puzzles after liminal halls becomes trivial quickly.I'd find a lot more fun in this concept if the Entropy Device was just released as a GMod addon.3/10 -Asteroid
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like puzzle games like Portal, Q.U.B.E. and Quantum Conundrum? Then The Entropy Centre is right up your alley.It's pretty obvious from the get-go that TEC takes major inspiration from the Portal games, with the sterile-looking puzzle rooms, large buttons, boxes, jump pads and more. What sets it apart from Portal is of course the core gameplay mechanic, which in TEC is a time-reversal-gun. Every movable object can be rewound back in time, which will feel immediately familiar if you've played games like Braid, or Singularity. And it works quite well.The basic premise of the game is that The Entropy Centre is a facility on the moon that can reverse Earth back in time when catastrophic events happen, and it's gone well so far. However, you wake up all alone and for some reason the centre is falling apart and the Earth is exploding. It's up to you to solve puzzles in order to charge up the Entropy cannon and reverse Earth back and save everyone, but things are not as straight forward as they may first seem. The story sets the stakes pretty early on, so you feel this constant tension all the way throughout the game and you feel like you need to hurry before it's too late. The game is roughly 9-10 hours long, but of course it depends on how good you are at puzzles. Getting stuck on particularly tricky puzzles can increase that time significantly, but just like with Portal, as soon as you find the solution and you take all the necessary steps and reach the exit, you feel like you're the smartest person alive! For... like... 5 seconds, until you hit the next chamber and you're stuck all over again. Personally I only had to consult a guide once, in a level in chapter 10, everything else seemed intuitive enough.In terms of bugs and glitches, I did not experience any during my playthrough, and the performance was excellent.So, if you like puzzle games, this one is a definite recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: NO SPOILERS :: Fantastic game! Definitely recommending The Entropy Centre for anyone who enjoyed Portal. Fun to play; whether it's navigating the facility, solving puzzles, or dodging the security bots. This game is GORGEOUS; I spent plenty of time exploring, and just admiring how lovely everything looks. Anyone who ENJOYS existentialism will absolutely love The Entropy Centre!
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe this game is as a Portal imitator. It has a similar world feel and game play structure. The sense of humor is not as dark, and more whimsical. That should not be construed as a pejorative description. We need more games attempting to replicate the winning formula of Portal. This game has unique puzzle mechanics that are clever. The puzzles are polished and fun. The difficulty ramps up slowly, and is never frustrating. Voice acting is high quality, and the writing finds an entertaining approach to  keep the puzzle mechanics lively.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals and some mechanics were "borrowed" from valve games, but the dialogues and the main time-manipulation thing is rather unique. Feels like a mod. BUT honestly i'm more amazed by the lack of delay on the mouse input and the fov slider. Good stuff. i recommend getting it on a heavy discount. A portal mod is not worth 25 bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I would usually try to finish a game before I share any final judgements, I think you can find gold even in the muddiest of rivers and the little nuggets you find can be worth getting through some objectively bad experiences. However, after getting nearly halfway through Entropy Center, I can't shake the feeling that the river has dried up and already revealed what little value it has. It's not a bad game per se, in fact it's way worse than that, it's simply a mediocre game with potential.Starting from the things I liked, the visuals are undeniably gorgeous. The "old laboratory/testing area overrun with plants" has got to be one of my favorite genres of puzzle game locations and this game sells it really well. The environments are rich in detail, the animations of all of the crumbling structures are stellar, the particle effects are really aesthetically pleasing and the lighting is just bright enough to highlight these strengths without making things look too "modern", as some of these games tend to do. Some of the places look straight up cinematic too.Credit where it's due, I think that the voice actors did a pretty good job and the sound design is generally alright. These are things that you don't really notice that much unless they're done poorly or exceptionally well. I would say they did a good enough job to comfortably fit between those two extremes.Lastly, I think the general idea behind the main mechanic is pretty good and could be used to make some good puzzles. The way your puzzle gun allows you to interact with the environment makes for a fun first impression for sure.Which leads me to the things I didn't like and that is the gameplay. If you're new to puzzle games it may not be as much of an issue but as a fan of puzzle games, throughout those 6 acts there was maybe 1 or 2 puzzles where I had to stop and think for a moment before seeing the solution. Normally I would say that it's fine because not every game has to have really high difficulty. The problem here is that none of these puzzles have any sort of meaningful complexity to them. At least half of these chambers had the exact same solution, look at the places you want the cube to go through, place it in those places in reverse order, reverse the cube. Sometimes you have to do it with 2 cubes, sometimes the object is not a cube. In all of those cases the methodology doesnt change a bit. It felt like I'm just going through the motions, to the point that i was trying to think of some more interesting solutions, only to find that I just didnt notice the second object in the room being there. It felt like I was still in the tutorial but I was being taught the same things over and over again, as if the developers ran out of ideas for what to do with the elements they introduced so far, resorting to adding more mechanics to compensate for it. You could argue that it's to ease in new players into the game but I honestly think Portal was able to do just that without any bloat, the puzzles didn't have to be difficult, just complex enough to force you to think about the correct solution after you try the most obvious one (which in the case of Entropy Center is usually one and the same). For a game that likes to stop you in your tracks and scatters a whole lot of exposition to find in the form of emails/logs, the writing is not great either. The voiced protagonist is a one dimensional punching bag full of "huh? whats going on? why am i here? why cant i remember anything? who are you?" and the quirky robot gun doing the punching isn't as witty as it wants you to think. It feels like it's supposed to make you laugh but to me it came off as simply unlikeable and annoying at times. There were also scripted events that could've been solved by simply using the gun which made them feel really forced. The concept behind the plot is nice but I think it reveals it's hand way too quickly and looking ahead, I was able to figure out pretty much every twist around Act 3.The escape sequences felt pretty trivial since I couldn't really see any time pressure and avoiding the obstacles is simply "look at the crumbling thing and shoot it". I also only just got to the introduction of fights against robots and that was when I decided to stop playing, the game didn't hook me before and I don't think making it less focused would improve that.Overall, I think the game deserves a mediocre 5/10 for it's visuals alone. Unless you're new to puzzle games and want a pretty looking long experience than what some of the older classics can offer, I just can't recommend it in good faith.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Played through it, had a good time. Portal vibes from the game in it's gameplay and presentation but that's a compliment. It's seems fairly short (i took my time reading logs and stuff) but it was quality time. To be fair if it had been longer it would have overstated it's welcome.It's great go for it if you remotely enjoy portal like games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: It has some slow moments, and there were times when I felt something was missing or some cheap plot points thrown in with no explanation, but overall, I thought it was a great story in the end and quite enjoyed most of the puzzles. It was fun and I grew to love the characters. If you are into puzzle games, not a bad buy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: They try to be a lot like Portal, but fail completely. Enviroments don't have their own identity, they pretty much just copied the test chamber design from Portal 2, except they literally call them "Puzzles" (It's like when they actually call zombies "zombies" in a zombie movie/game). The writing is super cringe. They do extremely worn out AI tropes, like the robot not understanding irony, and they do it in the most unimaginative way. The AI also sometimes does random insults to the player, because that's what Glados did right? Puzzle design is okay at best. Sometimes the puzzle mechanics feel really janky and they reuse puzzle ideas way too many times, just ever so slightly increasing complexity with each chamber. It's not really a bad game, especially for this price, but I can't recommend it. There are plenty of Portal 2 mods with way better puzzle design.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so, I spent 1.5 hrs trying to make ONE jump (I thought this was a puzzle game, not an infuriatingly small margin of error parkour platformer), the controls on xbox controller only work sometimes (???), mouse occasionally just breaks and wont work, jumping is slightly too low to where its just infuriating enough... seriously please make it just slightly bouncier (especially as this takes place on the moon)The office loop was spooky though and I did generally enjoy the story and ending.  Its just so fiddly that I ultimately can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Great Game- although it has copied off portal 1 and 2. some parts even made me sad. like how PEA (Astra) sacrificed herself to save the player from the reactor in act 12, yes shes annoying, but that doesn't mean shes not worth it. some parts are funny like when Astra suggest that the Entropy worker bots wanted to give you hugs in act 9. some parts are about braveness like how ''E'' withdraws the stun bots in act 15. this game isn't okay- its just that, it makes you have feelings and it helps you.So maybe the game is worth itcjw.cameron.white :)Oh and one more thing.Subscribe me to entropy cat facts lol
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Stunning visuals with easy to grasp mechanics. Yes it obviously has heavy portal inspiration but the only things that feels like portal are the pressure plates and cubes this game sets out to be its own and does a fantastic job at doing so. They pulled out all the stops and got super creative with the puzzle elements and always keep your on your toes by changing the way you need to think. If you're anything like me your going to constantly think you're ahead of the game and then feel like an idiot when you realize you didn't anticipate the next piece of the puzzle. Then you're going to overthink the hell out of the most simple things. Needless to say this game made my brain hurt so much in the best way. The story is very interesting and easily digestible in the form of employee E-mails that you as the player snoop through to gain context clues towards varying parts of the story. The dialogue shared in nearly every E-mail is written in such a way that it always kept me thinking about the over arching plot and what these various clues could mean. The game almost makes you feel like Sherlock Holmes in this sense because you piece these clues together and figure out probably commonly asked questions like "why am i the last one here", "why cant i remember anything" or "why is everything trying to kill me" are all answered this way. Also the gun was very funny both voice actresses did a wonderful job of playing these two characters and have some lines that will probably live in my head for the next few months.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Fun story driven puzzle game with some unique elements that kept me engaged. Several of the puzzles were fairly difficult, and a few of those I had to look up but was not particularly wowed with the cleverness of the solution. I think the game was maybe 10% too long but I enjoyed it and would recommend it to anyone that enjoyed portal.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent to good puzzle game. I had high hopes and this didn't get there, but it was still fun enough.The good: - some interesting puzzles with clever setups - decent amount of variety in puzzle mechanics with different cubes - pretty cool sci-fi story behind itThe bad: - repeatedly setting up some puzzle solutions all over again due to one part not working right - jump boxes. Probably 90% of my rework was from these - takes a while to get to the more interesting puzzles, felt like a long tutorial - some repetition in the puzzles - the story could use more detail and the ending felt drawn out to get to the final conclusion - rewinding time can be super slow and annoying if you go too far - battling the robots gets old fastOverall, it would've been a solidly good game with some more work. Jump boxes should be improved with larger hitzones, would be nice if you could scrub the timeline with a scrollwheel instead of just rewinding slowly, and shorten the ending by at least half.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I suck at puzzle games, and I’m also kind of dumb (those things may be related). Thus, I typically don’t mix well with pure puzzlers like Entropy Centre. So, when I say this is an easy recommendation, it means a lot coming from me. The room-to-room puzzles are excellent, and make up about 80% of the game. The other 20% is unfortunately very weak in comparison. This includes things like story elements, dialogue, and “walking simulator” type scenes. Still, it’s easy to look past that stuff and enjoy the main puzzle solving aspect.Most reviews here compare this to Valve’s Portal, and I think its justified. I found most of the puzzles in this game to be logically sound, which is more than I can say about 90% of other puzzlers. The solutions are cleverly laid out, and they all have a starting point (“work backwards”), so even the hardest puzzles guide you in a general direction.If the entire game was only puzzle rooms, I might give it a 10/10. Unfortunately, there’s a lot of “other” stuff. Long, drawn out story related levels that don’t really flow with the rest of the game. There are also “combat” levels where your only way to attack is to “parry” enemies. It adds variety, but it’s not good. All the “non-puzzle” stuff was too slow and tedious in my view.Still, it’s easy to look past that stuff because the overall package is very polished. The graphics and sound are good, but not necessary, so you can play at low settings.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and challenging game. Only needed to look up a solution twice, once was because the intended solution seems to have been borked by a later patch (1404 if I'm not mistaken). The game very obviously tries to emulate Portal 2 with its setting and humour, and it works. The main mechanic is very unique and fleshed out completely, this fits in the hall of fame of puzzlers alongside Portal, Talos Principle, Superliminal.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: It's a shame I can't leave a 2.5-star review, because I'm really on the fence about this. The game starts out like a fun homage to Portal, but some of the changes really make the experience feel more like a slog. In particular, the narrative tension in the story is a mess, and you constantly feel like there's something more important you should be doing than solving puzzles. The plot is very high tension early on, but once you realize it waits for you to perform actions before doing any scripted events, it kind of reduces the threat level to zero while still expecting you to be invested and maintain that same level of tension for literal hours. It really made me appreciate the fact that Portal's main motivation was the puzzles and not some external threat that would theoretically ruin everything if you don't do puzzles fast enough.The entropy gun mechanic is cool, but not as versatile as the portal gun. It felt like 80% of the early puzzles were just "Do the obvious steps in reverse order so that the time reversal gun can lead you through the level properly." It didn't feel like there were any clever solutions coming in until half a dozen new mechanics were added to support the main gameplay element. That being said, once they *do* actually introduce enough mechanics to support it, the puzzles can get some very clever solutions going on (even if I'm pretty sure I accidentally cheesed a few). Too bad each object has an arbitrary time limit attached to it which will screw you over at the very end of a level if you moved an object too much while preparing to solve the puzzle. When that happens, you have to start that entire object's time path over (and probably every other object too since you were probably rewinding them the whole time as well)EDIT: Now that I've finished the game, I feel that I should add one final complaint that the ending explained basically nothing. There was no satisfying conclusion to any of the questions raised in gameplay. Maybe the answers were buried in the random email logs floating around the world, but considering 95% of those were useless and the other 5% were basically impossible to miss and gave very little info anyway, I stopped bothering to seek them out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: ok I am not yet done with the game but I think I am around half way through and I have to recommend it as it is such a cool gamePros:- really cool visuals- really cool action sequences- cute and funny robots- rewinding time- level editor - music builds the mood wonderfullyCons:- (so far) basic puzzles that don't require much thought (except for like 2 of them)- some might not find the story engaging (but I do)- you don't have this gameIf you enjoyed portal and are ok with some easier puzzles then I cannot recommend this enough as it is super under rated right now understandable if you want to get this when its on sale but it is worth playing
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent enough puzzle game, but suffers from a critical flaw, which is that the puzzle rewind mechanic requires you to solve the puzzle before you can solve the puzzle. What this means is that you spend a couple of minutes figuring out the room, then much longer executing the solution. This isn’t helped by slow movement and an infuriatingly tiny jump. Later on if you misjudge a jump, well then it’s back to another three minutes of retracing your steps.The puzzles start out too easy, but later on devolve into a slog, but without the satisfaction of a good brain burn. There are a few good puzzles along the way -- I was especially fond of the river puzzles -- but it never comes together in a really satisfying way. The final puzzle felt no different than a hundred that came before it.There are some unfortunate combat sections which would have been better left out of the game. Same for all the sections requiring platforming skills or quick reflexes.The characters grew on me over the course of the game. It’s no Portal, but the writing is solid and the story intriguing. It’s let down though by the ending. It feels as thought the game either needs the ability to opt out of that ending, or for the protagonist to be a little more introspective before going into it. As it is, you know what’s coming, they know what’s coming, and yet you can’t avoid it and they dive into it with nary a thought despite the many, many hints that they might want to think it over first. It's an ending at distinct odds with the tone of the characters, which is why it needs the writing to engage with it more before rolling credits. You're left waiting for the twist that never comes.If you’re stuck for a decent puzzle game and have played through things like Portal and Talos Principle, then maybe this is worth it, but I was very ready for it to be over by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Mostly I agree with the other reviews - This game is not your average Portal clone, the story is unique and engaging, the characters are really engaging, the environments are fantastic.The puzzles are the only place where the game is slightly let down, as they can feel a little tedious, and if you're a puzzle addict, then they probably won't feel very difficult, but personally they were good enough, I did feel like I was dragging myself through them to get to the next story segment though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Draws a lot of inspiration from games like Portal or The Turing Test but stands on its own as an engaging puzzle game. While you can argue that the difficulty of the puzzles is a little all over the place, the game definitely leans on the easier side when comparing to some of the other puzzle games I've played such as Talos Principle, Portal, AntiChamber, etc. At the time of this review, the game is lacking a few minor quality of life improvements I'm sure the dev will add at some point like reloading checkpoints, a more intuitive way to track which levels you missed computer terminals, etc but those are minor things that don't take away from the core experience. Overall, the main characters Aria and Astra are likable and the game delivers a well rounded experience for the price. P.S. The fact this game was made by a single developer is absolutely insane. This man deserves your money for what he has delivered.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Great effort from a one person team - I am findings the puzzles at the right level - not bind bending hard but enough to give me enough to take a break and come back to it rather than hitting a wall. The story is also interesting despite borrowing a fair amount from its avowed inspirations but who cares? It's a great addition the the genre taking it to another level with a twist.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The game is nearly perfect. With some very simple puzzle mechanics, the developers have created interesting and unique challenges that never failed to keep me intrigued.  Other major plusses: the voice acting is top-notch, and the story line remained engaging and interesting. Personally, I would have liked to see a bit more clues about life on the station and Aria's role a little more (namely, why the bots turned on her in the first place), but that's a very minor nit and certainly doesn't detract from the game at all. Highly recommend for people who are puzzle fanatics (and fond of games like Portal).
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Short answer: No doubt a spiritual successor to Portal, but very much able to stand on its own merits. An incredible experience and a must-play for people looking for a challenging and charming puzzle-adventure game.Gameplay 10/10 - incredibly unique reverse-puzzle-solving mechanics. Incredible and tense setpieces between each chapters' 4-5 main story puzzle chambers (a total of over 100 puzzle chambers, excluding setpieces), most of which are relatively easy to solve but do require some thought and logic put into it. Several chambers are easy to cheese with jump pads, if you're truly determined. Moving between sections of the Centre also provide extra mini-puzzles and sequences. Incredibly well-paced, but you're in for the long haul.Story 7/10 - Earth is dead. The Entropy Centre is vacant. Where is everyone? Why are you still here? Aria, accompanied by her  I mean, Handheld Entropy Device with built-in Puzzle Exercise Assistant, Astra, must make your way through the entire Entropy Centre to figure out why the building is falling apart, and figure out a way to save the Centre and, by extension, Earth. The dialogue is funny and charming; Astra plays the "I am an AI and I am your friend" trope extremely well. The ending wasn't quite as satisfying as I'd have hoped, but everything else is phenomenal.Opinion on the ending, spoilers (obviously):Buy now, play it, love it, and please support these developers. I had an incredible time with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Way better than expected, a real quality piece of work. I worry that some people might give up on the game too soon, since it gets better around the halfway mark.Puzzles start off easy but get suitably more difficult over time. The game also has a lot more puzzles, and variety than I expected. Graphics wise, it is clearly a big budget production. I kept asking myself where they got the money to make all this for a puzzle game.The narrative is ultimately what won me over. It's a bold direction, to really commit to the message despite its alarming implications. I'm glad they did, cause it was pretty compelling, even though I guessed what the ending would be beforehand. That did not detract from the gut punch it landed though.Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Speaking as a Portal fan, it is pretty much undeniable that this game took inspiration from it, some sections are way too similar you just can’t tell otherwise. However, as the story progresses I can say I enjoy it a lot. I think I am half way through the game, some puzzles did make me think for a while, but not unforgivably difficult so far, I feel satisfied whenever I solved a hard one without a guide.I also like how the game’s main gimmick (rewinding time) could be used as the link between the plot (saving the world) and gameplay (puzzle solving). Actually this is something even Portal didn’t do, Portal gun and its principles were never given a purpose outside of the testing area, so in my opinion that makes the plot more creative and interesting as a result.Would recommend it to my friends, that’s for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The main character of Entropy Centre might be the only human left in our solar system and she is stuck on a tropical beach research facility on the moon that tries to save the Earth from self destruction and her only companion is a talking A.I. attached to her gun that can rewind objects for a limited amount of time. So yeah the setting and story is very intriguing, I like the rewind mechanic, the banter between the main character and the A.I. is good, and there is a big sci-fi twist in the middle of the game. The puzzles though are hit and miss in terms of good quality design and fair difficulty. But you should enjoy this game if you like first person puzzle games and science fiction stories.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, at first I wanted to critique the game on it's inconsistent level difficulty (ranging from way too easy (even in the last few levels) to pleasant head scratcher), the inclusion of out of place and unnecessary combat sections, and a lack of a satisfying ending. But then I saw that this nice 8+ hour, well polished (very good performance), well voice acted, custom level editor/hoster having, beautiful, and generally overall good single player game was developed by one person! My jaw hit the floor, big ups to you Daniel Stubbington! You have done more/better work as a single dev than I've seen out of many double or even triple digit dev teams. Bravo mate! Can't wait to see what you do next!
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The Entropy centre is the time-based counterpart puzzle game counterpart to Portal 2. By that, I do not mean to diminish either game: despite plenty of similarities between them, the mechanics of each are separate enough that they both stands very well on their own merits.The time elements are well used, the atmosphere is crisp, there is plenty to discover going on behind the scenes, and the storyline is interesting, if a little bit slow. (And by that I mostly mean that it takes  to get moving, which is funny enough if you think about it)But from then on I will be making heavy comparison comments about game elements between both Portal 2 and the Entropy Centre. A small disclaimer, before we enter the meat: it is hard for a 3D puzzle FPS not to be compared to what remains so far Valve's biggest surprise hit series (Portal started up as a lil' add-on to the Orange Box, remember?). It's even harder for this game considering the number of game mechanics that seems ripped off almost wholesale from its inspiration.To wit: you play as a female protagonist, waking up in a deserted facility, whose only companions are automated messages and AIs talking to you. You go through puzzle rooms, mostly because there's no other way to get answers and go where you need, using cube-and-button based switches to open the doors stopping you. As you go on, you discover more 'test elements' that increase the difficulty of the tests you have to traverse.This summary can apply to both games, and would not be too inaccurate in either case. Comparison also applies to these tests elements:- A modified gun that doesn't shoot bullets, but is able to grab cubes to move them- Cubes and switches controlling doors- Plates that makes you jump in a predefined parabola- Lasers to activate special switches- Ethereal bridges that can be redirected- Moving platforms and conveyor belts- Ways to traverse space independantly of gravity- Non-solid fields that the player can traverse but which will incinerate cubes passing through- Moon rocks helping space-time manipulation- And cutesy robots trying to kill you.But for all of these, the fact you can move most of these items  on top of by yourself, creates a wonderful experience. In fact, I'm even willing to say that these puzzle elements are tickling much of the same part of the brain as Portal 2 itself. And there's more to them, as well, including some you wouldn't be able to find  the time element!Storywise, Aria is not a 'silent' protagonist, mostly because she actually has someone to discuss with. And GLaDOS hardly cared for Chell the way Astra cares for Aria. To extend the comparison to story beats, the movements for both games are also surprisingly similar (Figure out what's going on along basic puzzles -> Goal 1 set by an IA -> Achieve goal 1 after tribulations -> Fall to the depths of the Centre -> Discover another facet of the facility you tested in so far, mostly on your own -> Reunite with IA companion -> Climb back up to Goal 2), but the ending is either... too straightforward or lacking in special sauce, if that makes sense.What I can say, however, is that the process in both games is also paced very differently, and I am not doing the Entropy Centre any favor by trying to match it point for point to its predecessor. I love very much this game for what it's doing. I still think the pacing could use some work, though. I understand it's hard to give a feeling of  for a  game, but the overall balance felt a bit too much on the 'shoddy' side?All in all, I'm still very much willing to recommend this game to everyone who wants to play "a different kind of Portal 2". The Entropy Centre will definitely sate that itch and more. And to close with a final mention, I would absolutely love to see test chambers combining both games - maybe with one player modifying space while the other controls time?
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game.Overall I found the puzzles fairly easy, which may be a good or bad thing for you.Even for the latest puzzles, the solution was often almost obvious and needed just a little tweaking to get it working. But at the same time I was never so blocked that I needed to give up or check a solution.I felt the difficulty stayed overall fairly constant, even when new puzzle elements were introduced.It took between 10 to 20 minutes for each of the latter puzzle so the sens of progression was always there.Beside the basic puzzles, some area are interlaced with "combat puzzle" that gets the blood pumping (a little) and there is a whole latter section, that is just ... different, in a good way.What I didn't liked the most is the environment art. You spend the whole game in what is the same environment with what *feelt like* the same 50 assets and 10 textures over and over and over again.Finally, be advised that there isn't a single cat to pet in this video game depite the lore making you thing so.You can pet the single non-murdery robot, but that's not the same feeling.Have a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Story is almost non-existent: soon after the start you find a smiling/talkative gun, which encourages you to complete more puzzles because... it's for the greater good! Off you go!Puzzles aren't challenging. The trick is.. you must solve them in reverse: holding an object automatically starts in-game recording of the object's movement path. Trigger the gun to rewind the path and pause when need to.Every 3-5 rooms the story takes a sharp turn - you rush up and forward mindlessly spamming the rewind ability to move falling walls, containers and stairs. However, it feels very imposed and doesn't suit the story. Just unnecessary drama.:I heavily loved the look of abandoned test chambers: neat surroundings and warm colours work really well with aged flora and space peeking windows. Some areas contain hidden monitors with emails sharing background lore (extra puzzle solving required!), but the progression is linear - no sideways!p.s. can I get a cookie for not saying that Entropy looks/plays like a Portal game? Oh no, did I just...
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzle games ESPECIALLY the Portal Series.People may keep comparing this game to Portal and I can totally agree as to why but it is still a unique game nonetheless with its own tropes etc. The commentary in this game (in my own personal opinion) was acceptable but i can see why some may find it a bit on the cringe side but honestly still gives character throughout the whole game.The graphics in this game was perfectly fine and ran smoothly apart from the occasional drop for only a split second due to certain scenes with a lot of debris and dust.... but almost any PC* will possibly end up doing that anyway (*every device is different, can't say how your own PC will run with it but i would argue that this is somewhat a easily accessible game to play) and is usually near the end of the game so "one off" situation i guess. The art design too reminds me of a mixture of both Portal and Portal 2 and arguably the original Mirror's Edge (only a bit) but still stands out as unique game in other elements as well.Overall for people who are more into ratings, here is my personal opinions down below but regardless of any of that, I would recommend getting this for anyone anyway :).Game play: 9.5/10Graphics: 8/10Art style: 9/10Music: 7/10Audio/Sound effects: 9/10Story: 7.5/10Acting: 6/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The Entropy Centre does a good job of scratching that Portal itch that you get every now and then. It sets out with an interesting core mechanic and iterates on it well, and importantly doesn't overstay its welcome, leading to a (slightly less than satisfying) conclusion in under 10 hours. If I had to complain about anything, its that the puzzle design doesn't really evolve that much. There are new elements added, for sure, but the puzzles themselves don't really evolve beyond the core concept of "get the box to the last place it needs to be, then move it to the first place, rewind as needed."
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game but it felt like they worried much more about visuals and not too much on puzzle mechanics and design, kinda feels a tiny bit repetitive at times, once you get the jist of what you're supposed to be doing it doesnt change things up too much or challenge you any more than just by putting more obstacles in your way. Was still overall engaging and a very fascinating and gripping story though, really great sense of atmosphere.Edited: After the level Editor update, I thoroughly enjoy the design aspects and capabilities and cant wait to see what new things emerge from future updates and bug fixes. It is the kind of level editor that I wish we had for Portal 2, its quite fun to design and make levels that look utterly gorgeous.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Portal, but the puzzles are tedious instead of fun.  Instead of looking forward to what concept each next puzzle would introduce, I really just got tired of seeing yet another set of boxes and switches where I had to determine the order in reverse.  The other aspects of the game are solid, but the puzzle design is lacking in creativity while increasing in complexity.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: If Portal is a 10 then this game is a good 8. _childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: A great portal-like with some genuinely unique ideas. The story was serviceable, though I feel like the premise left a lot to be desired. I certainly didn't end the game as emotionally invested as something like Portal 2, thought that's a high bar of comparison. The soundtrack was great, very atmospheric, though somewhat repetitive during the non-story sections. Visually, gorgeous, this game has a great art direction. The puzzle design is really good, almost every puzzle left me having to stop and think before execution- as much as I love rushing through games, when I'm forced to stop and think, I know the puzzle is well designed. (There are a handful that can be broken through manipulation of double bounce-pads, though that's just as fun.)Overall, as I said, a great portal-like. Worth your time, the story could've been more compelling but the puzzle design is very well done. I rcommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Very good. Mostly Portal 2 and Talos Principle level of difficulty (for me) but not as hard as the gray sigils or star levels of Talos except for maybe 3 or 4 levels that took me nearly 30 minutes to figure out, for whatever that is worth. But none that forced me to ultimately give up. I liked the varying puzzle elements. The story was pretty interesting. If you like Portal/Talos then I would definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game, a worthy spiritual successor of the Portal franchise. while there are ups and downs to all of it - the robot fights were a bit grating to some of the flow - it overall delivers a mysterious story, interesting ending, and a fascinating look at science fiction. my only actual wish for this game is an update that sees a codex of sorts added to the main menu for players to look at the messages they've discovered without returning to the location in-game. would make piecing together the lore easier.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: We don't get many Portal-like games these days, so when this game was announced, I was eager to check it out.  Unfortunately, there are too many drawbacks that hold it back from greatness. The first half of the game is really good.  It does a good job of teaching you new mechanics and easing you into the complexity of rewinding objects in time.  However, after completing the first half of the game, there's a significant difficulty spike, and puzzles become needlessly complex. The levels get bigger and longer, and if you make any mistakes, you'll have to retread many steps, or even start the entire puzzle over again.  You can also be attacked by robots while solving puzzles, and it's easy to get surrounded and die in a few hits.  A combat mechanic is introduced, but it feels out of place, and only makes the puzzles even more frustrating.  The biggest frustration of all though, is the performance.  When transitioning to each area, the game stutters, and the frame rate tanks during several action scenes and puzzle sequences.  It is all immersion breaking, and I'm surprised it hasn't been fixed since its release in November 2022. There's plenty of good things about this game that I hope to see expanded on in future games.  But with all my frustrations, I can't recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Some puzzles are bit too easy, especially if you've played similar games in the past, but apart from that the game is excellent. Interesting mechanics, a story that keeps you hooked and well designed environments.BUT, BUYER BEWARE. It ends in a bit of a semi-cliffhanger. The dev said on Reddit that a DLC is being planned and that was around 10 months ago.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Simply excellent.I have just finished my first playthrough and I knew maybe 30 minutes in I wanted to take the time to give this a glowing review, and after finishing it in ten hours play time (which includes probably 3-5 of leaving the game open whilst AFK) I still feel exactly the same.Puzzles great. Story/concept great. Graphics/art great. Voice acting great.I haven't read other reviews, but I am close to certain many of them mention Portal. That doesn't necessarily mean this, or any other game like it, "copies" Portal, but Portal is the absolute seminal game of first-person puzzlers that comparisons are inevitable. With that said, The Entropy Centre *does* involve being stranded in a breaking down science facility, with little clarity on who you are, why you're there, being guided by a personality-driven AI, doing puzzles in individual test chambers, being attacked by rogue robots in the aforementioned science facility, using a custom acronym-named gun device to utilise the game's unique puzzle mechanics, and a whole bunch of placing cubes on buttons, navigating light bridges, directing lasers, and transferring your momentum. Despite this, The Entropy Centre does a great job of being its own game. Sure the initial set up is pretty on the nose, but the story and reasons for the player character being there are fully fleshed out and realised and no way Portal-y by the end. And other than the putting of boxes on buttons (and directing lasers and light bridges), the puzzles themselves are entirely unique and not in any way related to portals. The difficulty of the puzzles was also perfect, in my opinion. There were a couple I had to stop and scratch my head for a while, but none that I ever felt were just so obtuse I would have to give up and look for a solution online like I did once or twice towards the end of The Talos Principle (especially in the Gehenna DLC).This is overall like a 90-95% score for me. The only things I would say bring it down a bit are pacing, lack of variety and weak/frustrating "combat" sections - all of which are related. Non-stop puzzling can be tiring, and despite thoroughly enjoying my time, I still played the game over 6 or 7 sessions despite beating similar games in one sitting in the past (The Turing Test for example). I get the feeling this was already anticipated by the developer (yes, singular - making this game all the more impressive) as there was one really cool "Entropy Centre Museum" section where there's a little bit of fun and world-building on display, and also a couple of sections where you aren't solving puzzles but are doing some very light combat/avoidance of malintent robots. Whilst the breaking up of puzzles was necessary, the robot battles weren't enjoyable and I would have personally loved to see more fun/relaxed sections like the first beach area and the museum.But that's nitpicking. In an AMA, the dev says there is more coming (it sounds like DLC or content updates to the base game), so I really can't wait for those! The story ends on, not so much a cliffhanger, but in a place that leaves me still with questions. Hopefully some of those are answered, but even if they aren't, the world of The Entropy Centre was brilliant and I whole-heartedly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The Entropy Center is easily my new runner up for best puzzle game of all time. If you loved the Portal games you will love this game just as much, it is super fun to play, a good level of challenging, and the story is very engaging! So many small stories are told with them then fleshed out by the environment around them, its so fun!cat.cat.cat.cat.cat.Followup, I have now beaten the game, loved it. _childDocuments_.review: If you love Portal, you love The Entropy Centre.I have been waiting for so long, looking up to play this game. I am not disappointed.
