_childDocuments_.review: The fact that Lunatea's Veil has finally made it off the PS2 is enough to recommend Phantasy Reverie. Klonoa's now more available than ever; no matter my negatives, that's fantastic.Thing is, Door To Phantomile is my favourite game. Ever. Period. It's arguable PR would've never satisfied me but I want to bring up a number of issues not present in the original:- Klonoa's jump height is fixed. In classic, you could control this and manoeuvre him through obstacles, with level design clearly built around it. PR flings him to his maximum no matter what and makes for a MUCH more fiddly platforming experience.- The wind bullet (your attack) has a smaller hitbox. If you're standing on a slope, Klonoa will fire directly in front of him and shoot cleanly past any enemy above or below him, making for some really annoying sections where before it wasn't an issue.- The switch to 3D models over the original's sprites lends a significant amount of input delay. Klonoa's animations now have to be taken into account when moving and neuters the excellent pixel-perfect feel from classic DP. Granted it's not a major sticking point if you're new, but the later stages aren't nearly as fun because of it and weakens one of DP's strongest elements.- Klonoa lost his drop shadow for some reason. In a PLATFORMER.- While I won't knock PR's total makeover as it's both subjective and based on the 2008 Wii remake, the presentation isn't up to snuff. Music doesn't loop properly and is mixed quieter, facial expressions are jittery and somehow less consistent than the sprites. Dialogue is ripped directly from the original and the audio quality clashes hard. Classic DP's cutscenes (especially a certain one) are the emotional drive of the game, it's very disappointing seeing them in a lesser state. Needless to say, I think the original looks WAY better but different strokes on that front.As for Lunatea's Veil, it does play closer to its PS2 counterpart but sadly carries over a few audiovisual issues, namely the looping and facial animation. Other than that, I've not seen anything as egregious and is definitely the better of the two, even if I miss the cel-shading.Idk. I'm conflicted. To see Klonoa get a new lease on life and in the hands of more players excites me more than anything. EVERYBODY needs to play these games, regardless of version. None of my qualms truly ruin the experience and in fairness, I'm in the minority.That's the rub though. I can't separate the pedestal I keep the PS1 original on from Phantasy Reverie and at best, all I see is my favourite videogame in a far less appealing form. It could've been so, so much more than it is. I still recommend these remakes, especially for the chance to play Lunatea's Veil, but I'm publishing this review from my perspective. I'm biased.

_childDocuments_.review: First I'd like to say I didn't play the original games on PS1 and 2. If you feel like that should invalidate my review go ahead and hit that thumbs down, steam wouldn't put that there if they didn't want you to use it.Klonoa is cute and colorful although it does that current trend of having whiplash from the dull late 2000s era of gaming where now where the colors are too white for both games. Stages are challenging but not to the point where you're grinding for 30 minutes beat or collect everything. The soundtrack feels like one of those dreams where everything is pristine and calm but still mysterious. The gameplay is unique for a 3D 2D platformer. I like how enemies have different contextual meanings to the player. One could be helicopter, the other times you have to precisely chain together jumps with enemies to access certain parts of the level. Despite levels also being "course clear" objectives many of them are nonlinear in design and are quite fun to navigate. It's got that vibe that kirby has with it's atmosphere and character designs. I don't want to say that it's "so dark guys lol" but it's got a neat story for both games that lightly messes with you. I 100% achievement it and as you can tell by my hours it's quite a short amount of time to do that. I played it all on my Steam Deck and it runs flawlessly if you're wondering. I had a certified "WAHOO!" moment with this game!

_childDocuments_.review: YES YES YES ITS FINALLY HERE!!!!!!!This is one of those few releases I've been anticipating on having pretty much daily since announcement. The only others of that kind for me are the System Shock remake and Wrath Aeon of Ruin. ANYWAYSYeah so this is a review specifically on the remaster itself, instead of the game. There's tons of reviews out there on the game you can watch or read. Though I will say that I personally really love this game and have since I first played it a year or two ago. I have no nostalgia attached to the game. And don't let its cutsey nature fool you! This game is extremely solid despite its simplicity. Story is great, and the characters are all lovable. The ending shocked me at first and without spoiling any plot details, I'd have to say it's one of the most depressing endings to any game I've ever seen. At least the first one - I haven't finished the 2nd one yet. Moving on to the remaster. You're probably immediately wondering about that price tag. That is quite pricey for a remaster. 40 dollars for a 25 year old game is pretty steep. Though it is a remaster of TWO games and not one, but that's still pretty high. And there's a dlc that should be maybe 5-10 dollars, but for some reason it's 20 here. So it's 60 for the full package, the price of a normal brand new game. Which is kinda horrible. But I bought the full thing anyways to show the devs there are people out there that really care. The first game is one that's been needing a proper rerelease for a long time, as it, since the early 2000s, has been the most expensive game on PS1 physically. Not sure if it got a PS3 digital rerelease but it did get a remakster thing on the Wii and a Sequel on the PS2. Neither of those which have been rereleased, but that WII version of 1 and the ps2 game are both of what have actually been remastered and included here. The visuals are very crisp, colorful, smooth, and fluid, and yes, better and more refined than their original counterparts. All the polish with today's tech, while keeping all the charm that played a big part of making the originals so lovable. The movement and mechanics are solid as they always have been and are pretty much untouched. Luckily on PC I have a 240hz monitor, so being able to play these games at that framerate has been an absolute treat to say the least. Not a ton of customization options, but that's pretty much expected as far as remasters go. The levels so far seems to be the same without anything new added, though this version does have extra costumes and achievements and whatnot, even though alot of the costumes are part of that expensive dlc. This version has local splitscreen which is awesome, though I haven't tried it yet nor do I know how it works. The music seems uncompressed which is awesome, though in a strange move they kept the original compressed PS1 audio. I'm not sure if that was intentional to keep the spirit of the og game, or it was an oversight but it's definitely a bit strange. Not necessarily a good or bad thing to me. Personally I loved the audio, it's just weird hearing that with the newer crispier visuals.And don't let my hours fool you either, I've played the original for at least a hundred or so hours (which is alot considering it's a short game), so I noticed the changes immediately. TLDR; If you enjoyed the original games, this is a great remaster and probably the best way to play the games now. If you want to show the devs that people still care about this series, I'd suggest buying this too and playing the crap out of it. If you've never played these games before, you're missing out! And if you haven't played them but want to try them out before dropping the cash, you can just emulate the originals and see what you think. Despite the price, it was worth it in my opinion. So happy to finally be playing these!
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: This game is aaahhh how do you say....like reconnecting with your best friend from childhood after not seeing each other for years. What can I say, except that game really does reopen those nostalgic childhood memories that have  been exploited thousands of times by those greedy corporate fat cats. It is a welcoming experience just as how you remember it. Now if you never played this before you will probably overlook it as it is a pretty simplistic game. Hell truth be told there are way better platformers out there. But if you are like me and Klonoa has a special place in your heart as you remember those few good moments of your childhood than this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay to remember to be sad. Klonoa's a bubbly game with some of the best platforming I've ever had the joy to go through. But in a lot of ways, it's more than that to me. What initially starts as an innocuous journey of a little cat thing trying to fight darkness and sorrow becomes something so much deeper. There's a level deep into the sequel, a game that holds for me as one of my top PS2 titles of all time, called the Maze of Memories. It's a place where people spend their entire lives reminiscing on the good times they had, no longer building what was new.  It hit me hard as a kid and still hits me hard now. It's a reminder that even though we attempt to distract ourselves from harsh realities and sorrows of the present, we can't just pretend it doesn't exist.  Klonoa is probably one of the best things Namco's ever made in my eyes. It's a sharply designed game with graphics that hold up even now... But it also possesses a heart that few games have ever been able to attain. If there's one thing this story deserves is a chance to give Klonoa a chance to find his way home. Wahoo.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh brother... i have mixed feelings here, i will mostly focus on Klonoa 1 here since it's the one i finished and to be honest, the more special game to me.First things first, it's an ok way to experience these games, hell i'd argue it's a great way to experience  of these games.Don't expect a Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy level of remake here, you are getting at best two PS2 games with some spit shine applied to 'em, this works well for Klonoa 2, since that was a PS2 game originally and i'd argue it mostly looks better than the original even tough i've played very little of it.Klonoa 1 on the other hand, oh boy, this was a PS1 game and to be honest, the PS1 version is still the best way to experience this game, this part of the remake fumbles. The original game might've been a PS1 game but it wasn't a pushover when it comes to graphics at the time and it had a consistent look, this part of the remake honestly wouldn't look impressive even on the PS2, and its so inconsistent, some levels look very good, some look bland, and animations during cutscenes are consistently stiff, more on that later. I will however compliment the character designs, they do capture the style of the original very well and probably save Klonoa 1 from being a total disaster graphically in this remake.The classic Klonoa gameplay is mostly intact, 2.5 platformer, you interact with elements in the background and foreground, however the new graphics i feel hurt Klonoa 1 here, unlike Klonoa 2, the first game was not designed with full 3D graphics in mind, in the original, your character and the enemies were 2D sprites, only the levels were 3D, as a result, it was very easy to tell when enemies were in front of you, in the background or the foreground, with the new graphics is not so easy and i sometimes tried to grab enemies that were actually in the background, that being said the gameplay is 95% intact, its not really a deal breaker on this aspect, and the game is super easy anyways, mistakes like this wont generate too much frustration.Now here's the thing, if you've heard of Klonoa 1 before, you probably know it as "that cute platformer that gets surprisingly sad towards the end", i'd argue the story of Klonoa 1 is crucial for the experience and the remake drops the ball HARD here, nearly every single dramatic cutscene is sabotaged by stiff character animations, SPECIALLY stiff facial animations, something very sad might be happening on screen and the characters might have a smile on their faces because animation is hard and someone was very lazy during development, this issue is compounded by the audio which was taken directly from the original, and while that's a plus for the music, which is as great as ever, its been horrible for the character voices which are bit-crunched to hell and back, everyone sounds as if they recorded their lines in a basement and underwater, the fact character talk is gibberish prevents this issue from getting worse, atleast you know you are not supposed to understand anything.Here's the thing tough, i recognize few people will care as much as i do, this is a game that made me feel sad as a kid and that was rare, it stuck with me, someone who didn't grow up with this game isn't going to give a damn, they will still be getting a decent platformer out of Klonoa 1, albeit a short and easy one, Klonoa 2 while not as emotionally impactful to me, is the better game in terms of gameplay, longer, harder and looks much better overall in this remake.i suppose the package as a whole is worth it so i recommend it, even tough i believe this is not the best way to play Klonoa 1.

_childDocuments_.review: The Klonoa games are special to me. Klonoa 2 in particular is one of my favorite games. And it saddened me knowing that in the twenty one years it had been out, the game had no re-release in any form. So seeing the game, along with the original game being re-released for every modern console and the PC made me pretty happy. I booted up 2 immediately and while I thought the game looked really nice in terms of the environments and updated character designs, all the little details seemed to have fallen to the wayside.Facial expressions have generally become worse looking and are outright missing in some cases. You have a couple scenes where a certain character is supposed to be smiling, but isn't. Part of what made the game so special to me is how expressive the characters are, and seeing that taken away almost ruins a few scenes. Apparently, a lot of the files that were ported over didn't transfer correctly and were overlooked. Music cues for certain cutscenes have been broken, so music plays over moments where it's supposed to stop in order to emphasize certain moments in the cutscenes.Background elements like the crowds in Joilant are incredibly low-poly creating a jarring disconnect with everything else.Random parts of the script got changed which leads to weird moments where characters repeat what they've just said and certain lines got replaced by ones that just sound awkward.As for DtP, the game is essentially a shinier port of the Wii remake from back in 2008, but with updated character models to keep in line with the original PS1 game's aesthetic. It tries elements of both via using the PS1's audio files in conjunction with the Wii's cutscenes, which creates a rather jarring disconnect. Still better than the Wii's terrible English dub, but not by much.Overall, this is not a very good remake and frankly I feel the Klonoa games deserved far better than this. It's frankly a sloppily made product. I would hold off on buying the game until Namco Bandai polishes the game some more via updates or until somebody decides to mod the games to try and fix the issues these games have.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful remake of the first two Klonoa games,  (from the PlayStation 1 era) and its sequel  - which is still one of the PlayStation 2's most highly rated games with a Metacritic score of 94 at launch. I fondly remember playing both at the time so I was delighted that Namco's furry mascot was getting a new lease on life on all modern platforms for his 25th anniversary. What surprised me the most about both games was how well they both hold up considering they came out between 1997 and 2001. Platformers have seen a creative renaissance over the intervening years thanks to the budding indie scene, so it was surprising to see both hold up so well against the more modern games in the genre. To say both games in the collection have aged beautifully is an understatement and this is only amplified by the loving restoration done by Monkeycraft on these lost platforming relics so that hopefully an entire new generation can discover them.  If sales are buoyant enough, hopefully then there is the possibility we see a third mainline entry into the series. Simple yet delightful to play,  is gorgeous visually, oozes charm, has clever level design that often allows the player to approach it from various angles, and is a winner for fans of the genre. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s been a long time since the last time I played this saga, probably somewhat around 20 years ago but I always wanted to return to both Phantomile and Lunatea, something got stuck in my head and those were lovely memories from easier and past times. Now let’s jump to the year 2022, the impossible happened, Klonoa is coming back with a remastered version of the main two games, Door to Phantomile and Lunatea’s Veil, with this Phantasy Reverie collection. Is it worth your time? Do they still hold up for modern standards? Let’s find out.Let’s start talking about both stories with Door to Phantomile which is the beginning of our story. We are Klonoa, a young boy from Breezegale, a small village from Phantomile. One day we experience a strange dream in which a strange ring drops from the sky and a strange entity appears, Huepow. To your surprise it seems that it wasn’t a dream and it really happened but things are about to start now, a strange aircraft crashes near your village, once you go inspect the incident you discover a strange figure and its minion are kidnapping a little girl, our mission will be saving her as we discover the truth of what’s going on.We don’t know what happened after our adventures in Phantomile, however, we are about to start a new adventure in a new land, Lunatea. We wake up in this world without knowing what happened but we (as players) know we are being observed by someone. Almost immediately after you wake up, both Lolo and Popka, our new friends in this adventure, will tell us where we are, who we need to talk with and what they think it’s going on. What started as a small adventure will lead into a much bigger one sooner rather than later.Both stories are quite liviane, keep in mind both games were designed with younger audiences in mind, however, I find both quite enjoyable no matter your age. In both cases there’s a great setup with their own rules, Phantomile and Lunatea have different sets of rules however, by the own nature of this saga, you will soon find shared elements between both places, it works as a bigger picture than their respective worlds. Characters are also extremely enjoyable in both cases.Huepow, Lolo, Popka, even villains like Joka or Tat (which, for some reason, I always loved the way she talked) are all not that deep but deep enough to enjoy their presence. Main characters do have enough presence to know them better and some side-ones too.Make no mistake, while both games were created with younger audiences in mind, that doesn’t mean they are exclusively for kids, in both cases there are dramatic moments, some extremely iconic nowadays as they were completely unexpected.There’s little more I can say about the narrative side without spoiling things but, What about visuals in both cases?Well, you see, Klonoa Door to Phantomile was a PSX game with a very peculiar but rather amazing visual style with 2D sprites and a somewhat 3D look, however, it got a remake treatment for the Wii which redo all the assets from the ground (likely got some inspiration from PS2 Lunatea’s Veil) and this remaster surprisingly drops in the middle of those two.Phantasy Reverie’s version is clearly redone, it’s clean but at the same time tries to emulate the original more than the Wii version. Klonoa’s character looks more like the original, backgrounds are less detailed than on the Wii and I think the reason for this is that they want to go after the original visual feeling. It’s more colorful and has a pixel filter that is great and confusing at the same time. I used it for a few levels but ended up using the vanilla visuals.When it comes to Lunatea’s Veil, you will immediately notice that it doesn’t look like the original, that’s correct. While no assets seem to be different, the visual filter changed to make it more streamline with the Door of Phantomile, that’s a good way of not making a huge difference between the two in the same collection. Lunatea’s Veil also has more details, more effects and in general it feels like a natural evolution for a game that came out 5 years after the original and on a completely different platform, If you ask me, Lunatea’s Veil is extremely beautiful at times, I might be biased given how I remember it when I was a kid and what I experienced but in general it is a great step up.Both games hold really well today and their level design is still extremely engaging. The way it moves as a 2D platformer but in a 3D environment makes it an extremely compelling experience, I don’t think there’s anything else like Klonoa right now and that’s something to consider as an achievement.Music is also a great part of the game and I’m happy to say that it sounds as good as the original movie sequences, there are great themes in both games, they too hold really well.I could say the same about the gameplay loop. There are two main actions to consider in this game: grab and hold an enemy to use it and jump/ hold in the air. As you can see it’s really basic but the way they designed the levels makes it an extremely engaging experience, sometimes there’s no room for a mistake, you do it or you don’t. You will notice this a lot if you try completing these games at 100%, mostly trying to get all the gems per level, you need to focus and jump correctly, run at the requested speed and not get hit during the process, and there’s also the side levels which are meant to be beaten only by those who are used with the controls and the movement, they are challenging but really gratifying once you beat them. Going after the 100% sure is an experience.I think it’s a good moment to talk about performance. I completed both of them on the Steam Deck, do not worry, they run perfectly out of the box, as a matter of fact, thanks to the pre-compiling shaders I think it eliminates some little stutters present on the windows version of the game. Battery held really well, performance was steady at 60fps with all settings at max and in general I would say I enjoyed it more playing them on a handheld than on my main computer, I guess they are that kind of game that for some reason I tend to enjoy more on a smaller screen due to memories.And I think that’s about it, Klonoa Phantasy Reverie collection was all I wanted for a proper comeback. Visuals are great, gameplay is still engaging and it transported me to my childhood playing them on the Playstation. Usually I would say “it’s not a game for everyone” but f*** it, I will say this is a great game for everyone, for those who want to revisit this old saga, for newcomers, for kids and for adults.Klonoa is back and for that I’m thankful, from the deepest part of my heart, thanks Bandai Namco for bringing back this old friend from past days, I’m glad to say that the final result is well worth your money and your time, heck, I went after all the achievements and the 100%, that shows you how much I loved this.I hope you enjoy it at least half of how much I enjoyed it, my best wishes to all of you.Thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: Its been almost two years since its released so I think its finally time to actually talk about the quality of these games in the package they come in. First off, I want to say that these games alone are fantastic on their own right, but you are much better off emulating the original games than playing them via Phantasy Reverie. The quality of these remasters are comparable to the quality of Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut. In terms of the game's visuals, it looks like they only saw the complaint about the wii remake being desaturated and decided to over-saturate the entire game which in fact made it look worse than the wii remake at times. This includes the second game as well. In addition, there are missing effects, broken textures and lighting, missing animations, poor audio mixing, alongside with some other new bugs introduced. To make matters worse, It also doesn't help that the first thing the games asks for when you boot it up for the first time is your location and to collect your data for a single player game of all things. You can easily get around that by disabling the games internet connectivity via your firewall settings. Regardless, there is absolutely zero reason for a single player game of all things to be asking to collect your data and you can't play the game if you reject it either.  I genuinely wish this remaster had more development time and wasn't treated as a rush job like most of Bandai Namco's recent remakes/remasters. Part of me wishes that they just brought over the first two games via emulation rather than a botched remaster if this was the quality we were going to receive. While this remaster sold decently enough in almost two years, I genuinely hope that if there is another Klonoa game in the near future, it gets the time and attention it truly deserves. It's a shame things turned out the way they did and that the most accessible versions of these games happen to be inferior versions when compared to their original counterparts.

_childDocuments_.review: This review was written after finishing both games and contains no spoilers.I've previously played the PlayStation version of Door to Phantomile and PlayStation 2 version of Lunatea's Veil.Klonoa immediately captivates by having an unmatched presentation with an appealing art direction and a soundtrack that draws you in. The whole experience leaves a strong, lasting impression, and playing the game is bound to produce sheer joy. The quality of the game stays the same throughout the whole package, the diversity of the areas is fantastic and none of the locations overstay their welcome. There are no padding areas and the stages are full of background eye candy. Klonoa really is the role model for a quality platformer.It's easy to pick up and play a Klonoa title. The games have aged well, with a timeless approach to 2.5D platforming. The controls are simple and responsive. Once you get the hang of the intricacies of enemy inflation, you're ready to tackle all the platforming and puzzles that the game has to offer.Both games now have 3 difficulties, an addition exclusive to these remasters, with easy and normal being available from the get go, while hard difficulty requires the player to finish the appropriate game first. Normal difficulty is "just right" and matches the originals, while hard is for those that have mastered Klonoa and want the extra challenge.Additionally, there's a toggle for tutorial pop-ups, which usually appear as soon as there's a new item or mechanic in the game. The completion is made easy so that the player is not required to gather all the dream stones. If you'd like to 100% complete this game in terms of achievements, then there's nothing to fear: the remaster remembers all of your collectibles and there's no need to pick them up again even if you've restarted a segment (something that was absent in the originals). The collectibles are used to gain access to the extra stages, which are the most difficult parts of the game. Finishing those extra challenge stages means that you've 100%ed all achievements.This partially removes the frustration that the original games had, as gathering all dream stones & collectibles is not an easy task. There are unfair segments that didn't age too well and the dream stone gathering can be a puzzle in itself, as there are power-ups that multiply the value of dream stones by two. Miss any dream stone during that power up or pick them up beforehand, and you're locking yourself out of the completion. On top of that, there's no convenient way of restarting a level or a segment (aside from purposely losing a life), so all dream stone collection is recommended only to hardcore Klonoa fans and platformer enthusiasts.The local cooperation mechanic is now available throughout both games. It originated in the second game and now has made it to the first one too! It's a neat little addition that allows another person with a second game pad to give the main player an extra jump boost, a sort of second chance in case you're falling down. With software like Parsec or Steam Remote Play, it's possible to have an online friend help you out or even switch roles.Lunatea's Veil has been rebalanced with stages having far less extra lives spread around. This could be the result of the game remembering collectibles, making checkpoint restarts less tedious. On the other hand, this game still features a notorious escape sequence that introduces a sudden difficulty spike and would have benefited from that rebalance touch.My first impressions of the Door to Phantomile remaster were... me being greeted by a stuttery mess of a first level, that was immediately apparent to the naked eye and highly distracting from the game itself. Both the original PlayStation and Wii versions of the game run at a stable 60 FPS with no frame time spikes, so this is not an inherent legacy code behavior. In a seemingly random fashion, the game tends to alter between the two states of either constantly stuttering or running the intended way, nothing in between: the first stage stutters through, then the next ones run perfectly fine, but when you least expect it, the game starts to stutter again and thus the cycle continues.After checking through some basic hardware monitoring stats, it's clear that the remaster is not resource-heavy and should not be pushing any recent mid-range systems against the wall. The stutter is not reflected on the RTSS (Riva Tuner Statistics Server) frame time graph, so there's something funky going on with how the game is wrapped in Unity. The game's frontend menu runs smoothly even during those in-game stutter episodes, so I have a suspicion that it's not possible to remedy this issue without a proper patch. I've tried forcing different V-Sync options and frame rate caps, but couldn't find a combination that would completely remedy this situation.Lunatea's Veil is affected the same way.If you know Lunatea's Veil by heart, then you're likely to notice that the character facial animations are either toned down or partially missing. Klonoa flying around with his mouth closed, the cutscenes having characters with poker faces or looking rather bored and unamused. Said changes negatively affect the mood of the majority of the scenes to the point where it looks ridiculous and laughable. As of now, there's a community-made patch "Restore Blend Shape Animations (Klonoa 2)" that restores the original PS2 animations and makes the game what it should have been to begin with.Another notable change about Lunatea's Veil are the visual effects. In the intro cutscene, the antagonists are supposed to be obscured in darkness, while the remaster has them perfectly visible. Later down the road there's a scene where the antagonist has a heat haze in front of them as they leave the burning area, adding that extra flair of edginess, while in the remaster the flame layer is completely removed. You could bunch these up as artistic changes, but I wouldn't necessarily agree that these changes are in the right direction.The Anti-Aliasing option is currently broken and does nothing. It's possible to use workarounds such as forcing FXAA through your video card's control panel or using vendor-specific downsampling methods from higher resolutions (DSR, VSR, DLDSR, etc.). The jaggies are especially noticeable on Klonoa and other side characters, therefore it's a shame that this option is currently broken, as it would greatly improve the image quality and presentation.But wait, there's more! Often times, Lunatea's Veil's soundtrack doesn't loop seamlessly, like it did in the original, resulting in awkward music fades with the stage theme starting from the beginning. Some cutscene music has broken cues, resulting in scenes with inappropriate music playing during them. But I'm not done yet, in Door to Phantomile there's a stage (Vision 6-2) that is missing a theme variation (themes are supposed to change based on your location during the level). There is one theme that has its loop fixed when compared to the original, but that seemed more like an anomaly.The remastered games give us a chance to revisit a dormant series that has been forgotten for far too long. The gameplay holds up even today, the touched up visuals are seamless and have the "just as I remember it looking like back in the day" effect. Despite all the flaws and inconsistencies, if you've never played these games before, or it's been far too long ago, then most of the issues shouldn't get in your way. That being said, I believe that these remasters need a little more of love, as I think Klonoa deserves to inflate these bugs and "Wahoo!" them away.Review copy provided by BANDAI NAMCO Entertainment.

_childDocuments_.review: Just to preface, this is not a game I grew up with. This experience has me reflecting on how it should have been. The mark of a great puzzle platformer is when knowing how to solve a puzzle often times doesn't make it any easier. It requires a lot of precise timing, but is much more forgiving than something like Cuphead. I found myself crying during the ending of what I originally thought was a very surface level story.I have only finished the first of these two games at the time of writing this (will update after completing Lunatea's Veil), yet I'm already satisfied having spent 40$ on the first game alone. Klonoa is going to be on my radar going forward, and I recommend you put it on yours, as well.The following passage was written directly after the completion of Lunatea's Veil. Do NOT begin playing the series through Lunatea's Veil. While not much of Door to Phantomile is in the sequel at all, the themes of the stories become stronger when experienced as a sequential duology. From a gameplay standpoint, Lunatea's Veil is definitely the more forgiving of the two, in spite of having your 6 HP cut down to 3. Very cool puzzles were added, like the creature you make larger by feeding other enemies to it to smash a color-coded crystal, or the boss fights. I didn't mention the boss fights from Klonoa 1, because aside from Joka and the true final boss, they were a bit plain. Each boss in Klonoa 2 has two forms, which are easy enough to understand. Yet, as I said before, knowing exactly how to solve these puzzles doesn't make them any easier. Coming out of the Klonoa Duology, I have a higher appreciation for the medium as a whole. The world wasn't ready for this series in the mid 1990s, as it was still hotly debated on whether or not video games were an art form. As a medium, video games did not get the respect they deserved from critics until Metal Gear Solid 4. (Which, admittedly, deserves most of if not all the praise it gets.)This is an intricate, existential adventure hidden behind the wrapper of an unassuming children's platformer. I will never forget the experiences I've had in either of these worlds. I look forward to whatever may lay ahead for the series. Given Bandai Namco's promise to revive the series, and the feedback it's received, the future looks bright for the Cabbit of Everyone's Dreams. Of course, not everyone is into 2.5D Puzzle Platformers, but especially for the bargain price these games come with, definitely give it a shot if you have a chance.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: The first game, Klonoa: Door to Phantomile, is a 2.5D platformer where Klonoa uses his Wind Bullet to grab enemies and solve puzzles across varied levels. The mechanics are straightforward yet satisfying, with the dual-plane level design offering depth. The creative puzzles and charming environments evolve as you progress, keeping the experience enjoyable throughout.Klonoa 2: Lunatea’s Veil builds on the foundation of the original but introduces more dynamic set-pieces and smoother visuals. The game’s level design is more diverse, with elements like hoverboarding sections that add excitement. The graphics and mechanics feel more polished, making this sequel the highlight of the collection. The gameplay remains lighthearted and accessible but with better pacing and variety than its predecessor.Throughout both games, Klonoa is joined by memorable companions who add personality and aid him in his journey. In Door to Phantomile, Klonoa is accompanied by Huepow, a spirited sidekick who offers support and guidance, while in Lunatea’s Veil, he’s joined by the energetic Lolo and the grumpy Popka, who provide humor and further story depth.Both games retain their signature vibrant, colorful art style, but with modernized visuals. The remastered graphics breathe new life into the levels, keeping the whimsical and lighthearted tone intact. The environments in Lunatea’s Veil are especially impressive, featuring more detailed backgrounds and lively effects. The hand-drawn aesthetic complements the nostalgic feel, even if the games aren’t pushing graphical boundaries.The music and sound design are standout features in both games. The charming, melodic soundtrack fits the whimsical nature of the levels, enhancing the emotional moments. Voice acting remains in the original “Phantomile” language, adding a unique flair. Sound effects are crisp and blend well with the overall atmosphere, making the journey through Phantomile and Lunatea even more immersive.The story in Door to Phantomile is simple yet surprisingly touching by the end. Klonoa’s journey involves saving his dream world from a growing threat. The narrative introduces themes of dreams, memories, and loss, which hit harder than expected, leaving an emotional impact.Lunatea’s Veil offers a more refined story, building on the dreamlike themes of the first game while introducing new characters and challenges. It’s more colorful and lighthearted, with a deeper plot that still carries a bittersweet undertone. The characters and world are charming, making it a more engaging experience overall.Both games are relatively easy to complete, with campaigns lasting around 6-8 hours each. However, for those aiming for 100% completion, there are hidden items, extra levels, and collectibles that add challenge. The difficulty spikes during boss fights, especially the end bosses in both titles, which demand precise timing and strategy. These encounters add a layer of challenge not found in the standard levels and are a highlight for players seeking a more intense experience.Hours to fully complete both games: 24Achievements: 25/25Playthroughs: 1-2Difficulty: 6/10Steam Hunter Points: ✪ 4,222The Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series is a must-play for platformer fans and anyone who cherishes nostalgic, heartfelt adventures. While the difficulty is on the lighter side overall, the challenging end boss fights add a satisfying level of depth to the experience. Both games offer unique, memorable journeys full of charm, creativity, and emotion. If you missed these classics during their original release or are revisiting them, this remastered collection is well worth your time—especially during a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played them before, but those two Caddicarus videos really made me want to play Klonoa. For many years I have waited for PC ports of the games which I never believed I would get. Yet, here they are, remade, actually, but the content is exactly the same as far as I know.Klonoa 1 is wonderful. Interesting physics and mechanics make your standard platforming adventure much more unique and twisted in a good way. The regular getting through forward path is almost like a puzzle half the time. Extremely creative and genius level design. Lovely world and character designs. I couldn't really get into the story until I reached the end and then the game ended with such a  ending. I was shocked. But I loved it. Music is beautiful too. Also, freeing prisoners unlock stuff like extra level and some bonus unlockable stuff which is so nice.There are two things I don't like about this game.1. Collecting all the crystals don't give you anything. There is no point in getting all 150/150 gems in all levels.2. Those timed 2x gem value enhancers are sent from hell. The time they work is very slim and you have to move absolutely perfectly in order to colelct all the gems you can collect while having them because their maximum limit you can push is what counts towards the total collectables of each level. It is painful. What's even worse is that if you fail, the only way to restart is to die before picking next checkpoint... But the worst is that when playing the levels for the first time, you don't know the limit, it never actually tells how many gems are you possibly supposed to get with them. Pretty often there are gems nearby the limit use and you can't know for sure if you was supposed to get those gems as well or is it impossible and you can't. It's a guessing game but also requires maximum skill. Very bad design. They should have scrapped those gem value enhancers completely. It also kind of contradicts itself, it is so hard to collect all the gems because of those stupid gem value enhancers, but you don't even need to collect all the gems to begin with as there is no point to it. I got them all in all the levels of the first game and it was all for nothing, I had hoped that they would unlock at least something.Still, despite those two complaints which do not even matter if you're not aiming for all the collectables Klonoa 1 is a wonderful game. One of the best platformers for sure.8/10Klonoa 2 is more of the same, but not as good. I cared for the story even less than in the first game and the ending I thought was a lot weaker. It adds some new mechanics and most of them I don't think are bad, but I don't think they are good either. Due to the very tiny grabbing area it is often too hard to grab stuff when falling. It was certainly easier in the first games as it did not have things as little as some are in this game. This game also has some clever and cool level design choices in many levels, but not as impressive as the first game and also I noticed a lot of repetitiveness in some of the level designs and loyouts. And I'm not talking about the fact that some areas have two levels in them, so it reuses the levels, but alters them a bit, which, luckily, was done in a nice way and not lazily like most games would do.It brings the same problem I had with the first game. Those annoying fairy 2x gem value enhancers are back. It wasn't improved at all, just as annoying if not worse. But they did actually this time make the 150/150 gem collection for each level matter. With each 150/150 level you can unlock 1 picture!!! That's very disappointing, but better than nothing. But collecting all gems in this game is much harder and those 2x enhancers are even more irritating than in the first game, I only managed to get 2 levels with 150/150 and one of them I had to replay like a dozen times, it is insane how precise you have to be. So I gave up and didn't bother.Overall Klonoa 2 is a nice game, but weaker than its predecessor.7/10Overall, I'm happy with this little collection. Never imagined that Klonoa games could be on Steam. I'm still waiting for Silent Hill, Disruptor, Alien Trilogy, The Mummy, Tunguska: Legend of Faith, Project Overkill, Hellnight, Vagrant Story, Nightmare Creatures 1 and 2, The Suffering 1 and 2, Dementium: The Ward, Future Cop: LAPD, Clive Barker's Undying, Diablo, The Thing, Medal of Honor + Underground and dozens of other games. If Castlevania, Klonoa, Turok, TMNT 2 and dozens of others made it, I have a very strong hope that those someday will too!

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series delivers remakes of the main two entries in the cult classic Klonoa series. These are both 2.5-D platformers revolving around picking up and throwing enemies, wrapped in colorful aesthetics and hiding melancholy stories. The versions in here have much higher resolution assets than their respective PS1 and PS2 counterparts, but hit detection feels a bit finnicky in here. Still, these are quite solid versions of these games, and the games in here are quite good.Klonoa: Door to Phantomile was novel in its original release for combining 3D environments and 2D gameplay, lending its world some literal depth in comparison to other 2D platformers of its time. It's put to good use with branching pathways and elaborate settings, but in this first outing, it doesn't quite reach its full potential. It's a solid start, but it's not quite an all-time great.Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil makes a much stronger case, though. It keeps the basic mechanical foundation of the first game but expands upon the types of enemies and puzzles encountered through the game, giving it more variety and pushing into more creative territory. It also introduces snowboarding levels which provide a faster counterpoint to the generally slow platforming levels. Even the story seems more substantial this time around, with more complex characters and motivations. A proper Klonoa 3 never materialized, but I'm not sure if one is really needed with a game like this.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe I haven't written a review on this game yet and it's been out for over a year at this point...I love this game. Plain and simple. This collection is amazing.After having barely known about the franchise because of a spotlight in a 2010 Nintendo Power magazine issue about the remake on Wii, to researching the entire series and trying out whatever games I could afford the physical editions of, it still feels unreal that this silly little cat-rabbit doesn't get the love he deserves.I had previously only played the Wii version of Door to Phantomile, which is what this collection uses for the remaster, and nearly everything is vastly improved. Klonoa maintains the phantomilian voice (no RPG protagonist sounding English voice) as well as an updated version of his classic design, the visuals are much more bright and colorful, and the writing is a lot closer to the PS1 original. From what I've seen and heard, the PS1 version of Door to Phantomile is still the best version, but chances are many people reading this (including myself) don't have the $300+ to drop on a copy of that, so this version is more than serviceable.Lunatea's Veil however? Absolutely incredible. Because the remake is directly based on the PS2 version, there's hardly any modified level designs if at all. The visuals are once again a lot more vibrant, admittedly too much so in some parts of the game, so whether you like this version or the original is entirely up to your own preference. They're effectively the exact same outside of visuals, so just choose whichever you have access to and prefer. Because this is MY first experience with the game however, I absolutely LOVED it. The characters, the puzzles, the story, THE MUSIC, even though I usually tend to gravitate towards faster-paced platformers this game still managed to skyrocket to one of my favorite games of all time. Definitely the major selling point of the whole collection.It's such a shame Bandai Namco doesn't recognize this series for what it is. I know that this style of platformer has a VERY niche appeal, but it was so heartwarming seeing the fans group together to make this game a success. Hopefully this review helps someone contribute to that success, because I really want to see Klonoa get a new adventure someday.And to Bandai Namco, PLEASE RELEASE KLONOA MERCH IN THE STATES. I KNOW PLUSHIES EXIST.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was younger, I had two levels from Klonoa 2 on a PS2 demo disc that I played over and over, trying to get all the secrets I can out of it. One of the levels always had me miss one collectible doll, and as a child I was endlessly frustrated with that. Now that I have finally played both Klonoa games via this collection, I know the reason why - it's because the level continued after the demo disc ended, which is where the final collectible doll was hidden! If only I could have told this to my 10 year old self...That being said, how are those games and do they hold up? Both games function essentially the same - you play as Klonoa and the main mechanic is that you can use your wind ring to grab an enemy and then throw it or use it to double jump. It's a simple mechanic and a simple platformer, but it works reasonably well. You traverse dreamlike worlds, find collectible captives (Klonoa 1) and dolls (Klonoa 2) and collect gems.I will say that Klonoa 1 is definitely the more fun game of the two. It leans much more into puzzles and using your wind ring to solve them by throwing enemies just the right way, finding keys and switches along the way. It is also much slower paced. Klonoa 2, on the other hand, ramps up the complexity by having bigger levels (some of which are recycled because you revisit them in a slightly changed form) and also suddenly tasks you with timed challenges or having to move quickly and precisely by grabbing enemies or platforms in quick succession. In my opinion, the controls just aren't made for that type of quick gameplay and the hitboxes can be a bit flimsy. It's very easy to miss flying enemies or not being able to hit platforms, causing you to fall to your death. It also has a few board levels, which can be fun, but here, too, the controls can be a bit awkward and feel slippery. Every level also has 150 gems, which is luckily not needed for 100 % completion as trying to get all them in every level will make your hair fall out.Even so, both games are definitely worth playing and experiencing and the remaster is done beautifully. If you take Klonoa as the simple game that it is supposed to be, you can spend a fun few hours with some nice music and some interesting, if a little cliche, stories and both games aren't too long overall. Recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Fine remakes of two great Namco classics! _childDocuments_.review: Phantasy Reverie Series is an ok remake, but there's unfortunately a noticeable lack of polish for $40.Here's a list of the (mostly minor) problems:- The game's core mechanic (the wind bullet) has been altered to be slower and smaller, making it mildly more difficult to use. This affects both games.- The above point is compounded by the high friction Klonoa has in this game. He can no longer slide as far after shooting the wind bullet.- The title screen for Door to Phantomile is out of sync with the music jingle.- Several cutscenes in both games have missing or worse facial animation (even compared to Door to Phantomile's sprites).- All of the FMVs in Door to Phantomile have been replaced with vastly inferior in-game cutscenes.- The art style for Lunatea’s Veil has been changed to be much brighter and more saturated. While it might be down to preference which look you prefer, I think the original look of the game should have been preserved.- A couple of sections in Door to Phantomile are made a little bit more challenging due to Klonoa having a pill-shaped hitbox that can slide off ledgesI don't think this collection is bad way to play these games, but I also don't think it's the *best* way to play them, especially for Door to Phantomile.Play these remakes, but play the originals too. They're all worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: How could I didn't know about this game? Klonoa is probably one of the best Bandai Namco original games out there. It's a shame that it was overshadowed by other popular Bandai Namco titles.Klonoa is an action platformer following our main character Klonoa on his journey to solve the problems of dream worlds. The main mechanic that revolves around this game is taking an enemy and throw it. It might sounds simple but it can also be use for double jumps, fly and much more depending on the enemy types.Klonoa 2 is a huge improvement on the first one. It adds lots of mechanic, fancier graphic and better story and much more. Still, note that I'd recommend playing the first one first so at least you can see the development changes of the game moreover the lore and story.The game itself is not really easy if you start on normal which is the way the game intended to be. For example, the mirror fairy that doubles the crystal amounts have a really tight time that a single wrong move in milliseconds can mess up the whole crystal you would gather. Also, the second game is a lot harder than the first one which is another reason I recommend to play first one first so at least you can get the hang of the controls. The side levels is also harsh and took me 30 minutes to conquer it 100%. Even though it's not aspainful as doing path of pain in Hollow Knight or getting true ending in Cave Story, it still gives the same amount of pain but a lot easier and faster to figure out.In the end, you should buy Klonoa NOW. I was shocked to know this was made in ps1 era. It really shows how Bandai Namco have changed over the years moreover with recent titles that doesn't feel like the way Bandai Namco used to be. For example, their newer Tales title doesn't feel like a Tales game anymore if you're an original fan who play many old Tales game from beginning like me. I hope they make more originals or cartoony like this again and please at least port old games back. I really want to know old and good Bandai Namco titles

_childDocuments_.review: Phantasy Reverie Series is an adventure platformer that's a faithful remaster with great visual enhancements & unlocked framerates while keeping it's core gameplay & everything else at the tones of the originals. It's a collection that consists of the first Klonoa, Door to Phantomile released for the PSX (1997) & KLONOA 2: Lunatea’s Veil (PS2/2001).You're a dream traveler and your task is to save the spiritual planes you wander & their inhabitants, before all perish & turn into nightmare fuel. The world is vibrant & full of colors, the characters cast is unique & somewhat peculiar while the story, starts in mellow vibes and turns into an unexpected plot twist that might shatter your expectations. It plays like a classical 3D sidescroller with most stages allowing multiple layer exploration, while the main gameplay mechanic & catch being your wind ring, which allows Klonoa to catch & inflate enemies, giving you extra mobility for extra jumps or air time.Both games have quite challenging precision platforming sections mixed with puzzle segments that stands out even by today's gaming standards. You will also encounter a handful of bosses that require good positioning & decent reactions. It's an experience that can & should be enjoyed by anyone, from folks who played the original games back in the day to newcomers & first timers, from innocent kids to life consumed grown ups. It has that magical vibe from the golden era of gaming& I'm more than grateful for that.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite Bandai Namco US trying as hard as they could to mess up the release of this game (No pre-orders, physical releases, and paltry marketing), it's heartwarming to see how the community surrounding these games are all coming together to celebrate the return of Klonoa.If you're looking for some simple yet fun side-scrolling platformers with cute aesthetics, head bop worthy soundtracks, heartwarming and endearing characters, and gut wrenching sad endings, don't even think of passing on this collection.The ports aren't entirely perfect with some odd audio issues and frame pacing on framerates higher than 60FPS. But considering Bandai Namco's history of PC releases, these run and play beautifully, and have enough graphical options to make sure even the most potato of modern PCs can handle them. Both games also work great on Steam Deck!With the possible future of the franchise hanging in the balance of this collection, I implore you: Pick it up, and get Stepping Wind stuck in your head for the rest of time.

_childDocuments_.review: The remaster didn't do good for Klonoa, and it mostly comes down to the controls and gamefeel. (Though I also think the visuals are just plain bad and if anything the original pixelated PS1 game has a better style, definitely better pre-rendered cutscenes, but I could get past all that.) I feel like this game wasn't tested compared to the original game. And I mean THE original PS1 title, not the Wii remake. I love Klonoa and I hope the series returns, but I also hope that the people who worked on this won't be the creators of the upcoming titles. I've cleared 4-2 and I decided it's not worth it, even though I finished the original game dozens of times and never felt bothered by anything.With that out of the way here are some things that bothered me through the whole time:1) Klonoa turns on a dime, but inching forward makes him slide forward like ~3 steps. In the original game Klonoa's direction was irrelevant, he just moved immediately in the direction you pressed. This is bad because the game has some tight platforms, making you unintentionally slide off them, what makes it even worse is, like I said, Klonoa turns on a dime in place, which means that if you wanted to compensate for this slide, you will not do anything because Klonoa simply turns around while continuing sliding.2) Jumping feels bad. Your input stays for too long, you start gliding way too fast after pressing X, and if you accidentally press X before landing you will do another jump. Klonoa has set jump height no matter how long you hold down X (which is exactly like the original) so having to accidentally jump is not something that should ever happen.3) Air control has momentum now. In neither of the original games there was any sort of preserved momentum of Klonoa while he was in the air. This was great because it made landing on the tiny platforms precise. Now you have to account for the added momentum, and once having landed on the platforms, you basically cannot correct your position because of the issue listed in 1)4) The wind-bullet is tiny, it needs to be around twice as chonky. There are SLOPES in the game where you can't grab enemies because the hitbox is so small. Flying enemies feel just about the same.5) So when you turn around you basically just turn in place, which makes jumping right after turning build up speed very slowly. You basically jump forward at half the speed. (Again these small things are bad because this is a precision platformer)6) Just when landing and turning around at the same time makes it so that you CANNOT fire a wind-bullet. This is inconsistent at best, but there were cases when my input just didn't register at all. I jump into the air, turn around, land, and my attack never comes out.7) I really wish they copied from the original game and not the Wii version (it has changed some things, most notably the 2-2 boss, the fish and king boss, where the middle part is now connected just so there is less challenge)In summary, I'd rather get the original games on an emulator because they feel so much better. Even though the original Klonoa 1 was much slower to grab enemies, actually it was so slow that you could jump, grab an enemy, have like 1-2 frames to preform a glide to stop yourself from descending (this was really good for the helicopter enemies), and then do a double jump. Klonoa 2 got rid of this, probably for the better, the game feels snappier and more responsive, however non of the problems I listed above had appeared in neither Klonoa 1 or 2. I'm hesitant to recommend the remasters and not an emulator. If you can by any means get the original PS1 and PS2 games, play those instead.8) They kept the original voice acting for the cutscenes but removed the Klonoa 1 WAHOO. That was my favorite wahoo

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa made from magical dream river. Its part of you and them combined together. What waits by the end of a journey no one knows. Its beautiful from outside but whole meaning unveils from deeper side of this story. This game is probably one of the unique platformers I’ve experienced. _childDocuments_.review: I'm so happy they remastered and re-released this game from my childhood! The nostalgia is unreal and playing The Door to Phantomile again brings me so much joy. This game always stuck out to me as a kid and in my memory for being such a unique platformer with a stylistic world design like no other. The game mechanics still hold up really well today and provide a really nice challenge while also just being fun to pick up enemies and hurl them across the screen or use them to go WAHOO into the air!The new graphics look really nice and are true to the original character designs without trying too hard to modernize it. Character models are nice and simple just like the original games but much cleaner thanks to higher resolutions without adding unnecessary details or changing character designs like the Wii remake did.The voices and music seem to be exactly like the original which I'm incredibly happy about. I remember a Wii remake that I didn't play changed the voices to speak English and I'm so glad to see they've kept the original voices here with their cute Simoleon like gibberish language that adds a really cute charm to the game. My only complaint for this would be that a couple of cutscenes aren't as good as they were in the original, since they seem to all be done in engine now but the intro pre-rendered cutscene in the original game looked much better with much more atmosphere to it. Overall this is an incredibly minor complaint though, as there was only about two or three cutscenes in the whole game that were pre-rendered in the original like that while all the other cutscenes were in engine. All of the new cutscenes like those are much better than the original thanks to being able to have new close-up camera angles and more expressive character models rather than just a single static camera angle in most of the scenes of the original game.So if you played and loved this game as a kid you will definitely love this remaster as it feels exactly like playing the original with a fresh coat of paint (you can also turn on a filter to make it look closer to the original game if you want that) and if you're just a person who loves cute platformers looking for something new and fun that gets progressively harder with a nice challenge and a good dramatic story then this is the game for you!

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa 2 is my favorite game of all time.  It was massively influential on me as a child in ways I did not even fully comprehend until years of introspection as an adult. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this to support Klonoa, and I'd do it again, but I can't in good conscience call this version of Door to Phantomile a good representation of the game. I can't even call it Door to Phantomile (DtP). 1.) Original sounds are great to have, and 2.) Updated graphics are fun to behold for longtime fans. Gameplay. This is supposed to be one of (if not THE) best platforming games to come out of the original Playstation's lifecycle, and I agree with that sentiment as someone that has played it since the late 90s/early aughts. However, this version of "DtP" completely botches the feel of the platforming—THE CRUX OF THE GAME. If I had to describe the platforming here, I'd use two words:  and  as compared to the PS1 versions' tight and predictable experience. Period point blank it is not a faithful representation of the original DtP in the most important area: .When Klonoa lands after a jump, the momentum abruptly stops for a few frames, giving the screen a sort of "hang up" feeling, which adds absolutely nothing to the experience. When Klonoa is fluttering, towards the end of the flutter, he will just as abruptly shoot forward. When Klonoa is near any ledge, it's all too easy to simply fall, or more aptly slip, right off it.Even with the original version's shortcomings, it blows this version out of the water in every important metric.Buy the collection if you must, but do yourself a favor and play the original by any means necessary if you're interested in the Klonoa games.

_childDocuments_.review: So as far as being remakes; they're pretty alright. Visually, they definitely upped the graphics. ESPECIALLY in Klonoa 2 (Klonoa 1 feels a bit weaker compared to the Wii-Remake, but still solid nonetheless).But there is some issues; Some audio bugs with specific (normally louder) SFX not playing properly, or visual bugs with animations not working properly, but relatively minor issues in most cases.As far as individual games are concerned; Some of the best Puzzle Platformers (though I use this term VERY loosely) in my experience.Klonoa 1 definitely defines the formula, both with a story that is easy to follow, yet hits some fairly heavy themes later on.  Great levels that make great use of the "pick up and throw" mechanics, and level design that intuitively guides you on how you can fully use these to equip you with the tools for later.Klonoa 2 improves on it with both new level styles, more options, and much more vibrant level design, without relying on some of the labrynthian design Klonoa 1 used for secrets and such (side routes for goodies in levels are a lot easier to tell). The story is definitely a lot heavier, than the first one, but it plays off of the first one regardless (It also tells some life lessons that I think many people could stand to learn; ).Visually, both games are a treat for the senses. They are very beautiful worlds with unique scenery (especially the second one) that really drive the "Unusual and unnatural" world vibe, without relying on some tried tropes such as simply using weird buildings.Audio; The music is fantastic, and the dialogue being in their own "Phantomillian" language really adds a nice layer of whimsy to the game.Challenge-wise, aside from devious bonus levels and 100% completion (and not even for achievements; I mean the TRUE 100% of getting all gemstones in all level), the games are fairly easy. You might take a few tries but they were made on the more forgiving side.Overall, it's easy for me to say Klonoa 2 specifically is one of if not my single all-time favourite games, and you get the first game alongside it which is a really good title in its own right. A VERY strong recommendation from me for those who haven't played it, and even for those who have and want to revisit these phantasmical lands.

_childDocuments_.review: I really thought Klonoa was a girl for so many years… the filthy things I did with his picture… makes me shudder to think about.I still can’t believe Klonoa is back and is getting more popular. Klonoa is the best platformer Nintendo never made. Klonoa just has that legendary design that makes you immediately fall in love with, and like Bomberman is the perfect blend of cute and cool. I mean if there’s one character that can rivalise Kirby’s cuteness, it’s Klonoa.Klonoa has been in the back of my mind forever, and not just because of all the masturbation. Of all the characters meant to be “the original mascot” of the early era of gaming… he was the one I always wanted to play, and by far is my favorite looking. So when I saw the Klonoa series getting a remaster… you know my childhood self felt complete.It’s one of the few games I vividly remember to this day. Something about it really captured me, despite the very simple gameplay. The story pulls at your heart strings sometimes. I still have fond memories of playing Lunatea’s Veil with my dad when game store rentals were a thing. Klonoa feels like the kind of game Nintendo used to make, with its cute characters and colorful worlds hiding dark undertones and novel gameplay style. The controls are tight and the overall aesthetic of the game is very pleasant to look at. They perfectly captured the bright and vibrant feel of the series as a whole. The gameplay also feels very good and engaging. It really gets you to think hard about your next moves and what you need to do to advance.There has also been some slight tweaks to movement, as well as how the wind bullet behaves compared to the originals. In particular, trying to catch enemies in the air or in inclines/declines is much harder as it seems the wind bullet has a smaller hitbox to capture enemies. You adapt to it pretty quick though.I think it’s worth noting that while the mechanics are simple, as the games go on the layering of all the different enemy types and puzzles get more and more complex and they’re a true joy to tackle. They do a lot with a little and it’s quite remarkable. It’s a really good remaster of two really good and fun games. I wouldn’t say that they’re perfect, but I’d say it’s mostly just nitpicking. It’s also a love letter to the PS1 and PS2 action/adventure platformer era. Really worth buying if you want to get into the series or just don’t want the hassle of old consoles.These are truly gems and it’s surprising how little known they seem to be. Klonoa still stands out because it shows mature story telling themes in a children’s media and if you’ve been paying attention to the quality of platformers lately, good story telling is in very short supply. Klonoa will always be a nostalgic joy for me.  I am absolutely happy it’s getting love even if just for a bit from their company.  Out of all the platforming series’ that have fallen into obscurity, Klonoa deserves another chance, and hopefully, if the Phantasy Reverie Series goes well, we might just get that long awaited Klonoa 3.10/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Well well well... as a huge, huge fan of the game on PlayStation, I obviously wanted to give a shot to the remake. And after finishing it, the word to describe is : missed, unfortunaly. We can see through the game that it got not polished at all.The graphics are faithful to today's standards, they look really good. Some details are missing, not a big deal ; but some are clearly rushed, for example the Ghadius little statues that instead of falling in sand, just go from one picture to another. The ghosts appears abruptely, the Moon Tower doesn't look anything like the majestic one that appears in the original game, in the fight with Ghadius ennemies appear and disappear abruptely, the transitions for boss fights are missing, for the 6-2 it doesn't make any sense ; the transition visuals between inside and outside Ghadius's wheel are missing ; and I can keep going on.Which brings me to the next point : in term of programing, it works, but we can clearly see it got made with speedrun in mind, but to a very bad extent. As a result, some ennemies go too fast, ending up in cheap deaths because of what looks like a weird hitbox during these times. The cage in 6-2 where we have to catch a bird was a nightmare to deal with, having to try 10 times before catching something clearly in sight ; the boss battle in 4-2 was bad, not being able to see properly where birds were close enough to be catched ; the transition of day and night in 5-2 very important to be shown and heard for the player is missing, and so on. I got hit and lost lifes due to all these flaws, when I go through the original game dozens of times flawlessly ; and I felt bad for players who want to discover the game for the first time, having to deal with all of this.And this brings me to the final point : the game is alas not faithful to the original. Not only the graphics are hit and miss, the programming is below average, but the pace of the game is too fast to be fully enjoyed, not being able to skip dialogs at our own will like the original, and with a default pace that goes too slow or too fast, like a bad rollercoaster. Add to that the details missing, the cheap difficulty and kills, and that terrible ending completely different from the original game : for the sake of "standards", it just lost the awesome gameplay and the majestic poetry that the original game offered, that made thousands of players remember as one of the best game ever made back then.You know what I thought when reaching the end of this remake ? Buy it to get the rights, then play the original ones with an emulator. This is the best thing you can do, and what I highly recommend to really get the full experience of the fantastic world of Klonoa.

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa has made a grand return with not just one, but two remasters. I’m a big platformer fan, especially for games from this era, so I was excited to give it a shot.The games play as 2.5D platformers, although the second game does feature a lot more 3D stuff. Both are good at what they set out to do: straightforward, yet fun platforming. The game mechanics are introduced at a steady rate, the environments are easily some of the best I have seen in this genre in years, and I was a really big fan of the dual purpose that enemies serve. One one hand, they are enemies and can cause you damage, but on the other, most have some sort of unique ability that can be activated only after you grab them.It’s a lot like Kirby in this way and it works really well with the level design, hiding just enough secrets to keep exploration interesting, but without going overboard to the point of tedium. There’s always something new to find, some new boss to take down, some new environment to explore - it’s pretty good at keeping up the variety, although it is also important to note that both games combined take roughly eight hours to clear. Sounds short, but honestly, it’s perfectly fine and might even be a bit longer than it needs to.I say that because the second game does resort to a bit of backtracking with some of its levels. A bit disappointing to see in place of entirely new stuff, but again, it doesn’t go overboard there.What it does go overboard on - at least in the second game’s case - is the story. There is easily like six or seven times more dialogue in the second game compared to the first and honestly, a lot of it is not necessary. Not to say that the story is bad, but maybe half of it could have been done away with and nothing of value would be lost.So while the second game may be a massive upgrade in terms of general gameplay and level design, it does have some faults of its own and I’m still struggling to decide which of the two was my favorite with this in mind. Regardless, I had a great time with both and the good vastly outweighs the bad in both games.On the remaster front, the game is solid. There's updated graphics, high resolution support, uncapped frame rates, customizable controls, and some new additions like difficulty options and a local co-op mode. I played it without any sort of technical issues at 4k 144fps and the controls are simple enough that it’s fine on both controller and keyboard and mouse.A few things to note though. The anti-aliasing option appears to be broken as switching it between off and 16x does not produce any noticeable difference, even when zoomed in. I was also not a fan of how aggressive the bloom setting was and ended up keeping that toggled off. Otherwise, the settings are fine.Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series is a great remaster of two fun games. Solid platforming, fantastic level design, great music, and the remaster does a nice job touching things up for modern platforms. It’s a nostalgic experience for sure and one I would recommend to platforming fans.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Tepidly recommending this if it's on sale. As someone who did not play the original PS1/PS2 versions I came into these games blind and am not influenced by nostalgia. Both games have a very dreamlike setting with floaty, ethereal soundtracks to match the visuals. Gameplay is typical 2D platforming fair but most levels require thinking to traverse as enemies are placed very purposely to help the player solve environmental puzzles. There are multiple difficulty options and visual filters which allow you to tweak things to your liking, although I will say I prefer Klonoa 2 over Door to Phantomile due to the latter having frustrating, uneven difficulty spikes in the 6th vision. Both games also suffer from some input lag and the controls can lack responsiveness at times leading to some cheap deaths. Overall I had some fun punctuated by extremely frustrating moments but the games have a certain charm you just don't get these days.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a hot minute since Klonoa has had... well, anything. We're talking the last entry being a Wii remake of the first game in 2009. Here we are again with both the first and second games remastered for modern consoles!Having played the originals repeatedly, I am a bit familiar with what was changed or done differently. This remaster seems to have overall weaker animations for cutscenes, and some scenes appear to be quite different like the first scene with Grandpa which now takes place outside instead of indoors like with the Wiimake. There also appears to be some minor audio balancing issues, and Balue appears to be less hilariously loud. While this can be a bummer to some, I find that some of the more positive aspects this remaster bundle brings to be nice. For one, Klonoa 2 is finally in more hands, which seemed like it'd be impossible. Secondly, Door to Phantomile now has level select from the beginning, no longer do you need to beat the game to get that. The levels are faithful to the original, with only minor changes like preventing the camera from drunkenly swinging around. Additionally, Klonoa no longer slides to a standstill in Door to Phantomile leading to a more responsive feeling flow to his movement. Overall, I'd say the remaster is fine. It's not a *perfect* one, but I'm overall just happy to have the boy back. I do kinda hope they update the cutscene animations at some point, however, as some do not capture the mood nearly as well as the originals.
