I think that Klonoa 1 is one of the cleanest, most concise and confident platformers of its era, and is a must play. I think Klonoa 2 is also phenomenal, but its levels tend to go on for just a bit too long for my tastes, which keeps it from reaching the heights of the first. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:Lovely crafted worlds where nothing looks out of place and everything pulls you in, perfectly designed platforming gameplay and level design where every game mechanic gets its due without getting stale, immersive and very emotive score, lovable characters, surprisingly touching and meaningful story that reveals an important life lesson.Cons:I think the graphics should've been polished a bit more, it looks like a Noughties' game. It was a bit sad comparing the way the game looks to the way it could've looked with current technological capabilities.The complete neglect of retouching the audio in any way really bummed me out when I first heard Ghadius' scratchy voice sounding just as awfully compressed as it did in the PSX original. Spyro and Crash showed how to do it right.I noticed a handful of localisation issues, but the fact that I'm even bringing this up shows that I've run out of serious complaints (the combined presence of these latter two issues points towards budget constraints though - the Klonoa franchise isn't on the same level of recognition as GTA, so at least they have an excuse for a flawed remaster, and it's still a fantasticatrillion times more polished than the GTA Turdogy).Comparison between the games:Klonoa 1 starts off easy but the difficulty ramps up quickly towards the end. Klonoa 2 starts more challenging than 1, but seems to have a milder difficulty curve.Klonoa 1 has more polished gameplay, whereas Klonoa 2's is more varied.Klonoa 1's dialogue is efficient and to the point, whereas Klonoa 2 sometimes gets lost in exposition and banter - in those situations it's like an anime, but the mediocre kind that lives off of goofy clichees and fan service. I doubt the writing direction was the same. Luckily it can be sped upIn general I think Klonoa 1 is a more well-rounded and pleasing package. Klonoa 2 sometimes tries very hard to expand upon its predecessor's mechanics, and it doesn't always work too well.All in all highly a very recommendable purchase, not the least because they're using it as a gauge for the future of the franchise. I really look forward to Klonoa 3!

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I love and recommend this collection, I think you should wait until it goes on sale, unless you're already a die hard fan of this series and don't care. It's absolutely not a bad remaster but it does feel kinda cheap in places, and £40 is pretty pricey for what it is IMO. Anyways, it's pretty damn good. I'm not a massive platformer guy but Klonoa has very quickly become one of my all time favorites. Gameplay, writing, music, environments, it's all great. If you're interested then just go for it, and go in blind. It's a simple game with simple abilities, but the complexity comes from level design and enemy placement, forcing you to gradually master Klonoa's moves. It's certainly not among the hardest platformers of course, but you will still be challenged in fun ways. I can't really talk about what I love without spoiling the game (also I'd need a full damn essay) so I'll just list a couple of things I think this remaster messed up. My main issues really just boil down to aspects of the game being serviceable, but they should have been better. Largely the visuals. Textures are kinda meh in many places, and I feel like more could have been done with the cutscenes. Character animations are just straight up reused in Lunatea's Veil, which isn't a terrible thing, but imagine how cool it would have been to have a truly modern remaster of the same game instead of just reusing stuff from the PS2. Animations in general are just kinda low effort here. More care in these places would really help to justify the price. I understand not wanting to go all out on a game franchise that historically has been a financial failure, but if you're not going the extra mile then drop the price a little.Gameplay wise, there's just a few minor bugs I ran into. Collision near the edge of platforms feels pretty jank, and I had a weird collision bug that completely blocked me from completing Door to Phantomile's Extra Vision, I couldn't go through an open passageway on flat ground. No idea how they messed that up but OK. Overall, I feel like this remaster is lacking a lot of polish and love. As cool as it is to see a beloved but dead franchise come back, I do wish they put in more effort to actually make the game feel like it was actually made in 2022 by a Triple-A company. Like I said before, it just feels kinda cheap in many places, and part of me can't shake the feeling that this is nothing more than a quick cash grab, with no real intentions of showing Klonoa any real care. I really hope I'm wrong. Regardless of the issues, it's a solid remaster of some pretty old games. I'm glad I played them and I'm sure I'll replay them again and again in the future. This collection is a great way for newcomers to play these games on a wide range of modern platforms, without having to spend stupid amounts of cash on original copies and hardware, or just pirating them. I just wish they did a little more. Or brought the price down.Edit time: I found out what caused that weird collision bug in DtP's Extra Vision. The collision in some areas bug out if your FPS is too high. Enabling VSync fixed it.

_childDocuments_.review: After completing both games, I feel it's time to make a review.Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series is a great remaster of the first and second Klonoa game during the PS1/2 era.These games were criminally underrated and i'm very glad people can experience these games again or for the first time.Despite the games having a cartoony and cute look, they do contain some serious story plotlines and keep everybody engaged whatever their age may be.The visuals of the remaster are much closer to their original games, even if the first game on the collection is actually based on the Wii Remake, but have made the visuals more cartoony and made Klonoa's appereance as he did in the PS1 game.However, it's disapointing that they've used the compressed voices of the characters in both games from the playstation games.This is much more noticable in the first klonoa game and I would had prefered if they used Klonoa's phantomille voice from the Wii-remake instead.The music still remains as good as it did before, especially hearing the windmill theme again.The Klonoa games on consoles are a 2.5D platformer and also has interactions with both the back and forground.Klonoa moves left and right and jump like most platformers, but is also able to pick up enemies and throw them as projectiles at enemies or out of reach objects.These enemies can also be used as a double jump and in Klonoa 2 some of the enemies have special abilities when you grab them to traverse through the level.Both games can be rather easy, but once you've completed the story, you'll unlock a hard mode to try the game again if you desire.they've also done a excellect job for newcomers of gaming or young players, to make a tutoial that explains enemies and controls as you play through the game (these settings can be turned off)I really don't wanna spoil anything storywise, as I feel this is one of the main enjoyments of the series, but believe me it's really good on both games.Sadly I feel this might be Klonoa's last chance to get a third mainline game, as Bandai Namco has mentioned wanting to see how intrested people are in this game before considering a third game (whatever the words are true or not I cannot tell).if you've played the game and enjoyed it, please do share your experience with other people!Our Wahoo boy definitely deserves to show he's ready for a third mainline game!

_childDocuments_.review: This collection is overall great. I've been a fan of Klonoa ever since I got into the series when I was a teen. Both are fun in there own ways, but there are flaws to be had. Klonoa 1 (my favorite) I still do like in terms of the gameplay, visuals and story. Thank god for the devs to use the original scripted for the game and also making characters emote more which is what made it touching. Yet looking at this and the wii version I'm more astonished with how this game looks in alot of areas. For some flaws, I'm mad that some things aren't fixed and some new problems are put in. Some of the visuals fail to do there job. Mostly in world 6 where the background is static. The model for the final boss looks like a Sonic adventure DX model and the ending is still the same as the wii. I have found issues with trying to grab enemies (This goes for both games). Not all the time, but it does mean I have to be a bit more percise. I'd also say if you're new to the game or you're not so good at platformers, take my advice and play the game on easy. The game is challenging and your result may differ. So just to save the trouble I'd say start on easy and work your way up from there (Not a flaw on the game, but something to just keep in mind). For Klonoa 2 I can tell ALOT of work was put into the game. The visuals are over the top great and I feel are what stand out the most. Gameplay is still the same. Not too complex as Klonoa 1 is, though it can be sometimes. I'm amazed by how the time took there time to go ahead and recreated all the artwork in the gallery. An amazing step up from the original. Would say I am disappointed that Klonoa and other characters don't emote much in this game. A big downgrade considering they emoted alot in the orignal, but I'd say it's ok. Some visuals I'm not a fan of. Pacifically the fun park level. Stuff like the lighting, the sky and the mansion part look dull. Also not a game I tend to come back to much. I do love this game, but alot of levels tend to go on longer then they need too and bosses aren't as challenging as they were in one. All in all, I had alot of fun with both games and it's SO good seeing Klonoa be alive again after so many years. On top of that if this game gets alot of love we might be seeing Klonoa 3 get it's wish. So I ask you to please buy this game and save Klonoa from sudden death again.

_childDocuments_.review: This collection has helped me to experience two great games at a somewhat fair price. As a first time player, I really liked my time with both games.Klonoa: Door to Phantomile is a charming PS1 game. Using the Wii remake as a base, the game has been wonderfully remastered with assets and aesthetics closely matching that of the original PS1 version: a best of both worlds. Charming presentation and characters give a long way to make this game the classic it is as well as the tight platforming which can get tricky by the end of the game. Some tearjerking moments are to be expected when divulging in with the story. You might not be ready for that ending.Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil is, in my opinion, a more polished sequel to the first game. Dropping into a new world with new themes gives this game it's own boost of identity, despite the gameplay remaining largely similar. Some neat gimmicks like a board are a welcome addition to the gameplay as well. The story this time can feel more thought-provoking and meaningful, which I think some people could really relate to. Presentation in this game is top-notch otherwise. The removal of the original iteration's cel-shading might take away from its personality, but this new look to match with the first game suits it pretty well.Overall, my experience with these versions of the game have been flawless with minimal to no bugs during my playthroughs of each game. As a first time player, it was a joy to experience these classic games for myself and see what all the hype was about. I cannot recommend this collection enough, just for the fact that it might potentially spark interest for more games in the Klonoa series in the future. Heck, I'd go as far as saying that Klonoa absolutely deserves a third mainline game. But please, enjoy these classics here in their near definitive forms.

There are a few awkward moments here and there, since it's more of a graphical touch-up than a full on remake, but having the game escape PS2 purgatory in a vibrant new light is extremely welcomed.This collection is well worth a platformer fan's time. _childDocuments_.review: We've been waiting for this title for years and I'm happy it's finally arrived.Here you get two quirky platformers in one bundle ($20 for each game in USD), both the first game,  (specifically the 2008 Wiimake version tweaked) and its proper followup,  making it's first multi-platform debut following its original 2001 PS2 release.Overall, Monkeycraft did a fairly good job on these remakes. There are quite a few issues, notably the sub-optimal performance of the first game, some physics jank on lower frame rates, audio looping bugs, and some subjective design choices that I personally wasn't fond of.But regardless, I still wholeheartedly recommend this compilation on any platform. _childDocuments_.review: Both Klonoa 1 and 2 are still solid platformer entries. Nothing that redefines the genre, but good for anyone who's looking for something else to play. Presentation for this series is one of its big strong points with the cute art direction and amazing soundtracks carrying the experience for both games quite a bit. The games themselves are short & sweet adventures that are to the point.Klonoa 2 as far as I see it is going to be the main reason to get this collection. It's the type of hidden gem the PS2 era was full of. Besides being the better game in my opinion with its more involved platforming and inventive level design; it just gets treated by this remaster the best. Klonoa 2 gets an almost complete overhaul here: Remodeled environments, new character/enemy models, completely new textures, modern rendering pipeline with lighting, shadows, materials, etc. It almost comes across as a brand new game at times, the uplift is pretty impressive. My main complaint is they changed the art style from the original which went for darker color tones and an almost cel-shaded aesthetic with its character outlines.Klonoa 1 is based off of the Wii remake and still feels very close to it graphically with the main differences being the few new character models, slightly sharper textures (with a few being redone), and lighting/shadows (the implementation of which is kinda spotty). Improvements from the remaster are more all over the place here compared to the second game. Also it looks a bit worse than the Wii ver. in some areas? Like the water in Jugpot lacking its reflection/refraction or the bloom missing from certain interior areas like caves. That said these are mostly nitpicks in the grand scheme, it still looks perfectly fine and is more than serviceable for anyone who's playing it for the first time.Keep in mind these games are short, like VERY short. Beating Klonoa 1 will take 3-4 hours casually and the second game is a bit longer but still is only a 4-5 hour playthrough. Going for 100% can a add a few hours to the runtime, but you're still looking at just 15-20+ hours total and that's a high estimate. $40 is probably going to be a big ask for a lot of people realistically speaking. If you can manage to get it on sale for $20 or less then it's totally worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa is very dear to me. These games helped me through a difficult time in my childhood, and DtP in particular really resonated with a freshly-depressed twelve-year-old me. Even if there is no more Klonoa after this point, even if he's wah'd his last hoo, I'm content. Do I have nitpicks? Of course. Do I care? Not really: It's Klonoa. It's a game so sure of its identity and so unlike any other game of its time. It's a game with Most importantly, it makes me and a lot of other people happy. Klonoa is a Certified Little Guy (C) and always will be. He deserves this and much more. <3

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa has finally returned from the ashes right on time for his 25th Anniversery and now has never been a better time to be a fan. It has been months since the announcement from that Nintendo Direct back in Feburary and now it's finally here~Klonoa 1 is pretty much a glowed up remake of the Nintendo Wii remake released back in 2008 but with major improvements such as remodeling the characters to fit closer to their Ps1 counterparts, a few facial and animation fixes, and best of all, reusing the original ps1 script where in the Wii Remake, Klonoa's dialogue was pretty much hammed down to him just being silent which doesn't work for his character being a happy-go-lucky child itching for adventure.Animation may have been slightly improved but it still uses the robotic and stiff ones from the Wii Remake sadly.Even so, the first game still plays decently well and is pretty much an accessible way to play DtP as opposed to the Ps1 version which is insultingly expensive as well as it's Wii counterpart.Klonoa 2 looks fantastic. This was my first actually playing the sequel so I sadly have no memories of playing the original version on Ps2. But looking at it graphically compared to the original, it stands out and looks incredibly colorful and bright, much like a lot of classic platformers of the past. Klonoa 2 is even more challenging than the first at least to me because I lost too many lives to count, but still managed to push myself to the finish line with a few left intact. Gameplay is smooth and incredibly fun to replay over and over.Overall, this is a solid product. I know a lot of people seem to harp on it being $40 (at least here in the US) but I think it's a fair price for 2 solid remasters of an IP that needs to come back. And come back he did.This should also be solid proof to Bandai Namco that we don't want the same generic anime fighting game released by them over and over and over again. We would like to have fresh new ideas, possible new IP's, and... maybe... just mabye... a well deserved third entry in Klonoa's future?if kingdom hearts 3 could happen, so could this. Here us well, Bamco! Klonoa deserves a second chance!!

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game to keep te franchise alive, but it needs work. tl;dr; bring back ps1 cutscenes of Door to PhantomileOh man, I've been waiting for this game for a long time. I've played Klonoa DtP alot when i was younger and it was able to make me feel a certain type of way no other game has done. That being said, this review of both games is from a perspective of someone who has only played DtP back in the day, it could come across as negative and nitpicky, but that's becouse I do really love these games and i want it to succeed, i bought the game on the switch and pc. If I refer to the "original" game, i'm talking about the Ps1 version, not the wii version.Gameplaywise it's still as fun as the original version. There are a few changes compared to the original game, but other than that, faithfull to the original. Through the journey I've stumbled upon a few audio bugs, where in 1 level the volume was to low of the background music, and sometimes there were sfx sounds not playing when peforming an action. They should also fix the dialogue boxes, it takes wayyy to long per sentence.The biggest problem I have with this remaster, is the lack of effort in the new cutscenes. The story is something that made the original game great, it needed the beautifull cutscenes and music to really deliver the story and the feel of the game, so i think the cutscenes are a  part of what made the game great. The cutscenes of the remaster is just, liveless and not well made, Klonoa smiling when talking when his grandpa get's murdered, the ending, everything is still green before the song of rebirth like nothing happend. and the animations were just bad and i could go on. I really hope there will be mods that could include the original cutscenes, then i'll actually will recommend it to people. otherwise they'll just get the wrong impression of what the game is in my opinion. Playing with the pixel mode on kinda fixed the bad facial expressions becouse they were harder to see. So that made it bearable. I saw there was a original sfx mod on steam aswell, will take a look at that too and play the game again. I don't want to ♥♥♥♥ all over the game and make it look bad, so here are the possitives. I LOVE the music of the original, i really resonate with that and i'm glad they haven't changed it. I still had a ton of fun playing this game I think the worlds and characters looked good, it still had the charm the original game has imo. The ending still made me cry, probably becouse of nostalgia, but I hope it delivers to new players aswell. I like the newly added features for replayability.Once again, it might come across as really negative, But i LOVE the game that's why i'm going hard on it. If you want it to succeed, it needs to deliver.I've never played this game in the past so i was really looking forward to it. I'll use DtP as a reference for this review.I start with the negatives again.Through the beginning of game, I didn't feel the magic the first game had. the music was less unique and it didn't feld like Klonoa music. Also the music didn't reflect the situation really, a reactor was about to blow up, and the game just played some chill jazzy music, which i think wasn't Klonoa-like at all, If you compare it to DtP that had different types of music for everything. I know this was never meant to be a DtP version 2, becouse LV takes place in a whole different world. I didn't like the dialogues and story as much as DtP's, to me it feels like this was more focussed to children, where DtP has some more serious ♥♥♥♥ going on with more scarier looking villains. I think that makes it more interessting for adults aswell.So i thought that was it and i'll just continue to play and enjoy what the game is, but halfway through, when i arrived at Ishras ark, the feeling of DtP came back. That ark looked awesome and is exactly that style that i like about Klonoa. Everything from that point was going uphill for me. The music started to get those lovely wacky panflutes again, the levels looked more fantasy-like and i just really enjoyed playing through that. I love the new creatures and mechanics in the game ,It was fun to play through.I loved playing through the series, and it made me appreciate the unique art-style even more, DtP needs some work as mentioned above. I really hope this series get the attention it deserves, I would love to see a modern Klonoa game with the technology of today. I don't know what direcion the devs would want to go. I feel like DtP is more child-ish looking, except for the villains. The story feels more grown-up.LV Looks less child-ish except for some characters, but the dialogues feel more child-ish. IF there is ever going to be a Klonoa 3, i hope it will have the feeling and music like DtP has, more fairytale-like and a more hard hitting story like DtP with the gameplay from LV. I'm biased becouse i've only played DtP in the past, so I understand that there are different standpoints and preferences and i respect that, please respect mine aswell.

_childDocuments_.review: The two games that defined one of Namco's most overlooked franchises.Klonoa is a 2.5D platformer where you can capture enemies and throw them as a projectile in five possible directions : down (for a double jump), left, right, front or back. The fact that you can interact with the foreground or background was innovative when the first game came out, and even today, it's still an unique way to handle combat and puzzle in a side-scroller.Apart from the gameplay, the games are known for their colorful aesthetic, memorable soundtrack, lovable protagonist, imaginative levels, fun bosses and bittersweet stories. They're a bit short and easy, especially the first one, but I prefer when games don't overstay their welcome. Both games are among my favorite plateformers of their era and I can't recommend them enough.To elaborate about this specific version:- Door to Phantomile is very similar to the Wii remake in terms of visuals, but the more contested changes are either optional (like the easier difficulty) or absent (like the redesign and the redub). I still think the PS1 classic had more charm, but that one is hard to find nowadays. This new version looks nice, plays well, is faithful to the original and is the most convenient to play.- Lunatea's Veil is pretty much the PS2 classic with cleaner graphics, a smoother frame rate and faster load times. I have no complaints whatsoever, this is my new preferred way to play this game.All in all, this is a great package and I'm happy these two games are finally available on PC and modern consoles.
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: Ah where do I begin.Those of you who grew up in the 90's might remember this adorable cutesy game on Playstation called "Klonoa: Door to Phantomile." A revolutionary 2.5D platformer that punches you in the gut with it's story. Bandai Namco trademarked this back in 2020 under the name "Klonoa 1+2 Encore" and then in 2022 they unveiled the official title after some trademarks showed up in December 2021 under the name "Klonoa : Phantasy Reverie Series" which of course is the final name of this package. If you have any desire to relive or experience a true platformer that has an enriching story and endearing characters and development, sit back as I review, Klonoa : Phantasy Reverie Series!What is Klonoa?Klonoa is a cat-rabbit hybrid or a cabbit if you prefer, he has huge ears that allow him to hover briefly for a moment, he has one source of attack, using the spirit in the ring to fire wind bullets that when impacting with enemies cause them to inflate, this can then be used as a projectile but also as a means of utilising Klonoa's strongest feat, his double jump.You'll come to realize how useful the double jump is by the time you get to Vision 3-2.This is a game that combines two of Klonoa's previous escapades into a neat little nostalgic package.Klonoa : Phantasy Reverie Series is a revitilisation of the I.P. by remastering the first two games in his series, the first being "Klonoa: Door to Phantomile" and the second being "Klonoa 2 : Lunatea's Veil".Klonoa is a dream traveller, and I mean he travels to different dimensions to solve their problems before eventually returning to his own dimension from which he came. And if you're like me, you probably bawled your eyes out at the ending of the first game or even the second game.He has a friend called Huepow in the first game and they bond more and more over their adventure as they take off in the land of Phantomile to stop an evil sorcerer known as Ghadius from plunging the world into a never ending nightmare, to do this he plots against the fabled moon kingdom only heard of in legends so people didn't know for sure if it existed and kidnapped the diva Lephise who is the only one who can restore a dying world with her beautiful yet sombre "Song of Rebirth". You'll utilise all of Klonoa's trademark moves as you traverse gorgeous environments, from windy green hills to a literal temple in the sky filled with lava traps and loads of hazards that want you dead. The game clocks in at about 3-4 hours if you go through in one run and collect everything, going for completion may take longer as you need to collect 150 dream stones in each level and free each of the 6 phantomillians trapped in each stage referred to as Visions when you keep to the dream aspect.Klonoa 2 has a much more driven narrative as it has much more diverse characters and not one but THREE main characters who accompany you, Lolo a priestess in training wants to save the world with her courage and desire for a better world, but she can come across as cumbersome as she's quite naive which you'll see in the game as the story unfolds.Popka which I have no idea what he actually is but he is quite quirky as he will not hesitate to take a stab at Klonoa when he fails a simple task. Speaking of Klonoa, he got a redesign in this game, sporting all blue outfit, his cap is now reversed so the front is at the back and the back is at the front, like a baseball cap, and he sports some vibrant Red and White shoes similar in design to Sonic The Hedgehog which in turn is why his design was changed, to look cooler.The villains this time.....well....that's the thing, there isn't really a main villain as Leorina and her subordinate known as Tat who is a white and black cat who can split into two halves that act independently but share the same mind so they are never unaware of their goal as you pursue them during play.Your main task here is to ring the bells of harmony and acquire the necessary power to traverse to the ruined kingdom of sorrow and "Save" the King of Sorrow. This game has another gut punching ending that I won't spoil so please experience it for yourself!Can I recommend this game?Absolutely, this game series has lay dormant for 14 years since the last game released which was Klonoa on the Nintendo Wii. Bandai Namco express interest in this series once again, please support this series and buy "Klonoa: Phantasy Reverie Series" today and show them that we want more Klonoa!Thank you for reading!Drax

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: I feel like they could've done so much more with the remasters. Right now I'd say it's just decent as a remastered collection, but if you're a fan of Klonoa, you might like this. And if you want to play Lunatea, this is a good (also legal) way to go about it.This is a lengthy one...So, I found out about this game in April (since I don't watch Nintendo Direct). Ever since, I waited to play it. Even while knowing that the first game was going to be the Wii remake instead of the PS1 version. I am writing this review after clearing both games, including Extra Visions.I'll try positives first.- I like some of the visual changes to both versions. Sometimes. Character models look great (especially both Klonoas, Lolo and the Priestess), colors are nice (even though it can also blend background and foreground together if the color tone is too similar).- This remaster allowed me to see details I'd somehow missed before (like how  and ). That, or it's just me.- The option to play without lives and with massively buffed health on Easy Mode is very welcome to those that might want to just play the game, without getting frustrated over Vision Overs that can set back dozens of minutes of progress. And, while I also appreciate having a Hard Mode, I think its conditions are absurd. I tried it and it's...well, really hard. One hit knocks you out, after all. But I think I can beat it...someday.- I also appreciate how achievements have nothing involving the mode you play or getting 150 Dream Stones in a Vision. It could've been Super Meat Boy's "deathless chapters" achievements all over again for me.- No English dub (especially as the default)...But again, a lot of rough edges on this revision of a lost gem.- I can feel how Klonoa's model is smaller in Phantomile and, while the model looks quite nice, his Wind Bullet's height from the ground was adjusted. There's a problem with that:  If you mess with heights of things, you should ALWAYS check that they still work. (Then again, this could be just a "me" problem.)- Speaking of Wind Bullet, I feel like it's actually shorter for me than it's supposed to be on Normal Mode? Is there something wrong with my setup or is it the game? I can't even tell anymore.- While I said colors were good, sometimes I find it hard to see pits or doorways since it's not as distinct as on the original versions. My first death was actually falling into a pit in Phantomile 1-2 because I couldn't see it at all.- I found both games frustrating to play at times. Sometimes movement felt unresponsive, even though I pressed the button. Especially when chaining grab jumps, oh boy... Also, why was there momentum remaining when I release movement inputs in midair? This is not good with tight platforming .- I found the animations too stiff to feel immersed in Phantomile. Might just be the Wii charm but it's not for me. I would've enjoyed the stories a lot more if the stiffer animations were updated somewhat. - There was still not a way to .- Small one: Text progresses automatically in Phantomile but has to sometimes be manually progressed in Lunatea. There's no setting (that I could see) that would toggle this for both games.And a few comments on top of pros and cons:- Is it just me, or is it harder to gain lives while playing in Normal Mode, compared to the original games? I remember playing the original PS2 version of Lunatea, having dozens of lives by endgame. Here, I had less than 10 which got me nervous about a possible Vision Over around the next corner. (Though in the end, I finished both games without a single Vision Over, yay me.)- - It took me 3 days to finish Spyro Reignited Trilogy on PS4 back in 2018, it took me less than a day to finish Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series. I feel ripped off a bit.- In Lunatea, music doesn't fade like it does in the original version during some cutscenes; examples include  and .Is it worth the price? I'd say...probably?You get a good way to play Klonoa (legally too) on all modern platforms, especially Lunatea's Veil which used to be only on PS2 since 2001.Even so, this collection still has a lot of rough edges so 40€ would've been a more appropriate price for me.(See, where I live it costs 50€, don't ask why)Despite all my complaints, it's glad to see Klonoa back after more than a decade.

_childDocuments_.review: klonoa, as a franchise, is probably one of the best out there. the style, the characters, the music and the atmosphere is all amazing. this collection of the mainline games is absolutely worth the money and the title of a proper "klonoa remaster". there's a reason why fans were begging for the franchise to make a return since it's last remake of klonoa 1 on the wii back in 2008.klonoa 1, while i feel it is the weaker of the two, is a wonderful platformer for it's time. the controls can feel a bit clunky at times, even in this remaster. klonoa 1 is still a worthwhile experience, and it sets the tone for one of, if not, the best games ever made.klonoa 2 is amazing in every way, and this remaster gives it a beautiful graphic overhaul that just makes the game all the more enjoyable. the story will pull you through all kinds of emotions, and will probably make you cry by the end. it's something everyone needs to experience for themselves. with an addition of difficulty modes anyone can play this masterpiece now.i hope this shows bandai namco that klonoa is a franchise worth developing. and i hope everyone experiencing klonoa for the first time enjoys these phenomenal games.

_childDocuments_.review: I wholly recommend both of these games. The fandom may beg you to buy it so Klonoa might be expanded upon but really, you should just nab the collection because it's a good and accessible port of two really, really good and underrated video games that recently reached cult-status.Klonoa Door To Phantomile is a charming introduction to 2.5D gameplay, but Klonoa Lunatea's Veil really steals the show and stands as one of my favourite video games of all time. So glad this little cat-rabbit-rat is finally getting the attention he deserves.So far I encountered no issues with the collection aside from some visual oddities. This is probably one of the most stable games I've seen at launch in recent years.I've seen some people complain about FPS drops, bad animation, etc. I personally only encountered a stutter once during a visually busy level and I noticed that some character models are fullbright while others are shaded. I think this may be an issue with the users' PCs rather than an issue within the game. Please use the options provided to you to lower the games' settings. I'm surprised I've seen no one talk about the compressed phantomilian voice-lines in the Door To Phantomile port. It's a shame that they never kept the uncompressed clips.I don't get the complaints about Klonoa's character model in Door To Phantomile appearing lifeless or poorly animated. It is far more expressive than the Wii version. The only thing I dislike is that they gave him this :3 kitty face mouth that doesn't suit him at all and somewhat hinders his expression. This is entirely gone in Klonoa Lunatea's Veil thankfully.
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: It's so good to see this series return with a vengeance, showing that even as almost two decades pass Klonoa is still here to show his stuff. The game feels polished and the platforming is fun as usual, Klonoa 1 being a fun little romp even if it's short. Cutscenes definitely look strange without some of the prerendered cutscene effects that really add the oomph you'd need. Still, super solid.But the biggest one for me is Lunatea's Veil. The fact that it hasn't had any support since its release back in 2001 is astounding, but finally it can be played here on PC and almost every modern console. It's such a relief to see it rise from the dead. That aside, 2 is my favorite and It looks absolutely gorgeous. I can't wait to bite into the rest of it and 100% this game. Hope everyone can give this franchise a shot, not just for the possibility of Klonoa returning in future titles, but just to play these 2 amazing games and have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa: Door to Phantomile, and Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil have been, and always will be, my two favorite games of all time.Ever since playing Klonoa 2 on ps2 as a child, I've been in love with this series and have been following it hoping for more games to come. These two games are incredible platformers with a fantastic story to each. I highly recommend giving them a try.Also if you enjoy these, try out the other games in the series.Klonoa: Moonlight Museum (a Wonderswan handheld exclusive, black and white only, but still very fun)Klonoa: Empire of Dreams (a GBA game that plays similar to Moonlight Museum, but now in color!)Klonoa 2: Dream Champ Tournament (another GBA game that plays the same as the previous, still super fun)Klonoa: Beach Volleyball (a ps1 volleyball game spinoff. Interesting choice of a game.)Klonoa Hereos: Densetsu no Star Medal (A GBA title that plays more like a top down hack and slash, probably my favorite of the handheld games)

Both of these titles run very smoothly and you probably won't experience any issues unless you're running it on a toaster.The pricing at $40 USD is a bit steep, but I've heard Bandai Namco completely butchered the regional pricing for this. _childDocuments_.review: I've played only a bit of this remaster so far, but i'm absolutely loving it.Klonoa is a game series that's gotten it's fair share of games/remakes, (one of those remakes was on wii). this is the first time that a remaster has been put on all consoles including pc. A quick little personal tidbit. I remember when i was 5 years old playing klonoa on my wii, whenever i'd get back from school i'd be super happy and excited to play more of it. countless times i replayed it and super mario galaxy 2. back then, everything just seemed perfect,playing this now, i can safely say: I feel like i'm reliving/revisiting a part of my childhood, and that makes me happy beyond belief. i'm glad they didn't mess this remake up, i'm glad it has the charm and appeal it did for me when i was younger. Back to the review though: The games ooze of charm and passion, every song on the ost tends to become my favourite song for the duration it's on for. i even find myself re-listening to tracks in my spare-timethe platforming is really polished and i love the mechanic where you can suck things up and either throw them or boost ur jump. The collectables also are very fun to get and find, they remind me of teensies from rayman legends/origins, The bosses are charming, I love the bright visuals, the cheery atmosphere. and also; the story is absolutely fun and charming, (ive used the word charming alot this review lol)Anyways; in total. you won't make a mistake by buying this game. As these two games are the pinnacle of 2d platforming.
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa, like many people before me, has left an impact when we were younger. To see this series dead in the water for so many years as it has is heartbreaking. I am happy to announce that this collection of the first 2 games is very much the definitive way to play both of these games, *especially* Klonoa 2. There have been minor graphical errors and strange audio bugs in Klonoa 1, but that is likely due to it being remastered on the framework of the market failed Wii remake, and as such are very minor nitpicks; Klonoa 2 however keeps everything in tact as is from the original version with much improved graphics and texturing. Original audio is mixed with the Wii-make's audio of Klonoa 1, but all original audio is used for Klonoa 2. As far as a remaster goes, this is perfect. While some may be upset at the lack of any additional features or some form of gameplay tweaking, getting the games as 1 to 1 as possible is exactly what you will receive here. And for Klonoa, that's all I ask for.

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa Lunatea's Veil was one of the first 4 games I ever got in a PS2 bundle back around 2001.  Of those 4 games Klonoa was my favorite and I have played that PS2 game several times since then.  I have a very strong nostalgia for this game, and it was great to find out that this franchise is getting another breath of fresh air for a new audience.  Though in classic Klonoa fashion Namco hardly advertises it so this release will probably suffer the same fate as the other releases.Now this game isn’t that hard, honestly if you don’t care for platformers or want a challenge I wouldn’t recommend it.  But if you do enjoy early 2000s platformers that also went the extra mile with a good setting, memorable soundtrack that uniquely uses alot of wind instruments, and a decent story.  Well this game became a cult classic for good reason.The remake is good, it has some quality of life stuff like the ability to skip cutscenese and all graphical options are always accessible.  Something some remakes make you have to restart or backout to change.  The sound mixing for the first game could be a lot better, voices were very soft compared to music. For the second game I really wish the baked lighting wasn’t so strong, it takes away from the mood the original was setting.  Thankfully the sound quality for the second game is great which I am glad cause I’ll say again Lunatea's Veil has a fantastic soundtrack.  Overall while I really wish both games would let you play with original graphics.  I can’t hate this remake too much.  It honestly is great to have the franchise in the spotlight again, even if just for a little while.  This remake/remaster works well enough that it isn’t just a cash grab (though it shouldn't be $40, that's a little too much).  I would recommend, though again if you care for platformers that are on the easier side.

_childDocuments_.review: These are no-frills remakes of two of the most incredible 2.5D platformers I've ever played. Stellar gameplay, lovely new visuals, and the same wonderful soundtracks place this firmly in the "must-play" category for fans of platformers such as myself. These two games are absolutely worth whatever price they may be listed for.Alright, now that you've read this review, go buy the game already!

_childDocuments_.review: To counter the devoted fanbase reviews of folks who are begging people to buy this to continue the franchise, I'm going to be a bit more real about it.I love the series, I really do. But this isn't exactly some people's idea of a great buy for $40. Depending on your skill at platforming, you might be able to beat this whole package in 7-10 hours. _childDocuments_.review: My original review went a little something like "please buy this game" like many of the other reviews when this game first came out, but I figured that I make a little more of a serious review. This game is a remaster of Klonoa (Wii) and Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil (PS2). As someone who played both the PS1 and PS2 game during as a child, I was hyped from the moment trademarks popped up for this game back in late 2019 and waited impatiently for this game to come out.The remaster of Door to Phantomile is bright and colorful graphically, occasionally to the point where it's overblown, but still a fairly welcome change considering the dull colors in the Wii remake. The controls feel very smooth (this game also has an unlocked framerate :D) and platforming feels very satisfying. Unfortunately, this remaster falls a little flat in its presentation of the story—something that the original PS1 game was renowned for. While this remaster does use the script from the original PS1 game, the animations still remain the same as the Wii remake, making core moments of the story (the  and the final ending) feel somewhat dull and expressionless. The developers also opted to use the original voice lines from the PS1 game in all its bitcrushy goodness, which could definitely turn some people away. I do appreciate the attempt to make the remaster closer to the original game, but the attempt does not feel complete here. That being said, if this is your first playthrough of Door to Phantomile, there's still a good chance that the story will make you emotional.The remaster of Lunatea's Veil follows a slightly similar trend, but I would  consider this remaster to be better than Door to Phantomile's remastering. The graphics are fairly hit-or-miss, as some areas are too bright, especially in certain areas where the game is  to be dark.But when the post-processing is done properly, the game looks  nice, arguably better than the original (wish I could put screenshots in a review lol).This remaster, like Door to Phantomile's remaster, has an issue in cutscenes where characters are just... expressionless. Bit of nerdsplaining here, but essentially, blend shape animations that were embedded in the animation in the original game were not transferred over in this remaster for whatever reason. The developers did reimplement them for animations where it was  necessary (e.g. the face Klonoa makes for "What's that supposed to mean?"), but the other animations where they did reimplement them are very minor. Also a bit of a self-plug, but I did create a mod to restore those animations from the original game, which you can download . Still, it is unfortunate that a mod is required to bring back functionality from the original game.Outside of those two issues, I don't have much else to complain about. Platforming is great, level design is a step up from Door to Phantomile, and the soundtrack is an absolute banger. It's a great remaster of the original PS2 game, and while some elements that gave the original its charm at the time (like the Gouraud + Cel-ish shading) are not present here, the changes to make the game more "up-to-date" are fairly welcome.Overall, very good remasters with a few shortcomings here and there that I really   wished they had fixed beforehand. Still the same great 2.5D platforming. Still the same amazing soundtrack. Still the same emotional storyline. Still the same wahoos. With that being said, if you're completely new to this series and looking to get into it, I cannot entirely recommend it at the base price point. $40 for a <12 hour game (usually), let alone €50 for Europeans seems too high. $30/€30 definitely seems more reasonable, and if it ever goes on sale for that price (or lower), I would recommend buying this game.Also, for nerds out there: This is a Unity game compiled using Mono rather than IL2CPP, meaning decompiling this game is trivial and modding capabilities are pretty much endless :D

_childDocuments_.review: This is a damn blessing that these two games were made accessible for everyone to play. Not only is the port decent, but the game functions very well. Great way to get into the series. Out of the two games, I think Klonoa 2 got it better in terms of the visual upgrade and just being able to play it. My only few nitpicks has to be with the 1st game. While it looks and plays good, there were some weird audio and visual issues. The game uses the voice lines from the PS1 version of the game, but has the cutscenes framed in the manner of the Wii remake which was jarring sometimes. Plus there are certain moments where it uses the Wii voice lines instead of the PS1 making at bit inconsistent. Plus certain models didn't express as much emotion as the sprites from the PS1 version. Not being able to Pause scenes was a bit of a downer as well but not the end of the world. These two games are damn good and are well worth your time. Hopfully Bandai-Namco will notice people like these games and do more with this IP.

_childDocuments_.review: I no longer have to dust off my PS2 and Wii to play my favorite childhood games, that alone is worth the price of admission.The PC port itself appears to pretty good, gameplay is very smooth with no stuttering noticed on my R5 5600X/RTX 3070 and I was able to change video settings to 1440p without any weird hiccups that you sometimes see on remasters of classic games. The graphics and menus are pretty basic, but I expect that for a by-the-numbers remaster for a niche series that hasn't seen a new release for over a decade, and they get the job done just fine.I'm just happy Bandai Namco hasn't forgotten about our good little Dream Traveler and I finally get to WAHOO on a modern system.

_childDocuments_.review: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series brings back "Klonoa: Door to Phantomile" and "Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil" remastered in one collection to fans new and old. Get ready to set off on an adventure to save the world. Released initially in 1997 by Namco, Klonoa is a side-scrolling platformer featuring a colorful character roster and vibrant game world, it's up to you as Klonoa to embark on a journey to save Phantomile. For the franchise's momentous twenty-fifth birthday, Klonoa: Door to Phantomile and Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil are receiving the remaster treatment in a two-in-one set—titled KLONOA Phantasy Reverie Series slated to hit the Nintendo Switch™, PlayStation®5, PlayStation®4, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, and Steam. The graphics have received an elegant revamp while Klonoa's beloved world and classic gameplay have been faithfully preserved. The remaster also features an adjustable difficulty level, allowing franchise newcomers to delve right into the action, and long-time fans to get reacquainted with ease.

name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie
detailed_description: Special Edition Includes: • Main Game • Little Prince Costume • Katamari Damacy Series Music Pack • Little King Costume *Contents/specifications are subject to change without notice. *The main game is also sold separately. Be careful of duplicate purchases. About the Game The King of the Cosmos once accidentally destroyed all the stars in the universe. He sent his son, the Prince, to Earth and ordered him to create a large katamari. The Prince rolled the katamari and made the katamari bigger and bigger, rolling up all the things on the earth. The katamari that he created floated in space, sparkling, and brought back the lost starry sky. As the starry sky was restored, the King's fans gradually grew in number all over the world. The King wanted to respond to the wishes of his fans for his success, and the Prince kept rolling the katamari to make everyone's dreams come true. •We Love Katamari Damacy has been powered up! We Love Katamari Damacy, the second title in the Katamari series released in 2005, has been remastered. The graphics have been completely redesigned, and the in-game UI has been revamped to make it even easier to play. •New additional features such as Royal Reverie are also available! In his youth, the King received a strict education from his father, the Great King. New challenges have been added where you can roll around as the King in his boyhood! The days of hard study and intense training can all be rolled through in 5 all-new challenges. Will the young King be able to clear the tough challenges? In addition, a selfie mode has been added, allowing the Prince and his cousins to take quick photos while rolling through the stages! •A simple but very deep game! Roll the katamari, roll up objects, and make the katamari bigger. You can roll up anything from paper clips and snacks in the house, to telephone poles and buildings in the town, to even living creatures such as people and animals. Once the katamari is complete, it will turn into a star that colors the night sky. You cannot roll up anything larger than the current size of your katamari, so the key is to think in advance about the order in which you roll things up around the stage! * This product is based on the We Love Katamari software that was released in 2005 on another platform. Some specifications are different.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm embarrassed to say that despite loving the first Katamari Damacy, I never actually played We Love Katamari. Not even after having the PS2 game sitting on my shelf for 15 years...BUT, all of that has changed, and I'm now a rounder, fuller person for it! We Love Katamari is in almost all respects an improvement over the original. There are more stages, more cousins, more collectibles, more challenges, and above all else, more The King of All Cosmos. You can't go wrong with more of the King. To be honest, it almost feels like the devs realized how insanely popular he was in the original and doubled down on giving us more of the narcissistic, yet lovingly benevolent ruler in this sequel. The ONLY part of the game that is a step down from the original is the soundtrack. Not that it's bad; there are some truly fantastic tracks here, but nothing can touch the masterpiece that is the first game's soundtrack. And the music is nearly as important as the gameplay itself considering how much time you'll be listening to it as you roll up every little (and big) thing in the game. Really, there's not much more to say. We Love Katamari is a fantastic, addictive, highly enjoyable game with an entertainingly quirky sense of humor that'll have you smiling all the to the end. If you were even  thinking about picking it up, DO IT! Only a curmudgeon could play this game and not instantly fall in love with it. And are you a curmudgeon? I didn't think so!

_childDocuments_.review: Katamari has once again rolled back into our hearts. We Love Katamari offers a fresh take on the beloved formula that fans have come to adore. With this remaster, it is back with its catchy soundtrack and charming visuals, but bigger and better than ever! We Love Katamari delivers a thrilling dose of wacky fun that is simply irresistible, with addictive gameplay and a world ready to be rolled up into a memorable experience!The plot is a doozy because it is quite literally a self-referential story about how fans REALLY wanted a sequel to the beloved game Katamari Damacy. The King of the Cosmos wants to respond to his success and give people what they want: more Katamari! While the story may not seem like much, its true appeal lies in the underlying messages and commentary on the nature of sequels, which makes it fascinating.There is, however, a supplementary story that focuses on the King's troubled youth and upbringing, in which he lived a strict lifestyle inherited from his father, the Great King. It is very odd, but it surprisingly has a lot of heartwarming moments to it and is ultimately enjoyable to watch pan out.Katamari's gameplay loop is a delightful symphony of simplicity, chaotic fun, and gratification. Push the katamari around to roll up objects, and with each absorbed object, your katamari gets bigger, unlocking new areas and granting access to even grander things to roll up. While not mechanically rich, its refreshing concept sets it apart, providing a captivating and engaging experience that serves as a reminder of the entertainment value found in simplicity sometimes.While the controls may feel clunky initially, they become more manageable with time, though the dash mechanic remains awkward throughout.We Love Katamari's level design improved drastically, with a significant focus on variation and originality. The design focus has shifted from a singular emphasis on "How large can the Katamari get?" to a more expansive question of "What can you do with the Katamari?" and because of it, each level feels like a unique experience: one submerges you in a pond with water physics and unique obstacles, and another immerses you in a scorching challenge where you find yourself continuously on the brink of extinguishment, reignited by collisions with objects.These unique interactive elements add depth and variety to the rolling experience, keeping the gameplay dynamic and enjoyable without becoming repetitive.Roll with a friend or roll against a foe! You can compete against a buddy of yours for some intense one-on-one, but if that is not your cup of tea, you can fumble together to roll a katamari in sync for an entertaining but chaotic experience.It is important to note that there is no Steam Remote Play option as of this review; local split-screen is the only option for Co-op.Through each level, you can discover and absorb your adorable cousins. Once absorbed, these endearing characters can be found in the main hub, allowing you to switch and play as them. You can also find presents that unlock various types of hats and accessories.As a remaster, We Love Katamari boasts numerous quality-of-life improvements and additional content over the original. It introduces a quick menu selection for ease of level selection. Navigational cues for the next size-up zone are also triggered once you reach the requirement.You can also create a playlist consisting of your favorite music in the music player. Prince Look (photo mode) has also got revamped with a selfie mode.Then there is Royal Reveire, which has five additional challenges where you can roll around as the King in his boyhood. The levels are based on the cutscenes and are more challenging than the base levels. However, for a more relaxed experience, the Endless mode offers boundless enjoyment, granting the freedom to roll endlessly without the constraints of time or objectives.The visuals are genuinely a treat to look at. The world is imaginative and filled with a delightful blend of quirky characters, playful environments, and visually captivating objects. There is so much joy and wonder in its unique art direction and distinctive aesthetics, which capture that whimsical and lighthearted atmosphere. The vibrant color palette, with lively animations and surreal landscapes, contributes to a visually enchanting experience that immerses you in the bizarre and fantastical setting.However, if you are not fond of the new visual changes, We Love Katamari has you covered because it allows you to switch between two different visual styles. "Gorgeous" features a variety of changes that improve the game's graphics, such as real-time shadows and lighting. "Usual" changes the visual style to resemble the original game.We Love Katamari delivers an exceptional soundtrack that rivals the prequel's OST. The unconventional mix of instruments, unique vocal performances, and genre-fusion music create a captivating score. The music becomes more than just background ambiance; it becomes a driving force, infusing every moment with a sense of enchantment and leaving an indelible mark in your mind long after you have finished the game.Sound effects combine minimalism with charisma, be it the satisfying sound of forcefully stopping or the playful collision sound; each audio cue evokes a sense of wonder and delight, immersing you deeper into the whimsical world. While the voice acting is not the central focus, the few VA performances are remarkably well executed, capturing an endearing essence that adds an extra touch of lovable charm to the overall narrative and tone.PC: i7-9700K, 24GB of RAM, and a RTX 2080 Ti.SD: 800p, 60 FPS, ~3 hours battery, ~13.3W, ~57-59 C.Both platforms ran smoothly, without any prevalent issues encountered on either one. We love Katamari defies expectations by delivering an incredibly entertaining sequel that surpasses the charm and joy of the first installment with its addictive gameplay, improved level design, visuals, and exceptional soundtrack. It will keep you hooked as you roll up an ever-growing assortment of objects into massive katamari. We Love Katamari is as close to a perfect sequel as possible. It flawlessly builds upon the foundations of its predecessor, embracing and expanding upon everything that made the original game so special.

_childDocuments_.review: Picture this if you can...You're a Japanese salesperson, and you're walking home from work. All that can be heard are the honks of horns and disgruntled drivers as you make your way through a crowd of citizens desperately trying to make their commute as much as you are. The noise is deafening, and the only way to get through it all is to disassociate and float above your body for the time being as you make your way to lord knows where. You are married, and your relationship is strained beyond reasons you can hardly fathom. You have a wonderful child whom you dote upon yet feel that the march of time only strives to separate you from the beautiful creation that was made in your image, and made in the image of your former love. You often drink, regular as clockwork, and imagine yourself walking into the sea and being washed away with the sand. On this thought, you hear a low rumbling in the distance, that shakes you to your core, but you hardly notice. You suddenly realise that you despise your work, and you despise your suffering, and through this epiphany, you finally decide to quit your job and retire, so that you can make things right, and be with the ones who used to bring you such immeasurable joy. You smile bitterly, knowing the pain this will bring in the short term, full-knowing that when you do manage to reconnect with your lost happiness, the difficulty will have been worth the trouble. You call your spouse and tell them how sorry you are, and reassure them that everything is going to be okay. They sound surprised, yet hopeful. They support you, and they care. You've made it through the traffic, and the crowd recedes as you reach the bus line. For the first time in years, you feel hopeful. The rumbling you heard earlier is now louder than before and seems to be coming from a few blocks away. What can now be heard are screams, and cars honking their horns yet again. You care little, whatever may come matters not. You turn your gaze towards the junction across the street, and you see an enormous silhouette blocking out the sun, turning the day into night. It is moving towards you slowly, until it spins itself up to an incredible speed and crushes you beneath it, adding you to its contents. Your last memories are of the screams that became louder, the splintered bones that pierced your sternum, and the ultimate silence that followed the life being squashed out of your body. It didn't matter, in your last moments, you were happy.Then you woke up, in a beautiful meadow with your spouse and child, they were unharmed. Everything became clearer, and a man appeared in the sky. His presence was reassuring, and you knew everything was going to be alright. Then the man in the sky asked you,"Have you ever been to Thailand?"

_childDocuments_.review: While the original Katamari Damacy was designed and made by one man, Keita Takahashi, this game was only led by him and developed by Namco. Keita himself said he never wanted to make a sequel "as it went against his ideologies of the industry's reliance on sequels being detrimental to employee creativity." Namco then told him they were going to make it with or without him, and he reluctantly took the role of project lead, leading a team of Namco developers. Despite this, it's still an excellent game. Do I recommend you play this before Katamari Damacy? Well no, not that you will miss anything integral to the story, because the story itself is not integral. But the first game really still stands out as the better one, solely because of two things.1. There is not much music from the first game, which I would have been fine with, if this music was just as good, but its not. There are some good songs sure, but the overall ost really makes the game in the first one. Not that this music is unlistenable, but its not as good2. The comic strip cutscenes of the block people from the first one are gone. There was something about those that were just so surreally hilarious. The story in this isn't funny or really even trying to be. Not that that matters, but I'm just sad they didn't include that.The game as a whole tries to be a sort of fan service to the original, where your missions/quests are helping out fans of the original game. And it still does have some great silly dialogue.For example, one mission a fan states they need you to help save the red pandas. If the red pandas don't eat enough strawberries, they'll turn into regular pandas. So you must roll up enough food of equal monetary value to buy the strawberries. Once you complete it, and give her $50,000, she says the strawberries are only $4.50 and you can keep the rest. Idk its the silly little moments like that that sell it for me.The game mechanically doesn't change up much, but that's exactly what people wanted because it works. Its just goofy stupid nonsense fun. The remaster doesn't change much, other than that its HD, and you can run it without crappy emulation. The cow/bear level is also back, and is just as infuriatingly enjoyable.If you liked the first one, get this.  sale or no sale its 1000% worth it. But play the first one first if you haven't Also youre going to need a controller

_childDocuments_.review: We are pleased with this return to Katamari. But we will also probably wear our thumbprints off while playing it.  The game has an excellent framerate, and we are impressed at the loading times considering how many objects each level needs to render, but the Katamari itself is slower than ever, needs more force to get going, and turns with no precision at all. We have remapped the Quick Turn function to the shoulder buttons in order to relieve a bit of stress from the thumbs, but there is nothing to be done for the controls for ramming into things. We used this to ram into an island in the final stage to progress faster, but hit the side of a glacier instead and went sailing into the sky. As the sluggish Katamari has not landed yet, we are writing this review from the heavens. But, even with the difficulty of steering the recalcitrant Katamari, we are likely to return many more times.

_childDocuments_.review: Thinking back to the glory days of gaming for some going as far back as the mid-1990's with the rise of the PlayStation up until around the time gaming went into it's seventh generation in 2006, this was a great time for all sorts of wonderful, wacky and occasionally weird ideas for many different kinds of developers to come up for games, seeing how a fair few did flop fantastically (such as Kowloon's Gate on the PS1, a weird survival horror version of Myst, and Chu♥lip, a most bizarre game involving winning the affection of the town's residents to kiss them via obscure puzzle-solving, neither of which having sold much at all) whilst other such quirky titles (God Hand and Killer7 come to mind) were lucky enough to have received a 'cult following' of sorts that gave them some form of success despite how 'weird' it was perceived to mainstream gamers at the time,Such is the way that goes when it comes to the Japanese game development cycle back then, where they often experimented with such weird concepts, threw a whole bunch of them at the wall and seeing what stuck, rinse and repeat until you came across that fabled 'golden goose' that'd serve as the company's bread winner by carrying any future profits solely or mostly on said franchise's back.Having said all of that, this is what eventually came to what again sounds like a very strange concept for a game here but, as time and history has told us since, those who have experienced such a game as Katamari Damacy when it originally first released in December of 2004, having taken a large portion of the gaming community back then by storm with the simple yet revolutionary creative idea of rolling up a sticky ball with round spheres pointing outwards that is called a 'Katamari' in order to roll up small objects like erasers, pencils and mice as you steadily grow in size, starting off from as little as a measly 5 centimetres tall and working from there, such a straightforward concept yet it is so irresistibly fun and addicting to pick up and play for hours on end!That is once you get used to the controls, since I should give a word of advice for those looking to play this game that, although the keyboard is a serviceable way of playing the sequel to this game, We Love Katamari, it does come across the usual problem of games designed with consoles and their controllers in mind being ported over to a PC platform with said 'controller' being a keyboard, as several things stood out to me prior to chancing it with linking up with a console controller for specifically this game here, as turning is made more difficult than it needs to be without full analogue control, dashing forward is especially hard to pull off with mashing the forward + backward buttons to initiate the dash (since, again, the analogue sticks on a controller makes this more intuitive to pull off without wasting valuable time trying to get it to work on a keyboard) and using one of the most helpful techniques, flipping over a katamari to the other side for quick turns, is nigh-on impossible to do properly with a keyboard, hence why I plugged in my PlayStation 5 DualShock controller which thankfully worked and made the game's control FAR better to play in my personal opinion here!With that being said, I should get into why fans of the old PS2 classics alongside newer people curious about such a wacky game should look into what is essentially a remastered version of the second entry here as, alongside the usual increase in both graphical fidelity and performance boosts to FPS and the likes, We Love Katamari REROLL introduces some extra fun additions that makes this more of a convincing purchase than it's previous remaster, Katamari Damacy REROLL.Starting off is the most evident of the lot, that being the small but notable 'expansion pack' of sorts that is the Royal Reverie, a short selection of five scenarios that features the titular (and arguably the main 'attraction' as far as what 'story' this game has to offer!) 'King of All Cosmos' back in his younger years at a similar point in time as The Prince and his many 'Cousins' do now that offers alternative scenarios for similar challenges, some of which are the usual standard fare but others are actually quite fun and exciting to try out, either by further improving upon existing scenarios in the main game or adding straight up new ways of playing that compliment the overall gaming experience!Though to touch directly upon said 'gaming experience' here, obviously the main goal for these scenarios is to get as big as possible within a time limit (that or how quickly you can reach a specific height with said katamari) although most scenarios will task you with much different objectives that is based on the 'dream' of what this game showcases as a fan's request, directly breaking the fourth-wall as a good-will gesture of showing the studio's appreciation to many of their fans, both within Japan and from abroad, by directly making this sequel to appeal to them in a manner of 'fan service' that is entirely antithetical to that of the usual appealing to gamers' lust by instead focusing on more wacky scenarios thought of directly by the fans of the original Katamari Damacy themselves!To give just a few such examples outside of those 'Large as Possible' scenarios, one involves dashing around a local town to roll up items of value to raise as much 'funds' as possible for a Red Panda cause which puts the focus not so much on the size of the item but rather it's perceived value, another requires the player to carefully navigate around a zoo filled with various sized animals and items whilst doing their best to making the biggest katamari with just 50 items rolled up and even a fan request taking place on a remote island that is home to a fully-kitted circuit where various participants (both humans and animals in different vehicles) drive around in a rapid-pace which befits your katamari also being forced forward constantly and adds a fun extra degree of challenge to what would normally be a more simplified scenario!Given all what I have said thus far, I truly do believe that the remaster of We Love Katamari is deserving of love and praise for having brought back what is argued by some to be the best of the entire series in part due to it being a lovely 'send-off letter' of sorts by the original creator himself, Keita Takahashi, who made this sequel as passionate of a project as he could muster with an improved budget by Namco wanting a sequel on the spot, which the results truly do speak for themselves here!It also helps that it brings about a brand new 'selfie' mode of the sorts when using the camera accessory, another key part of the Katamari series whereby rolling up various 'Royal Presents' in each level unlocks new cosmetics for each of the 40 cousins to wear with some changing depending on who wears it, that helps to give experienced players something fun to mess around with and make for some funny/scenic screenshots and the likes!Honestly, if I had to mention any general critiques, outside of this game not being the best to play with a standard keyboard, it does have somewhat of a learning curve that is unusual for what could be described as a 'puzzle' game of sorts, seeing how one must learn which items to roll and at what height alongside the ideal pathing so that one can grow their katamari as quickly as possible for the best score possible, something that may not be for everyone given the nature of the gameplay itself, alongside one map in particular being a tad overused compared to the rest.Otherwise, to conclude my review, We Love Katamari REROLL + Royal Reverie is a gem from the PS2 era brought back in a time of gaming where fun and creative titles inspired from Japan's finest are much-needed where gritty and realistic games have become the norm in today's mainstream titles and I wish the people behind MONKEYCRAFT nothing but the best in their future remaster endeavors!

_childDocuments_.review: Katamari Damacy REROLL became a game I always went back to ever since I played it, so when they announced the remaster for the sequel I was incredibly excited yet worried; I have played so much of the first game in different versions that I was afraid of disliking the sequel because it's common for sequels to have a different vibe or soul to it, but We Love Katamari felt amazing. It felt as if the designer(s) were able to fully explode in creative freedom. I found myself laughing multiple times at the dumb scenarios like a salesman offering a spinning grilled pork to someone else or a tiger entering a carwash and leaving as a tiger rug, stuff like this is why I love Katamari. Katamari is not afraid of being silly and this entry embraces all of its sillyness by making the main premise of the game "people liked the first game so much they asked us to do more; those people are the ones that will give you the directions on what to collect" and it's just so greatI love the king and how his story was expanded in this game. I've always loved his chats in Katamari Damacy but I've grown bored of them. Here his egotistical personality shines so brightly it's blinding. The levels this time do make you use the spin dash thingy which I used to hate, but with how much We Love Katamari makes you use it for higher scores, it growned on me how good that mechanic is, I was just bad. There's a lot of different types of katamari. Hell, there's a level where you make a sumo fighter get fatter and fatter by collecting food to defeat a rival. There's also gimmicky levels that can be difficult like carrying fire and if you touch water, it turns off and being fully honest, with how many levels there are and how much I've played the prequel, I really enjoyed these levels. They felt like fresh air and they're just perfect imo.The cousins and presents are the best here because most of the cosmetics you get from presents look different when you use other cousins. For example you can get a bikini early on and that bikini on a character can have a skirt and bra, sometimes it's more like a swimming outfit, there's lots of different things that really makes the cousin's personality shine with just their cosmetics + animations. I'm so glad they made the cousins playable outside of multiplayer because I had so much fun switching around and collecting every single one of them.this remaster added new content; Royal Reverie, where you play as the King when he was just a prince. Most of the levels are not great imo in the sense of them just being gimmicky and difficult. Given the context of his father and his youth, I understand why, so while they're the least enjoyable of all the levels, they do add a bit to the story and I really enjoy them.one thing I didn't like is how the stickers force you to use the camera costume, making it so if you want the 100% you can't really wear a cosmetic place, as the camera occupies a slot. Truly a shame, but just minor nitpicking on what is an incredible game.At release this game had some drawing distance issues but they've been resolved and it's now the same as the original. I really wish they incremented the draw distance for PC because sometimes getting cousins/gifts can be tedious as you are waiting for something invisible to pop in and be visible but once again, this is just nitpicking.Overall, a 5/5, absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ peak. I don't think any other katamari game will top this but once again, I thought the same about the first game so I'm really hoping they port the rest too because I'm so in love with this franchise.
