_childDocuments_.review: I'll assume you've never heard of the game for the sake of this review.The Katamari Damacy series is an interesting game franchise, in part because there's not really many games like it. You roll a physics-based object (called a Katamari) around a stage, to roll up items smaller than itself, attaching the items to it and changing how it rolls. Each item makes the Katamari bigger, allowing you to roll up more things.It's a sort of... action-third person game where you explore a limited area, usually under a time crunch of some sort, to make your Katamari as large as possible, in your average stage. Other stages have gimmicks, like "Only roll up 100 things" or "Your ending score is determined by the monetary value of the items you rolled up, not your overall size."The game has a very nonstandard control scheme, where instead of motion being locked to an analogue stick and the camera controls being on the other, you instead have to use both analogue sticks for movement. Pointing both sticks in a given direction will move the Katamari in that direction. Pointing one stick forwards and one stick backwards causes the Katamari to turn, maintaining the momentum of your Katamari's movement prior to initiating the turn. You can also click both sticks to immediately flip 180. Lastly, you can do a "charge n roll" akin to Sonic's spindash by alternating both sticks forwards and backwards in a specific rhythm.(I have not tried the keyboard controls. I do not plan to.)It sounds complicated, but the controls are VERY intuitive. When I played the first game, it took around 30 minutes for the controls to click. The Katamari grows more and more unwieldy as it grows and gets heavier, thus needing longer to start and stop movement. This is the only time where the controls seem to struggle: when the game is intentionally making itself more unwieldy.In the narrative, the game relies on a strange sense of humor, often at the player's expense. The game makes fun of you for failing, and even criticizes you for succeeding only at the bare minimum. If you're salt-prone and weak-ego'd, this may not be the game for you.You play as The Prince Of All Cosmos (or one of his many cousins, as you unlock them) and you solve people's problems by rolling around the Katamari in stages of various sizes. If you succeed, your accomplishments are underplayed by everyone involved (both the NPC you helped, and your father, the King Of All Cosmos, whom you always interact with before and after every stage) unless you get an absurdly high score at the stage. Your katamari is then tossed into the sky to become a celestial body, like a star, planet, or orbiting natural satellite. You have an eventual goal of rolling up the Sun, using a Planet-sized Katamari and rolling up The Sun using the celestial bodies you created.I recommend playing the first game (Katamari Damacy REROLL) first, as this game is a direct sequel which acknowledges the first game many times, but they're very much the same sort of game. If you like the first game, this is more of the same, with some minor control differences, some fun stages, and a new storyline focusing on The King Of All Cosmos backstory. Worth the cash if you like the first game. I recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: [03JUN2023 EDIT] Reroll-related post-game comments have been added below.This review will gloss over the game in both the context of a remaster and the context of a sequel to Katamari Damacy. TL:DR - 100% worthy as both, and if you have the choice of picking up either this or the OG, I'd say go for this one. As of this review, I cleared nearly all the main game stages once and all the Royal Reverie levels. I know my gameplay time is short but I played the original extensively as a kid.Katamari Damacy was one-of-a-kind when it released in the west nearly 20 years ago. There was nothing like it, and it was strange but wildly entertaining. The stages had so much charm and silly interactions, the characters were silly, and the music was top notch. It was a success, and We Love Katamari ended up coming out soon after, and it really expanded on the base game. More unique level goals and designs, bigger heights, ability to play as the cousins, more plot, more everything. In my opinion it was almost the perfect sequel; The only thing it didn't have was Eternal mode. Step forward to 2018 when Katamari Damacy Reroll came out. Reliving one of my favorite games of all time was a fantastic experience but oddly underwhelming given what's come out since then? Still no choice in music, no ability to play as other cousins etc. Thankfully Namco took notes because WLK is a more substantial Reroll, adding ETERNAL MODE and even small things like better song management (you can pick your favorite songs etc), all while holding the same level of high quality visual appearanace that Katamari Damacy Reroll had, not to mention a day 1 stable release which is oddly uncommon anymore. The only thing WLK didn't add that I noticed was additional time in some levels like KD:R did, but I think that's because WLK was more relaxed on its time limits to begin with.The Reroll also added a few new levels where you play as a young King of All Cosmos. These are short levels that remix a few levels from the original game, but they're nice free additions and I felt they still held a level of charm comparable to what the OG levels had. I enjoyed them. There is also a mini objective where you can find little stickers from other Namco games like Pac-Man. If you wear the camera and take pictures, you "collect" these stickers. It's a neat little way to encourage more replayability and I'm all for it since the Katamari games are about that in the first place.Other small things I noticed worth commenting on... some of the sound effects have a lower pitch which caught me offguard as I wasn't used to them. Some objects I noticed were renamed or redesigned, such as the American Guy being renamed. These things don't affect gameplay at all and the renames/designs likely won't go too noticed.In terms of why We Love Katamari was an overall great sequel, it just expanded on what Katamari Damacy did... added more level objectives, more levels, bigger goals, more replayability incentive, actually playing as the cousins in single player, a soundtrack just as good if not better than the original, and every level is fun with some having multiple layers to them, such as the "guesstimate" level having 3 variants instead of just the one. The original Katamari Damacy had a couple levels I was "eh" on, but I never felt that way with WLK when I played it back in 2006 and I certainly don't feel that way replaying its reroll in 2023. Overall, Namco did an excellent job with this remaster, even better than the Katamari Damacy one. It's rare for me to buy a game Day 1 at full cost anymore, but I'm glad I did with this one because it holds up well.[03JUN2023 UPDATE]I have now finished WLK:R. I acquired all achievements, cousins, and presents. Still working on stickers, collection & speed comets. The comments I made before with lower-pitched sound effects and renames do get more noticeable as you replay the levels. Examples include the Taiwanese flag just saying "TW" in the space level, and cousin Colombo being renamed to Njamo. The discussions have pinpointed far more differences than I could, so check them out if you're curious.My other post-game comment pertains to Eternal Mode. It does exist, and I am happy about it... but it only exists for ALAP3-5. Fun levels, especially ALAP5. However WLK has a lot more unique setpieces than KD, and part of me was hoping other levels such as the Campsite, Lake, and Save The Pandas levels, would get the Eternal treatment like in later games. This may just be a petty point, but wanted to comment on it in case others expected more like I did. Maybe they'll patch it in a future date especially if they fix the sounds.I have not picked up the DLC, but taking a look it's very expensive for what it is and you don't even get MP3s or FLACs. They did a good job at picking a lot of hits from each game though.My recommendation still stands as it is a genuinely fun game and Namco still did a great job, better than some other companies would. Skip the expensive DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: this port of we love katamari is admittedly less than perfect. the sound effects seem weird and low quality compared to the original, the new graphical style looks kind of bad (though thankfully there's an option to make it look more like the original), and the draw distance isn't as far as it was in the original, particularly in the zoo levels, which have now become a real pain because of thisbut with all that being said, most of these are issues you'll only have if you're intimately familiar with the original like i am. and even despite that, we love katamari is still an absolute joy to play nearly 20 years later. it expands upon and improves upon the original in every way that it can, and even as a standalone game, it still feels just as fresh, innovative, and fun as it always has. being able to play it at 60fps in a higher definition is nice, too. despite my nitpicks, this is a perfectly good way to experience one of my favorite games of all timealso the new stages are fine. they most certainly exist

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first time playing a Katamari game!! So this review will be for other newcomers that aren't comparing Reroll to the og games, etc. The movement/camera during the tutorial made me worry that I was going to dislike/refund it, but once I started playing the actual levels, I got the hang of the controls. The movement is Supposed to feel a little stiff because you're pushing a heavy sphere. Don't let a couple wonky tries discourage you from pursuing the game! I do not recommend playing with keyboard whatsoever; if you don't have a controller, I don't think you'll enjoy yourself.The music is fantastic and lively. Something about it, combined with the game's weird little premise, makes me feel happy and enthused. The colors and aesthetics are great. The item and character designs really wrap the game with a cute bow. My favorite thing was collecting all of the cousins. Lean into the game's shtick, don't ask why things are odd, and enjoy the sounds of screaming people as you roll over them like an adorable bulldozer. This is a fairly short game; there are about 20-ish levels that you ideally play through 2 or 3 times each. I don't think I'd pay full price for it, unfortunately. If you're unsure about whether this title is for you, wait and get it on sale. One must imagine Sisyphus small, green, and happy to be here.

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I wait for games to go on sale but this was a "OMG BUY NOW" purchase as soon as I heard news it was released. It is still the same basic premise. Using your twin-analog sticks you skid-steer the prince around an environment and roll things up using your ball into a larger diameter thing. You then get berated by the King of Cosmos for being a bit crap even if you have done quite OK in a level.This is the way of the Katamari. You are never good enough and therefore you just have to try harder, right?The menu and navigation system in the game has been thoughtfully updated to make level navigation far more logical. You don't have to roll a ball around to try and find the level you need. You can open a menu and have a easily accessible stages menu that lets you get right into the action. You can keep releasing Katamari games as much as you want and I'll definitely keep on buying them. They have been remastered and look fantastic, and are well worth the price of entry.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Katamari, but more of it. And yet, strangely, worse too. The game is still as incredibly addictive to play compared to the original Katamari Damacy, a game I went for 100% in not just the achievements, but filling out the entire item catalogue in game... but there appears to be considerable Nostalgia Glasses being worn for the reviews for this sequel on Steam, as in many ways it's a large step back from it's parent too.In particular, the main game screen becomes unbelievably messy, especially when you start opening up worlds to visit and the landscape is crowded out by huge NPC shouting messages at you; I gather compared to the PS2  original, there are sub-menus to get around the utter shambles of layout, but it still rapidly becomes very, very ugly and frustrating to use. Likewise the information on what you've collected wastes far too much of the screen adding a useless roll-wheel, there appears to be no way to track which Cousins you've rescued this time (but you can track the stickers you photograph in game), and the solar system display is just plain badly laid out.The camera angle compared to the original seems much, much worse; there are fixed cameras around the Prince and the Katamari to help look around, but doing so costs you precious time in game. I think this may be to try and limit the amount of items rendered, as there's a much higher number of rollables in this sequel, something also hinted at by the loading mid-level, which was never a problem in the original. But  so many times I just found myself with no clear idea of where I was supposed to go because the view distance ahead is so very, very short.But then again, levels get reused again and again, so after a while memory of the layout built up; but this is a flaw, not a benefit of the game. And most disappointing of all, the soundtrack is noticeably weaker than the original. There's a reason why you see "Katamari On The Swing" referenced online so much, but very little of the rest of the soundtrack. There's some good tracks, but again repeated far too often and some of the good ones are just remixes of the original OST; where as the original had almost every single track being unique and memorable, this one has way too many bland, hardly even notice they're there tunes.All of which sounds like I hate the game... I don't, it's still great fun when actually rolling, and I'd recommend this game without question to anyone who enjoyed the original. There's some fun variations on gameplay I've seen so far too, especially the feeding the Sumo to make him big enough to roll up his opponent, where he literally eats the pick ups and gets fatter. But if you're absolutely new to the series, I absolutely wouldn't recommend this one despite the almost universally positive reviews; Get Katamari Damacy first, which I think still holds up far better.  And if you have KD, and were only "Meh... Ok" on it, the annoyances here will make it We Love Katamari not something you're going to grow to love more, I'm afraid.

_childDocuments_.review: My childhood was clearly stunted - this was such a delight to experience. Reverie doesn't really offer much more, but the game itself holds up really well. The controls never really feel good, but you'll get used to them quick. The main thing holding the controls back is the inability to turn fast enough, which is more of an issue in the Simple control scheme (you have to completely let go of movement to turn faster) so I'd recommend against it. For the game levels, as they progress, it's worth noting that things get a fair bit easier and less stressful. Levels are filled with fairly unique items & goals, with a bunch of goofy easter egg situational placements strewn about to keep things interesting. I'd still love an option for unlimited time, but I think this game does a good job at keeping it fair for the most part. Many of the special levels will still mark as completed even if you fall short of the completion goal. The remaster itself seems to hold up very well in the modern day, but I never played the original so I can't properly compare, but I had no issues with it. I do appreciate the option to switch between old & new styles.Try the game!

_childDocuments_.review: I really love the Katamari series, but I can't really recommend this one over the first one or as the introduction to the series.☆ Frequently freezes entirely. It doesn't crash, but will freeze for several moments. This has happened multiple times throughout many stages (for me).☆ Objects don't load in from a distance always. Sometimes they randomly appear or fade in when re-rolling through certain areas.☆ Not sure if it's just me, but the camera frequently gets caught behind large objects for extended periods, or gets placed at strange angles that can cause motion sickness.☆ The music is not nearly as good as the original. It's not as fun destroying the world with a ball listening to what sounds like a sugar plum fairy entrance theme song. The original had much more fun upbeat, jazzy, unique music that made you want to be a menace. It was a huge aspect of what made Katamari so enjoyable to me, and it's not here in this title.The songs also aren't quite as randomly placed throughout levels? One song is usually tied to levels, and once it's done playing it just re-loops the song. In the original, it would play a different track as to not give the player a headache listening to the same thing looped for up to 14 minutes. ☆ The levels are all over the place. The first Katamari had a sense of slowly growing and upping the stakes as you progressed through different stages. Here, it's much more random and features gimmicks rather than a gradual climb.☆ The maps aren't as fun. Probably a very personal gripe, but some of them do genuinely become a headache to roll through, such as the school for example. Also, while increasing size, the game actually pauses to load and increase the map, completely halting your roll and making each level much less smooth to play through. This was never an issue in the original.This game just seems to have a lot less care put into it than the original. The people aren't specially named, the items aren't as meticulously placed, the music is soulless and unfitting, there are bugs, everything's all over the place. I hate to constantly compare to the original, but I only played it for the first time recently (no "nostaliga" or memories to cloud judgement) and WE LOVE KATAMARI is just so subpar to KATAMARI DAMACY.I can only recommend this game over the original if changing the playable character is the only way someone will play a game, to which this game allows you to exchange the Prince for his Cousins. ✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧˖°˖✧

_childDocuments_.review: Does almost everything a sequel should do; it iterates on the previous game by adding more variety in the levels where you get as big as possible, adds more interesting maps overall, and new gimmicks to keep things fresh. Item placements feel more natural, and levels don't always place you in the same spot when you retry, so replaying levels doesn't feel like a chore.There are some nice QoL features added in the game and the port: faster retrying, better control of the katamari, easier traversal, and it runs at 60 fps now and autosaves.The game's presentation is as ridiculous as ever with how over the top everything is. I like how it contextualizes the previous game's story into its own and how it isn't afraid to poke fun at itself. There are so many little details littered across the game that didn't need to be there; you can just tell the devs were passionate about this one.The major downside of this game for me is its soundtrack. I think it pales in comparison to the previous game. That's not to say it's bad, but I just think Katamari Damacy's soundtrack works much better than this one does. The port also has an issue with not rendering objects in the distance which can get annoying and there's no option to change it. I don't think even the original game had this issue on PS2The new content added to the game is okay. It's not as good as the base game's levels, but it's more katamari, so not much to complain about.Overall, if you had to pick one, this is the one you should choose since it's just more of everything the original had but done better. I still think you should try the original, though if you can.

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from having a few more minor flaws, We Love Katamari is a sequel awesome enough to roll up the first game. That's pretty impressive given that Katamari Damacy is one of the greatest games ever made. You know what's even more impressive? This sequel was released 1 YEAR after the first game. Early 2000s developers truly are built different.I'm quite happy that this remaster was released, it's such a joy to be able to experience more Katamari. This game is more katamari like that it's entire identity, probably more so than someone would expect coming into a sequel. It makes comparing these two games interesting. The first game is special because of how confidently it is able to be itself: it's weird and wonderful and expects you to just roll with it. Then this 2nd game is an entire parade that strolls in exclaiming "isn't it wonderful how weird katamari is".This intent turned me off at first, but I quickly was brought on board as I realized that this parade was outdoing the very thing it was celebrating. Imagine if a composer made an iconic song, and someone loved it so much that they assembled an entire live orchestra to play their arrangement. Sure I can find places where I don't like choices the cover made, but I'd probably find myself saying this tribute sounds much better.The main way this game overshadows the last is with its levels. Katamari Damacy levels are memorable as a set, but the variety is mostly clever ways to recontexualize what they already have. Meanwhile each level in We ♥ Katamari is incredibly memorable. Its packed with interesting objectives,twists, and most impressively unique environments. Not only are the gimicks more creative, but there's just more cool places to roll around in.The only levels that felt like padding to me were the Royal Reverie additions, which I'm not a big fan off. They're all remixes of levels in the game, unlocked right after you do the original. This does some strange things to the pacing, I'd probably recommend saving them to do some time near the end of the playthrough. I didn't find them especially interesting and I'm not sure the more "expert" style is actually that fun.Anyway, back to the main levels. They're way more gimicky than what you see in the first game. If some of these levels were in the original it'd feel like they're stretching the focus too much, but here in the context of this game it feels like they really shine. I adore many of these levels. Its full of delightful suprises and I constantly found myself with a feeling of "that's neat!".I'm going to resist going into detail about each level. Unlike this game, my praise wouldn't hold a candle to the thing I'm referencing. I will specifically mention that I didn't like Just Right or Cowbear {the latter is a joke that isn't funny the 2nd time, and in fact they didn't understand the comedic timing at all since you can fail the very second you start rolling due to cheekily hidden objects at every spawn point}. It's also worth mentioning that the "As fast as possible" alternate are fundamentally antagonistic to the core appeal of the game, since you'll finish before the soundtrack pops off.The main "as large as possible levels" are excellent. It's quite unfortunate that hitting a milestone in turn hits you with a loading screen. I could have sworn the first game didn't have this problem. Sure these environments are more ambitious, but this feels like an eggregious thing to allow. {Now that I think about it, I think the 1st game cleverly hid loading screens with the way you traversed barriers, in this game you can simply roll up this barriers which is neat, but also probably had the explicit cost of requiring loading before you arrive at them. }. It's pretty baffling to me that this remaster didn't remove these loading pauses.[especially given how fast the levels load from the main menu area]The final "as large as possible level" here is a fantastic experience. It makes the memorable final one of the last game pale in comparison. The specific way they 1-upped themselves makes for a level that's a joy to explore.The intro video stutters a bit on my machine. That was kind of a vibe killer the first time i booted up the game, but luckily I didn't have any problems for the rest of my time here.Speaking of Vibes, the soundtrack is as you'd expect a masterpiece. It's rightfully what carries the game and transcends the great mechanics into the experience katamari is known for. I love a lot of the tracks in this one and the album feels incredibly different to the first one. Jarringly, there's actually 1-3 tracks here I'd skip if I was listening to the album. [The Animal one I can respect because it's incredibly high effort, but that can't make it escape from sounding like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (which is funny when you're playing the orginal level, but doesn't make for a great song to relisten too) . That's ok because everything else is so awesome. Shoutout to Bluffing Damacy, Katamari on the Swing, Everlasting Love and Blue Orb.

_childDocuments_.review: The art of Katamari is eternal, unchanging, sublime. If you have experienced Katamari Damacy once before, it won't surprise you now. While the sounds of the Katamari are still as gratifying as ever, what accompanies it does not have the same... flair? Such a deficiency could be remedied with the music from past and future Katamari outings for... $20!?! Why punish us so? Was the Katamari too small? Too slow? Still Katamari is... joyous! _childDocuments_.review: This title is a remake of the original PS2 classic We Love Katamari.It's a delightful, fun and funny game with a devilishly simple concept - roll things up to grow bigger.It's the sequel to the original Katamari Damacy game (which it references heavily), and is an improvement in virtually every way.In the game you play as The Prince, and you assist various inhabitants of Earth by rolling things up with your Katamari.The game design is top-notch and while the concept is the same, every level feels and plays differently.It is a game with extremely strong game essence - it's hard to play it and not have a smile on your face.From the colorful graphics, awesome cheerful soundtrack, funny quips and addictive gameplay, every inch of this game is made to be fun.On a technical level, it's a remake of a PS2 game. It's honestly surprising there are still some loading screens, but they're not long.If you want a non-complex, fun game that you could play for a few minutes to a few hours at a time, I would absolutely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm shocked at how good this remaster is considering how lacklustre the last one was.144FPS support, a bunch of graphical upgrades to give it visual parity with Beautiful Katamari (I wonder)and as a result of both, it feels very fluid and polished in a way far beyond the original. Kinda funny the best game in the series gets treated this luxuriously while the original is stuck with a really basic portjob. Not you're missing a whole lot by skipping that one and just coming here instead anyway. It's good, sure, but this is better, y'know?As far as you could go both for gameplay and graphics, this remaster would be perfect if not for one thing they hopefully patch soon and that's the draw distance. Your visibility is vastly worse than it was on the original PS2 game and my only question is why? It was changed for no discernible reason and can become a problem when you need to be keeping track of items to roll up. It's maybe 20 polygons at most, it's not a graphically demanding game, come on.There's also the elephant in the room, the music DLC. It's severely overpriced on its own. If you can get it bundled in with the game cheap it's worth it for the music variety, but going out of your way to buy it for even half its price, no, just no. Any more than a fiver and you're being ripped off.

_childDocuments_.review: The same thing! This was the very first thing We ever rolled up! I am truly blown away by this Re-roll. The Katamari Damacy Re-roll was good, but *this* one is thoroughly spectacular. I grew up very poor, and We <3 Katamari was one of the very few PS2 games I ever owned. The only reason I got it was because I begged my mom to get me a copy of it from some second-hand game shop (my PS2 itself was third- or fourth-hand, IDR). What a strange treasure it was. I was, for a long time, almost certain that I'd dreamed it up, as no one in school had ever heard of this bizarre little game. Anyhoo, this remake checks all of the right boxes for me. - The soundtrack is as incredible as it ever was, and they've added a "favorite tracks" feature which is very nice. - The graphics have been upscaled wonderfully-- better than expected!-- while still preserving all the style and color of the original. - Gameplay remains faithful to the original but the controls have been updated to contemporary standards, making them feel buttery smooth. No trouble at all getting my Dualshock 4 to work as soon as I booted it up. All in all, a fantastic remake, thoroughly enjoyable for those who loved the original, and I would highly recommend it for those curious to try it out for the first time, because... My, Earth really is full of things.

_childDocuments_.review: As a remaster, it's alright. The new content isn't all that exciting and there's some minor changes, intentional or not, that can be a bit jarring, such as a handful of sound effects being weirdly pitched down and very obvious pop-in in some levels. As a game, however, it's still a long-awaited remaster of one of the best damn games out there. At it's core, it's still that energetic, addicting rolling fun with an amazing soundtrack you know and love, now with a higher frame rate, better resolution and is a lot more accessible than it originally was, thanks to the multi-platform release. Take it from me, a big Katamari fan, that if you still haven't played We Love Katamari but don't have a PS2 with the original game, then I very much recommend this remaster.

However there is lots of replayability to replay levels in order to find more secrets or get a higher score.The gameplay might sound boring but it is challenging and cute.If you are looking for a serious game to sink time then look into something else, but if you just want a good, happy time then this is recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: It has been about 5 years since I played the first Katamari Damacy game, so I decided to pick this sequel on sale to enjoy more of the uniquely fun gameplay! Long story short, if you enjoyed the first game you'll enjoy the sequel!It's the same gameplay with new levels, new gimmicks, and new characters to customize and play as (Marny is my personal favorite)! In addition to this, the OST is great and supplements the game perfectly! I beat the game in about 6 to 7 hours, and it took about another 3 hours to get all of the achievements. So if you are tight on money, maybe wait until a sale to buy the game as it is short but sweet.If I was to give any critiques (more so nitpicks), it would be how to unlock the Cousins (playable characters) and the new content added to this remake being pretty underwhelming. The way you unlock Cousins is fine for most of the game except when it comes to the final level. The reason why is that although a level may have 2-4 Cousins to find in it, you must find the first one in your first run to be able to find the second one on the second run and so forth. The reason this is bad is because the final level has 4 cousins, and if you know the final levels in Katamari games you know they are the longest in the game.When it comes to the new content, it was very small and nothing too notable. So if you are planning on picking up this game solely for the new content, I wouldn't recommend it. The first new gimmick is stickers that are hidden in the levels that you can collect. I found a few in my playthrough, however you have to have a camera cosmetic equipped to "capture" it and since I wanted to use a different body cosmetic I never touched it the camera and this feature. Furthermore, there is no achievements tied to this, so you don't even need to think about it. The other feature was the 5 new "King's memory" levels which are all very short and simply re-use pre-existing levels with new gimmicks and item layouts. They were all pretty forgettable besides the tire one which was probably the most enjoyable and the night school one which was a pretty annoying stealth mission level.I know I typed out a lot for the negatives, but again as I said at the beginning it's a very fun and solid game! If you haven't played the game, check it out on sale. If you have and purely want to see the new content, I would definitely suggest waiting for a cheap sale or passing on it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fantastic to see that the second Katamari game has made its way to the PC, only.. um, 5 years after the first one (quite a thing when the original games were only just over a year apart). As with the original, the game is a cult classic, so you probably already know if you're interested in trying it or not. Let's start with the good bits. The gameplay. The gameplay is simple: you have a ball that rolls around, anything you touch sticks to it and makes it bigger, which allows it to collect even bigger items, and you try to roll it up to a certain target size in a given time. There are assorted variations on this, but that's the basic mechanic. If it sounds a little bit repetitive, then you're right, but it's made up for by the artistic effect of seeing each level in very different ways as the size of your katamari changes. Something that's impassible now might be a huge bonus to collect later. The stages are designed around this, and also have a sense of sheer innocent fun to them that's remarkably uncommon in modern games. It's not often you'll replay a level to wonder if it's possible to feed a sumo wrestler an entire hippopotamus but it's nice that you get to. The game design, Keita Takahashi, was a visual artist who wanted to design children's playgrounds and it shows (and, by the way, if you do have kids this game is almost perfect for them)Then the music. All fully studio recorded, sung and  and a huge variety of melodies built around the catchy Katamari theme. While there are a few tracks that are slightly grating after a while, and some of the classics that were in the first game like  don't really have parallels, it's still fantastic and unlike things you'll hear in 99% of other games. The beautifully surreal  on one of the climactic levels still gives me the chills.But it's not all rosy. The graphics have been upgraded to HD, but the actual models are still the lego-like representations they were in the original. That's fine - it's part of the character of the game - but it may be displeasing, and there's still the odd moment when the camera allows you to see an ugly flat blank part of the map with a repeated generic texture. What's annoying, though, is that there's pop-in. When your katamari gets big, suddenly small objects stop appearing until you're close to them, even if it's not so big that those objects don't matter (and on some of the levels, small objects have to be specifically avoided). Hopefully it's patchable but it's a bit irritating that a 2023 PC game has graphical issues that didn't exist on an 18-year-old Playstation 2 version.There's no meaningful story - the original story wasn't great, but it worked as a unifying theme. In this one, you and the King are just rolling katamaris because the King saw that people liked it when they rolled katamaris. That's it. There's new content added, but it's kind of limited. There's Eternal modes for three of the size-based stages, which weren't in the original.  There's also a set of five extra missions that are supposed to represent tasks the King did for his own father back when he was the Prince, but it doesn't go into character that much and the mission are rather half-baked. They reuse existing map bases and most of them have limiting gimmicks - the only one with a classic Katamari "roll up size" experience is the very first one, and that has a time limit of 1 minute. By far the worst is the "Night School" stage which is a very difficult stealth/evasion game packed into the Katamari engine. It's being praised as an original idea, but hammering a square peg into a round hole is technically an original idea - it just isn't much fun in the context of the game and its controls.And there's the last problem. The timing. You can finish We Love Katamari in 4-8 hours. There is a single final mission that takes  to complete, is constantly repetitive and doesn't achieve anything (which has the strong feel of a CLAMP-style piece of author's pique concerning previous complaints about how short the original game was) but leaving that out, you'll be done pretty quickly and while you can keep rolling to improve your scores, it won't last long (and there's no online leaderboards, which is a surprise)This might not matter to many people, but I'll mention it anyway - the original Katamari Damacy Reroll was in straight Unity C# which made it very easy to mod. Sadly, this one doesn't share that property, being il2cpp protected. If you don't know what any of that means, you can ignore it.At the end of the day it comes down to the money. The original Katamari games were budget titles to begin with, and while the price is still probably lower after inflation, you're still putting down a fair chunk of change for something that'll be gone quickly. If you've got kids who like the style or you're up for one of the best quirk games ever published, it's worth it, but you might want to research a bit first otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Rolling a katamari allows one's troubles to be tumbled away, the worries of life all balled up into a soon-to-be star. Allowing oneself to roll is allowing oneself to see the true nature of the cosmos, to experience joy and love, and to find purpose. Moons roll around planets, planets roll around stars, stars roll around black holes, and the galaxy rolls around the universe. What does it mean to live? Simply roll, and you will find out. "But I have to stop rolling and do my silly little activities like eating and talking to family!" No. You don't need to eat if you roll all your snacks into a ball. You don't need to talk to your family when you may simply roll them. Friends? Roll them. Pets? Roll them. Fear of what comes after death? Not a problem if you simply focus on rolling. There is not much that one can find joy in, but everyone enjoys rolling. There is no self, only the spirit of rolling that has lost its way. Return to rolling and you will find joy, peace, and happiness. Our fundamental nature, our entire existence, everything that is, was, and ever will be is only a means to an end, a means to roll.(Also wait until the game costs less than 20 dollars, you get like 20 hours of gameplay max)

_childDocuments_.review: A remake of a sequel that still retains a few of its predecessor's flaws (e.g. inability to rebind controller controls), but still manages to improve on nearly every aspect of  core design. More levels, smoother gameplay, and longer runtime make it a much more fleshed-out experience; while still holding on to whimsical humor and charm that made the first game so endearing. Make sure you have a twin-stick controller before playing, and avoid wasting money on the Special Edition or DLC.  is a remake of the 2005 PS2 title  and the sequel to , which got  a few years ago. Following the events of , the King of All Cosmos discovers that he and his son's previous antics resulted in a bunch of fans back down on Earth. In an effort to please these new fans, he sends his son the Prince (that's you) to help them with their problems and wishes, which always inexplicably involves you rolling a katamari or katamari-like object around for them. As you progress, you'll also get cutscenes that dig into the backstory of the King when he was a boy; and this remake expands on this further by including five new stages that let you play as the young King, hence the "Royal Reverie" in the new title. It's just as bizarre as the previous game; and as far as sequels go, it's by and large an improvement across the board.Just like the first game, the core gameplay involves rolling up objects around each level using this big sticky ball called a katamari, adding their mass to it and allowing you to roll up bigger and bigger objects as a result. There are 5 "main stages" that feature the basic objective to get a katamari as large as you can within the time limit, and the remaining 27 are special stages that include some kind of twist, like only counting certain objects towards your score or switching out your katamari for something else. , both in how far they push the core gameplay loop and the actual quantity of levels that do it. If all that wasn't enough, many stages can also be replayed with different objectives, such as aiming for a certain katamari size as fast as possible instead of trying for the largest you can get within a pre-established time frame.Something to note is that, despite the casual-friendly look, .  had its tough spots, but the threshold for marking a level as beaten was extremely low, and it didn't require too much effort to get what the game considered a high score. Just finishing every level is still easy to achieve in , but earning the highest rating has become a much more demanding task that can require a lot of replays—and even a little bit of luck at times—to accomplish. There's no official rating like a letter score to indicate how you did; you have to parse it out based on the dialogue the King provides in the results screen (e.g. "It's good, but We could have done better"). Getting anything below the highest rating has the King berate you in some way or another, which can either motivate you to try again or simply move on out of spite depending on the type of player you are—I admit to being the latter, save for a level or two where I got stubborn. If you're a glutton for challenge , you'll have the opportunity to spend a lot of time working towards that perfect score and the King's approval; but even if you prioritize fun over perfection, the abundance of levels and their variants will still give you plenty to do.As for everything else, the positives of  design are either retained or improved upon, and the negatives are either mitigated or, at the very least, not made any worse:One final warning before I wrap up: . As of writing this, the only DLC available is the "Music Bundle", which adds 25 songs cherry-picked from other Katamari games so that they can be selected as the backing track during gameplay—and that's all you can use them for. It doesn't provide actual files to let you listen to these songs anywhere other than the in-game music player, and that's just not worth the $20 they're demanding. Buying the Special Edition cuts that down to $10, but given that you have no other way to access the music you're paying for, I'd argue that's still asking for too much. It's a weird and almost insulting cash grab, and you should not buy it.That said, buying the base game is still very much recommended. , and I could easily put more into it if I wanted to grind for more top rankings or grab all the achievements. The higher difficulty means it's not quite the "zen-like" experience the first game could be, but that doesn't stop it from feeling just as satisfying to play.  It's not entirely required to play  first, though the abundance of self-referential humor may fly over your head if you don't. That said, if you're tight on cash and can only pick one,  will definitely give you more bang for your buck.

_childDocuments_.review: We Love Katamari is one of my most favorite games to ever exist when I played it on the PlayStation 2, and this REROLL+ Royal Reverie port is exactly what I have been craving and scratched that replay itch for one of my favorite titles of all time. Much like the previous Katamari Damacy REROLL, this port is technically sound and faithful to what I remember with some nice quality-of-life updates to help adapt to more modern habits.I feel like the gameplay expands and improves upon Katamari Damacy in such a fun and satisfying way with new levels, new premises, and new goals to achieve. For those who may not know, instead of trying to roll up the larges Katamari you can in the fastest time, there's much more variety, such as rolling up snow off the ground to create a snowman, rolling up valuable items to get the most expensive Katamari you can, and rolling up food off the ground to fatten up an aspiring sumo wrestler. There's so much wacky imagination going into this that easily makes it an admirable comfort game that I can appreciate on a new level as an adult. It brings so much offbeat fun that seems to be missing in a lot of titles I end up playing nowadays.The graphics, interface, and sound is all great in this remaster, although the only issues I have encountered so far are just some minor audio bugs (pitch shifting, incorrect timing, etc.) but nothing super distracting from the overall experience. The visual style is so faithful to the rest of this series, and with better shadows and post processing effects, I feel like I am experiencing the game for the first time again, like this is how I remember the original game looking. The music is also bizarrely catchy in a genre/style that I don't typically enjoy, but I love it here. I played both on my desktop PC and Steam Deck and it worked flawlessly from both experiences for me.The new content added to this game with the King of All Cosmos reliving his childhood was also a welcome addition, and I appreciate adding new things to one of my favorite games rather than replacing any aspect.If you remember the Katamari games and haven't picked up We Love Katamari already, or if you are completely new to these games and want something different, I think this is a classic and easily the best in the series for my opinion and you will have a blast with it. Maybe wait for a sale, since the current price is a bit high for a game that is not very long. I highly recommend this game, I'm glad I got to it when I was younger and am still able to enjoy it now, this one will stick with me forever.

_childDocuments_.review: My review of the game:We <3 Katamari made my childhood, and is back to make me smile again. The perfect sequel to the original Katamari Damacy, this is a game that everybody should play at least once. It's not a triple A experience with an incredible narrative, but it's beautifully simple and deeply satisfying. If you haven't played Katamari and are thinking, "That doesn't seem like it's for me," I encourage you to keep an open mind and give it a shot. As silly as it may seem, this game changed my life and gave me a new appreciation for what makes something art and what makes a game fun.As for the quality of the remaster: I'll admit, the remaster is decidedly lazy in certain areas. Several things have been executed poorly or incorrectly, and the brief Royal Reverie sections lean too heavily on preexisting gimmicks to feel original in most cases. Most of the Royal Reverie levels are basically re skins of levels that already exist in the game. Certain sound effects throughout have been somewhat broken when compared to the 2005 version. Walking in the plaza makes a faster and higher pitched sound than it did when I was a kid, and the little dancing sound you can make in the plaza has a similar issue and no longer loops. Some other minor sound effect issues and broken loops exist as well, which a keen ear may or may not notice.Additionally, certain cousin names have been switched without explanation, and certain cousin descriptions in the collection menu no longer reflect their "upgraded" designs. Nostalgia negatively alters my opinion of the way the cousins look in the two remasters that have been released, but I must say I have been coming around to them, as they are still adorable and an absolute blast to collect. Notably, I think I actually prefer Jungle's new design with the little background image it always shows now. That might be a controversial opinion, but I think it's neat.Overall:The issues are far from game-breaking, and seeing my favorite game remastered in HD with some new lighting effects has been an absolute joy. Is it enough to make this the definitive version of the game? In my opinion... probably. It's not like I'm going to recommend that newcomers to the series go out and buy a PS2 to play the original, especially because the issues I've presented would only ever be noticed by a veteran player anyway.If you're reading this review and are on the fence about whether you should buy this game whether you've played the original or are entirely new the series, the answer is simple: GET THIS GAME! It's worth every penny and then some.

_childDocuments_.review: Katamari Damacy was one of the pinnacles of the PS2-era of gaming, a time where technological advancements had finally made ambitious and novel game concepts possible without too many restraints, but also when the cost of development hadn’t risen so much that big game studios still greenlit such projects. But even this period of gaming wasn’t a bastion freed from the yokes of capitalism. Creatives still needed to grease and gaslight executives into greenlighting such creative projects, and if that project became a meteoric success, said studio execs wanted to milk the ♥♥♥♥ out of that success until all the magic had evaporated. Such was the fate that Keita Takahashi, lead designer of the Damacy games, found himself in.We Love Katamari is a blatant and self-aware reaction on the roll-away success of Katamari Damacy. Taking place after the first game, instead of reacting with abject horror at the rolling-up of Earth by the King of All Cosmos, mankind has now become fans of the King and ask him for random katamari favours. The King, bored by the prospect of the job but not immune to even the most superficial praise, sends his son and cousins to do the fanservice for him.It is a satirical frame to what is basically the same gameplay as the previous game. You roll your ball via manipulating both control sticks independently, adhesing small objects to your ball in order to grow it so it can stick to even larger objects. Katamari Damacy used a very logical progression of scale: with every level, you would start with increasingly larger balls until at the final level, you would roll up the entire world. We Love Katamari trades this progression for variety; next to the standard missions akin to the previous games, you are also asked to roll up different types of items like fireflies or snow or tyres, in order to satiate the fans.And the fans will never be satisfied. Even if you roll up a mission with a high score, you will be chastised by them for not living up to the impossible expectations that they have cooked up in their dreams. It makes them downright more dismissive than even the King, contender for Worst Father in Video Games.This frame, which would be downright cynical if not for the same absurdist vibe as the previous game, puts you in the shoes of the creator. You feel like, in a way, you’ve been there before.. Even if it’s “”””objectively”””” a better game with more varied missions, a higher difficulty and even more swag for your player characters, this game can’t quite capture the same glee and surprise as the original game because it’s obviously not an original game. It is still a great game, don’t get me wrong, but We Love Katamari also wants you to move on and find joy in the unexpected, rather than the tried and true.

_childDocuments_.review: I am morally obligated to recommend this game, because when the first Reroll came out, I said this would be the superior choice for a remaster, and here it is. We Love Katamari is the absolute best of the three main games, and I played it an ungodly amount as a child. But is the remaster good? No. You want to know why? Because PS2 games, like this and Spongebob BFBB, looked bloody fine as they were. This one even more so, because its low-fidelity art design was part of its charm - that's why everyone has box heads and the textures are pixel graphics. Art direction is far, far more than texture size, and the remaster team (correctly) decided to leave most of this be with only a handful of touch-ups. But that begs the question: why bother remastering it at all?Yes, I think the 2005 version of the game is better than the 2023 remaster. They screwed up a lot of the sound effects' looping and pitches for some reason, and artificially sped up some things that had no business being sped up, which breaks the positive vibes even more. Also, the bonus levels are just remixes of existing levels, so you're not missing much there. I can pick this stuff out a mile away playing remasters of games I'm a subject matter expert on, and I will not tolerate it. That sounds harsh, because it is. If you remaster a game that is already highly polished, I expect perfection, and I am tired of being made to pay for anything less. If you aren't going to commit to that, just re-release it on new platforms, original and fully intact.If this is your only available route to play We Love Katamari, then by all means, vote with your wallet on this feel-good fever dream masterpiece. But as for me, I'm firing up my emulator and going back to 2005.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love the Katamari series, you might enjoy this. I wish there were a neutral rating to give a game, though, because it's one of my least favorite Katamari games.The REROLL of the game is really nice, and it does address a lot of issues that the original had. It still has some really bad pop-in though, and there are still some annoying camera issues that make me wonder if they did as much work on this as the original game's remaster. The visuals are very nice, though, and they give a pleasing, though slightly different, visual experience.Unfortunately, We Love Katamari was a game that decided to change it up a bit. The original release didn't have any kind of Eternal Mode, which was a huge misstep that fortunately, subsequent games remembered. REROLL does provide Eternal on a few stages, but not all of them, which is kind of a mixed thing for me because the real crux of the issue is this: We Love Katamari is about gimmicks.Rolling underwater, rolling up specific things, there's a wide variety of these challenges in this game. Some of them are fun enough, several of them are just horrible, and almost none of them were fun when Katamari Forever decided to make half of the game a series of increasingly questionable challenge gimmicks. It doesn't help that the King and a lot of the fans basically voluntelling you to do things are super ungrateful and annoyingly rude. Some games, they're funny or shady and entertaining, but this is not one of those games in the series.The credits game is terrible. There are some unlockables, but you probably won't want to go to the trouble. There are just too many levels in this that you'll never want to play again. You'll get close enough, and you'll decide that's okay.There's a DLC pack with some extra tracks, and they are really good ones, but I think the bundle when it's on sale is the way to go, if you want that. Unfortunately, they didn't get some of the tracks that I would have liked to see, like my personal favorite, "Sayonara Rolling Star". The sound is good, though, and of course the soundtrack is enjoyable, though not as good as the first game's soundtrack.I do want them to keep going with the REROLL series, because I would love to play Beautiful Katamari, my favorite of all the series, again. I'd also love to see Me & My Katamari, the PSP release (better played on the Vita), REROLLed on Steam. I'd buy all of the games, just to enjoy them again without having to dig out old consoles or coax them into working. So I did buy this one, and I do recommend it, but only to big fans of the series who, like me, want to support the releases so that there might be future games in the series given this same treatment.I hope Beautiful Katamari will one day be REROLLed onto Steam. If you want to check out We Love Katamari, get it on sale. If you don't have the original Katamari Damacy REROLL, get that first. This is not an introduction to the series. But it is nice that they're still giving love to these fantastic, iconic, and very much classic games. Even if I like We Love Katamari among the least, it's still better than most games, and it's worth playing through at least once.Just maybe get real chill before you try to tackle some of the stages. You're not going to like some of them.

_childDocuments_.review: The original game on ps2 is my favorite game of all time. Making this remake "good", but I feel like its lacking in a few ways.1. Sound effects are weird. This isn't the biggest deal but it still bothers me a bit. To my understanding when converting the sound effects they get messed up. I feel like some further effort could have been put in just to make sure the sound effects sound the same as the original. 2. The game is google translated from the Japanese version. This is especially weird considering that the original game had a full translation, and I can't imagine that it's that difficult to rip the dialogue from that version. I mean come on, its already translated. The results of this are only obnoxious, little things like saying "planet dust" instead of star dust, and "that sun..." as opposed to roll up the sun. Again, this is trivial but still effects the overall quality of this remake. 3. A lot of the textures look weird, almost like they we're upscaled by AI. A lot of the textures look a bit off putting, but it's nothing jaw dropping or game breaking. Just obnoxious. That's about all I have to complain about. The extra challenges are goofy, nothing too special, but I guess I'm glad they're there. They don't interfere at all with the core game which is nice. Otherwise this is a faithful remake of the original. While it is better and more convenient then to emulate the game, I just feel like they put in the minimum effort just to make this port good enough. It's a good thing this is already an amazing game in the first place since this is almost just an HD downgraded version of the original. Nevertheless I'm glad this exists. I love this game and the most important aspects of the game are left untouched. The mechanics and music are timeless and hold up incredibly well 18 years later. I hope if we see any more Katamari remakes, or even new entries in the series, that we get see the love and effort that this series deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: "We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie" stands as a monument to the gaming industry's unyielding commitment to repackaging the familiar in ever so slightly shinier foil, proving that innovation is merely an optional garnish in the feast of mediocrity. This title, if one could grace it with such a designation, endeavors to recapture the whimsical charm of its predecessors, yet manages only to ensnare itself in the sticky web of its own nostalgia, delivering a gaming experience as fresh as last week's sushi. The developers, in their infinite wisdom, decided that the zenith of creative achievement was to take a beloved classic and give it the digital equivalent of a fresh coat of paint, expecting applause for their courage in not altering a single pixel more than necessary.The gameplay, a term I use as loosely as the developers applied their effort, remains a Sisyphean exercise in futility, rolling up objects ad infinitum in a quest for size that mirrors the game’s own bloated sense of self-importance. The controls, as intuitive as a Rubik's Cube for the colorblind, only add to the existential ennui that permeates every moment spent in this kaleidoscopic hellscape. It’s a digital odyssey that promises the joy of creation but delivers only the monotony of accumulation, a metaphor for consumerist society wrapped in the guise of a 'fun' activity. One cannot help but ponder the philosophical implications of dedicating hours to rolling up virtual clutter, a sobering reminder of the hours of real life irretrievably lost to the void.Investing time in "We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie" is akin to pouring your life's sands through the hourglass of mediocrity, each grain a testament to the moments you'll never reclaim. The game, with its relentless repetition and superficial charm, serves as a stark warning against the dangers of nostalgia unchecked by innovation. It’s a vivid demonstration of how the gaming industry, in its relentless pursuit of profit, can take a concept sparkling with potential and reduce it to a tedious chore, leaving players to wonder why they bothered in the first place. In the end, this title will likely be remembered not as a crowning achievement but as a royal reverie best left forgotten, a dream from which we wake, regretting the waste of our precious, fleeting time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a much better port than the previous game, as this one actually runs at a proper 60 FPS.If you got into the first game, you'll get into this one as well. However, you don't actually have to play the previous game to get into this given that there's no real story to these games.It's mostly more of the same ball rolling, ball size increasing, item gathering gameplay with a lot more variety in goals aside from just simply making your ball bigger.There's a lot less jank in the physics, but controls feel a little slower compared to the first game.All those cousin characters you unlock are finally playable in single player, not that they change anything in the gameplay.Overall though, it's a very simple game to play like the previous one. Despite being easy to clear, the game likes to tell you you're bad at it if you don't reach the hidden goals.It's good fun though. Lots of charm in the visuals, music, and gameplay.The "Royal Reverie" part of the game is terrible though as it's just five short bonus levels taken from the base game with no real changes.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game all about picking up small items & adding them to a ball so that you can pick up bigger items.The sky is the limit in the later levels where you'll be picking up literal continents.Crazy controls make a comeback, but you can always turn on the simplified controls if you're having trouble.Def better than Katamari Damacy & I recommend getting this one if you're looking to get into the series.The only things I dont like about this game are1. If a stage has multiple player characters to be unlocked, you have to replay the stage as many times as the stage has characters. For example the last level being the longest you have to beat it 4 times to unlock all of the characters it has to offer.2. The stickers that appear all over the place are a collectable that you're most likely going to miss out on even if you manage to find a couple of them, as the only way for you to pick them up is to take a picture of them with a camera thats hidden in 1 of the earlier levels. Miss the camera & you'll miss 100% of the stickers.3. The game has amazing music & a dlc that gets you more songs. You'd think that you will get mp3's of these songs, but as it turns out they're only available as background music in the stages.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: This is a review of the game as a Remake not a review of the game itselfBut as a game itself: We Love Katamari is an amazing game worth your time with creative uses of foundation set by the original Katamari Damacy with an even better soundtrack and fun dialogueIf you want a Solid Remake of an Amazing game then here it is! We Love Katamari Reroll + Royal Reverie is pretty competent as a remake. It does it's job being another way to play the best game in the series and then some. For the first time since Katamari forever this game boasts original and interesting content courteous of the titular Royal Reverie. It adds an extra half hour of content with Sonic Mania Encore mode levels of remixing to the base game levels. Although if you ask me, I still prefer the Original We Love Katamari. Unlike the remake of the first game Katamari Damacy Reroll which I can confidently say is a straight up replacement of the original, We Love Katamari in of itself was a vast improvement over the first game that only thing you could do for a remake besides enhanced graphics was to add more content and Fix the fact that you have to replay a stage up to 4 times just to get all the cousins in a stage since some cousins are locked behind future replays.  Reroll only does one of those two things and in fact has made some parts of the game (albeit a few) kinda bollux. the Cousins stage is a pain to get a good score at because the two cousins circling the tree are nigh impossible to roll up in a reasonable time for instance. The credits scene feels needlessly hard and I can't put my finger as to why. Heuey has Knees and should not have any if anything doesn't belong in the Katamari series Heuey's Knees is one of them. Also due to the redesigns that the remake of the first game introduces, the collection description of Ace is inacurate as he no longer has a spiky butt. These are nitpicks I know but the first two Katamari games is full of fun little details to the point that missing things like this is very weirdOutside of accessibility, If you Liked the first game's remake than you'll love We Love Katamari's remake, If you have the original like me then outside of the fact that it's on PC and has songs from the series later half, then you don't have much of a reason to get this remake outside of brand loyalty (I guess)

_childDocuments_.review: If you're like me and played this game as a kid, it's exactly how you remember it and then some! It's just as fun, just as colorful, and the soundtrack is just as bumping.The game comes with several new additions. Such a sticker hunt, and a Selfie mode, which are at their worst, wastes of precious time. I wish the timer would stop while I was using the camera! There's also small quality of life additions such as something guiding you to the next area (FINALLY.) And a way to quickly select a fan without having to walk alll the way to them. Said little updates add so much to the game despite being so little!Oh yea and for some reason this game has keyboard and mouse controls. They are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You NEED to play this with a controller.As for Royal Reverie, it's a pretty neat addition. A couple of extra challenges of varying difficulty based on the King's childhood trauma. While it's not a bad addition to the game, I can really only describe it as.. More Katamari. No complaints here but I found myself avoiding it to play the original game.I have one complaint. This game has really weird lag spikes. I've seen people get it worse but for me, there's this massive lag spike when the timer starts its 60 second countdown. It's really irritating, and I can't figure out why it does this.Despite that, this has always been one of my favorite video games and I cannot recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have ever even seemed intrigued in these weird ass games and their gameplay, this is probably the best accessible way to play the second (and best so far imo) katamari. This game goes "meta" with the people's wishes you help complete in the levels because of the success of the first one, which ironically is repeated again with these remasters. _childDocuments_.review: A sizable improvement on the first game, if not one that adds too much to the formula.This game goes straight for fourth wall breaking to an intense degree, especially when compared to the first game. It works well, given the general sense of humor of the games. The fans are consistently fun, and the game's snarky attitude at anything less than perfect performance is refreshing given the current atmosphere of games coddling the player.The music in this game felt slightly less memorable than the previous game, though not by much. The main theme is fantastic, of course; some of the normal stage music less so, though. In general it felt a bit more formulaic, and less insanely eclectic like in the first game. There's no real low points, unlike some of the music in the original game. Of particular note is that the music for the collection screen is good and not awful, which improves things immensely.The gameplay receives a few subtle but important improvements from the first game. It's substantially harder to get stuck inside objects when the katamari is very large; this makes a huge difference on many stages. There's many, and more varied, stages, especially compared to the 3 stages total in the first game. There's a few extra rules introduced, but not many. By and large the goals are identical (and the bear/cow stages make a return). In this game the end goal is to roll up the sun; having this separate from the main stages worked very well in my opinion, and the ending was satisfying. During gameplay I thought the king was much more passive; in the first game he would often interject with absurdities, but here he rarely says anything at all. The various absurd scenarios on the stages themselves continue on from the first game.The end-game content in this game is very odd; the achievements end more or less where the normal game ends, with nothing for the post-game content. There's a bonus stage with an insane victory condition, plenty of rare objects to roll up, stickers hidden throughout the stages, and the various presents from fans which are not tracked as far as I can tell. There's not much in the way of rewards for finishing the stages from the King's memory either. As usual, the gameplay is its own reward with this kind of thing; I would have preferred a few more achievements, but it's no real issue.In a lot of ways, this feels like what Katamari Damacy was trying to be, and that the original game was more of a tech demo. That's pretty incredible, since the original game was fantastic on its own; this game then is even better. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: A loving remaster of a game that was out of place even when it first released, let alone now. There's a playfulness and a willingness to be weird in We Love Katamari that had been sorely missed almost two decades ago, and in the time since then can still mostly only be found in smaller passion projects. But it's on display here with the budget and scope of a small-ish dev team working at a big studio, and I like to treasure when corporations accidentally fund a thing like this.We Love Katamari is still the sequel the creator of the series never wanted to make, though. In a way, for this one sequel, that was actually kind of a blessing. Faced with the task of figuring out how to make a second one of these that actually feel original enough to be worth making, the team decided to explore what strange and niche tasks you could hand to someone stuck in the Katamari engine. The standard "roll 'em up and get big" levels are still here, but there's so many one-off level ideas. In one, you roll a sumo into food to make him bigger so he can win his upcoming match (it plays with the concept of what counts as food is, of course). In my personal favorite, you're tasked with rolling up the biggest cow or bear you can, with the stage ending the moment you roll a cow or bear up; the game is extremely impish about what it considers a cow or a bear, and even more mischievous about where they'll place those things. The variety on display means that We Love Katamari ends up feeling so much more playful than maybe any game I've ever played. It's here to make you laugh, and it's here to show you a fun time; the game doesn't have need of any other trappings. The colorful toy room-like graphics are still there, and the music is still an upbeat delight, but the core of what made this game stand firmly in the memory in a way further sequels didn't is that focus on its playful spirit.As for the remaster, it's good! No complaints whatsoever. The graphical update is pretty well done, but I do think there are some areas that needed work (water), and that the lighting effects have slightly less charm than the flatter colors of the original; fortunately, if you end up feeling the same, you can revert the game to its original lighting and shading effects in the in-game settings! The addition of Endless versions of some stages is a great update. The new photo mode is, honestly, kind of confusing and inconvenient, but it's a nice idea for an extra thing to do. New stages were added almost in the form of a small new Katamari game stapled on called Royal Reverie, and they've got some interesting ideas, though the levels are ultimately kind of forgettable. There's a "Series Music Bundle" that comes with the Special Edition; it almost feels like a must-have for how good some of the tracks on it are, and it's the kind of thing that would have just come with the game during the era this originally came out in, but that's just the era we live in now. So yes, I recommend this game. It's a little slice of joy, a game firmly interested in making you smile. I downloaded it, played a bunch of levels, and then started playing one level a day, like a desert I was keeping squirreled away in the fridge and picking away at here and there. You might enjoy that, too.

_childDocuments_.review: My first Katamari game is finally remade, with a fresh coat of paint and a new lease on life. Is it still great? Yes.Are some levels still infuriating? Yes, thank you very much CowBear level.For anyone unfamiliar, Katamari is a series where you roll a ball of stuff to roll up other stuff. You use two inputs (either two thumbsticks or WASD & IJKL keys) to roll it around. You typically have a limited amount of time to roll up bigger and bigger things in order to get a high score. It's very fun and surprisingly challenging.The soundtrack is both strange and beautiful, with most songs being about Katamari itself but done in surprisingly interesting styles.Overall, it's a very fun experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Cosmos... A world of mystery both tantalizing and terrifying... Not a very well publicized world, you understand, but a glamorous and influential world nevertheless. Both yet sensitive, and rugged to boot. Tolerant and compassionate with a heart deeper than the oceans. Such is the Great Cosmos, and the King that rules over it is marvelous to behold. Except for the one time that he destroyed all the stars in the Universe. No big deal really. Having come to and realized the folly of his ways, the wisest of King sent to the planet Earth his beloved son, the Prince, and commanded him to make a katamari of ample proportions. Tossed unceremoniously to Earth, the valiant Prince rolled the katamari entrusted to him by the King, rolling up more things than you can count. Vaulting boxes, pencils, erasers, postcards, ramen, robots, cows, sheep, this girl, that boy, moms and dads, bicycles, motorbikes, homes, buildings, rainbows, clouds, islands, hopes and dreams. The Prince rolled them all up, rolled and rolled until the katamari was big enough to be lifted up to Space to replace the shiny stars that were so grievously lost. And that, dear friends, was the plot and purpose of the fabulous game called:KATAMARI DAMACY Its popularity recognized no boundaries or borders, and it rolled right out of the game to bundle away the many and sundry ills that blight the modern world. Overnight, the King found himself a superstar. The adulation of the crowd knew no limits."I want to meet the King!""I think it should be bigger!""The King is so cool!""I want to roll up more stuff!" Oh dear, such a chorus! Fans crying out from all over the world for the magnificent King to do his thing.Wooooowww!!! Woooowww-w-w-w-wooooo!!!Hmm... Still not enough stars here...

_childDocuments_.review: I ADORE the Katamari games.A unique and strange style, sense of humor, soundtrack, and gameplay is already enough to get on my good side. Every time I see a ball pick something up in another piece of media I think of this series.I honestly just do not feel the need to convince anyone this series is wonderful. It's so imaginative it makes almost every other game look like they're barely trying.The physics of this PS2 Era game where everything can be picked up is sometimes a little janky or confusing, but that's the closest thing I can think of that's an objective flaw.Also, this game is silly. I'm hesitant to call it jokes, stacking 15 cows on top of each other doesn't feel like a joke, but it's certainly silly, and Katamari fully embraces being silly.Try one of these games if you haven't. There is nothing like them, other devs just straight up do not try to emulate what Katamari did. You don't know what it's like until you try it.
