_childDocuments_.review: This game takes the first one, Katamari Damacy, and expands on the premise greatly. Instead of each stage being simply "make the Katamari bigger than the last" (and there still are stages that are that), there are also fan requests where you have to get as big as a Katamari as you can make with only 50 objects, rolling the head of a snowman just right, collecting up to 1000 paper cranes, keeping a flame burning to light a huge bonfire, and so much more. It helps to keep the premise fresh and fun, while still being at its core the same Katamari we love.The Royal Reverie is short but fun. Staring the King of All Cosmos in his childhood, he has to go through his dad's tough training to be a good king. There are only five stages, remixes of existing stages, but they're overall tougher than the main game, requiring you to reach the goal quicker, avoid obstacles that can end the stage early, and finding hidden objects. It's a fun little mode that gives the King some backstory.If you love Katamari, or are looking for a place to start loving it, this is an excellent game to go with.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games on the PS2. One of the better games on PC. If you liked Katamari Damacy, if you were curious, grab this one. This game is better than what came before. Better maps, more interesting scenarios, equally solid music, and a better plot. Very weird, very japanese game. I adored it as a kid. I still love it now.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I have the original PS2 game and this port is fantastic.  The refreshed graphics are very bright and colorful and the controls are smooth, though this Katamari always had better controls than the first one.  One difference I noticed is that the voices of the characters you have to help are speaking in Japanese, while in the PS2 version they speak in English.  There are probably a few other minor differences as well but I haven't played the original in a long time and don't remember it well.  This version also has a little extra content such as more songs and some story content involving the King of All Cosmos when he was a boy, which is a nice treat for those who have the original game.  The Katamari Damacy series is one of my all-time favorites, so it's great to now have them on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I love Katmari. We Love Katamari. This game will certainly make YOU Love Katamari!Honestly my only complaint is that the ending and transition to post game feels really abrupt. I didn't feel as satisfied when I reached the credits compared to the first game. And if you disliked the gimmicky levels in Damacy this game is your worst nightmare. A lot of people also complain about the soundtrack being weaker than the first game and unfortunately I have to agree on that.Basically, this game really is just a giant filler game for fans who wanted more Katamari. And, well, I am one of those fans who wanted more Katamari, so this game is perfect for me.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: How do you make a sequel to a game like Katamari Damacy? Well, exactly like this.I have to say, for a PS2 game with a deliberately low-poly style, this game looks fantastic. It's really aged well and has a bright, pleasant pastel vibe going on. Really easy on the eyes.The game controls better. You can be a little strawberry prince, or a little cow prince, or a little fat prince. The music is, again, amazing. It has more innovative levels. It tries to push the longevity of the concept through various challenges. It's a proper sequel and definitely worth playing if you're a fan of the original game.The cutscenes deserve an academy award.It's such an upbeat, joyous game that it might cure your clinical depression.Still opens in window mode but you're able to change it faster than the original.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Explaining a Katamari game to someone who has never played it is a bit like explaining portrait to a blind person.  Let's try this.  Imagine a joyful imaginary game a kid with Synesthesia (google it, it's wild) comes up with about gobbling up the world with his little toy ball.  Now give that kid acid and set him loose in the park.  The first one was easier to fall in love with, but the core of these games is just weird, senseless fun.  Unapologetic in it's campy weirdness.  10/10 would sing along to the theme song again.  I've bought these games on every system I've seen them release on because I'm just addicted to madness.  TLDR; buy the ticket, take the ride.  Get theme song trapped in your mind permanently. na-nanananananana katamari damacy

The get big then roll something up was cool- Cool collectible cousins- Cool collectible giftsA few issues I have:- Score boundaries are much harsher. Expect to finish levels way over target and be ridiculed for how bad you were- Score boundaries are not displayed anywhere. If you finish under the top score, you'll just be told "Do better" with no idea how much you need to do.- You have to play time trial versions of the stages before you can replay the original stage. The one with fighting spirit is literally the firefly level with the sprites changes. Thematically it was cool though.Nitpicks:- Music is worse in general. There's only a couple good tracks. Katamari on the rocks is here but it's an inferior remix :'(- Stage select plaza is extremely cluttered and annoying to navigate and definitely nowhere near as cool as the original planet menu.

_childDocuments_.review: When Katamari Damacy REROLL suddenly rolled into existence less than 5 years ago, I absolutely loved it. And my biggest complaint was the lack of We ♥ Katamari content, as it felt to me that a new title mixing both the original and the sequel would’ve been a far better choice. Well We Love Katamari REROLL is here now, with lots of improvements, a little added bonus in the form of Royal Reverie and, sadly, with a few unfortunate issues.Just like the original Katamari Damacy or it’s enhanced remaster, the gameplay of the title is very unorthodox, but also fun, simple and exciting. As the Prince of All Cosmos, you are sent on tasks by your father King of All Cosmos, all of which involve you rolling a ball (though there are exceptions) that can be rolled over other objects to get them stick to it. Which objects can or cannot stick to the ball fully depends on the size of the ball itself and usually at least one of the objectives for the game is to simply get a bigger Katamari ball before the time limit runs out.Unlike the first game, however, We Love Katamari has lots more levels where simply getting the Katamari as big as possible isn’t the main task and instead you have other goals. And many levels in the game also have several stages of completion, from one that lets you consider the level complete and move on, to the one that fulfils the ultimate goal that is often very hard to achieve. Doing so, unlocks more fun stuff and specifically in the remaster, more levels in this new Royal Reverie mode, where you play as the young King of All Cosmos and try to complete the tasks his Papa set for him, all of which are usually harder than the main game and all of which are somewhat based on the little scenes you see when you’re playing through the story.The only huge complaint with the game is that it has several odd technical issues that are either entirely new and were not in the 2005 PS2 original, or are remnants of the old design that was kept and sometimes feels at odds with the game. The new issues include the horribly small draw distance for a lot of objects, that actually makes the game harder in stages where you need to collect specific things, as you don’t see them from just a dozen meter away and can lose precious time when going for best scores. Another issue is the fact that the game can occasionally freeze for several seconds for no apparent reason, before continuing as if nothing happened. And finally, as a remnant from PS2, every time you get bigger than a specific size, some levels have a bit of a loading before you can continue, which seems odd for a game like this in 2023, but at least keeps the cute dialogue boxes from the King.Other than that, a lot of little improvements were introduced and the game is more fun to play. I’m also glad that unlike Katamari Damacy REROLL, that for some reason lacked autosave (at least when I’ve played it), We Love Katamari REROLL does have it. The visuals are more beautiful than they were in the first remaster. The music is as amazing as it has ever been, remaining catchy and fun and you will be singing along before you realize it. The controls are as finicky as they used to be, which is a shame, but also a part of how these games work.I loved We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie and while it’s hard to choose between the two, I tend to prefer the sequel. If you were to choose which of the two games to start with, I’d suggest this one. But really, you owe it to yourself to play both now that they’re available on modern systems. They’re absolutely lovely.

_childDocuments_.review: I sunk countless hours of time in younger days into Katamari Damacy. During the pandemic, I fired up my old Playstation 2 and played through We Love Katamari with my roommate, finding every cousin and present along the way. Having recently played the PS2 game to its completion, I can confidently say this.This game is what your rose colored glasses remember We Love Katamari to be. The sound and visuals, though improved, remain true to their source material. (Yes, the motorcycle guy still makes his ridiculous v-v-v-vrroom vroom when you snag him.) The textures are all enhanced in such a way as to make things clearer while still maintaining the cartoonish charm. The controls are responsive to boot.I would recommend using the normal graphics if you're on an older or lower end computer rather than the enhanced ones. Though the game ran on my computer at max settings remarkably crisply, it did have framerate issues when I booted it up on an older machine that I would have said were on par with the original PS2 game when several items were on screen and a lot of chaos was going on.I do wish the Royal Reverie added more levels rather than just applying some rules to levels and giving me a short time frame to get some King time in, but they're fun enough little sidequests that can eat up an hour or two of your time.Final Verdict: If you love Katamari, buy We Love Katamari Reroll+ Royal Reverie and teleport yourself back to 2005 for at least 10 hours of play. If you don't already love it, snag this or its predecessor on a sale and discover that love without the pressure of its full price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: We Love Katamari REROLL is the well anticipated sequel to Katamari Damacy REROLL, being just like the original releases, a second shot to hone the craft of the games, done well with, in my opinion, great additions to quality of life and graphical capability. This review will just detail We Love Katamari and this rerelease, if you want my opinion on the series as a whole, my original Damacy review is lengthy enough to get an idea of that, so I'll spare some words on this one.Katamari Damacy is now a hard sell to people new to the series, simply because We Love Katamari evolved on the original recipe and, in my opinion, completely compromises the existence of Damacy. WLKR brings with it not just more of the incredibly unique and beloved Katamari gameplay from the PS2 exclusive to updated consoles and PC, but even more updated QOL features and graphical features into the new games that both streamlines the game much more than it already was on release and brings the vision more in line with Keita Takahashi's most recent renditions of the game and cast's style- subtle, but it is there.Functionally speaking, it runs great at 1080p and can easily take advantage of high refresh rate monitors which is by far the best advancement any old game can get. The controller inputs from what I can tell are just about as responsive, if not better (please use a controller, not keyboard). The only issue the game has is a down-pitch that is applied to a lot of sound effects, mostly on random people voices, but this should hopefully get a patch soon if it hasn't already. The included Random and Favorites list with shuffle for BGM is by far the best feature in any Katamari game, especially for those longer Eternal runs.The additional parts for Royal Reverie are in a weird spot where they are fun little additions, but also very trivial both in challenge and in why it needs to be there in the first place, which in itself is a double-edged blade. I have not noticed any say of the aforementioned Takahashi's involvement in the reproduction of the Katamari series, so without his input, I would be skeptical about how faithful new storied parts or new stages would come together. So, I'll call it the cherry on top that isn't necessary, but it's generally an appreciated gesture as a nod to the series. But, maybe fingers crossed that a new entry is coming down the horizon in a few years.$30 in my opinion is a well worth price for WLKR, especially if it funds more Katamari projects, but I could see arguments made to go down towards $20-$25, maybe $15 if you want to stretch it, and fair play to those people. The Soundtrack DLC however is really only for fanboys like myself, as it doesn't even give Steam Soundtrack access or MP3s or anything, it's purely in-game, quite an awful value proposition even for the bundle discounted price of $10. It's a good set of songs, but horrendous price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great remaster of a great videogame.   There's something really appealing about the sensation of rolling around a clunky and oblong ball that remains really satisfying across multiple plays of each stage.  A different path can result in passing through an are at a different scale, leading you to recognize details that you never really had the opportunity to notice in the previous five runs of the map.  The soundtrack is one of the greats, the music DLC is good (but clunky in how you select the tracks to play in a level), and the Royal Reverie levels are nice (but small) additions to the overall package.At the time of this writing there's a pop-in issue that badly hurts a few of the levels, but I think that is one of the things that will get patched.   Other noted changes like "voice samples are less repetitive" or "musical cue happens too soon" are IMO improvements.   Some of the sound effects in tertiary game modes or features need to loop better than they do.

_childDocuments_.review: A few years ago Katamari Damacy ReRoll hit steam, a remastered version of the game that started the series. I'd never had the chance to play it, it not releasing in my region, but I tried it and was amazed. Ever since then I've tried to find a few of the other games, but We Love Katamari remained out of reach. Colour me gleeful when the ReRoll version was announced. Bought it on the launch day and have been rolling, rolling, rolling happily since. So what's the deal with this ReRoll of what many call the best game in the series? Updated graphics, cloud saving, modern hardware optimisation and a crossplatform release? That, but they've added more things to this version in the form of the Royal Reverie and the expanded ingame OST that includes the Yuri mixx of Sayonara Rolling Star. So you not just have the base game levels, their speed-run alternate versions and the original ost... but 5 new levels with their counterparts, playing as the King of all Cosmos (prince form) and you can set ANY track as the music.Like in KDRR you can roll up practically any object in the game world if your Katamari is large enough. From a thumbtack to a house, from a child to the entire school, from simple bushes to all the continents. If you can make it big enough within the time limits. Some levels have alternative rules, extra effects or goals and there's a ton of creativity in finding objects combined to depict something else... Even then, the game has tons more basic objects than its predecessor, nevermind the amount of cousins and presents you can also acquire by rolling them into the Katamari and finishing the level. You can then talk to a cousin to switch with them to replay a level as a cousin.We Love Katamari is a fun action puzzle game with so many things to discover that its a solid recommend even if you played the original gray. Get it, get it full price or at a discount, but don't miss out on this amazing game.

We♥Katamari was always my favorite game growing up, and it's so nice to see it get the love it deserves from namco. it's the same game, but with extra challenge levels, new QoL changes with level selection and menus, and some cute little additional details you'll find as you progress through the game. the special music pack adds 25 tracks from other games in the Katamari franchise, which, in my opinion as a huge fan of the series already, was worth the additional price, but only get it if you know you want more than the original ost in game. theres some quirks with the audio throughout the game, like sound effects being different pitch, not looping properly, and some other small bugs like that, but these do not affect gameplay. everything else plays just like the original game!i've been waiting for this game to come out for years and it did not disappoint! i would recommend this Reroll over the original Katamary Damacy Reroll to a new katamari player since this game feels easier to control and has a much more fun selection of levels and additional content than the OG. please give this game a try, you will love rolling up the whole world in your katamari!

_childDocuments_.review: We Love Katamari is my all time favorite kid from when I was growing up -- to the point where I pull out the PS2 emulator every year (or less) and give it a replay. This is my comfort game, for sure. And Reroll knocked it out of the damn park, not only delivering the same game with no cuts but improving on it by including details that the previous Reroll overlooked. The entire game now runs at the determined framerate, so it's possible for the game to run at 144 fps. Better graphics options and the ability to change display settings from the start screen. Including both the classic graphic style and the revamped "Gorgeous" style that simply looks fantastic. Even going so far as to include tools to help players play the game, such as better tutorials and a guide system that appears mid-roll (and obviously, allowing you to turn this guide system off).Just phenomenal. God's perfect video game is looking better than ever.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: This is an awesome remake and even includes more (playable) backstory of the King of All Cosmos regarding his own relationship with his father. I never thought I'd be writing about Katamari Damacy lore on Steam but there you go. The only real complaint that I could have is that the Katamari feels as though it's rolling extremely slowly and that they seem to have taken out the Dash option.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so happy this port is here! I used to play the Katamari games a lot when I was younger, so seeing this series get ported over to both PC and newer consoles is very exciting for me.I can't wait to get my fingers all prune-y 100%ing all that this game has to offer. Aside from the steam achievements, there is a new stickers collectible that will be an interesting challenge. Plus completing the 1 million roses, and discovering all the items in the collection. I'm also liking the new stages with the King!It's really nice to hear this game's soundtrack again as well. It brings back feelings of warm nostalgia.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely AMAZING game compared to the original Katamari Damacy REROLL. Unlike KDR, the game has been completely remade with actual graphic settings (finally), new levels, a whole new area to play in and TONS of new content. First of all, every Katamari game in the past has been capped at either 30 or 60fps (with most of the games never even getting close to 60fps). We Love Katamari REROLL is the first Katamari game to have fully unlocked fps and it is BEAUTIFUL. I have a 280hz monitor and seeing the game this smooth is seriously something else. The game performs perfectly, with so far only one bug and zero frame drops.Second, this game has SO much new content. I'm only 3 hours into the game and I've already noticed so many new things. There's new levels, new characters, an entirely new stickers section? I don't wanna spoil everything but the amount of just new stuff in this game is awesome.Lastly, whether you've played the rest of the Katamari series or not, this is such an amazing game in general and I highly recommend buying it. Hours of fun, amazing music and such an adorable game.
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

_childDocuments_.review:
The King of the Cosmos once accidentally destroyed all the stars in the universe. He sent his son, the Prince, to Earth and ordered him to create a large katamari.
The Prince rolled the katamari and made the katamari bigger and bigger, rolling up all the things on the earth. The katamari that he created floated in space, sparkling, and brought back the lost starry sky.
As the starry sky was restored, the King's fans gradually grew in number all over the world. The King wanted to respond to the wishes of his fans for his success, and the Prince kept rolling the katamari to make everyone's dreams come true.

•We Love Katamari Damacy has been powered up!
We Love Katamari Damacy, the second title in the Katamari series released in 2005, has been remastered.
The graphics have been completely redesigned, and the in-game UI has been revamped to make it even easier to play.

•New additional features such as Royal Reverie are also available!
In his youth, the King received a strict education from his father, the Great King. New challenges have been added where you can roll around as the King in his boyhood!
The days of hard study and intense training can all be rolled through in 5 all-new challenges.
Will the young King be able to clear the tough challenges?
In addition, a selfie mode has been added, allowing the Prince and his cousins to take quick photos while rolling through the stages!
_childDocuments_.name: We Love Katamari REROLL+ Royal Reverie

name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars
detailed_description: Game Editions Get the main game, future DLC, and digital products in one great value package. Asterigos: Curse of the Stars - Ultimate Edition includes: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars original game Asterigos: Call of the Paragons DLC Asterigos: Curse of the Stars Complete Soundtrack Asterigos: Digital Art Book Asterigos: Curse of the Stars - Deluxe Edition includes: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars original game Asterigos: Call of the Paragons DLC Join our Discord About the Game Discover the long-forgotten secrets and hidden paths in this high fantasy world, featuring exhilarating battle encounters, interconnected maps full of places to explore, and an immersive story where every choice matters. Play as Hilda – a brave young warrior from the Northwind Legion who embarks on a journey to the cursed city in order to save her lost father. The gameplay elements inspired by soulslike games alongside a lighter, dynamic combat system, create a fresh take on the modern action RPG genre, providing you with a harmonious difficulty and exploration balance. Explore the magnificent city of Aphes inspired by classical Greek designs and unveil the truth behind the city’s curse. Combine and change your weapons on the go. Equip two different types of weapon at once and become unpredictable in combat. Battle more than 60 different enemies and encounter 22 bosses in the main story and side quests. Decide the fate of Aphes. Every decision you make in Asterigos matters and will affect the story. Find over 100 collectibles, complete numerous side quests, and forge your destiny in the NewGame+ mode. Test your combat skill in the brand new boss rush mode: Gauntlet of the Stars. Welcome to Aphes – a city-state full of magic and wonder inspired by ancient Rome and classical Greek designs. From the mist-covered bazaar streets to gloomy sewers, the enigmatic forests at the city’s outskirts to deep chasms full of glittering crystals, the landscapes of Aphes are full of beauty and dangers. Choose from a variety of ranged and melee weapons on the go and combine them as you wish! The talent system allows you to pick and expand your combat style by choosing two out of six completely different weapons: sword and shield, dual blades, spear, hammer, staff or even magic bracelets . Equip a magical staff to obliterate your foes from the distance or switch to a gigantic battle hammer to squish them in a close combat. Whilst Aphes might distract you with its breathtaking views, this city is not for the faint of heart. Fight your way through 60 different monsters and encounter 22 unique bosses – each with its own unique battle mechanics. Every choice and every decision you make matters. Your journey in Aphes will lead you to discover the truth behind the city’s curse, letting you piece together its history through conversations, discovered documents and cinematics, as well as Hilda’s own diary, which she’ll update with sketches and observations. The world of Asterigos is full of secrets and untold stories. Complete numerous side quests , find collectibles and win rewards from Gift of the Nexus , test your combat skills in the brand new boss rush mode: Gauntlet of the Stars and build on your legacy in the New Game+ mode !

_childDocuments_.review: Not bad, but could have been better without the way too much dialogue in this. Story isn't that much interesting and some side quests are ridiculous (that simp quest for example.) I get that they probably didn't want to go the whole Dark Souls route with the lore explained by reading item description and such, but some dialogues and echoes take WAY TOO LONG and it breaks all the pacing from this action title.The gameplay is cool though, but we need proper key bindings because, using the C controller preset (the one with RB and LT as attack buttons), I wonder what was going through devs' head to make the Y button the sprint button.Also having to hold the sprint button to jump isn't good design.Really loved the demo and somehow enjoying my playthrough but yeah, not a perfect game because of the pacing issues (faulty long dialogues) and weird button placement.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: As far as the general gameplay, the game is good.  Not exceptionally different from other action games. Choosing your weapons is nice, but it would be nicer if there weren't so many menu selections to change weapon sets, because sometime you might want the staff for distance.What I am thoroughly disappointed about is that the game advertises, "Decide the fate of Aphes. Every decision you make in Asterigos matters and will affect the story." However, you can't make any choices in the early game, and others who have played it through, say there are only a couple toward the end.  If you weren't berated for her actions in the beginning, which you cannot change I might not have been so annoyed.  If you don't care about choices in games, and just want to mindlessly play through the game, you will probably like the game. I am disheartened by finding out long after I purchased it.  As such I do not plan on buying any DLC, at this time.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: I will keep the game for the Bonus Dlc but the 10% discount at launch is a slap in the face Thanks Acme and tinyBuild. Good game though.Now that I have about 12 hours into the game I will say that its a blast to play. There are some little glitches in combat but overall has a good flow to it. The world is open but with a central area to upgrade weapons and trinkets. grab stored items complete missions etc. The missions feel very organic to the game and while there are no puzzle elements the exploration factor is a puzzle in its own with twists and secrets to uncover. This is by no means Dark Souls as it is a Souls familiar with its own feel if that helps. So far this has met my gaming expectations from the Demo. I picked up Kena a few weeks back and finished from my Epic games save file. (Epic yes I am sorry couldn't wait). Any way I was unable to complete it from that store so it was great to add it to my steam collection. Bottom line kingdoms of amalur style combat with some Dark Souls sprinkled on top. The pre-order debacle aside this is a good game worthy of the price tag so far.UPDATE at 14 hours..I have opened up Fast Travel and the story/lore is growing on me. The game is still more about the exploration of each place for me and generally enjoying the combat still. I am looking forward to the DLC later on.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: After finishing the game, here's what I've got -The combat is great.  There are a good variety of weapons and enemies.  The staff is probably OP tho.  Story didn't grab me, but the main character is cute and likable because she is well voice acted.  So bravo to Christie Cate.The exploration could use a map and a better side quest tracker.  I think the dev's were thinking too much about the souls games.  The game they made does not lend itself to ambiguity. Overall I really loved it.  I'm too old to play every game I like through to the end.  This is one I did.  So that's my recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: As Souls-like games go this is kind of a hit or miss.On the positive side of things I do like the story, attractive characters & aesthetic of the game nails the 'pixar' character with kind of a bleak classical Greek setting, but mostly lighthearted & not grim as most souls-likes goes.It has the souls like save / load system, boss designs & level designs but It falls short in several areas:1. Player progression is kinda meh, limited amount of weapons .2. Player skills and powers are based on the weapons you invested points into. Not many other options available worth a difference in game-play.3. Difficultly even on the hardest is generally easy compared to other souls-likes, the bosses are fun to fight but might be a push over for many and some have cheap one shot mechanics which i found annoying.Overall if you are a Fromsoft souls enjoyer you will feel disappointed because even as a AA game it is no where as complex and satisfying as Fromsoft earliest games. But if you are open for a more simpler less complex less bleak tone souls-like this might be your pick.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: My initial impressions were that it is a "poor man's Darksouls game". Similar exploration and hack-n-slash combat themes. The combat is a little less "smooth" than Darksouls, but still fun. Animation-lock will be your biggest annoyance during combat.Although I was a little unsure of how I'd like the game, it quickly grew on me. The story and character development are quite good, and the game is longer than I initially expected.I would have appreciated a bit more of an interface for tracking of side quest progression and objectives (the journal doesn't always record important details), but I'm guessing they were going for more of a Darksouls "no hand-holding" style.I also wish NPC dialogue options would have some sort of indicator when there are "important" dialogue options that will progress quests. It's rather annoying having to check EVERY dialogue category EVERY time you speak with them just to make sure nothing new has been added since the last time you spoke with them.Overall, very pleased with the game. Looking forward to achievement hunting, and doing the DLC content.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Built a glass cannon on hard. Turned it back to normal after being 1 shot and realizing it just gave -75 all resistances. Despite being a glass cannon enemies felt generally beefy. Combat low key reminded me of Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning: Reckoning where you just pick 2 weapons and that's your build. This became even more painfully apparent 20 hours in when I had maxxed out the skills for the 2 weapons I use. I'm not metroidvania's biggest fan and this has some low key metroidvania aspects.Overall the game was alright if a bit bland.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars is a game with an interesting atmosphere and plot, as well as well-written characters. In my opinion, the game is distinguished by a very good combat system, we have a lot of weapons, you can play as a mage, assassin, warrior and so on, we just choose the weapon we want and choose spells for it and that's it. I think that the game offers a lot of different cool options and thanks to this we can play however we want and there are no limits to us, we can even combine these weapons and spells into sets and make, for example, half a mage and half a warrior, and such a solution changes the way we fight.The game does not have any specific errors that I could criticize here, and the game time itself is also satisfactory because the game is not too short or too long. First of all, I recommend it to people who like challenges and, most importantly, the action genre. The game is not overly difficult, but it is not easy either. As for the negative comments about the game, I don't agree with them because the game is really good. I am aware that it may not be the highest level but the game is still not that bad, it has limitations resulting from the game's budget and you can feel it, but apart from that the game is very well made.My rating is:9 / 10
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: The game's a ton of fun. Good combat, good level design, good soundtrack, pretty to look at. While the story is interesting, the story-telling, the word choice in particular, feels very amateurish. The text also frequently contains errors - syntax, conjugation, typos... It's not downright terrible, but it is a blemish on what is otherwise a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: An easier Souls-like experience than you’d find traditionally, but still has enjoyable combat. The world is pretty well fleshed out and there’s definitely been effort put into the lore. The story is half-decent, nothing phenomenal but it still feels rewarding when you finish. Visually they’ve done a great job thematically and nailed the Greek Mythology aspects. Really love the art style. Would definitely give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars is a good game combines the style of traditional RPGs with a soulslike template, resulting in a challenging but more accessible game that’s able to forge its own identity without hiding its influences.  Despite these shortcomings, the gameplay is still enjoyable and the emphasis on storytelling and world building helps make up for it. The biggest divisive factor with Asterigos is that it tries to appeal to both fans of more traditional RPGs and Souls games by combining elements of both, and as a result doesn’t excel at either. But if Asterigos is approached without a purist mentality it can still be a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Jank controls. Why is jump on R2? Interesting hit boxes. A curious approach at a morality system.Questionable script writing. Definitely done by someone that speaks an Asian language as their mother tongue.No map, no compass, no quest log, no world markers except blue arrows painted on walls for the main story.There's still some enjoyment here, and it might be worth it when the game is on sale. Otherwise - Pass.

_childDocuments_.review: Generally a decent time filler. Large scale feel to the world and areas and lots of exploring and side quests to investigate. However, the journal system for tracking quests is pretty much useless so best to find an online guide if you want to try and get anywhere with most of them.The combat system is ok, good array of moves and weapon choices but the camera tend to get lost at points and timing your heals needs decent timing and putting some space between you and the baddies while you do it!
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Odd mix of a standard adventure game with the combat and bonfire system of a Souslike, which steadily wears away at the fun of actually playing the game with little frustrations. A lack of anything meaningful to reward the player with really kills exploration motivation and I'at no point did it feel like any character upgrade I got actually made me better at fighting.The characters range from blandly average to actively aggravating and the game has an awful habit of stealing control form the player to walk you to were it wants you.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing! I really love the art style, and the combat system they have in place feels really good! One point I also really like about this game is the way they go about the story and the characters. While playing an absolute unit that single-handedly solves the world's problems alone can be fun at times, it was very nice playing as someone trying to prove her worth in a legion of highly skilled warriors. Which also gave agency and value to the entire supporting cast, instead of the cliched fall-back of "just leave it all to me" easy way out kind of narrative that's much, much more common.Also, the main protagonist, Hilda, is really well designed! She has a great look to her, and the way they animated her movements and expressions gives her an extra sort of cute charm!As far as the combat goes, the two weapon system they have in place is incredibly fun! I found myself experimenting with the different weapon classes and really enjoyed mixing and matching them to find weapons that had great synergy, but also finding combos that were just plain fun to pair together!
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: this game for me thus far is very fun. I felt bad I bought it on sale because of how much I am enjoying it so I gfifted it to a friend too. combat feels *very* smooth I was instantly impressed. I love the visuals. main character talks alot doesnt bother me because her voice isnt annoying to me but that's subjective and something to note. unlike what you may expect when you see souls like it doesnt rely on indirect story telling which I am fine with. the main character to me is fine. I like her thus far. it has a direct story that you will follow that seems interesting thus far. These are mostly just my first impressions. to expand a bit on The combat though is very nice to me. it feels very polished and made with great care. all the weapons feel nice. having the second weapon be sorta a weapon you can combo into and use as a secondary attack feels well implemented and I already find myself using it to chain combos when I stagger enemy's and such.very impressed with this one. highly reccomend it based on my first impressions  with the combat which to me is always the most important thing with games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly the product of a number of highly skilled games industry folk but features a number of deep flaws that feel due to problems at the producer level within the studio.Asterigos is clearly inspired by Dark Souls but seems to just miss the underlying fundamentals of why Dark Souls works as a game.Show Don't Tell: The story is interesting (despite Hilda not being the strongest character), but there's just way too much of it. I quickly hit sections of the game with exceedingly long sections of dialogue in the span of what felt like 5 to 10 minutes of just characters talking. Now, I like story, I am ok with long periods of dialogue, but these plotbumps are just everywhere. You can't go more than 50 feet before finding another note with anywhere between 5 to 30(!) paragraphs of text or another echo that amounts to a cutscene that would be an audiolog in another game. I eventually found myself just skipping any and every amount of dialogue, only putting the briefest amount of effort in to skim the context. Just too much text.Mostly Empty Space: Many sections of the game are wonderfully crafted and just gorgeous to look at, but for every section of village there exists an equal amount of invertly drab and exhausting space to travel through. Fast travel comes midway through the game, (and thankfully you can use items to warp to and from the hub before then), but with or without it, getting from A to B within a zone sometimes feels like a chore and an exercise in thumb cramps as you'll click the left stick in over and over to burn through countless stamina gauges worth of terrain in sometimes weirdly immense spaces. The Barracks area of the game is an especially strong example of long periods of travel, especially if you're trying to clear out the zone of collectibles. And, if you do go hunting for collectibles and side stuff, (which, to steal from Robert Palmer, you might as well face it you're addicted to loot), you're going to do a LOT of pushing run and/or dash. I all but know for a fact that their QA recommended a better way to mitigate the long stretched of running which was surely veto'd by Production.So Many Skills, Little To Do: I only used a handful of skills the whole game and was never even curious about all the ones I had access to. That said, I used the Staff all game and even was spec'd hard towards skills but found that I built up AP so slowly that using skills on the regular was just wildly inefficient to just maxing attack and HP. Maybe I would have been more interested in skills if I hadn't just stuck to blasting stuff with charged shots (a manually aimed long range attack you can almost always dodge out of). I even stopped using the ultimate stance for the staff, which wholly uses your main attack, largely because the final staff attack rarely hits anything and has long uncancelable animations. Whereas, Magic Breath (a charged attack that does lock you into an animation) did so much damage in a window that I would largely just hop around and wait for a window to start standing and deliver. All this is a real shame as the skills are all just amazing to look at and the few I did use felt very crunchy, I just never had any AP to use them.Let Me Innnnnnn!~: There's just a lot of story gates in the game. In Dark Souls you have locked gates, but often you have some clear path forward towards some new boss or zone. In Asterigos, you have several major story gates you just Can Not Pass until X moment and plenty of minor gates within zones themselves. Did you find an area you're meant to be in later too early? Welp, go back and progress the plot because this door don't open until you've finished your meat. At least three times I also found myself just unable to figure out where I was meant to go next, but this is probably because I was skipping dialogue. On the other hand, I wouldn't need plot text to make forward progress.Conclusion:So to be honest, I'm still playing Asterigos and expect to finish, mostly because roaming around and blasting enemies with the staff and daggers became reasonably satisfying after getting pasted in combat trying to block or parry things. (This is on me for forgetting Soulslike Rule 1: Never Fight Fair, Hidetaka Miyazaki said it's cool dudes, cheese is legit, but you play the way you want to play, you are valid.)And a number of the boss fights are pretty good even if the melee combat feels a little clunky. And the game is quite pretty. But, I'm invested at this point. If I could go back, I'd tell past-me not to buy the game. So, here's me warning you as a proxy for past-me: There's better stuff out there to spend your time on.It's just a shame that Asterigos didn't have stronger Producers.(oh and Devs, please don't take this too harshly. You did a lot of good work here, I wouldn't have taken the time to write all this up if I didn't think there wasn't something here. Respectfully, Monster)
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen the term 'souls-lite' to describe this game, and with my limited experience in the genre(Elden Ring and Code Vein, neither finished yet), I'd say that fits. The HUD, overall feel of combat and weapon progression are familiar, with the big difference that character leveling in separate, with a more traditional exp system. This exp is not lost in any manner on death, so it feels less punishing to die. And in addition, you only lose some 'Stardust' (the money side) on death, although it is instantly gone, and not dropped.The game as a whole feels more forgiving than the other games I mentioned, which, combined with the exp, make this feel like a good option for someone whose intimidated by the genre, and can scratch the itch of veterans that want a slightly 'tamer' experience.A few negatives though.Lack of a map, no mini-map, nothing, can make it frustrating to get from point A to B.Side quest tracking, made more obvious by the prior issue, it can be a chore to remember what side quests you have active, and where/what you need to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Right, so let's talk about this game shall we? Coming from a background of a lot story driven games as my favorite choices, I can confidently say that on story telling this game delivers big time. The only issue I find in it, is the pacing, there are times where you feel like you need have rewind button to get all the indepth details. Especially when some of the side quests come into play. But overall, the story is a gripping adventure that keeps you engaged from start to end.Gameplay can feel a bit wonky, it is a learning curve with weapon and skill combo's you can have, and in that lies the real challenge, as upgrading your weapons, talent points etc. is something you don't -just- reset without paying a price. Mobs and Quest have a decent difficulty and some depending on the how you've upgraded yourself, can at times feel like fighting a Dark-souls-esc battle.Is there anything I would have liked to be different? Well, a longer story for one, perhaps a bit more varied end content that lets it feel like you've now truly become a master of your weapon and skill. A plot-twist somewhere there as well and of course, a sort of multiple endings deal... Why the multiple endings? Well, there were some encounters that gave the heavy vibe that different outcomes could be reached depending on dialog, but that wasn't the case, and felt really unfulfilling.I recommend giving this game a go if your looking a fabulous story with fun fantasy hack'n'slash.7/10 - would play again.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't know much about this game upon purchasing, didn't even know it was souls-like. I just had it on my wishlist for a long time, looking at potential purchases I looked into the game more and most comments just said combat was good which is what matters most to me. To preface this, I don't actually enjoy souls-like games, too shallow combat wise and what I normally associate with souls games is a vague story you learn about through objects. Well this game definitely fir's the bill with the die and lose some resources on death, but this game has a full story the whole way through with the collectibles giving you MASSIVE lore dumps about the world.The story was entertaining beginning to end and if you like a ton of background lore in the world there is massive amounts and found myself reading everything everything I came across,  which is most everything in the game. My biggest complaint about this is while it is nice getting this info, getting notes titled NICELY HANDWRITTEN NOTE, OR NOTE WITH TERRIBLE HANDWRITING. But the font is the same no matter what, if it's neatly written SHOW IT don't explain that, you can have an option where you press a button and you can easily read it. But instead they definitely went with the "tell don't show" option here.Combat which is something I care about the most is actually quite enjoyable. you have 6 weapons to choose from pretty much right at the start and can upgrade any as long as you ave the materials to do so. (MAX 3 WEAPONS PER RUN CAN REACH HIGHEST LEVEL IF YOU FIND THE MATS) Each weapon feels different and great in their own way I experimented a lot in the beginning until I fell into my favorite two weapons to use for the remainder of my first run. You have several skills for each weapon and perks that change how certain moves work that you can toggle on and off. It isn't the deepest combat system but it is enjoyable with a good variety of enemies to fight. The game had a good amount of difficulty throughout and never felt like it got easier as you go on. You also get to choose difficulty at the beginning I do recommend doing Challenge at the start if you are looking for a bit more difficulty. Although, if you are looking for a brutally hard game this also is not that.Speaking of difficulty there is a point in the game where it turns to night and a bunch of hard bosses spawn around the world, these bosses are definitely the hardest part of the game and the fights are VERY fun.The story itself was good, but the greatest story ever told. It dragged me in enough to reed the lore, listen to what the characters in the shelter had to say about the current and past state of Aphes. The devs really put as lot of care and attention to the world taking a ton of inspiration from Greece and Roman mythologies. The only complaint I have about the story is that to get the "best ending" is super extremely vague that absolutely requires a guide to get. You have to meet certain requirements and a certain amount of them to get this ending. A lot of it is hidden and a nice chime happens when you meet a requirement and you can check how many you have on the corner of Minerva's desk at the shelter.Now arguable the biggest problem with the game is the "quest log" or lack thereof. Therte is no map so exploration is up to you entirely, which bothered me at first but not in the grand scheme of things as this game is a lot more linear than it appears to be, there is always only one path forward. The problem is the main quest it does tell you what you need to do it's up to you to find what to do which really isn't an isn't an issue. The real issue is the side quests, you better have a damn good memory or a guide because once you are told something that is the last you will hear or read of it. Hilda writes a vague entry in her journal that explains nothing. Most things you can do on the spot but some you can't do anything about until later in the game and you get a quest item and you just think "I dunno wtf to do with this" because you spoke to some one at the earlier parts of the game that wanted it. Well you better start going to any NPC you can talk to you if you don't have a guide, or write down what/where people are.I am dedicating this  sentence at the end just to say I LOVE the soundtrack it's REALLY good.Overall it was a very enjoyable game and I loved just about everything in the game, it is rough around the egdes in a lot of ways but the pros outweigh the cons in the end. I enjoyed it enough the get all the achievements and plan on returning to this game again sometime in the future. I recommend people to try this game if you like a linear-ish souls-like with a story inspired by Greek and Roman mythologies and a good but not particularly deep, but satisfying combat system.

_childDocuments_.review: Asterigos is an ARPG with lockout combat animations, invulnerability frames, and generic 'action' button (F) to prompt your toon to execute some random task like opening doors, climbing walls, pick up an object, vaulting, etc..    This game VERY story driven.  I mean, you will get frustrated with how in-your-face the story is.  You can click though dialogue to skip it at least.  Some parts of the game basically require you to click-through all the 'talk' options with NPCs in order to open certain parts of the game, or to advance sequences.Asterigos is NOT sandbox, open-world, or free choice.  It has a linear story, following a predetermined sequence of events.  Levels/zones are like streets with platforming. Platforming in this game sucks, due to the 'jump' key being "G" for no good reason, and TONS of invisible object collision.  If it looks like a clear path, you will probably hit an invisible wall.  Vaulting can only vault things that are knee high, and only if you get the prompt that you can click on it to vault.  Clicking on the prompt means you need to get the prompt to vault to properly show up on your HUD.  (Proper facing, distance). Thanks to trashy unreal physics, your character doesn't turn, as much as they drift around an arc to get a proper facing.  This makes aligning the UI a PITA sometimes, when trying to interact with some object.  Gotta run a ways back, get lined up, and calculate your deceleration trajectory to land in the hit box for the prompt in the correct facing.  Attack sequences are basically, 'hold down button' to see your character execute a series of animations in an action-packed wow swinging around and flailing in random directions while you are getting mobbed!  So cool! At least they allow you to interrupt attack frames with a dodge or power.  Alternatively, if you want to avoid the chain-combo attack, you can mash the attack button to repeat basic attacks.  You CAN lock onto your target, but your attack combos often send you past your foe, and continue executing attacks away from your enemy's backside.  Like, you for real get stuck into a wild weapon-swinging-fest like your dude can't stop randomly failing at thin air.  It would be great if the enemy was moved along with your toon, but nope.  You just attack right past the target and keep going!  It is also possible to attack right off a cliff.  Watch those ledges.Suffice to say, combat leaves a LOT to be desired, due to ARPG lockout garbage, and action-spectacular attack animations.In conclusion, wait for a sale.  To me, this game is worth maybe $10-$15, it is graphically appealing, but otherwise a clunky click-through action story.  I dislike click-through action games, like assassin's creed, dragon age, witcher, and similar.  If you like those games, you will probably enjoy this one too.  If you don't like click-prompt ARPG with lockout animations?  Then check other titles.  This game is at least pretty, even for being so basic.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a gem. It's a big fan of Dark Souls, and I've tried several Soulslikes and Soulslites, and this is definitely a great example of a good Soulslite. That is, it's similar to Dark Souls in having engaging, difficult combat, but it's a little easier because it doesn't punish you as severely for dying. Better yet, it has more of a story than the typical Souls game, plus an attractive and lovable main character named Hilda. Hilda's beauty, style, and spunk add a lot to the experience.While Asterigos isn't perfect, it's really a worthwhile and fun game. I do think it would've been better if it had a greater variety of weapons and if you collected weapons like in Dark Souls. Instead, you start out with all of the weapons. This does give you a lot of flexibility in playstyle, and you do unlock new skills for the weapons as you level up.For anyone who likes a good Souls-style experience but is not expecting an exact clone of the Souls formula, this is game is a good choice. Alternatively, I think it could also be a good way for younger players to try out the Souls experience without it being prohibitively difficult for them. My kids enjoy watching my play Dark Souls and similar games. I think my pre-teens could get into playing the game soon.In short, I highly recommend Asterigos. I'd really glad that I bought it, and I bet you won't regret it either.

_childDocuments_.review: Asterigos is likely one of my favorite games of this year. I've played Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous, Elden Ring and the Horizon series for most of the year and this game has scratched the adventure RPG itch for me quite well.The latest update improved a lot of the main gripes I had (especially the stamina drain while dashing in the main hub).I've not completed the game, yet, but so far the story (especially all of the lore you find around the game) has really kept me interested in finishing it. The skill trees are all very interesting and lend themselves to multiple playthroughs to see how you enjoy different playstyles. There are hybrid weapon combos that are hidden and only discoverable through experimentation.At the end of the day, though, the game is very easy to grasp though difficult to master. It would be nice to have a harder difficulty to play through in the New Game+ because the enemies in my current playthrough are pretty easy to beat once you get their attack patterns down.Overall, I'm a major fan of this game. I'll be following this studio for future releases for sure, and I'm excited for the DLC. I will update this review once I beat the game and add some more detail.

_childDocuments_.review: I really kind of hate this game..This is a mostly fine action adventure RPG. I hesitate to say it's Souls-like because it does a few things to set itself apart from Souls games that I find put it more in line with a more traditional action RPG, like across between a Souls game and something like Devil May Cry, or Castlevania Lords of Shadow.The things I like, in the interest of fairness, are the character designs, the world building, and *sometimes* the combat, although I'll get to that. It's.... it's not technically competent, there are absolutely a ton of bugs and design flaws, but it is a STABLE game. I don't get unexpected crashes and the performance has been admirable. I'm able to mostly maintain a high framerate at ultra settings, so credit where credit is due.I like that the game gives you a variety of different weapons from the get go to experiment with as opposed to something like the classic God of War that just hands you 1 weapon and has you continually unlock moves and combos with it-- although you can also unlock different perks and moves for each weapon with a talent point system.The things that are frustrating in it are unfortunately things that I see many Souls-like games try to do to great detriment to the quality of the game; try to pack it with a ton of extra mechanics and systems that add nothing and overcomplicate the game to "differentiate" it. For example, the game not only gives you a compliment of different weapons to try with their own playstyles, but it  forces you to use 2 at once. This is a horrible mistake. While the idea of choosing two weapons to use that compliment each other-- maybe 1 slow, heavy weapon, and one quick weapon-- sounds cool, the controls are poorly optimized for this, and the game is bloated with so many other systems during combat that I mostly find myself cursing whoever made this decision. The game, aside from the weapons, also has an element system that you can change on the fly, a Dark Souls-style item quadrant for quickly using consumable, a special technique system that has special, mana-fueled attacks for each of the weapons, and 'special' attacks for each of the equipped weapons. This is too much. The best demonstration of this I can give is the game's comical control rebinding screen that has so many things that are required to sit in specific places in the controller I don't know why they bothered to allow rebinding. Any attempt I've made to rebind these has failed because it left a required control, wired to one of the games many systems,  absent. And I think this is the deepest wound that shows how overly bloated with unnecessary things this game is, if you can't already tell from the combat.And in the midst of having these convoluted systems, you get oddities like a required, dedicated jump button that is used extremely rarely, to the point that I'm baffled why it's there. Dark Souls resolves this issue, maybe not elegantly, but it at least understands that the other controls are more important. Asterigos wastes your controller space with this thing you almost never use expect to access some secret collectibles or resources.The combat. Ugh. It really is a spectrum between classically satisfying action game combat and a cheap system that uses tricks and artificial difficulty to imply a level of challenge it never earns. The game is lousy with projectiles. More than one of your weapons allows you to make ranged attacks, and they do not consume mana, they consume your stamina, so essentially you have unlimited ranged attacks. If you think this breaks the game to a degree, you'd be right. It compensates by making enemies have tons of projectiles they can throw, or summon, or conjure, and these are usually awful. Your projectiles stop at the first enemy they encounter. You'd expect enemy projectiles to behave identically, and you would be wrong. Enemy projectiles can pass through whatever enemies are in front of them to get to you and this is not OK. Certain enemies can conjure a ranged attack to trigger under you, and they don't require line of sight which is also not OK.But there are plenty of other problems. Your character's attacks can't handle different terrain elevations, so you'll be trying to attack an enemy on stairs slightly lower than you and miss every attack. Bosses are cheap and poorly designed, often not telegraphing major attacks, or having horrible hit detection that sometimes winds up causing damage for attacks you successfully dodged. They all also essentially follow the same formula of having 1 attack that can be comboed over and over just "until you take damage." AOEs are too broad and deal damage to you (LOTS of damage) when you're not near them.The game also has bugs. In the briefing after the black streets, the overlay with documents wouldn't go away so I couldn't see what I was doing. When I tried to keep pressing cancel to clear it, my character closed the dialog entirely and was chided by the NPC. In the same dialog, the left and right arrows indicating more pages were set on the document instead of to either side, and for some reason the designs thought that these arrows should be the SAME COLOR as the parchment.There's a light you eventually get to help you in dark areas, and the light also has some helpful exploration functions, but it's relegated to an inventory item that you need to use in order to turn on and off. This should just be a thing that's allocated to your character and stays on, since I don't see any reason why you'd ever take it off. It's a weird design decision.As I sit here and type this, the thing that pissed me off enough to finally stop giving this games chances was a boss that appears in the area as part of a scripted sequence. The sequence ended, but doesn't do anything to communicate to the player that it's over, so I took a ton of damage from an incoming attack. I left and did the whole bonfire thing to start over, since I consider this pretty cheap. The next time I hid behind a wall, and wouldn't you know it, the ranged attacks go through walls. So now here I am just trying to make it to a place where I can even start observing and seeing what kinds of things this enemy can do other than cheat, and I've already wasted 2 rests on it. These are the kinds of things that betray that the game doesn't respect you and doesn't respect your time.I cannot recommend this game. I have hopes that they'll eventually fix the weird walking animation for Hilda, curb projectiles, stop making me go back and 'select' that I accept a mission after my character has already agreed to accept it in dialog, and that some of the bloated mechanics will be trimmed down to be accessible and useful in combat instead of a steamer trunk full of bad ideas. But I'm not holding my breath.

_childDocuments_.review: Another reviewer described this best, as a "Souls-Lite" rather than a "Souls-Like." A lot of the familiar elements are there, and there can be a more challenging experience if you want one, but the game is vastly more accessible with both a "normal" mode (which I found to be slightly challenging at times) and an easy mode, which I can only imagine must be pretty darn easy.If the mere existence of an "easy mode" turns you off then, well, there you go, but you'll be missing out on an absolutely fantastic game.It's much more mobile than a true souls-like, where you can not only dart around faster and utilize a greater degree of weapon movement, but can even gain a trait to make your dodge much more responsive (at the cost of shorter I-frame duration). With all of the different weapon/build combos there's plenty of replayability for gameplay alone, and this is one of the few games where I enjoyed combat as much on the last boss as I did at any other point in the game.Speaking of bosses, there are no more than you'd expect (one for each zone, give or take a mini-boss or a boss for the zone's expansion). However, the variety of them and their mechanics makes this another rare game where I looked forward to the next boss fight, rather than dreading it. A couple of them even made me grin like an idiot as they were introduced.It's also visually and auditorially quite pleasing, not just in terms of the models and sound but the use of color and space. Weapons feel impactful (you definitely want to use a controller for this one), animations look fluid (mostly), and there were only a couple of zones where I wasn't at any time distracted by the environments or some of the characters.There are a lot of characters of course, and many of them have a lot to say. Not all of their dialogue is voiced, but when it is, it's great. When it's not, there's a lot of reading. There are also a lot of hidden things to find for more reading. If you don't mind reading a lot in a game (and I don't), and you find the story interesting enough to look for more details (and I did), you will get a lot more out of it than someone who ignores exploration or skips through text.However, on my second playthrough, skipping all text was pretty much a given, except after exploring different choices and options. It's a one-and-done sort of story, despite the allusions to alternate paths (they're not too meaningful) which brings us to the game's weaknesses.First of all, all of these elements, from style of gameplay, to aesthetics, to characters and story, are subjective, and you may take or leave them, hating everything I loved. But there are a few glaring issues which are more or less objective. They were not too big of an issue for me, but they may be for you.First is the A.I. I couldn't ever quite tell if enemies just had really low poise or were just freezing up. Using the staff is easy mode on all levels, as you can range and kite just about anything to death, sometimes before it even reacts. Enemy mechanics are quite fun, but they're not always consistent. Some will stop mid-fight as though having forgotten they were trying to kill you. This considerably increased the game's easiness.Second is the backtracking. Almost every large level has a means of creating a shortcut to its beginning, but these are not always obvious, or they may be delayed to very late in exploration. The Academy (which I otherwise loved) was probably the worst offender here, and where a lot of running back and forth over long distances became the most annoying. You gain  at around the 60% mark, which helps a lot, but is an ability that would have been welcome much earlier.Finally, the jumping mechanics are terrible, which can make one particular jump  absolutely maddening, especially as it's necessary to progress. Seriously, I wish I could skip that jump on every successive playthrough, it is so wonky. Add to that the weird combination of inputs to jump in the first place (one prone to sending you rolling off, rather than jumping, or jumping, rather than dodging), and you have a big thorn in the game's side.But to be honest, although memorable enough, I was still really reaching for those flaws. Not since Skyrim have I wished I was playing a game whenever I wasn't.Great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars

_childDocuments_.review: Asterigos: Curse of the Stars is a game that exceeded my expectations. Initially, I anticipated an average soulslike experience, but I was pleasantly surprised to discover a well-crafted souls-lite game.First and foremost, the gameplay mechanics in Asterigos are impressively refined. The combat system strikes a perfect balance between challenging and accessible, allowing players to engage in thrilling battles while still providing room for growth and improvement. The precise controls and responsive actions make every encounter feel satisfying and rewarding. The combat in Asterigos: Curse of the Stars strikes a delicate balance between the weighty combat mechanics of Souls-like games and the more agile action RPG style. This middle ground may not appeal to purists from either camp, but approaching it with an open mind reveals an enjoyable combat system. Initially, the combat may feel a bit slow, but as you unlock more abilities, it becomes increasingly thrilling. However, there is a slight issue with balance in the game. Certain weapons, such as spears and daggers, outshine others, making them feel superior in terms of effectiveness. Despite this disparity, all the weapons are undeniably fun to use, allowing players to experiment and find their preferred playstyle.In terms of boss encounters, most of them are well-designed from a mechanical standpoint, offering engaging battles. However, some bosses lack interesting visual designs, which can take away from the overall experience. It would have been even more captivating if both the mechanics and aesthetics of all the bosses were equally remarkable. Speaking of difficulty, it's worth mentioning that the game leans slightly towards the easier side, even when playing on the hardest difficulty setting. This might disappoint players seeking an extreme challenge or veterans of the genre. Nevertheless, this accessible level of difficulty ensures that players of varying skill levels can enjoy the game without becoming excessively frustrated.The story in "Asterigos: Curse of the Stars" can be described as serviceable, although it occasionally ventures into overly ambitious territory. The game features an abundance of information dumping, numerous optional dialogues, and an extensive lore to delve into. The developers aimed to flesh out the world and provide a rich narrative experience, but the sheer amount of content can feel overwhelming at times. One notable aspect of the storytelling is the inclusion of "echoes," which are essentially mini cutscenes showcasing past events. These echoes aim to provide additional context and deepen the understanding of the game's world and storyline. While this feature adds depth to the narrative, the abundance of echoes can be a lot to take in, particularly for players who prefer a more streamlined storytelling approach.The soundtrack of Asterigos is generally solid, providing a fitting accompaniment to the game. However, it follows the usual trope of gothic priest humming that is often found in Souls-like games. The soundtrack successfully sets the mood and atmosphere of the game, enhancing the overall experience, while a staple in the genre, can feel somewhat clichéd or predictable. While it may resonate with fans of the Souls-like genre, it doesn't bring much new or innovative to the table in terms of musical direction.Nonetheless, the soundtrack as a whole remains a solid component of the game, effectively complementing the gameplay and contributing to the overall atmosphere. One of the standout features of Asterigos is its exceptional level design, which sets it apart from other non-FromSoftware soulslikes. The game showcases a remarkable blend of Romanesque architecture, creating a captivating and immersive world to explore. The interconnectivity of the game's environments is particularly impressive. From the opulent hallways of the academy to the mesmerizing crystalline caverns, each area seamlessly flows into the next, offering a sense of cohesion and depth. This interconnectedness enhances the exploration aspect of the game, as players discover hidden paths, shortcuts, and intricate level layouts that create a rewarding sense of discovery. The attention to detail in the level design is evident, with intricate and visually stunning environments that showcase the game's unique setting. The Romanesque architecture adds a touch of grandeur and splendor, making each location a feast for the eyes. Exploring these meticulously crafted spaces is a joy in itself, as they provide a sense of wonder and immersion. Moreover, the level design in Asterigos encourages players to engage with the world and its various mechanics. Navigating through the environments, discovering secrets, and finding new paths not only adds to the sense of exploration but also rewards players with valuable items, upgrades, and lore that enriches the overall experience.In the end I had a great time with Asterigos and will most likely be doing a NG+ run, if you're after a more souls-lite experience with  great level design, you can do much worse than Asterigos.8/10 my final score

_childDocuments_.review: (Spoiler free)I finished the game after 50 hours and I have to say it ist pretty damn good, especially for an Indie-Debut-Game. Technical:The game is extremely well polished, I had no major bugs throughout (except a few spelling errors) and the sound- and art-design was absolutely phenomenal.Gameplay:I really enjoyed exploring this game and finding all the hidden materials in the world. The combat is very simple and straight forward but in a good way and I always had to think on my feet to survive (I played on medium difficulty). Trying out the different weapon-combinations was a lot of fun and the fights are pretty well balanced to make each weapon viable, though I am pretty sure you will have quite a difficult time without the staff.Story:The history and lore of Aphes and how the curse came to be is very interesting, the characters involved are quite well written and interesting and the way their relationship develops is believable. Hilda struggling with her lack of experience as a character-arc is an interesting idea, though I feel the payoff of her learning that there are consequences for her actions could have been given more weight by actually showing those consequences directly (perhaps in the ending slideshow).Bossfights:None of the bosses drop the ball as far as I can tell. They all have varied movesets that develop throughout the fight with the second boss being a particular standout. Unfortunately the last boss (no spoilers) did not really deliver anything memorable. It was well balanced and by no means bad but I feel like it should have been something more unique and interesting, to make the ending of the game feel more climactic.Conclusion:A great choice for fans of the souls-like genre with only a few rough edges that do not detract from the rock-solid experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend this game because it is a fun game, but there is no map nor a quest tracker. I played for a few days in a row, skipped a day, and when I came back had no idea where I was or where to go next because the area all looked the same. If you are playing a section straight through you are mostly fine as it is pretty linear, but many areas have a strong consistent theme, which looks good but is very easy to blur together. And since many of the side quests are knocking different doors that don't look different from other knockable doors that give non-relevant gossip, you just have to go through the entire area again just knocking random doors. One early side quest has a guy, behind a door, demand you bring him multiple items, but I forgot instantly what they were, he wouldn't speak to me again, and the notebook Hilda writes in just gives her thoughts, calling him grumpy or such, not what he asked for. I just have to hope I grab the items and somehow find his door again. I've put off continuing the game as I don't want to look up a guide, but I know I'm going to have to.

_childDocuments_.review: I  wanted to like this game. It seemed like a scaled-down Dark Souls for those who don't have that kind of patience, or a more fleshed out Kena Bridge of Spirits. While it shares qualities with both of those games, the lack of map is absolutely infuriating. If you've got a poor sense of direction, little patience for reused environmental assets that add to that confusion, and even less patience for unclear directives, this game is not for you.It has a lot going for it - different weapon styles, a deep upgrade system, what seemed like it could've been a cool plot if I could figure out how to keep going, etc...I have high hopes that whatever this developer does next is great, there's just so much potential here. There's a lot to like about this game, but I do not have the patience to spend backtrack through identical looking environments - hoping I haven't been there before - to find the next objective.
