_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of roguelikes of various kinds, here are some thoughts I have after playing similar games like Dead Cells and Skul extensively:Pros:The artstyle and music are both pretty goodDecent variety of weapons to choose fromThere are a reasonable amount of moments you are left with a decision between two or more things that actually make you weigh your options (which is a great thing to strive for in roguelikes vs the alternative of one option always being best and making the randomness obsolete)I've beaten up to Breakdown IV so far, but it seems it goes quite a bit past that, so it's nice that there's depth to the difficulty (I can't say at this time whether the upper levels are "fair" however)Cons:Balancing could use some work. Some abilities together can make a run effortless sometimes ("Gain 1 max hp every time you get hit (not take damage, but receive an attack)", along with something that gives you enough defense to take no damage, suddenly getting tons max hp for absolutely free for just standing still in front of an enemy for a while). On the note of balancing, the rarity of curse rewards don't quite line up. Sometimes a common reward is way more useful than some of the epic or even legendary rewards. I think it's weird that you can be offered some that are contextually useful or useless (EG: Legendary curse that doubles defense...which is useless if you have no defense curses or weapons that give defense like Parasol).There's also a noticeable gap between enemy difficulty and boss difficulty. Enemies are pretty easy as you can just mash the scythe and stunlock them as you go through the rooms, while bosses typically require constant dodging. The flow of combat between these two are a bit dissonant from each other.Some spells' usefulness doesn't seem to quite match their rarity, or perhaps I haven't found the application that makes them worthy of the rarity given.Reaching Breakdown IV there only seems to be a handful of things left to unlock with Ingots, so perhaps more things to unlock to encourage longer playing is an idea I'd suggest to the developers as well.Neutral things:Like most/all roguelikes, the game often is very difficult as you learn how the game works and learn patterns. The game is pretty difficult on the whole, but I'd ignore reviews calling the game unfair. It may take 5-10 hours to really get the hang of things, but a lot of the difficulty can be overcome by not trying to mash your way through everything (which unfortunately the normal enemies encourage because it's so effective), and actually stop your combo to give time to dodge attacks.In terms of the speed/flow of combat compared to other action roguelikes, I'd say it's slightly slower than average, but not by much. I wouldn't mind if the game was slightly sped up on the whole, but it's nice that most enemies project their attacks ahead of time.This game has limited healing items to find, and finding them is random, so it's similar to Dead Cells in that optimal play encourages getting hit as little as possible as your focus.Overall Score: 7.5/10It's not bad, it's not great. I am having fun right now, but I'm not sure if this game will be able to capture me to complete its hardest difficulty challenges like other roguelikes have. There isn't enough depth to make this a game that you'd replay for hundreds of hours, so much as unlock the things/beat the challenges and be done with it in my opinion.Feedback for developers:Fine tune balancing on the whole, maybe consider making healing a little more accesable to acquire (Relaxation room is incredibly rare to find in runs, and anima being mostly luck based is annoying sometimes), clarify some descriptions (specifically with "X do more damage in this department", making it disappear or cross out when you're done with that department and doesn't appear as ongoing despite the description). A way to see more status buffs you have would be nice too (food effects on pause screen, or hover with mouse at least on the UI, a timer with how much of the effect is left would be great too). Soulary Department could afford to offer more soulary for choosing it, it feels like a weak room choice unless that extra 10 soulary would really make the difference down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: It looks great, and the writing is humorous enough, but the game is just boring and has some truly puzzling design decisions.So, combat starts with your basic attack. Mash attack 3 times, and you have a combo. The enemies get dizzy if you do enough damage to them, which prevents them from hitting back. Usually simple to do on smaller enemies, and for larger enemies you have an i-frame capable dash. Fine. No problems.The stages however, are devoid of ANYTHING. Most of the first stage has you walking right. You can go up and down (think Dead Cells).... but there's nothing there. Sometimes a small enemy.... sometimes. I don't expect to find the best item in the game every time I venture out of a straight path but... something? No? Okay.Your meta progression is fine. You collect gold and unlock "weapons", which are not actually weapons, they are abilities that are good for that one run you are on. These range from overpowered to completely worthless, and RNG determines what you get. This is my first problem. Roguelite/roguelike games are all about making a run work even in the most awful imaginable situation. Well, aside from a very few things, almost every case is awful, and none of it works. You do so little damage and the mobs just keep eating away at....your health. So here, we have a bar of health. It goes down when we get hit. Cool. Wait. There is also a grey bar. What? So here's how it works. When your main health bar goes down, you have a grey health bar. If you happen to find a (almost never dropped) healing item, you only recover some of the grey bar. So essentially, you LOSE max HP... by getting hit. Look folks, I beat Contra back in the day, but Contra was designed around that. Here, I'm traveling right across (5?) boring stages, please don't ask me to be perfect, just make them more interesting. Once you get over THAT hurdle you discover that the once nice looking graphics are just... green. And then you see that after beating a level boss (if you get overpowered in a few hits, or if you are underpowered in about 10 minutes of dodging around), you come to a fridge that gives you +defense for 10 minutes. A side scroller, a linear one at that, offering an MMO style booster of 10 minutes of +attack or defense. You can even unlock more of these with meta progression currency! They doubled down on this idea. Oy! And shortly after, you come to the review section and make this game sound like it made you eventually feel; bored, annoyed, and wishing you never bought it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is wonderfully animated and quirky, not taking itself too seriously with all the dark humour throughout the entire experience. I especially like the character design, it’s really clever and fits the overall theme. Combat is fun, fast and responsive, it’s satisfying to use attacks that connect in a cool combo sequence and the attack/skills animations are just fantastic! Music is mostly sombre but picks up when fighting boss and arena style encounters, makes for a dynamic change! I wasn’t that invested in the story but there are many fun moments that made me giggle.Progression system is straightforward but a bit tricky. Due to a limited arsenal of abilities you can carry there is little incentive to experiment with various upgrades and attacks you pick up during the run. You can always experiment on consecutive runs but usually you’ll stick to the abilities you find early in the run. I like the Curse system but I find Blue Curses to be mostly redundant. It might just be me but I haven’t picked many during my play through. I feel they are lacking momentum and impact compared to the Red and Green ones. Some are too specific to even consider during a run when they pop up, they don’t excite me. I had a bit of an issue with the rarity system. I often couldn’t tell if abilities/curses I pick up are of a higher potency. Overall I would totally recommend the game to people who like rogue likes and appreciate a cool and fun visual presentation!

_childDocuments_.review: Competent. It's damning with faint praise, but that's the only real word that can be used to describe Have A Nice Death. In mechanics, tone, aesthetic, structure, and story nothing in this game hasn't been done elsewhere and done better, but what's here is rarely outright bad. It's just even more rarely outright good. This sort of psuedo-metroidvania combat is always tricky to get right and with its bloated HP totals and ferocious enemy damage this game misses the mark. What's worse is that while powerful defensive and healing abilities exist they often incentivize waiting around for slow cooldowns to tick over. The writing is decent enough if you enjoy this sort of Dilbert-tier lampooning of office culture, but it has no insights or clever characterizations and what few characters are interesting are archetypes portrayed with more love and more finesse in Hades. The muted color palette makes it difficult to distinguish enemy attacks during larger fights, and the movement is too floaty for some of the precision platforming they occasionally demand. It's a death of a thousand cuts where if any facet of this game was phenomenal I could see myself sticking around despite the rest, but there's just nothing to look forward to once you've run through the basics. If you just want to hit buttons for a dozen or so hours until you get sick of it, this will certainly do the job and there's worse options out there, but there's nothing here you haven't already seen.

_childDocuments_.review: Have a Nice Death feels like the devs thought "What if Hades was a platformer instead?" which is a great idea, but the execution falls slightly short. The art and style are phenomenal and the music is good - I love the theme of the game. The combat feels very tight and satisfying, and the boss fights in particular are super fun. The core loop of the game feels very similar to Hades: you clear several levels within a stage then beat the big boss to move to the next stage, within each run you can collect some items or xp that will let you come back stronger next time, and after each run you get a new set of dialogue with the games cast of characters and, if you leveled up, some new items to play with. Unfortunately, the positives kind of end there. While procedurally generated levels don't /have/ to feel generated, HAND's really do. It's missing the hidden secrets that make the levels in games like Hades, Dead Cells, or Hollow Knight feel worth exploring. The pathing of the levels also often feels a bit random - many times I went down into an area only to realize it was completely empty and pointless. And whereas the combat has some depth and challenge to it, the platforming here is very simple - it clearly isn't meant to be the challenge. The game is also missing the control over your run that makes Hades so fun to keep going back to. There's so many fun weapons to try out, but they're all gated behind RNG. Why can't I choose my starting weapon, at least? In conclusion, the game is carried by its style and satisfying boss fights but as you get deeper into it the levels between those boss fights may start to feel like a slog. I still really like the game and I think with a couple of tweaks (or mods) and a steady stream of fresh content it could be one of the best rogue-lites out there. The game's biggest 'problem' is that it's far more shallow than its peers while costing the same price. If regular updates can shore that up, the future looks great for Have a Nice Death.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, gather round my children, for I have a review to tell...Have a Nice Death is a wonderful game for those who enjoy a face-paced action and dynamic combat. The style of the game is its best aspect though; the colors, animations, art style, and visual humor is what makes this game truly unique from other games. I am one who enjoys action roguelikes, and despite this game's lack of build opportunity, it makes up for in cool ability synergy. A run in this game can determine slight variations into your playstyle, but it won't be as diverse as...let's say...Hades. I believe the intention of this game is to provide enough of a challenge to keep your attention, but doesn't complicate it to make it feel like a chore at times: a perfectly relaxing game for myself.The story isn't complete, nor is it deep. _childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing! The controls are buttery smooth and the action is addictive. The lore is interesting, I particularly like the office aesthetics and kitchen gossip. The art is unique and the action is never obscured. My only grip i that the spells seem to somehow fire in the wrong direction from where you are facing for some odd reason. Being in EA, I assume this will be addressed.Above is my inital review - This review is for March 19th 2023: The combat is fluid and enjoyable, there is very good feedback when enemies are hit and distinct sound effects for each weapons. Visually, this game is very unique , it stands out, has its own aesthetics and is just thematically sound. Technically, the devs have fixed all the issues I had initally, health has been rebalanced and feels more fair. Starting weapons can now be selected and you have some ability to "curate"your own run. That said,  I struggle to find the same ability to fine tune my run that I can find in other rouge likes. Let's use dead cells for an example of this. I can decide to do a run with oil and fire, lightning damange, etc. And curate this experience throughout the run for synergies that make you feel powerful. HAND does have an ability to "curate" with curses, I just feel like i never had the control I would like and the random options don't seem to consider what you chose before.Specific spells are hard to find if not impossible, there are some spells I have seen only once. The fun in these games -  for me  - is the variety in spells , weapons and having a different run each time. I do not feel like this achieves this for me. This is just a personal opinion, but by no means is this a bad game and I think everyone should play it. I am just struggling to have the type of fun  I expect from this genre in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a roguelike. Roguelikes are fundamentally flawed for what I like in games, the level design is either incredibly boring out of necessity, and they're inconsistent, also out of necessity. You can't really master them because they're always changing. This one feels pretty good to play, but it's also really annoying to get a really good item one run, destroy everything, then get nothing the next and get destroyed. This one also doesn't explain it's mechanics super well, such as what the symbols on the select screen mean. Other games have that, sure, but that doesn't mean it's not bad. You're just at a deficit for the first few runs, when you're already at a deficit because you haven't played the game yet. The movement feels pretty good, and the attacks are quick, but taking more than one attack to stun an enemy like the Pyromancers, or whatever they're called, doesn't seem like a great choice, given that you can't see what they're doing when you're attacking them. If the scythe's trails didn't last so long or didn't cover the enemy completely, that issue simply wouldn't exist. Enemies immediately turning around during wind-ups in a game where every single hit matters is also really bad, especially considering it's 2d, and being close enough to get behind them during the wind up time is already a challenge. It feels really good to play and it has nice charm, but there are plenty of mechanics that I don't like so far, mostly due to it being a roguelike. It's not a bad game, but it's not great, either. I guess this would be a recommend if you like the things that I dislike about roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: For me, this game is a 5/10. Now please remember what that means, average. This is an average game. It isn't terrible by any means, nor is it particularly astounding, it just an okay game. The game isn't a broken buggy mess, nor does it employ anything particularly new or profound.In terms of style I commend the art team for making something as grim as death and its topics look so absolutely cute. Character designs are unique and play along with the character's punny names or defining features.For story, it isn't really anything grandiose, just a bunch of co-workers with their boss stuck in an eternal job together just doing their own things with those who mess around or slack off being put in their place. For those who work a regular 9-5 office job, the story will resound particularly well.In terms of combat, it is swift and flashy but also is very "swingy", as in your own experience with how easy or tedious combat will be is entirely dependent on what curses or drops you are able to find throughout your run(If you can find any). Any one particular run can feel either like an episode of one-punch man or death by a thousand cuts, emphasis on the thousand. Given that all drops are random and you can't force the game to have you start with a specific weapon you've unlocked (other than another RNG starting armory), you can't really make a character "build" per say when you start a run either. Unfortunately this makes it very hard to take any sort of accomplishment as a player to have any sort of meaning when a fight can take anywhere from 10 seconds to 4 minutes simply on RNG gear alone.In terms of resources throughout a run, unfortunately that too is very "swingy". Even with all items unlocked, you could kill an entire genocides worth of enemies and feel either like an unkillable millionaire with way too many resources or a pauper constantly on the verge of death with how frequent or infrequent soulary, anima, or general consumables drop. Even if you do get a decent amount of resources, shop or upgrade prices make you feel like your 30 minutes of killing mobs and mini-bosses is tantamount to only 1 shop purchase or upgrade. This is a shame for each weapon and ability can be upgrade up to three times but you will be hard pressed to even get even one to level 2 let alone level 3 with the price spikes. Now lets talk about Prismium. Prismium, this all powerful resource that allows you to upgrade your base scythe or upgrade the shop's inventory is more scarce than a drop of water in a desert. Not only that, but when you finally do find this mythical resource and spend it, lo and behold after you die you find out that the upgrade to either the shop or the scythe isn't even a permanent thing. So I ask you, what is even the point of this resource if it can take you literal hundreds of runs to encounter it once, only for it to mean literally nothing?This brings me to the feeling or sense of progression, there isn't any really. Other than story progression and slowly unlocking the chance to encounter weapons, abilities, or consumables, there aren't permanent character upgrades. Yes there is a level up system, but its passive bonuses are only there to alleviate problems that the game creates itself. You will always start out with 65 health, you will always deal 10 damage, and bosses (and some general mob enemies) will still kill you in just a few hits. In addition, weapon and ability upgrades you get in a run don't carry over to the next so even if you do somehow get enough resources to get even one weapon to level 3, know it will revert to level 0 in your next run.All in all when I first played my first couple of hours, I did genuinely have fun and that's what counts, and at the same time I slowly became dissatisfied with its experience as I played more to the point where I don't even want to achieve my first full run clear. The game has a periodic tendency to remind the player about "burn out" and while I took this as a funny 4th wall break joke at the beginning, its message soon started to resonate with me as I played more and more until I reached the point where the second half of the devloper's message set it. If you feel burned out, please do not hesitate to stop playing this game. To me the short experience was worth the 25 dollars and now its time to put it into my library where it will stay until I ever feel like playing it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Look the game is really good, especially for an early access game. It's charming and funny, with likeable characters and a beautiful art style. The combat feels fluid and the boss fights feel fun and engaging.However the level design outside of boss fights is weak, calling this game a platformer is stretching as some of the levels are very basic. In addition there is no real incentive to explore as the levels are mostly boring. While the art style is good it can often be distracting as the backgrounds have a lot going on. I can make it past brad but the healing mechanic seems flawed to me. I don't understand the injured mechanic, sometimes i can heal past it sometimes i cant. So without a way to actually heal that much health. The game becomes extremely challenging to the point where you essentially have to beat the first boss flawlessly if you even want a chance to make it to the second boss. Something else this game sorely needs is a parry mechanic it would add something to the combat. In addition I'm guessing each of the different levels mean something? But i cant tell what each level is as there is nowhere in the game that tells you this. In addition to this i feel like i get no real reward for making progress. I can unlock new weapons sure, but I'm only unlocking a chance to get those weapons so whats the point really?All of that being said. The game is very well made and enjoyable. It gets a bit stale after a while but that's to be expected off of an early access game. I hope to see these issues get improved as the game goes through early access, if so it will make one hell of game!

_childDocuments_.review: The art style is honestly absolutely gorgeous, easily one of the most stunning I have ever seen. This needs to be stressed because I am in love.The characters, the world, and the story (all the little arcs, too) are so lovely. It has a unique charm that I simply can't get enough of.The combat is, mostly, fluid, fun and pretty fantastic - the controls take a bit to get the hang of, but not because it's clunky: it's just so dynamic, anything you do seamlessly blends into the next move. It feels so full and intense, and yet also really simple. It's also REALLY fast - not a bad thing, just takes a bit to get used to.The gameplay and difficulty... this is tricky. I put these two together because the difficulty forms a crucial part of the gameplay - of course, this is true for all roguelikes, but this one, even more so, and not in a good way, imo. I think that it's got some serious downsides. Part of the charm of many roguelikes is that when you die, it's not just a bad thing - you are stronger / better. Hades is an obvious example, from the mirror to the weapons to even just the talismons, and ofc the "god mode". This game has that god mode, sort of, but it caps pretty early and is really weak. You can unlock new weapons (endless weapons, so many weapons, how are there so many weapons), which does help keep runs fresh, but you can't CHOOSE your weapon. You just gotta hope you get a good one, and then during the run, pick between rolling the dice again to try get a different weapon or getting things like health or mana bar upgrades. Which, again, isn't something you can upgrade in between runs, it just stays pathetic, so upgrading it feels crucial during the run. Overall, when you die, it often just feels like a waste. I gained nothing. I gained practise, sure, and can get better in that way, of course, but it doesn't always feel great, just demoralising. It can also feel really hard, unfairly hard, unless you cheese it a bit. The bosses mostly need you to just wait out their attacks, dodging. The minions come down to about two strategies - they mostly need to be stun locked, which happens after 1 hit, and then working from there. Mostly, it seems like keeping enemies a w a y from you is what's best. Picking a ranged weapon seems to be the smart thing to do, for both minions and bosses, as it will get you the best results... which sucks, because all that fluid lovely combat and game play doesn't translate to simply standing as far away as possible and just taking pot shots, or other, very similar, cheeses. You don't HAVE to do that, of course, but it is way easier, and the game is pretty hard with absolutely no way of improving your character. So having all those weapons doesn't feel like a good thing, it's just another obstacle. Dying changes nothing. The enemies somehow manage to be both a lil too hard, a lil too repetitive, and not rewarding - and honestly, that sums up how the gameplay ends up feeling: a lil too hard, a lil too repetitive, a bit too unrewarding.I think this ended up as a fun beginning, and then just... I don't know. Mixed feelings. Love-hate. I still enjoyed it. It still has loads of good. I plan to keep playing it, at some point. But there's pretty important parts that just feel... unfriendly. I'm still going to recommend it, because I think it's genuinely stunning, has loads of charm, and feels unique and fun. It has huge potential, I adore it. But the downsides are definitely there.

_childDocuments_.review: After 5 hours of gameplay, I can officially say that I do like this game. However, there are a few things that frustrate me while its in the Early Access, and I hope they get fixed:1. The clearly inconsistent Anima drops. Sometimes i'll get dozens in a run, even when on full health. Then next run I will need them, and I will get absolutely none until after first Biome boss. Definitely needs to be adjusted. 2. The fact that there is no real 'reward' for repeat runs. Having played many rogue-lites over the years, my favourite thing about them is that you do actually feel some kind of progression, even when dying and having to start over. This doesn't have that, you have the same exact run every time, with the difference being potentially you may find new spells/weapons. You always deal the same damage, always have the same start of currencies, etc. Its my biggest gripe - I wish they rewarded you for continuous play. That's the one thing that's going to stop me from playing this over and over sadly - unless they introduce something like this to keep you playing. Overall - 7/10 so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, combat feels sharp and quick, and though oftentimes there are moments of unfair projectiles it's really not enough to bother me.I like a lot of stuff about this game, don't get me wrong, but there are a lot of flaws as well.oh boyI just want to note that I can understand difficulty. I get losing over and over again can often be beneficial, and I get rogue-like games are literally built around the concept of dying over and over.But there's a difference between fun difficulty, and frustrating difficulty.The movement in the game is super imprecise, which isn't really that bad usually, but the straight, slow dash can often end up just moving you into a different attack, since it can't be cancelled early, and it doesn't have enough invincibility frames to compensate. Some enemies (I don't really wanna spoil much so I won't note them) have attacks that are ridiculously difficult to dodge, or projectiles that home in on your position far too well to be fair. In terms of area's, there's only two I have a problem with.(SPOILERS FOR THOSE AREA'S BTW)The addiction department is just absurd.Every time I attempt to get past it, I'm hit with the stupidly unfair range of the jack-in-the-box style enemies (haven't looked in to them so I'm not sure what they're called) every hit is negated by the enemies that make other enemies invincible, and it's basically a nightmare.And then of course it puts you up against maxx, a boss that's so much more difficult than Hector Krab it's actually a bit goofy.The second area I have a problem with is the inevitable time department.Most of the enemies are actually pretty fair, and are fun to fight against!Except for those big guys with the hammers.Even with insane defense buffs, they still dealt FORTY damage with one hit, which, if you don't know, is usually around a fourth of your health. If I could, I killed them with attacks that didn't require me to be anywhere near them to do damage, or just ignored them, because otherwise they could potentially end the run that had already gotten pretty far.And the boss of the area is pretty ok actually, he's kind of fair and you can start to learn his patterns pretty-Sorry what was that?Oh yeah right, the boss of the area actually ISN'T the boss of that area.Yeah so he's basically a guardian to the actual boss, but he's so difficult, and placed in the exact position the boss normally would, that it makes him seem like the actual boss.So you're tricked into thinking he's the boss, and when you beat him and find out he's not, it ruins that moment of fulfillment where you're like, "this was a really cool super tough challenge and I beat it that's so cool!"Nah there's just another, harder boss waiting in that exact same room.In terms of characters, they're decent designs, fun and interesting and their dialogue can be pretty funny, but after a few runs I found myself skipping through pretty much everything they had to say that didn't give me key story points. They just became... not interesting, so quickly, which is a shame, because I do WANT to care about them. I think they're fun and cool and have a ton of potential! But... Idk why, but I just started to care more about finishing/playing the game than interacting with them.And I want to end out saying that again, I do understand difficulty, and I'm willing to roll with it and lose a ton of times, but it's just so much more frustrating and annoying to die than fun to go for another run after completing the first.It just stops being rewarding, and there's not much you can look forward to or work on, mostly just passive stuff that you get for playing the game that you just stop by to collect from time to time.And of course, it was a fun game to play, but I just... I can't muster the same excitement about it as I can other games, like Hollow Knight or Hades.Anyway, you didn't read all that, so byeEDIT:I'm now just realizing that I didn't even talk about how annoying the anima system is.Oh well I'll summarize my beef with it really quick1. Some runs you'll get basically no anima2. The wound/injury system is horrifically explained 3. After gaining three golden anima, all other anima earned are completely useless4. Making the only healing item in the game also basically being the only way to unlock some area's that often don't even lead to anything useful is kinda jankAnd also, I just wanna let the devs know (though they absolutely will NOT see this) that this is still a game with a ton of potential, and I can see how awesome it can still beKeep doing what you're doing, and you can make something even more awesome

_childDocuments_.review: first of all the game is game is great! the animations, the style, the characters, the story, the music, the sounds, everything is there. there are however a few things to that needs to be resolved on the gameplay side because it honestly is too frustrating at the moment.First of all, fighting enemies outside of arenas where you get rewards is pretty much pointless. Enemies have a chance to drop items but it is way too small to be worth fighting them. The only thing you're risking is loosing HP which bring me to my second point.Second of all, like many other people have said, you have absolutely no sustain whatsoever. enemies can drop healing orbs which heal a tiny bit of hp but as i said before, it is very rare (i've had multiple runs where not a single enemy has dropped one). I was expecting to find a healing spot after the defeating the boss of every level but again no. most of the time the resting spot gives you a buff you don't need when you're 25% HP. These 2 problems the best strategy is to rush past every enemy outside of arenas because you don't get anything other than loosing health which is way too hard to recover. A third and final problem and this is maybe on a personal side, the camera isn't very good. when i move foward, the camera is following my character but too far back which means i can't really see what's ahead of me.I also found the levels weirdly short. if you expect the levels to be as long as they are in hades for example, you'll be in for a shock because they are really small and it doesn't help that you have to rush past all the enemies because fighting them isn't worth it.I can't recommend this game right now because it simply is too hard and not rewarding enough. The game is still in early access however and these are problems that can easily be fixed. Fixing these issues would make the game so much enjoyable and really unlock it's whole potential because it really has a lot of potential. Hopefully, an update in the future will resolve these problemsEdit after the infrastructure update : The situation about the lack of healing is a lot better. enemies have a bigger chance to drop healing orbs, there's a thing in the break room where you can buy healing orbs at increasing prices, getting a blue orb while you're already holding 3 blue ones will upgrade one to a yellow orb and there's a new room that literally just heals you. All these changes have honestly made a big difference in terms of gameplay and it's a lot more enjoyable. The developpers seem to really be listening to the community and have added a lot of content with the latest update. i would say that the game is now worth buying

_childDocuments_.review: While at first I had a lot of fun with this game in the past few hours it's become increasingly frustrating to play. There are a couple of reasons for this.Boss balance is just not there. You can choose different paths but depending on how good your built is you tend to avoid a few bosses/levels just because they're SO much more difficult than the other option. Bosses also need clearer or longer openings. Curses aren't balanced at all. It's like 20% of curses are worth picking up, others are just not worth it. You usually blow through all 5 of your rerolls you get to get something worth picking up. This should not be the case. I shouldn't be feeling that my runs are down to LUCK with curses. It's literally possible not to get curses you need at all. The final boss of the game takes away your cloak skills and spells. Meaning you can only fight it with your basic weapon. This negates more curses because it makes any build that doesn't focus on the scythe, worthless and this makes the game much, much less fun.You have a variety of scythes to choose from but one of them is just SO vastly better than the others that it's better to reroll your run to get the scythe you want. The reason for this is that that specific scythe does % health damage. The other scythes NEVER get enough damage with their special effects to make up for the difference % health damage does.  Runs are too samey. Due to the way the game classifies skills/spells you end up using the same few skills/spells over and over. I shouldn't feel like resetting if the selection of scythes i get isn't good. I shouldn't feel like resetting if the first curses I get are all horrible. This game needs some serious balancing. A LOT of the curses need buffs, a lot of the scythes bar the diss scythe need changing. Right now this game is no longer worth my time because it's just not fun anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is an EXTREMELY CONFLICTED "thumbs down" that I've considered multiple times over the course of writing this as giving it an EXTREMELY CONFLICTED "thumbs up." Bear with me here.Really stunning visuals for a game that's pretty average in execution. The concept is interesting, but for a game that seems obviously geared to be plot-heavy, it's quite weak in that area. It's loaded with interesting characters, but there's never enough of a presence for any of them to be memorable. Progressing through each area gets old very fast, while also being pretty vague when introducing any new variations, like "consequences" for certain perks.When it comes down to it, Have a Nice Death ends up being like a lamer version of Hades by most measures of gameplay. You start each run through with a choice of base weapons, pick up perks and upgrades along the way, while helping side characters progress their own narratives as you get further through the game. But all of it is so watered down that it almost feels like the developers decided they wanted to make a game that looked Hollow Knight and played like Hades, and cobbled together a game around that....That's way too mean, though. I don't think Have a Nice Death is a hollow shill knock-off of better games. It's not a soulless cash-grab. I bought this game in Early Access because it looked right up my alley, and honestly I think there was a lot of love that went into this game. But the couple times I played it before its official release, the game was honestly a mess. It was confusing, frustratingly difficult in unintentional ways, and much more boring that it is now. I think Have a Nice Death was a well-intentioned labor of love that the devs couldn't quite make work the way they imagined, and defaulted on a similar structure as Hades because it was the closest to the game mechanics they wanted.I don't want to be mean. Plot-wise, it's nothing like Hades, and aesthetically, it's not that similar to Hollow Knight despite the graphics. And I've played many, many Metroidvanias that suck, and this isn't one of them. The best praise I can give it, and maybe its biggest selling point, is that it's a much cozier version of those other two games. There's no deep lore that takes extensive gameplay to unfold, there's no convoluted plot that requires a lot of thinking to keep straight, and there's not that much strategy to consider. It bills itself as being Soulslike, but it's too easy for that, and it's probably a better game for it. You can just jump right in, play for a bit, and leave it alone for however long before jumping right back in. Plus, it's actually pretty good at humor? It's not laugh-out-loud funny, nor is it really clever, but it's goofy and doesn't take itself too seriously.This isn't the game I wanted it to be, and it's not the game it's trying to bill itself as. But it IS a good game, I guess, for some people. I might've enjoyed it more if I had a better idea of what it was going into it. I don't regret buying it, and though it's not something I plan to play more of any time soon, I could definitely see a day when it's exactly the kind of game I need, and I'll already have it ready to go.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great entry into the rogue-like genre.  I love the art and the quirky characters.  The controls are very tight, it's like if Dead Cells and Hollow Knight had a baby and Tim Burton was the god father.  The weapons are creative but need a bit more balancing and I'm hoping the variety will continue to expand with further updates.  The story-line is simple and cute. I actually preferred the game prior to the major update. My biggest criticism right now is that I now have to choose between the Environmental Disasters and War worlds instead of getting to do both worlds at once.  This has had a huge impact on the design of the game.  It feels a bit too short now and I actually miss the power spike that I'd get from additional resources (esp curses, and shop visits) that come from having to do an extra world.  Getting to fight an extra boss is just more fun. The character just feels...less well rounded when going into the final stages of the game and then the enemies are suddenly way too strong in the final zone. Overall: 8/10 would recommend!

The characters, story and visuals are definitely my favorite part of this game.I say that also because in my opinion the gameplay is not the most innovative, it feels like your standard platformer, however a lot of weapons and your scythe have additional attacks depending if you're airborne, aiming up or down, and I really appreciate it, it makes the gameplay, while not the most unique, still feel good to play with. Movement is fairly simple, but mastering dodges with dashes and aerials is something that might take a few runs to really start utilizing well.Progression feels decent, doesn't lock you into a specific playstyle or achieve specific achievements to unlock items.Runs can get long which is somewhat tiring at times, but you're able to leave the game and return to right where you stopped(at the start of the floor you chose) so you can take a break and come back later, which is really nice.Overall, very solid game, with a lot of soul put into it. _childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one, but generally as I’m a glass-half-full kind of person, I’m going to give this a recommend. I was originally interested in buying this game because it shares various similarities to the metroidvania game,  and therefore, it looked like something that I might enjoy. However, after playing it now for around eight hours, I am slightly conflicted with whether I really like this game or not. This is mainly because it has no story at all and a frustrating death mechanic that resets nearly all but a slight amount of progress upon dying. At first, I found this mechanic to be quite frustrating, and if it weren’t for some solid gameplay mechanics, it would have been a deal breaker for me. But, as I’ll explain, there are many positive elements to this game too that still make it worth playing overall in my opinion.  Have you ever wanted to play as Death, claiming souls with the hack-and-slash of a scythe that has cool animations and upgrade pathways? Great! Because this game lets you do that, and it is honestly the best part about this title.The gameplay is honestly the only thing that made me open up the game again after my initial disillusionment with it after realizing that progress is mostly reset upon death. The combat feels fluid, challenging and satisfying and there is a genuine sense of progression when it comes to getting better at it. There are three available weapon types that you can equip Death with: the cloak weapons, spells, and the main weapon, the scythe. All of these weapons feel meaningfully different from each other and using them in tandem can create the opportunity for interesting combos that add some variation to the gameplay. The feeling of deciding to keep fire arrows equipped so you can have a long-range option for a particular boss while using a cloak item such as daggers for a close attack option genuinely adds a nice layer of nuance to the gameplay which feels satisfying when executed correctly. The whole thing feels fluid, responsive and balanced. So, it’s great! And no other complaints there.(The same goes for the art style, which, although in early access, is still really gorgeous and looks markedly different for each area). The only real problem that I have with this game, then, is the repetitiveness. This game is REALLY repetitive (at least in its current early access stage). I don’t see how a game developer in 2022 can expect their player base to play through the same levels just to end up dying to lose their progress and do it all over again. It’s strange. Especially when you consider that there are so many games out nowadays (many of which are free) that offer the opportunity for emergent gameplay upon each playthrough and many of which actually reward the player with permanent items that have more of an impact on gameplay than those  do. Runs usually go this way: start off by killing a bunch of low-level mobs, get curses which unlock branching powerups, collect weapons through the various sub-levels, beat the end of area boss to buy heals, and then do it all over again for a different area with a different end of area boss. This formula would be okay if there was a genuine sense of reward at the end of each run, but there kind of isn’t. After the completion of a run all the player gets in return is a few gold pieces that they can use in a shop to purchase items such as cloak weapons that can be unlocked on the next run or food that gives certain powerups for a small duration. I really would have liked something permanent in return for my progress in this game, even if it’s just a cosmetic item such as a new robe for Death or something. I think that this would have broken up the monotony of repeating the first levels and added some much-needed meaningful variation to the game. is a game with fun mechanics, a solid identity, and a lot of promise. However, due to issues such as lack of meaningful rewards and the requirement to repeat the same bosses, it just doesn’t feel complete enough at this stage. Hopefully, this will be resolved when the game launches fully, which should bring much more dimensions into the game for hopeful players such as myself to tuck into. However, despite its feeling of incompleteness and sometimes frustratingly repetitive gameplay, the game is fun. I would like however, to see in the future more variation in terms of bosses, levels, cosmetics, and weapon upgrades to add more variation to the gameplay because it desperately needs it. In short, I would say that if this game is in the sale, then buy it, if it’s full price though, then it still just about justifies a purchase (for me).

_childDocuments_.review: This game still needs a lot of work before it's released and I can give it a nicer review. Long story short: a game that has enemies scale with increasing difficulties while your character has no scaling between runs is a bad design. After the enemies gain defense, status ailments can be nullified or some weapons with weaker hits literally deal 0 damage...The only thing you can unlock between runs are weapons, items, and contracts, which is good and all, but having very little ways to upgrade your weapons in game or have unlockable buffs between runs makes it very painful. The game also lacks a lot of variety, but that will be addressed in future updates. There are also a handful of bugs such as incorrect flagging of conditions in contracts or gaining discounts in the unlock shop. Also each run, no matter what difficulty, gives the same rewards both in game and out of game (gold ingots), so your time is not valued whatsoever. Just making a run more difficult for the sake of difficulty without any incentives is a terrible choice, and I hope that the devs fix this before this game gets out of early access. Also this game is absolutely not a metroidvania game as there are no ways to explore the world differently from the start of the game to the end of the game other than selecting different routes. Since there are no ability unlocks, you are not going to change anything between runs other than experience more pain. This game can be fun and has lots of cute dialogue, but it needs way more improvement before it can be acceptable.Also another issue with scaling is that only very rare curse buffs can increase your healing scaling, so when you are playing higher difficulties when you need more than 100 HP, getting a heal for 10 HP is pathetic given how rare and expensive heals are.

_childDocuments_.review: Have a Nice Death is a very nice game. It was in a rough spot through early access, but it's in a much better space now.The environments, character, dialogues and Art direction the game have a lot of work put into them, and it shows.This definitely doesn't feel like a generic rogue like, it has a huge amount of charm. The boss design and fights, while very hard, are well made and fun, and they don't feel unfair. Some patterns can be hard to read though.As far as the main gameplay loop goes, building up your character using various spells, capes, scythes, upgrade and curses is a real joy. The game will always propose different things over each playthrough and there are many ways your character may become strong. The reroll system allows you to steer your build in the direction you want, but that's not to say that you aren't going to have to play with the cards the game dealt you. The balance is well found here, and it's not often the case in these kind of rogue likes.That being said, there are some areas where the game falls flat.A few features and options seem like they haven't been thought out completely, like the power attack,  the  A few curses seem completely useless.The  The biggest problem is the levels between the bosses. Running through the levels is much less dangerous than fighting the bosses, but the level are still quite long.The environments lack events or variety to keep you on your toes. it's mainly just running through them with the occasional arena fight .That being said, fighting is still very fun because the controls are slick and tight. Moving around feels very natural.Overall, I would recommend the game without a doubt. Be aware that it's brutally hard. I hope the developers will keep updating the game as they have integrated feedback from the community with a lot of success.

Characters like Death and his book however look great during gameplay, the various animation also helps liven up the world.The gameplay is a good start but needs vast tweaks. There is a large delay that often comes in for dashing and causes more frustrations with the controls than an actual challenge from gameplay. Have a Nice Death is a 2D action roguelike where you play as an overworked Death, whose employees have run rampant, completely throwing off the balance of souls - and his vacation plans. In order to restore order, you'll have to grab your trusty scythe and show your employees who's boss.

name: Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space
detailed_description: Join the Freelance Police on a bizarre adventure from the North Pole to the Fountain of Youth, from outer space to Hell and back. Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space is a remastered version of Telltale’s second season of episodic Sam & Max games, lovingly updated by a small team of the original developers. Sam is a six-foot canine detective with a nose for justice. Max is a hyperkinetic rabbity-thing with a taste for mayhem. Together, they’re the Freelance Police—an irreverent comedy duo whose esoteric crime-fighting style has been entertaining comic book and video game fans for more than thirty years. In this five-episode collection of interconnected cases, Sam & Max are back on the crime beat in a showdown with Santa Claus, a race to subdue a giant volcano, and a face-off with a Eurotrash vampire. And then things get even weirder. Is paranoid shopkeeper Bosco on to something with his talk of a grand conspiracy? Is diner proprietress Stinky hiding the truth about what happened to her grandfather (also named Stinky)? Will flaky neighbor Sybil Pandemik ever find true love? Did someone say… BIRTHDAY?! Hop into the DeSoto for a hilarious outing that won IGN’s Adventure Game of the Year award the first time around and now looks and sounds better than ever, with gorgeous HD graphics, overhauled lighting and lip-sync, finessed cinematography, remastered audio, and eight all-new musical tracks featuring live jazz musicians. Zombies will dance. Mariachis will sing. A giant battle robot will trash the streets. And when their friends’ lives are on the line, Sam and Max will risk their very souls to set things right. Features: An adventure game that makes you laugh: Explore unexpected places, chat with eccentric characters, and tease out brain-tickling puzzles in an interactive story that has a joke hiding behind every hotspot. Beautifully remastered: Lighting, lip-sync, cinematography, audio, music, and more have been updated and enhanced to bring Sam & Max’s second episodic season up to modern standards. No walkthrough required: The game detects when you’re stuck and provides subtle contextual hints. Hint frequency can be customized to accommodate all playing styles. Optional driving mini-games: Take the wheel of Sam & Max’s 1960 DeSoto convertible for fun diversions from the story. The hood decals and car upgrades you win carry over across episodes. Localization: English voice with subtitles in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess it's only fair to compare remaster of second season to the previous remaster. And I gotta say, it feels even better!- DeSoto mini-game progress now works better (decals progress is saved properly and you don't have to play episodes in order), that progression checklist is also pretty nice.- Personally, Bosco's VA perform better than first season. And I don't think it's just because I got used to his new voice.- Quite a handful of areas got revamped with new decor and actual lighting. New lighting is especially nice to look at in zombie factory and night time streets. Pleasant references for true S&M fans sprinkled everywhere.- Nipple keyring is back.- Most obscene (and therefore hilarious) original jokes didn't get cut so I assume nothing else got cut too (as promised by Skunkape devs) - New music is really great! And don't worry, you'll get to hear all original compositions too!- I didn't notice at first, but I'm glad they added skip button for closing credits so you can see original post-credits scenes!- And I also gotta thank Skunkape Games for letting me beta test the game and report various bugs and oddities. _childDocuments_.review: Originally released back in late 2007 through 2008,  is the second season in Telltale’s trilogy starring the beloved, somewhat niche, crime-solving duo.For a little more than a year now, it has been available with a fresh coat of paint, exceptionally remastered by Skunkape Games, a team founded by ex-Telltale developers back when the you-know-what hit the fan at the ol’ office. Skunkape has since been the home of the six-foot, fedora-wearing dog and his "hyperkinetic rabbity thing" buddy, and it is thanks to their hard work that the duo’s worst adventure can now be enjoyed on modern systems, with improved visuals, audio, and an updated soundtrack.Hold up! "Worst adventure" yet a positive review? Look, If you’ve got four games in a series, it only follows that one of them has to be the worst. It's just that you can’t pin it on the original LucasArts darling that gave these two their first time in the spotlight, and it can’t be the game that brought ‘em back, nor the dramatic sendoff. Therefore, the title of “worst” has to fall in the middle, even if the game to bear it is quite alright. But I've got gripes!The second season follows the freelance police on their most colourful journey of ‘em all. Through five episodes, each with its own outlandish location and bizarre villain, you’ll be battling (pointing & clicking through puzzles until the credits roll) the supernatural, urban legends, and none other than Santa himself. It’s going to be a bit hard to take a step back and evaluate  on its own merits when it so clearly wasn’t designed for newcomers to the franchise. Usually, the cases Fido and his lagomorph pal take on are one-offs; standalone stories without explicit continuity between ‘em. You don’t need an overarching plot hanging above the entire series for good seasonal storytelling, yet Season Two picks up a couple of background tidbits from  (Season One), cranks ‘em up into a proper plot, and rounds off some fan-favourite characters. In that sense, it’s quite bold to try and build something new and cool off of what was left over from the previous game. The execution here is narratively satisfying, yet it lets the past have too much hold over everything new, to the point where it feels conflicting.Point & click adventures live and die by the writing, but more often than not, they die by repetition. offers a lot to appreciate. Its writing is as biting as ever, surprisingly relevant, and most importantly, unrelentingly hilarious. It's a more cohesive whole than , making it all the more suitable for a solid binge. Still, “is repetitive” is a recurring item on the “Cons” lists of almost every review of a game from this genre written since the dawn of time.  was served those same complaints when it was released, but managed to rise above ‘em because of how fresh it was.Even with all the new bits showing that  has more than enough ideas to be its own thing and keeping in mind that its story is building up on  foundation, there are  so many reused characters and locations that are hard to take in earnest. Almost every time something from Season One comes back around, it feels like a cost-cutting technique, rather than necessary continuity in a trilogy of games. Even worse, the centrepiece puzzle of every episode follows the same pattern, including a repeating, ridiculously easy minigame.  Anyone who thought Telltale started abusing tried-and-true methods only after  is in for a surprise.To someone who’s hooked on the storyline connecting these two seasons, getting over the cardinal sin of point-&-click adventure games that’s been committed here might not be a tall order. The same goes for Sam & Max fans, especially those who’ve gone through the necessary hours of bludgeoning yourself with a hammer to be on board with this kind of humour. However, they might be turned off for different reasons, depending on how intimately familiar they are with what makes these characters work.The world these characters inhabit is one of finely-balanced absurdity. Everything goes. Animals are anthropomorphized, store owners sell mundane items for billions of dollars, giant stone statues run for the presidential office, cockroaches serve in the military, self-help gurus build bases on the Moon, wars erupt over forgotten birthdays… Yet, it’s paced and delivered in a manner that never feels overbearing or incoherent. leans a tad too hard into that absurdity and puts the pedal to the metal until you’re desensitised. It becomes farcical; as if whoever's in the writer's chair is just thinking up ludicrous scenarios with little regard to anything else. Travelling to the Easter Islands, where Amelia Earhart has been kicking it back with DB Cooper ever since the two had disappeared seems a lot less clever when the previous episode had you  over to the North Pole to deal with a rogue Santa Claus. Following that up with an episode where you battle disco-dancing zombies in an old German castle turned night club seems like a downgrade. I don’t want to go “Ah, okay, right, that makes sense—I’m playing a  game”, but rather “Oh, that’s right, this is a  game!” when weird things happen.Aside from the sharp writing style, this is where most of the humour comes from. The slight disconnect is needed to make the game work as the satire that it is. The joke isn’t that Sam & Max are doing all these weird things, it’s that they’re doing them within the logic of a point & click adventure game, where MacGyvering it goes unquestioned. You’re not supposed to accept it, even when making sense of it is necessary for the solution of most puzzles, but rather laugh, ponder, or flinch from the downright cruelty it usually implies when it comes along.My dislike of the tone is passed on to the soundtrack, a lot of which is rearrangements of tracks from the previous season, to go along with those same old locations you’ll be revisiting. While new music was again contributed as part of the remaster by the original composer and legend that is Jared Emerson-Johnson, neither it nor the rest is as memorable or catchy as what was in . The silver lining is that it still makes for some enjoyable jazz, except for the quietly mixed title track that has just a tad too much nervous energy, with its bongo beat and sudden blares of trumpets. Even the dark and gritty third season had the guts to include something fun, like a theremin!An ambivalent tug of war that pulls strong enough in neither direction,  travels between past and present so much it ends up in a chaotic loop, eventually spat out somewhere in the middle of the road—six outta ten, five on a bad day. With three whole other games in the same series, each offering a better experience, it wouldn’t be hard to pass up were it not part of a trilogy and a well-written bout regardless.Speaking of the trilogy, the third season should be getting its remaster at some point this year, and I’d much rather we go out with a bang rather than a whimper. Just thinking about it gets me all tingly, or maybe that’s the intracranial hematoma from all the hammer blows acting up.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond time and space is an exceptional remaster, and not just because it brings this 2007 relic to modern platformsThe developers have clearly put their heart and soul into making this remaster as great as it can be, making it easier for new players to get into and understand the game as well as giving long time fans a reason to play the game again if they played the 2007/08 original. The Save the World remaster was all about reinvigorating season 1 and while Beyond time and space does this as well for season 2, the changes this time round are also about re-imagining certain scenes in the game. This is best seen with the new lighting, where STW sought to only make the game look nicer and modern with the real time lighting, the new lighting in beyond time and space is often more stylistic. The best example of this is in episode 2, 'Moai Better Blues' where the gloomy, overcast appearance of streets contrasts nicely with the other main setting of the episode, Easter island. Not only that, but the changes and additions to the game also allow beyond time and space to distinguish itself more from Save the World. With the original release of Season 2, A lot of content was re-used from Season 1. Most likely to keep the series releasing as quickly as it did in 2006-2008. However, this to me always made season 2 seem less like a proper sequel and more as DLC. Additional episodes that told a different story from Save The World while also reusing the same assets, music, etc. There were new things, however, it always felt as if the re-used content outweighed the new content just based on it's prevalence within the game (Even though there technically more new set-pieces, music, etc used in the game than re-used). However, this remaster removes this feeling entirely from the game. There still is re-used content, but it's now usually only reserved to small sections of the game you may only visit once or twice. The new music alone makes all the difference, with the new City Streets theme making the streets feel completely different compared to the original STW theme (Which is should considering the streets are torn apart in the opening of the game). Another area the game differs itself is Camera angles. From what I've played, I'm pretty sure every recurring location from Save the World is now shot differently to give an alternative perspective on the room you're in. Whether it being looking through Flint's office into Sam & Max's office to being able to see more details on the back wall of Sybil's office. The game now feels complete unique from Save the World, having a more consistent theming with recurring motif's (Like the portals) that weren't really front and centre in the original. On top of all the usual QOL changes, updated controls, improved inventory and UI, new easter eggs, this is a top quality remaster (Especially so, considering the recent reputation of remasters in the past year)

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the previous remaster of "Sam & Max Save the World" you're gonna like this.I think the biggest improvement besides character models has to be the lighting,  it's beautifully crafted and breathes new life into the game. Artistic choices like camera framing in gameplay, new additions to cutscenes, lots of little details and even certain effects have been added to enhance the overall experience while still being faithful to the original. For example, in Moai Better Blues, it's now overcast gloomy weather when Sam and Max are in the city, which helps juxtapose the beautiful sunny and vibrant colours of Easter Island when travelling back and forth between them. Skunkape Games really did a fantastic job and I can't wait to see what they do with the Devil's Toybox. Overall fantastic work, it looks slick and modern which is a testament to the artists considering it looked dated even by 2008 standards when it initially released. Disclaimer: Yes, Bosco still got the new voice actor, I've liked his performance better in Season 2, he's doing his best, but if you weren't sold in the first one, this one won't change your mind.

_childDocuments_.review: It maintains the cleverness and quality of the previous game. The puzzles are more difficult but mostly remain in the "solvable with time" realm. There is greater variety in the environments.TECHNICALThe game slightly slowed down in the third chapter, as it features rain effects. I did not encounter any crashes, glitches, or anything of the sort.AUDIOVISUALThe microphones are more consistent, but not wholly consistent, with some characters having slightly worse microphone quality between lines. Aside from this the quality of graphics and sound is the same as the previous game. GAMEPLAYThe puzzles are harder. A good portion of this is because some of them are "hunt the object" puzzles where the solution involves finding an obscure prop object. Some of this is due to legitimately requiring more thinking. I think each episode is also longer, but I don't know if that's a matter of more stuff to do or harder stuff. Something interesting here is the presence of car minigames: one per episode. They aren't just there for puzzle purposes, but also to obtain optional collectables in the form of car decals. It's interesting as a concept but the games themselves are rather boring. WRITINGThe writing in this is a bit better than in the prior game, but the prior game had great writing, so there wasn't much to improve on. While the previous game had some distinctly 2000s jokes, this game is more timeless, though some lines can all but carbon date it. Aside from this, the only thing to note is that this game is slightly more politically incorrect, but I doubt it would actually offend anyone. Like in the previous game, the overarching plot is nothing deep, but it seems that there was more focus put on creating something cohesive. There's foreshadowing for later episodes, for example.

_childDocuments_.review: 2020's Sam & Max Save the World was a fantastic way to cap off that nightmare of a year. It's developers, Skunkape Games(despite some controversy), made, in my opinion, the definitive way to experience the Freelance Police's first season of their Telltale exploits.Now, just a little over a year later, they've done it again with the follow-up Beyond Time and Space, the fresh new reprint of Sam & Max’s second season.Much like Save the World, the base game is largely unchanged. It's still five episodes of unfiltered chaos as Sam & Max face-off a killer robot, tango with Santa, become volcano gods, and rap battle a vampire as they descend further and further into hellish madness. As always you're still pointing, clicking, and using an inventory system to solve various puzzles, alongside the occasional dialogue tree, wrapped together with the same never-miss dialogue that'll probably have you cackling like a damn hyena. Each episode is about one or two hours long to complete if you know what you’re doing. If you don’t know what you’re doing, then don’t worry too much, as there’s a handy hint system that can guide you in the proper direction.Before getting to the presentation, let's start with the writing, because those allergic to inconsequential changes will be happy to know that absolutely NONE of the dialogue was cut or altered in any form or fashion. Even the more obscene topical stuff, like Timmy Two-Teeth and his coprolalia, have been untouched.Bosco's new voice has also improved significantly. While still being voiced by Ogie Banks, his direction and delivery are way better than in Save the World. He conveys much more emotion and energy this time around, making him sound like a proper paranoid maniac.The presentation is still on top, like last time, with updated textures, lighting and character redesigns with input from Steve Purcell, and a live jazz soundtrack packing eight new tracks that are absolute FIRE.This extends to the more technical changes too. There’s new camera angles and interface tweaks, uncompressed voice clips, the driving minigames are now optional, the decals you can earn in those minigames are a lot easier to keep track of, there's just a lot of great changes to make the experience more cohesive.Overall, Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space is another great remastering of another great graphic adventure. With a ton of new bells and whistles, this makes for the finest way to play the funniest Sam & Max adventure yet. (And if you’re still on the fence, you can still play the originals, in all their janky-ass glory.)

_childDocuments_.review: OK, so I so far have played "Sam & Max Hit the Road" and "Sam & Max Save the World", but this game, "Sam & Max Beyond Time and Space" has the best jokes/gags so far! It seems like the banter between Sam & Max in the first two tried to carry the humor, but it just didn't seem all that funny to me. This game seemed to let the other characters provide some of the humor, which I did enjoy! The robot quoting 80's music lyrics I enjoyed, and little Timmy (or was it Jimmy) with turrets I though was funny, and I did catch myself laughing out loud with the parking break gag! Is the game perfect? No, so far it had the best jokes/gags. Some of the puzzles/solutions were like, "WTF?", but at least there are plenty of guides out there, although I couldn't find the perfect guide for me that included just the right amount of information to help me solve the puzzles. I started to use a Youtube video walkthrough, but they were clicking on every item possible, which I can find and do on my own, so I abandoned it and found a text and picture walkthrough guide, but it looked like it was translated from Russian, so there was some bad grammar and it seemed like it left out some details, so I had to go back to the Youtube video to visually see how exactly the puzzle was solved. I was going for all the achievements, which the "Desoto Dominator" was the one that gave me the most problems in obtaining, since it spanned 4 of the 5 "episodes". Since this is a point and click game, I was using the mouse and keyboard on my computer, but I found that a game controller seems to make the driving mini games easier, especially on one of the games where the left stick can not only move you right or left, it can also speed you up or slow you down, depending on if you push up or down while moving left or right. After I finished the game, I thought I did everything to get the "Desoto Dominator" achievement, but it did not pop up for me. I used the poster next to the Desoto to check to see if I was missing any decals, and noticed that none of the decals from Episode 1 got transferred over to the final episode. Also, upon further investigation, I noticed that the very last sticker will turn "gold" when you reach a certain threshold (run over x number of Torture Me Elmers, deliver x number of discs to zombies, etc.). I had to go back to episode 1 and redo all of the decal challenges, and go back and do the bagpipe challenge until the sticker turned gold. If the last decal for each season isn't gold, then you still need to complete the next threshold challenge. You will need to obtain the gold decals in order to get following DeSoto upgrades: Ep1: Turbo Charger, Ep2: Dashboard Hula Girl, Ep3: Flame paint job for DeSoto, Ep4: None/NA, Ep5: Demonic Grill Teeth/Super Upgrade:Police Lights. I thought these only applied to the console versions of the game, but they are in the PC version as well!

_childDocuments_.review: As I said in my review for the first game - I never played the originals, so I cannot comment on changes to the source material.What I can say is that these games are extremely funny and entertaining. The humor and gags are great and make me nostalgc about old games with character. The story continues where the first left off is engaging throughout. _childDocuments_.review: Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space is a wonderful continuation of the first game. The humor is still top notch and the charm is as good as ever. However I'm going to have to place this game a bit lower than Save the World, purely because of the way the puzzles are handled in this game. Season 1 had absolutely solid puzzles that made sense and were reasonable enough for you to figure them out. Season 2 however I found the puzzles were more troublesome and confusing, especially in Episodes 2 and 3. The Moai island was probably the worst time I had with this game purely cause of how often I got stuck.Another unfortunate thing about Season 2 versus Season 1 is that there is one less episode, which is compensated by increasing the length of each episode. While in Season 1, you could finish each episode in one sitting which gave me great satisfaction, Season 2 takes multiple sittings to get through each episode which is probably also a consequence of the worse puzzles this game had. Both the actual duration of the episode and puzzle troubles increase the time it takes to complete each episode.With all that being said, Beyond Time and Space is still a good Sam & Max experience and well worth it. I just wish the puzzle solutions weren't as obscure and confusing. And now that I finally completed this, I'm greatly looking forward to The Devil's Playhouse remastered!

_childDocuments_.review: From the creators of The Walking Dead games, and The Wolf Among Us, comes an exciting blast from their past. Sam & Max, the second part. Play as Sam, the dog, as he solves puzzles with questionable solutions, and quirky jokes. Meet a range of recurring characters as they either aid or hinder your way through the game, then get annoyed at how the game works, and search the solution up online. Play through 5 stories worth 5 hours at the price of the prequel, then realize that this game has barely any replayability. But I mean, you had fun right?Starring:RabbitDogThe three annoyersDo you have anything that could help us?Therapy could help, but screw thatLiteral Abraham Lincoln. I can't make that crap upBetter actor than Jared LetoT.H.E.MWhere I'm going to end up after I dieAnd... a cool as hell car.Woof cop, Mad cop: It's about time

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get why people say this is the weakest of the Telltale Sam and Max series.  It does have an abysmal 2nd episode, and the 3rd episode isn't that great.  However I still feel like even the weak episodes are funnier than even the funniest episode of Save The World.  The writing in this game is the best in the series, even better than my favorite Sam and Max game, The Devil's Playhouse.  The music is far worse though, it either reuses Save The Worlds OST or it has new tracks that are not at all memorable. This does have a lot more cryptic puzzles as well.  The puzzles here are a lot worse than Save the World and The Devils playhouse.  I would still give this one a higher score than Sam and Max Save The World because I feel like it's much more of a memorable game than Save The World.  I'm giving this game an 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's weird, silly, and complete with charm. Get it for the music alone!I will say that the writing + narrative this season feels much less cohesive -- even if they deliberately try to tie in elements like the Mariachis, Santa / Satan, etc. -- and makes for a deliberately more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane product. Which has plenty of solid jokes... but also, a lot of misfires or awkward moments, hampered by some irritating voice acting and sound effects esp. from the season's overarching antagonists. I know that Sam & Max is an inherently irreverent brand; this season just gets a little TOO irreverent for my liking. And the Devil's Playhouse ups the stakes by keeping the irreverence, but also adding some stakes + poignancy so you get more invested; here, it's all so flippant that it can be really grating at points.But beyond that -- it's still fun puzzle-solving. The best episode is the Moai episode; I think Jurgen's is my least favorite. There are plenty of excellent challenges to figure out -- even when some border on purely frustrating. (I hate that rib puzzle in the 5th episode, man). I can't wait for the third season.
